This game is a very fun FPS, full of humour and parodies of 80's action films. It doesn't take itself seriously at all which is a key point of the game, it even makes fun of it's own tutorial level for example. You get the impression that the developers wanted to have as much fun making it as you will playing it and the result is similar to what Saints Row does with the GTA-like games with all the Sci Fi silliness you could want from a game.
Overall it will take between 4- 4.5 hours to complete the campaign missions with additional optional content (hunting and checkpoint clearing (called garrisons in this game)) available.
I have not played Far Cry 3, but what I can say is you absolutely do not need to have played Far Cry 3 to play or enjoy this game despite sharing its name it is a definite standalone (does not require the base game in order to play either). I am a completionist. Meaning that I try to do every quest I can get. The downside of this is that the low level quests don't give so much XP. Still I like doing the quests. I like the compelling and sometimes ridiculous stories, and I love the beauty of the environment.

Budget RTS done right - Infested Planet is equal parts manic and intriguing.
------
The game has an almost "flash game-esk" aesthetic, but don't be put off by this. You'll find the game to be a delight to play, combining fast-paced action with a surprisingly deep strategy layer.
The gameplay consists of giving orders to a squad of marines and making good upgrade decisions with the limited resources you are given. There are a ton of upgrade options for you to choose from which unlock as the game progresses, but are available from the start of each mission, making your upgrade choices a crucial part of your strategy on each mission.
The enemies follow suit with a variety of enemy types, defensive buildings, mutations and sporadic waves of particularly challenging special enemies to keep you on your toes.
If you like a strategy game, have nothing to do with a weekend and see this on sale, then you'll certainly enjoy your time with it.
Awesome and challenging tactical RTS.  Well worth the money.

Let me say this first: Brawlhalla is a fantastic free game with quirks. I have a lot of fun playing the game but frustration is extreme at the same time.
My experience is near exclusive with the legend 'Teros', so keep that in mind.
While devs work hard and keep improving things, balance of legends and weapons is not that great yet. I play a Teros main character which only very few people do due to the severe downsides that come with it. A victory against an equal or better opponent feels like in football, when your team scores in the 95th minute of the Champions League final.
Most play super quick 'legends' like Hattori, Lucien, Queen Nai because they are easier to use and make for more fun games. Teros is slow and strong. That's bad because his weapons are also hard to land hits with. His game style is about running away from enemies 90% of the time and attempt to get a hit down if your opponent screws up. And if YOU screw up punishment will be severe (this is fine because of Teros' strength stat).
Playing Teros means you want to smash your controller 5 times every session but when you pry a victory from someone you see the angels of heaven and a six pack of fresh beer descending down in a ray of light.
Many people get annoyed by Teros' play style but given equal ELO level / skill there is zero other way to win with Teros. All other legends will hit you faster with better combos and their attacks have higher priority. So get out of people's way and hit them only when you're 100% sure that you will land it.
Servers have been a mixed experience and although you can choose a region and I have pretty a very good connection, I keep experiencing rather bad lag. It's especially bad if it happens in ranked matches. It's sort of hard to play against teleporting players or when your hits are locally registered (sound and animaton is played) but 500ms later your enemy is behind you unharmed (hit not registered on server).
Matchmaking is also a mixed bag. It happens all the time that you will play someone you JUST finished a match against because all people will mash the continue button after a match so they enter matchmaking at the same time again. Waiting 5-10sec alleviates the issue but it would be nice if recent opponents would have a low priority for a match-up.

If you love Super Smash Bros. then you'll like this game. This is my first ever review so I'll give you my experience with this game. FIRST OFF, Gameplay.
When I first started playing I thought it was very difficult. And it is! But the more you play, the more you learn. I suggest playing against Bots in Singleplayer maybe 3 times so that you get comfortable with the controls. Then move to Online where it's 4 player free-for-all. From my experience, use Scarlet because her attack strength is high and attack speed is better than her stats say. A lot of people believe her to be overpowered when they themselves don't understand the definition. She a very VERY strong character in the right hands but she is very slow and has a pretty low defense which makes it suicide to even think about using her if you aren't the fastest learner. You've got to be quick in this game because IMO speed beats strength. If you can attack and evade enough to weaken your opponent then you'll be able to finish them with a sig.
Every character has the same light attack whether it's S-Light, D-Light, or N-Light. This makes it so that the characters are balanced TO A DEGREE. Treat Signatures like Smashes is SSB.
Now when it comes to sig. (or signature) every character has their own unique moveset. This really changes how you use your Light Attacks because with different signatures, you can combo differently. For Example: A basic combo would be with Cassidy and her Hammer >> D-Light + N-Sig. When she kicks the ground, the enemy pops up in a hit stun leaving them open for a mere split-second. Press N-sig so she lassos them in for a hammer hit.
Like Smash Bros, the game offers a dodge system. However, being a 2-D based fighter, the dodging takes time to get used to. You can dodge in every direction and it helps when you need to get away OR close in on an enemy for a combo. Speaking of which, there is a mechanic that seems odd at first but is REALLY helpful for a last minute attack. When in the air, simply press the dodge button WITHOUT using any directional command. Basically, N-Dodge (While airborn). You'll freeze yourself in the air for a split-second allowing you to follow with a Sig. BUT, your sig will be used as though you were standing on the ground. Think of it as.. Creating a platform beneath your character.
Now about other things I've noticed.
The Community- 50% of them are tryhard wannabe competitive players. If you lose to them then they'll rag on you for it. One experience I had when i lost was to one player who never gave me any breathing time. Now, I'm man enough to say that he was a great player for attack FAST and using his dodges properly. And I would've been fine with that. But afterwards he said, "That's a nice White Character Color. Dunno how you got it with you awful skills." I responded with, "I play to have fun and entertain myself. I'm not competitive." To which he said, "I can see why. You f***ing suck. Wish you were better." Then left.
30% are spammers. Who think to only use Ada's S-Sig and Down-Sig with her pistols. OR Orion's S-Sig with his spear. Then when they win, they think they're the best. Or when they lose they start freaking out.
20% are actually very nice people. It's a low percentage but you'll find these people very often. After an intense match with someone you've been exchanging hits with, they'll say, GG. Or may even go out of their way to actually type something like, "Dang man. That was intense. GG. You're Koji is way better than mine." You may even find someone to partner up with in 2v2 ranked.

ReignMaker is a match three game where the novelty is waves of attackers coming from the side of the board - meaning you need to focus your mathcing areas at the right height. This basic mechanic is pretty good, and quite well balanced for the most part - the only problem with it being that on bigger board, clearing the bottom row mindlessly is usually enough. In addition to that there's a "home village" which you grow as you clea boards... except it grows more like a free to play town.
I don't recommend it though for a few reasons:
- It has little "quests" (clear 5 gems, launch 30 attacks) that mostly frustrate and are often impossible (randomly requires certain equipped items or match 5s where the board is only big enough for 4s.
- A gold collection mechanic that means constantly having to click tiny piles of gold on the other side of the screen from the board. Very irritating.
- Free to play style resource collection (even though there are no IAPs). The progression feels totally wrecked and resource collection is
.
- Skilled at landing chains? Doesn't matter. Chains only count for basic damage, and if you pop a line of 3 to chain react a 5, the 5 will not count for anything. No bonus gems, doesn't count toward quests... argh. Oh, and get a "match 30 quickly" quest? Chained matches don't count. Same for "match 5 airs". This seems... well, broken.
In summary, this game is so very "below average" in every respect, that you'd be better getting some other match 3 game.

ReignMaker is a match-3 game similar to Bejewled or Candy Crush Saga, where your matches are used to kill invaders coming after you. Overall, this game is a mediocre time waster that falls way short of its promises. I'm going to copy/paste the first line of its Steam store page: "ReignMaker is a city building political strategy game with match-3 tower defense combat." Calling this game  a city builder, a political strategy game, or a tower defense game is a serious insult to those genres, and this is coming from someone who enjoys those types of games.
You technically build a city, yes, but the "city building" is little more than waiting to collect resources and upgrading buildings. The only choice you make is what order you build things in. There's no real planning, no infrastructure building, and really, nothing interesting at all about this city building parts. They only serve as a vessel to get you upgrades, and are absolutely no fun on their own. Also, resource collection is really annoying. I never had nearly enough lumber, so I had to wait for hours, checking in every 30 minutes to harvest. Another annoyance is the gold, which appears on the ground as you fight. It spawns so frequently that it's a huge distraction from the puzzle, and you won't get nearly enough if you don't pick it up. Scouts are a necessity if you want to progress since they take that element out, but that's one fewer person you can take into tough levels.
There is technically political strategy, yes, but it amounts to a series of questions, one per level, that almost never have any consequences at all. When there are, they're minor at best. It has all the depth of an Internet quiz. After making choices, you can find out your city's "culture", which matters none at all, really.
When it says it's a "tower defense" game, though, that's completely misleading. In a tower defense game, you place towers strategically to impede and attack units that are trying to get through, and that's not what this game has. In this game, you defend towers with match-3 combat.
Now, for the match-3 elements. The core match-3 gameplay is present in this game, and it does provide some challenge. The spells and the people you hire are interesting additions that shake things up. This game suffers from poor design decisions overall, though. The difficulty curve is a mess, with a huge spike at level 10 before varying wildly between really easy and very difficult. The boss battles are mostly luck; you have to attack very rapidly with matches and spells and hope that you get enough combos to win before your opponent murders you (even worse, you can defeat the boss but still lose the match and be forced to replay). Also, some of the levels are excessively long, which really sucks when you run out steam and lose 20 minutes in to a level.
This isn't the worst game I've played, not by a long shot. I still played this game to the end, probably just because the match-3 combat was enough to hold my interest for a while. This game is really heavily flawed, though, and it spectacularly fails to deliver on its promises. Sadly, this game is little more than a time waster, which isn't good enough for me. It looks like this game is still being worked on, however, so hopefully some things can be ironed out, but it will never be a "city building political strategy game" with "tower defense combat". Ultimately, this game is just a second-rate Puzzle Quest. This game's a joke at $15. I think I can only recommend this game if you can find it for $2 or less.

This game is a cross between Bejeweled/Candy Crush and Tower Defense.  When you make matches, bolts of magic fly out from that row towards the oncomming enemies.  There isn't really any "pathing".  Enemies simply advance toward your city and start attacking your walls until you lose or you beat them.  You can also "build a city" that simply exists for you to unlock items, spells, and heroes to use later on.  The one downside is that you do not know how many waves of enemies remain, so it can get frustrating at times to plan out how you'll make some of your matches.
There are a LOT of acheivmements in the game, but you get many of them simply by playing.  They are more about you playing like you normally would and you'll just magically get them.  There are probably only a few that take a little bit of planning.
During each round, you can get special missions that when completed give you a few resources.  In the end, they are often not worth the effort because you may end up losing resources when you are required to use an item.
Some of the boards are very difficult to play since you have a narrow opening in which to make matches, making you rely on spells.  Spells are recharged by making matches, but don't cost any resources, at least.
Overall, the game is fun and combines multiple game generes pretty well.  I recommend it! :)

Fun casual game in the "match-3" puzzle genre with a cool twist. You make matches to "shoot" a variety of ranged attacks on approaching enemies. Some enemies are more resistent to different attacks (minor void minions are resistant to void rune attacks and I think the turtles might be resistant to water rune attacks).
You can also use spells, weapons, and NPCs to defend your tower. You manage a town with automated resource gathering (a nice feature!), spending those resources on building upgrades, hiring NPCs, spell and weapon research, weapon inventory, and town population growth. Currently it seems that the demand for wood resource far outpaces your collection rate. Each farmer/lumberjack/smelter NPC hired will increase the gather rate for that resource by 1% (currently capped at 20%).
Wood, food, and ore resources accumulate in real-time in each of their respective buildings. Just don't forget to click on "Collect" to move the resources out of the building because each resource building has a limited capacity and won't accumulate beyond it. Upgrade buildings to increase the cap.
If you get too serious about gathering resources, this game can be a bit of a grind as you repeat levels over and over to earn triads (game currency used for equipment and upgrades) - so just relax! It's a casual match-3 game.
The game developers participate in the steam game forum - they're quite friendly and helpful.

Blood Dragon is just a super streamlined version of the main game - many items are made much simplier to obtain, and many abilities are unlocked straight from the beginning. This doesn't mean you are godlike at the start of the game - it also starts with the difficulty higher to match your character.
It does follow Farcry 3 in it's gameplay: find enemy bases, clear them out, and move on to the next through the dangerous wildlife. However, this time the "wildlife" is ♥♥♥♥ing dragons. Each one is like a miniboss - you don't even want to mess with them until you're well into the game and you have the weapons and health to take it down.
It's perfect for it's price even without the sale, and it's a pretty good introduction to the full game of Farcry 3 (even though there's a fair bit missing) Don't take this game as an expansion or DLC - it's something very unique.

After hearing all the rave reviews from critics and from friends, I was excited to check Brothers out. A game that has a story that shows more than it tells is exactly what I like, as I prefer to play the story than I do to watch it.
Perhaps being excited is what has essentially ruined this game for me as my expectations may have been too high, but all I can say is that I didn't enjoy Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons. While the graphical style is nice, I personally did not find much else in this indie adventure platformer.
The game mechanics are so incredibly frustrating, many times the characters wouldn't grab a ledge properly making me need to restart seveeral times, other times I would simply get mixed up with which brother I was controlling on which stick, making me need to think for a second and readjust. My friends have told me that they "are intentionally bad" but I don't see that as any excuse for any game. No game should make it's mechanics difficult by frustrating the player with clunky controls or ones that simply decide not to work when they please.
As for the story, I didn't really "get it" either. I will admit that I gave up before I finished the game, but nowadays I expect more. It doesn't need to have voice acting or text, but I never really felt like I related to either of the characters from their simlish esque speech. I didn't really know either of the brothers either, other than the younger one is better with people and kind of a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(but only sometimes). I won't spoil the premise of the game but from what I've played of it, it seems to be a typical coming of age story with the aforementioned brothers learning to grow from their loss, which I think is a story that has great potential to flourish in a game but this game just fails to hit the mark.
All in all, I came to Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons with high expectations but left with high disappointment.

Most of the bad reviews seem to center on the following objections:
- One city, Prague: Seems like lots of players are used to having wildly varied levels, but truly they just bore way too easily. I think the story makes a lot of sense in and of itself; going to a thousand different settings can be detrimental to story-telling.
- Micro-transactions: Again, the level of indignation seems disproprotionate. I didn't buy anything and had a good gamne.
- DRM: sucks. Often more trouble than it's worth, and projects players into criminals.
- Crashes: With one playthrough, had one CTD.
Now that that's out of the way, it's a good 8/10 (or $40-50) game. Graphics are above average (although animation is a bit choppy and lacks the fluidity of modern games), gameplay is good, story-telling is above average. Not a stupendous game that will be talked about for years to come, but still a good game by today's standards.

I still recommend to play this game, despite I am a bit dissapointed. The gameplay is great, the characters and story are interesting, yet I find it incomplete. I hope there will be expansions (in reasonable prices) that clarify things.
The thing that pains me the most is the breach game mode. I think that was a waste of developers' time. Instead of making a horribly looking grind-fest with opening packs like in some CCG, they could just invest the time to make more interesting side quests in the main game. Maybe add a new city-hub. I took very long time to play my first playthrough, cause I like to search every corner. I still missed a lot of secrets and that's fine, I will surely be playing one more time.
Deus Ex HR was great because of the story. It didn't need any endless game modes, I just wanted to play the main story several times and it did not bore me.
Another thing is the season pass. It's actually a one time use item pack with 2 DLC stories. I am a completionist and I want to get all the achievements. It's really annoying that I have to buy that really expensive pass to be able to play System Rift and get the achievements. I would definitely prefer to buy just that one story for a reasonable price.

This is an interesting premise ruined by some awful and baffling design choices. The initial game starts strong, where you have a small squad and you're slowly unlocking more powerful gear as the campaign unfolds while the aliens get stronger and more varied. And for an RTS mixed with a tower defense, I have to say the user interface is a lot better and more responsive than many other indie games I've played.
However, it all goes off the rails very quickly. The first problem is that several campaign stages are escort missions. Escort missions are never fun and, frankly, people who make them should be publicly shamed. Defense or tower defense missions can be made well. It is simply not possible to make a good escort mission. That might seem like a petty complaint, but it's 2017. Everybody should know better at this point.
Otherwise, Infested Planet's economy is completely and utterly screwed up. You can research more powerful gear, but you always start with a handful of almost useless basic guns and the better stuff is prohibitively expensive. The only way to get more resources is to take over enemy bases, which gives every enemy a random beneficial mutation, but you only get enough resources to upgrade a single guy or put down one turret. The turrets aren't strong enough to actually defend anything, while after two or three bases you need to have a fully kitted-out squad to even have a hope of blowing up the rapidly upgrading swarm of foes. The best you can do is buy one-time upgrades at the shop to use in the next mission, but all that means is that you now have to replay levels multiple times just for cash.
Then you can also be screwed from the very first second of a map by the map's procedural generation. I repeatedly had it spawn my starting base right next to multiple enemy strongholds, who instantly started overwhelming my grunt's peashooters with sheer numbers. The RNG will also frequently put multiple enemy bases right next to each other, so by the time you are through one line of defense the others are already shredding your squad. You can, potentially, get through this kind of situation if your squad has a bunch of powerful weapons but we've already talked about the problem with getting to that point.
Finally, I just gave up on the levels where the enemy bases sent out a respawning bug when they were destroyed. You will not be able to kill that bug with your starting weapons, so it will escape and the enemy bases will eventually all be crammed right next to each other, with a ton of overlapping defenses and shields and a truly massive amount of bugs heading towards your pathetic little squad.
I don't know what kind of person enjoys the type of grind you have to engage in to get through this mess of a game, but I wish them well and I hope I'm never trapped in an enclosed space with them.

Here's what I said about Trine 1:
"I'm sure this is going to get downvoted by diehard fanboys of this series, but really. The graphics are nice, yes. The music's decent. There's a good premise for a game here. So why is it /so bloody boring/? There's very little variation in the levels here, aside from one or two notable exceptions most every level plays the same. Even then the only notable departure is the last level, which is instead just flat-out flawed. The game focuses far too much on its combat system and too little on platforming or creative puzzle design. There's about three different types of enemies throughout the entire game, and they're all over the place in each level. So fighting them gets... really boring, really fast. Though the bats never stop being annoying. Ever. The puzzle design is mostly physics-based and can also be entirely broken, basically defeating the point. I have plenty of fun playing as the thief and doing neat platformery stuff, but that's fairly limited throughout the game... I kind of wish the game was based more around that mechanic than the combat or physics puzzles, really. But as it stands the game just felt like it dragged on forever to me despite not even having that massive of a play time to it overall. Not going to say it's outright terrible but it's not particularly impressive either."
This is mostly still entirely true about this game. The combat is a bit more diverse, there's a few more gimmicks in the level design, the graphics look nicer, but the improvements end there. In many ways this game is actually /worse/, at least in terms of the collection side of the gameplay. Trine 1 has a green, bright color for the experience pickups that stands out, and I don't recall them ever being entirely hidden/not visible. Trine 2 on the other hand has a bright blue color that frequently blends in with the background, and experience pickups that are entirely hidden behind rocks on many an occasion. The interesting item system of the first game is also gone, instead replaced by a larger skill tree, but really, why bother... at least in this game you can eventually pretend the knight doesn't exist at all (since you will literally never need him after a few of the unlockable skills).
I bet this game is really fun in multiplayer, yeah, and maybe more fun if you just play from beginning to end ignoring the experience gathering, but really, as a single player game, it's one of the most tedious and uninteresting games I've ever played, so much so that I doubt I'll ever be finishing the "expansion". I sincerely hope they don't make a Trine 3 and beat the corpse of this horse even more.

Video:
Text:
As always, watch the video for a much more detailed analysis.
Urban Empire looks pretty - that much is uncontested. The various time periods, design choices and distinct detail in every nook and cranny ooze personality. From character art to research screen, everything looks fantastic. It also has pretty good PC Performance with no dips below 60 at any time and smooth gameplay on any level of zoom.
Sadly, this performance is achieved in part by just having almost no simulation of life in the town. Street look empty, sounds are subdued when available and everything just moves at a snails pace that doesn't really fit with the "month per tick" cycle of the game.
But, it's not the visuals that make this game bland... It's the gameplay. Between having very limited information (that has almost no detail or depth) and very limited control over the city building that makes it for a very hands of and very frustrating experience. Not being able to assign districts directly, and not being able to build your infrastructure beyond a "draw a box, call it a district and yay" is not that fun and more than that ... everything is ridiculously expensive that keeping a solid balance is nigh on impossible... oh and keeping your economy running doesn't matter anyhow, there are no consequences
Also, the expected political gameplay boils down to a sliderbar with a score on top. The expected depth of political gameplay or intrigue really never shows up and all voting boils down to is how often you've done one of 3 random events.
Also, almost anything is put to the vote, but by and large the parties don't really oppose you in any way. With neither real counter plays or divergences in ethics being apparent in their per-vote look at things. And nothing you do will have any long or even mid term impact.
Overal a shallow experience that fills a few hours before you crave either City building or Political gameplay, and it provides neither in any real way.

Revolution Ace is definitely NOT one of the best shooters in its genre. It has frame rate problems, the bullets blend in with the background, and generally it's a bit of a mess. But somehow when I was playing it, something made me look past all that and I really did have a good time. It has an upgrade system that definitely helps with the sense of progression, a fun but challenging boss at the end of each stage, and a neat system of air bullets vs ground bullets, forcing you to pick between whether you're shooting in the background or in the foreground.
But by far the best part of the game is the multiplayer. It takes all the problems I mentioned and kinda blurs them out of your mind, because, at least for me, I was more focused on playing a game with my friend and the issues became less glaring. There's also a cool multiplayer versus mode, which I've never seen implimented into a top-down shooter before. It works pretty well.
As a whole, Revolution Ace was like a fat guy sitting in front of you at a playoff game. It's annoying at first, sure, but if you can look past the problems, you have a great game in front of you. It's a fun experience, and you should definitely consider picking it up if you have some friends to play it with.

Being a huge RWBY fan, I was curious to see what this game had to offer. I had just finished Volume 3 a few days earlier (and was still emotionally suffering from its DEVESTATING finale), so I wanted to have something related to the series to keep me occupied before Volume 4 came out. And this game did NOT disappoint. I don't even know where to begin.
For starters, the visuals look like they were ripped straight from the series. Every level feels like an episode itself. Whether you're traveling the Emerald Forest or venturing through Forever Fall, you will instantly recognize the beautiful locations from your favorite episodes. The level design is terrific, as well. No two levels are alike. You'll be seeing different layouts from start to finish. Some levels have their own twists to them, and some even have separate paths that the game will open at random. This means that every playthrough of a level will be different than the last. The variety in the levels makes for a great experience.
The gameplay is pretty much exactly what I wanted. While each characters' fighting style has only minor differences between them, they are still satisfying to play. Every character uses their respective weapon from the series; Ruby slashes at everything with her Crescent Rose, and Yang beats up enemies with her fists. The upgrades you can unlock for each character allows you to use even more amazing abilities and witness even more impressive finishing moves. Every character is a ton of fun to play. This is brought out further with the multiplayer. Being able to team up with other players to get through each level is a worthwhile inclusion.
Speaking of the characters, you won't be disappointed hearing them speak. The beloved voice cast from the series is all here. Hearing a character taunt that now-dead Grimm is both satisfying and hilarious. Every character's personality is retained, as well. Not once does anybody sound out of character. Rooster Teeth knows consistency when they see it, that's for sure.
The game's soundtrack adds to the excitement, as well. While traveling through the levels, you will be blessed with truly brilliant orchestral scores. While locked in battle with Grimm, you'll be pumping your head to amazing rock pieces. The ninth chapter even has its own exclusive techno music. However, the absolute best piece of music in this game is the instrumental version of Time to Say Goodbye, the opening song of Volume 2. I can't help but sing along every time it starts playing. The soundtrack never gets old, and it's always great to hear it.
Every game has its flaws, though, and this game is no exception. First off, while the characters retain their respective voice actors, their performances sometimes fall flat. There are some moments where a character's line sounds poorly recited. This is especially noticeable with Blake. There are times when it sounds like it was the actor's first time reciting the line ever. This is surprising because everyone has decent acting in the series. It's a wonder how the final cut of some of the voice-overs ended up so poor.
The game also has a terrible issue with the subtitles. Most of the time, they're fine. But there are several instances where a character's recited line and the subtitles do not match. These inconsistencies range from minor errors to literally two different sentences. The lack of proofreading is just inexcusable.
Sometimes, a character's line is played at a moment where it clearly was not meant to. There's a spot in Chapter 5 where you hop across pillars to reach an artifact (you get an achievement by doing this). If you reach this spot while playing as Ren, it plays an unrelated line from Pyrrha. It's bewildering how this bypassed the game's testers. These voice issues are cringe-inducing, and it really detracts from the quality. It's nowhere near perfect.
The multiplayer has some quirks, too. The only way you can communicate with your teammates is by bringing up a chat menu, meaning there's no way to communicate and fight at the same time. You always have to stop to talk to your teammates. This not only stops you from helping or reviving them, but it also makes you an extremely easy target for every enemy attacking your team. You'll be overrun by enemies and be unable to fight back just because you're typing in something to say. The lack of voice chat makes communication with your team incredibly stiff. It's not even worth it.
Overall, though, RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is a fun and memorable experience, and one that no RWBY fan should miss. If you're waiting for a new episode or volume to come out, this is just the thing to keep you occupied. This is a gift to fans of the series, and I highly recommend it. You will not be disappointed.

IMPORTANT: This game requires a resonably good and consistent connection to play online coop. A friend of mine experienced frequent desyncronization.
A significant improvement upon its predecessor, Torchlight II is a solid step forward on the road to the ideal ARPG. It's charming art style, overall fast paced gameplay and mostly forgiving features, including a choice of difficulty setting, also make it a good entry point for those new to the genre, as well as offering a good challenge to the experienced dungeon crawler. The major change this time around is the addition of up to six-player cooperative play online, where the first game bizarrely lacked any multiplayer at all.
The story is still somewhat sparse, again shoehorning the player into the role of damage control regarding the actions of a villain who, infuriatingly, will always look cooler then your character, and your character has no spoken dialogue with other characters. The classes do however have satisfyingly varied and powerful abilities and the combat feels very chunky, thanks to good sound design, enemies exploding on a critical kill and an overall focus on powerful single attacks. However, this installment inherits some of the first game's biggest problems: you are required to mainline potions to both to stay alive and keep your mana up, you may go hours without finding better gear and the champion monsters are much more powerful then the actual level bosses, sometimes outrageously so. I found myself dying regularly in the final act even on normal, though this costs you nothing should you choose to respawn in town, coupled with a total lack of an item durability mechanic (a huge plus that other games could learn from- I'm looking at you, Diablo 3). In addition, only unique gear is actually flavored towards your class, leaving you looking like a scrappy scavenger for most of your playthrough. You can also only refund your last three skill points spent and cannot redistribute your attribute points at all. Any of the above issues are easily remedied by using the game’s integral mod support or the Rapid Respec editor, the latter of which also allows you to resurrect a dead “hardcore” character.
After playing through the game once as an Engineer without mods, I played as an Outlander using several mods, most notably a "double points" mod that gives you 10 attribute and 2 skill points per level, and a mod that scales all enemies and bosses to your current level whenever you enter a different zone. Having the right mod setup really enhances the game experience overall and I recommend giving it a shot as soon as you feel comfortable doing so. The pet system remains very useful, now including the ability to have your pet buy potions and scrolls for you in addition to selling your vendor trash, and this time around it seems your pet can take more then being looked at funny before losing all its health. This game also retains the absolutely enchanting musical talents of Matt Uelman, the music man behind Diablo's equally compelling soundtrack. In spite of its problems, Torchlight II is an excellent title with excellent mods, and well worth your time.

While not a BAD MMORPG, I have to say as a Tolkien fan I was a little saddened by how linear the gameplay felt. "Go here to start the quest, talk to this person to complete the quest, kill exactly this many creatures to complete the quest"...It just doesn't feel as if anything you do has any real impact on the world. If they had given it more of a sandbox feel while still being story driven (think Skyrim or Oblivion), I think I might have enjoyed it more, and yes I understand that a lot of MMOs are limited in this way. I suppose I was just expecting a little more from an established series; I get more enjoyment and feel more freedom in Star Trek Online. Visually and thematically it was appealing and I did love seeing the various locations, but it wasn't for me--especially after taking nearly 48 hours to complete the initial install as well as patch it. LotR fans might enjoy it if they are looking for something that's just LotR themed to play with friends, but if you're looking for something that feels like a Middle Earth experience you probably won't find it here.

What. The. Hell, Eidos.
I honestly thought that after
developers all over the world would finally learn their lesson and get that VIDEOGAMES ARE NOT TV SHOWS. You can't cut the plot in the middle and write "To be continued..." with a smirk. A TV Show season takes about a year to get released, but a video game sequel? Three, four years. And if the game suddenly failed to sell well, there might not be a sequel at all.
I'm torn in this review, honestly.
The titanium augmented heart of
is still beating in here, and Eidos' famed attention to details is present as well, so the game DELIVERS. There is a big city hub, with huge amount of secrets, side-quests and sub-plots, adding to the whole story and expanding the Deus Ex universe greatly. A few new characters feel interesting, however many just don't get enough screen time. Adam as a protagonist has matured as well and is not
anymore. The gameplay had received minor improvements, but it was already nearly perfect in
anyway.
The problem is just one, but it's big.
The game had most definitely been hastened towards the release, and moving the release date for six months did not resolve the issues entirely. The main storyline and some unfinished side-quests serve as proof: the game creates an illusion of being non-linear, but it's simply false: the only consequence of your choices can be seen in a final
news program before credits. Hardly satisfactory. Many sidequests begin prominently, but are later dropped without a second thought.
The main storyline takes ages to develop, but when it finally does and you think "Great, things are finally getting interesting", the game just ends almost instantly.
Human Revolution had a solid main plot, with three endings, each concluding the story by the end credits.
Here? An abrupt ending and classic
after credits scene teasing another sequel.
Oh, an by the way, know how many bosses there are in the game?
One. One, Carl. And he appears in the launch window every time you launch the game, so you know the final boss before you even begin your playthrough.
What. The. Hell, Eidos.
--
Anyway, Mankind Divided is still a good cyberpunk experience. But sadly loses to its predecessor. I just feel I'll be lying about many hours of fun I spent in the game if I give it a thumbs down, but... That was not cool, Eidos. Hope you learn on your mistakes.

But the overall direction taken by the game publisher in order to get more and more money from us gamer is frightening.
If, as a community we continue to support games that agressively push micro transactions in game, DLCs that should have been included in the base game and other suspicious marketing strategies, we are going to witness the worst gaming era ever.
For a game that in its philosophy and story points out the injustices of a particular system, it is a shame to see that those behind the game are the one perpetuating those said injustices and unfair systems.
What does the industry needs to realise that they are being the bad guys ? More Piracy ? Probably not, the way to get rid of a system is to progressively replace it with a new system. And the way to do it is for buyers to put their money on games that are a reflection of this new system. Hopefully the Indie scene will be the one providing.

Here's what I said about Trine 1:
"I'm sure this is going to get downvoted by diehard fanboys of this series, but really. The graphics are nice, yes. The music's decent. There's a good premise for a game here. So why is it /so bloody boring/? There's very little variation in the levels here, aside from one or two notable exceptions most every level plays the same. Even then the only notable departure is the last level, which is instead just flat-out flawed. The game focuses far too much on its combat system and too little on platforming or creative puzzle design. There's about three different types of enemies throughout the entire game, and they're all over the place in each level. So fighting them gets... really boring, really fast. Though the bats never stop being annoying. Ever. The puzzle design is mostly physics-based and can also be entirely broken, basically defeating the point. I have plenty of fun playing as the thief and doing neat platformery stuff, but that's fairly limited throughout the game... I kind of wish the game was based more around that mechanic than the combat or physics puzzles, really. But as it stands the game just felt like it dragged on forever to me despite not even having that massive of a play time to it overall. Not going to say it's outright terrible but it's not particularly impressive either."
This is mostly still entirely true about this game. The combat is a bit more diverse, there's a few more gimmicks in the level design, the graphics look nicer, but the improvements end there. In many ways this game is actually /worse/, at least in terms of the collection side of the gameplay. Trine 1 has a green, bright color for the experience pickups that stands out, and I don't recall them ever being entirely hidden/not visible. Trine 2 on the other hand has a bright blue color that frequently blends in with the background, and experience pickups that are entirely hidden behind rocks on many an occasion. The interesting item system of the first game is also gone, instead replaced by a larger skill tree, but really, why bother... at least in this game you can eventually pretend the knight doesn't exist at all (since you will literally never need him after a few of the unlockable skills).
I bet this game is really fun in multiplayer, yeah, and maybe more fun if you just play from beginning to end ignoring the experience gathering, but really, as a single player game, it's one of the most tedious and uninteresting games I've ever played, so much so that I doubt I'll ever be finishing the "expansion". I sincerely hope they don't make a Trine 3 and beat the corpse of this horse even more.

You know that guy who slaughters all the noobs with highly advanced weaponry that makes everything feel unbalanced? I'm that guy. I was the dude who looked up all the stats for every gun, knows the armor thickness and speed of every tank in the game, and consistantly topped the leaderboard. I played for a while, not as long as some, much longer than others. And I had a lot of fun. I paid about $15 once because I figured all the problems in this game could be fixed if I helped out a little bit, but all the rest of it, the OHK sniper rifle, my super high level American, I got that all through grinding. And it wasn't even a grind sometimes, I had fun.
But I can't recommend this game. If you don't already have at least my amount of time in this game, you're done. It used to be that you started with one soldier from each faction and had grenades to go with your starting weapon. You had something to get you up on your feet. Not any more. I've seen the expenses of every item go up nearly double. It went from being bordering on unreasonable to almost insane. But I already had the good gear on one of my characters, so I kept playing. Firing thirty bullets from my rifle cut into half my earnings and other equipment brought me near to breaking even. So I had to nerf my own character to continue playing, and I couldn't go back to my nub characters without being so badly killed I didn't have fun. "Git gud" doesn't apply here. I've been on the other end of the slaughter. There is nothing a new player to stand against someone with better equipment except take pot shots at a distance and hope to scrap together some XP, which isn't fun. And if a game isn't fun, its not worth playing.
The real nail in the coffin is the technical issues. It got so bad that I couldn't stay in a match for more than a minute before the entire game went bonkers. After a couple days of this, I just stopped trying. It really isn't worth the trouble.
TL;DR
It was fun, now its not because grind/technical issues/not new player friendly. Give it a shot if you want, could be your cup of tea, wasn't mine. This is an opinion, just like every review. Treat it as such when you are making your decision, and bear in mind its free-to-play, so there's no harm in trying it yourself.

Despite the resemblance to other city-builders such as SimCity and Cities: Skylines, Urban Empire is first and foremost a political simulator.  You play the role of mayor of a city located in the fictional nation of Swarelia and you'll be responsible for guiding your city through five different time periods, from the industrial revolution to the modern era.  Like the city-building games mentioned before, you will oversee the growth and development of your city, zoning residential, commercial and industrial districts as well as adding service buildings (police stations, hospitals, churches, etc) and issuing edicts.  However, you do not rule with absolute authority - the decisions you make are subject to approval by the city council.  The council is made up of multiple parties, each with their own agenda, so it may be necessary to appease the voters order to get them to see things your way.
Here is a quick run down of the pros and cons of this game.
PROS:
- Good quality graphics - any changes are visually displayed on the city view screen such as adding street lights or upgrading roads from dirt to cobblestone, etc.
- Extensive tech tree that allows you to upgrade your city in a variety of ways.
- Detailed statistics screens on a variety of subjects.
- Game features multiple dynasties to play as, each with their own strengths and weaknesses, adding some replayability to the game.
- The political wheeling and dealing you engage in is quite fun.
- Detailed tutorial that offers advice as you play the game.
CONS
- Some of the statistics can be a little confusing.
- The UI is not the friendliest.
- While the tutorial is detailed, it can also be intrusive at times.
- There aren't that many maps to play on.
- Gameplay can feel repetitive at times, I suspect the developer is looking to flesh this out with DLC.
- The city-building aspect is a little basic.
CONCLUSION

A difficult game to review because it's very difficult to tell whether it's fun or not. It's also very difficult to tell just about anything happening in your city. I very much enjoyed the opening half-hour, getting involved in city politics, forming likes and dislikes towards certain parties that opposed the type of city I was trying to create, and unlocking different services for the first time.
This quickly fizzled out when I advanced to era II and wanted to try to stimulate my industrial areas to provide taxes to further improve my existing districts, and I realised I had no idea how businesses actually work. Sales demand is counterintuitive (lowering it is...Better?), extra sales, efficiency, quality, and lots of nice other words that the game fails to explain the significance of. After some prodding, raising and lowering business tax and keeping track of the finances of certain businesses I've managed to work out the general gist of how things work, and yet I still feel woefully underinformed about what policies to implement regarding the industrial and commercial sectors, and consequently have little intution about what to build in my residential districts.
Is the economy growing or shrinking? I'unno.
Is my city business friendly? I'unno.
Should I take steps to improve conditions for doing business, or can they handle a 2-3% rise in taxation? I'unno.
And it's a game where information is key, half of the difficulty comes from an irritatingly unhelpful UI. Which is just unacceptable for a game considered to be in a finished and playable state.
So, I'd suggest saving your money for now, at least until one of the great sages among us have figured out how to play it and post a guide, because it promises to be quite fun in the moments of clarity you experience from time to time.

Please note: at time of writing, I have only played the base game and Vergil's playthough, and I'm going through Legendary Dark Knight as Vergil. So I have no informed opinions of Lady and Trish. However, I believe I've seen enough to make an adequate review.
So, this is my first Devil May Cry game. I've played games with various degrees of similarity to the series and had a blast, so I decided to jump in. It was a good decision. As such, this review will be aimed at newcomers of my variety.
Level design: As any newcomers may have heard on review, the base game is only part-done due to only having a few environments and nothing new for Dante in the base game. Fortunatly, this level design is really good. It has neat touches   designed to ease you into mechanics you'll see later and are as fun to traverse as a game of this genre should be. Whilst there is the much-maliagned backtracking, at least on this phase each level for Dante, with the exception of his last level, has a gimmick that changes things up in some way (mostly around some penalty for tardyness), so whilst the environments are the same, at least the experiance isn't.
Enemies: Again, there are sadly a small number of enemies. Again, happily, they are fun (or at least interesting) enemies to fight. With the exception of two, each enemy has a normal version and a bigger, more dangerous version that fights similarly, but not identically. They appear less frequently and are often there to boost the challenge of a situation. The two exceptions are odd, since because of how one of these enemies works although they are the same enemies that behave the same way, them appearing in the same area makes it more like the more dangerous versions.
Bosses. There are seven bosses. They are each unique and challenging with their own unique strategies, and are annoying to fight in exactly the way a boss should be. However, you fight each multiple times. Fortunately, it's a little different each time, so that's nice.
Nero: the posterboy of the base game, and a nice way for newcomers to get in. He has three attack buttons: Blue Rose (gun), Red Queen (sword) and Devil Bringer (grappling hook/enemy stand). Each does it's own thing and is used for particular purposes. He has a small moveset, but it's a useful one, and stylish, thanks mostly to the Bevil Bringer.. Plus, in the base game, by the time you want more...
Dante: Far and away the character with the most moves. Dante has six weapons to contast Nero's three (counting the latter's magic arm) and four uses for the third attack button. By using specific button inputs (D-pad on controllers) you can switch Dante between four (eventually five) styles on the fly. Trickster (grants a dash and limited teleport), Swordmaster (gives Dante a second melee attack button), Royal Guard (grants the ability to block and parry) and Gunslinger (give Dante a second ranged attack button). The ability to switch these is key to Dante. Dante's fifth style is spoiler-y so I won't go into much detail, but it's pretty limited anyway. For refrence, Dante's weapons are: Rebellion (Longsword), Gilgamesh (Gauntlet and Greaves), Lucifer (Exploding... Spikes?), Ebony and Ivory (Dual Pistols), Coyote-B (Shotgun) and Pandora (Transforms, but is usually a rocket launcher of some description. Standard attack for usual attacks,  gunslinger gives screen-nukes when enough damage is done with normal gunfire)
Vergil: Dante has the most moves, but Vergil's no slouch - plus he's way more streamlined... and badass. Whereas Dante has a style and weapon combination for every scenario, Vergil has only four weapons - Yamato (Katana), Force Edge (longsword), Beowulf (Gauntlet and Greaves) and Summoned Sword (summons swords in a number of formation). He also has only one style - Dark Slayer.
But oh, what a style and weapons. Yamato is fast and variable, able to deal good damage in most situations. Force Edge is a bit slower, but is good at early setup for combos or payoff for an opening. Beowulf is slow but does a lot of damage. Summoned Sword are like Ebony and Ivory mixed with Pandora, but better in every concievable way. The multiple attacks of Pandora with the speed of Ebony and Ivory. They can surround Vergil or his enemies, rapid fire or rain down on foes. And, as they manifest around Vergil, not held or thrown by him, he can unleash Melee attacks and ranged attacks at the same time. Dark Slayer has two effects - concentration and teleportation. Concentration improves your attack capabilities (for example, giving Yamato more reach), but neccesitates that either you maintain a constant stream of damage or stand around not attacking enemeis to build it up. Running, missing or worst of all getting hit reduces concentration. At full concentration, and in Devil Trigger (explained in a moment), Vergil can use Judgement Cut End. This basically deals huge damage to everything in front (and some things behind) Vergil in a very flashy manner. A nice way to finish bosses or fights you just don't wanna deal with. Vergil can also teleport to any enemy that has a summoned sword imbedded in it that isn't behind a wall.
General: All characters generally work by having range being weaker, but safer than melee and having Melee being more powerful and cooler looking. And that is vital - you are judged partially on how cool you look. Repeating the same attacks is generally less good looking (except for the occasional DBZ Vergil teleport combo or basketball game with lesser demons), so you are encouraged to switch things up, which makes the game more fun. Additionally all characters (except the pure human, Lady) have access to the Devil Trigger. This generally buffs the character hugely - for Dante and Vergil it's a general buff, wheras Nero (since he can put enemies in stunlocks with ease), gets a massive DPS increase. Plus, all these characters feel good to play (though, as you may be able to tell, Vergil is my current favourite), and a lot of that is how excellent the animations and controls are.  Everything is responsive and does what you tell it to, and you know what to tell it to do very diagetically.
Story: A fun little romp for Dante and Nero. I won't spoil it, but for what it is it's decent. Unfortunatly, the new characters gameplay and story are incongrous with each other, and that story is barebones anyway (Vergil's is basically "one day Vergil went for a stroll around Fortuna. Demons died. Nero happened (possibly). Vergil left. The End, cue DMC3") and the gameplay is non canon at that (Vergil has weapons he gets over the course of DMC3 before it happens).
Soundtrack: I have no idea what genre of music this is, but it fits perfectly in this sort of game.
Overall thoughts/TL;DR: An excellent game, if one with a lot of untapped potential. Gameplay is more than solid, it's diamond hard and fun as you could want.

No spoilers for anyone wanting to buy the game but the flow of the story is very much; a routine day of Grimm killing for our (maybe not yours but definitely my) favourite team of heroines (and possibly the secondary team if you bought the DLC) when you discover something that eludes to something greater and that is when the main story ensues. At the ending of the game i didnt feel compelled to replay, didn't feel like i wanted to delve into the Rank system when there is almost no reason to actually use it, but i still ended up going to rank 5 as of this review. The replayability is almost non-existent except for the aformentioned Ranking system or for achievement hunting.
My Final verdict? The game is a good hack and slash, the game has a good story, the game has no replayability and is most likely experienced as a single runthrough. I do recommend this game for RWBY fans and I do recommend it to my own friends but it may be hard to find more entertainment out of it besides the same repetition.

Let's be honest for a moment, let's get into some
talk, yeah?... Half-Life 3 is likely never going to happen at this point. The same could probably be said of a Portal sequel, and maybe even Left 4 Dead, as well. It's sad, I know, but that's the bitter pill we have to swallow until Valve tells us otherwise. But the good news?... People are still making really great mods for all these games in the meantime. Yay! Pan to stage left and cue the entrance of Transmissions: Element 120, the latest mod set in the Half-Life universe.
A lot of mods can tend to just take the existing parts of a game and cobble them together in ways that are essentially a remix of things we've already played, but what I like about this is it actually brings a couple of new ideas of its own to the table. The interesting use of light at times being one in particular that I'd actually really love to see expanded upon. In fact, that's pretty true of the whole game, with it only taking little more than an hour to complete and with no real incentive to revisit. It's a minor let down, but considering the content is largely the work of a single individual, you can hardly hold that against them, and it's a small miracle in itself that they managed to make something that feels so true to the series that could easily fit right alongside it.
If anyone's played either of the Half-Life games then they'll already know exactly what they're getting with this and will feel right at home - a perfectly solid shooter with a light dusting of physics based puzzles and a high degree of polish (even if the game engine does feel old as all hell by now). It's completely free whether you own any of the main games or not, has some easy achievements for anyone interested in them, and is an entertaining excuse to reacquaint yourself with your old Half-Life stomping grounds.

I'm writing this part early, because of all the people that are booty-tickled about all the microtransactions. There's something they clearly don't know how to do, which is completely ignore them. They don't shove them into your face, and say "BUY ME!" No, they are there for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that actually spend money on it. Don't listen to these reviews that have to do with "microtransactions" and other ♥♥♥♥ that's going on. If you're a fan of the Deus Ex series, you'll love this game. Play the game, don't worry about the company's business practices. Now, to get onto the meat of the review.
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided takes place two years after Deus Ex: Human Revolution. After the whole biochip incident, and everyone going insane, people are very skeptical about augmentations. In fact, the city, Prague, where this game takes place in, augs are looked down upon. Train stations are segregated from Natural to Augs. Police are arrested augs for no reason, or with little suspicion. Adam Jensen, is a new Interpol agent. Sarif Industries, the place we last saw him working for, went down and went bankrupt after the biochip incident. TF29, an Interpol agency that is located and based in Prague. There are many more groups involved in this game. None of the groups from Human Revolution, are either disbanded or, not heard of. The Juggernaut Collective, a group of vigilante hackers, ARC (Augment Rights Colltion), a group dedicated to making sure that augs gets rights, and equality, and The Illuminati. All, but one, are very mysterious groups, the Illuminati, they don't know much about them at all, they just know they exist. Jensen, has an insider in the Juggernaut Collective, Vera. She helps Adam throughout the game, with details, and secrets. In the first mission, you encounter the Illuminati, disguised men, that wear black suits and gold masks. In the heat of all that's happening the world, Adam Jensen is back at it, and is trying to stop these secretive organizations, from causing or performing more terrorist attacks.
This game plays almost identical to Human Revolution, just with an UI overhaul (Thank god the health and energy are bars now, not numbers), and a whole new skill tree, in the matter of new augments that you find out are secretly in your system. In my playthrough, I was doing stealth. It was pretty enjoyable. Going around, traq'ing people, or knocking them out. I enjoyed it a lot more than running and gunning. There were points where I was running and gunning, but I tried my best to be silent throughout the whole game.
The graphics of the game, are an overhaul to Human Revolution. The character models, the city, and gun models, look beautiful. With the graphics engine of this game, Prague felt real, and like I was there. Sadly, the PC copy of this game isn't optimized too well. (Running a GTX 980 4gb Strix edition with a i7-4640) Running the game on High, was optimal at some points, but in populated areas, the FPS would drop to 30-40. I ran the game on Medium, and it was fine. Just, I wish I could have played this on High, but that's ok. I was more entranced in the story.
The story, was very enjoyable. In this game, I decided to most of the side missions, explored the world, hacked a bunch of ♥♥♥♥, and more. I didn't just rush through the story, and beat the game. I wanted to see what there was, all the other content this game had to offer. The story of the side missions were actually really good. I don't think I've enjoyed side missions in a game, since, I don't even know. Now, speaking of the ending, it's a bit of a cliffhanger. I'm not sure if they're leaving that for DLC's, or even another game. The fact they are making two DLC's, makes it hard for me to believe they'll rap it up with those two. Unless, they are really long.
The mission that comes with the game as a pre-order exclusive (we all know everyone will be able to buy it sooner or later) called Desperate Measures, is a side mission that should have been in the game, but it wasn't, and is now considered "Jensen's Stories". It takes place somewhere around the beginning of the game, when one of the bombing happened, and you find someone that might have evidence about who did, and why? Now, most games these days cut out content for DLC, I'm not gonna take points off my score, I'm just saying it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥.
The other content this game has is called The Breach. It involves hacking in vitrual reality. You are called a "Ripper", someone who hacks secure corporations, inside of vitrual reality. Vitrual reality in the Deus Ex world, is done through something that is mentioned in the game, and later used fully in the game, called NSN, or Neural Subnet. So just a more high tech vitrual reality. I'm actually happy this is in the game, as a seperate story and such. The fact that there's only one mission in the game that has the gameplay, is saddening, but the Breach allows you go through a map of servers, and different server levels, to satisfy your hacking needs. The gameplay is very neat. You're inside a server, going around, solving little puzzles, and extracting data needed for the Blades, the organization that you are part of. You even have weapons in the NSN. This is honestly cool as ♥♥♥♥.
Now, after beating this game, I am saddened. When I found out they were making a new Deus Ex, I was pumped. I loved Human Revolution, and I loved this game so much. I'm most likely going to re-play Human Revolution, do the side quests, and then play the original Deus Ex. Right now, this is my favorite single-player game of the year. 9/10 Buy it if you're a fan of Deus Ex, but if you're not and you're still skeptical, check out ♥♥♥. They may have the game for a cheaper price than what Steam has.

: A good loot system let down by a bad aesthetic, with the combat feeling really bad compared to Diablo 2, 3 and even PoE.
As far as the looting system and progression goes, TL2 is quite good. It has that good "always-feels-like-im-upgrading-and-being-rewarded" feel that good action RPGs - except release Diablo 3 - have. This is probably the biggest strength of the game.
Character customization and weapon types are good too, at least compared to other aRPGs. Each type of weapon does actualyl feel different and has a decent effect on how you play.
The first and most immediately noticable problem, for me, is the aesthetic and visual design. Firstly steampunk is done to death, and as far as steampunk based games go this is one of the worst looking/sounding. Bioshock and Dishonored did it (somewhat) well, but for me personally steampunk wasn't the best thing to begin with and is now so, so overdone. Independent of my personal dislike of steampunk, the colour palette isn't the best: there are far too many purples and pastel shades of blue green, and everything appears like a washed out cartoon.
This is underlined by the game being devoid of an immersive and compelling atmosphere. The atmosphere in this game is like Borderlands 2. I'm not against pop culture references, satire or humour - I loved GTA 5's atmosphere - but this game, like Borderlands, seems like it's confused with it's own atmosphere and as a result is never going to immerse anyone. The guys who designed both TL2 and Borderlands' atmospheres ren't the best in my opinion. You can make as many nerdy jokes as you want but when there's no atmosphere at all, that isn't enough I'm afraid. I don't think it's because I dislike the atmosphere, my tastes are pretty varied; I think the game just lacks a compelling one which can draw people in. This would be less important if the game was really good fun, but it isn't.
Perhaps more importantly, the actual combat gameplay isn't good enough, particularly with the high standard set by Diablo and old Blizzard games. The combat feels very shallow and the characters and spells feel too "floaty", not crisp and responsive like Diablo and other good "feeling" games. The actual combat mechanics are also lacking. It's very stop-start and doesn't flow. Any spell which requires standing still to cast feels TERRIBLY clunky. This isn't aided by the sub-par sounds that the spells make. As a result everything feels just
, which makes the game hard to return to in the long run, unlike Diablo 2 and 3.
If Torchlight 3 is ever made, the aesthetics and overall "feel" of the game, particularly the combat, need a serious rework. As it is, it's not even an acquired taste. I do imagine some people may enjoy the aesthetic, but from my point of view it looks like it's even more divisive than marmite. Some things were done right, but overall this game could - and perhaps should -  be so much better than it turned out.

Far Cry: Blood Dragon is a love letter to the eighties and more specifically to that decade’s magnificently cheesy science-fiction and action movies. Someone savvy at production company Ubisoft, decided to use the basic building blocks of Far Cry 3 and to repurpose them, giving them a fresh lick of paint. Blood Dragon has clear similarities with the main game, but can be bought and enjoyed as a stand-alone. There are, again,  enemy bases to liberate, collectibles strewn about the landscape you traverse and plenty of faceless enemies to kill in a manner of your choosing. The experience is more streamlined, with less padding than the main game, but the gameplay is familiar. There is leveling up, though this time it is an automatic process. You can get upgrades to weapons by playing through some optional missions, but there aren’t so many of them that doing them all feels like a chore. Especially if you are just coming off the main game, the shorter playtime is a good thing as Blood Dragon could otherwise easily have worn out its welcome.
The plot doesn’t bear much pondering and its tongue is in its cheek so hard it’s a wonder it doesn’t puncture it. Basically, you are a Good bionic soldier who has to stop an Evil bionic soldier. The meat of this story, in so far as there is meat, is told in lovingly crafted 16-bit cut scenes, which especially older gamers will be able to appreciate for reasons of nostalgia. However, the parts where you are in control, are rendered in glorious current-day graphics, with a first person perspective. The esthetic is futuristic retro, with a lot of neon, and the color scheme is predominately purple with splashes of green, red and blue. The music pays homage to Blade Runner, The Terminator and also seems influenced by Daft Punk’s Tron soundtrack. Aliens and Terminator veteran Michael Biehn does the gruff voice-acting honors for your alter-ego.
The island you find yourself on is populated by Blood Dragons who have lasers for eyes (naturally), disposable mercenaries whose hearts you can rip out (with a purpose, though also for laughs) and scientists whom you are supposed to protect, although it really doesn’t matter to the plot whether or not you succeed. I witnessed on at least two occasions, presumably scripted, that a scientist accidentally offed himself just after having been liberated by me. There’s a cheekiness to it all, also evident in the mission objectives (“Unique Horn Dragon. It’s Magical and Wonderful. Now go kill it.”), your character’s baffled response to the stupidity of them, his random tough-guy one-liners (“This little piggy went to the morgue.”) and during the loading screens (“Need credits? Pilfer bodies. There’s absolutely nothing morally objectionable about that.”).
If you play Blood Dragon right after Far Cry 3, it is entertaining to spot the redressed elements and game mechanics. For instance, I have a suspicion that the ‘bear’ A.I. is at work below the pixilated surface of the Blood Dragons. Be it with added laser eyes, of course. Not all of the re-used elements make sense, however. Among the otherwise high-tech opposition are fidgety-looking guys specialized in throwing Molotov cocktails, who make the same nervous jumps their equally pyromaniac counterparts did in Far Cry 3. If you didn’t play the main game, I imagine that kind of stuff will have you scratching your head at the randomness of it.
The Blood Dragons give you some welcome new options for taking over a an enemy base. Find a power generator located at a back entrance, lower the protective force field at the entrance and then lure a Blood Dragon inside by throwing some cyber-hearts in the direction you need it to go. Sit back to watch the Dragon zap all your enemies and lure it outside again to finalize your hostile takeover.

This is a RTS with very simplified building management, few units, and a couple of concepts from the Tower Defense genre. The result is probably not great, but it is pretty decent, and if you like RTS and/or TD games, you should really give it a try.
The game starts _very_ slowly,  and within the first couple of hours, you'll feel like doing the same thing over & over again, without much challenge. Fortunately, the game picks up after that, even if the strategy doesn't really get too deep. This is mostly a game where the thing that matters the most is your clicking speed.
The campaign is pretty simple, a bit repetitive, and short : count between 6 and 8 hours to complete it on a challenging difficulty, without doing the optional missions ; and this was enough for me to get around the game. So I'd recommend you to get it on a 50%-sale or cheaper.
- Simplified RTS + a bit of Tower Defense = concept fresh enough, but without revolutionizing anything, so the genre amateurs will be at home right away
- a few campaign missions are well orchestrated and bring some interesting and unique challenges
- good handling of difficulty during the conquest of big maps : the more you steal control points from the AI, the more it mutates and get special new powers ; like this, it avoids to have a super hard start and then steamroll once the shock point is passed
- upgrade system lets you buy new stuff in the order you want, and it's balanced enough
- Visuals are the exact opposite of badass : aliens look ridiculous, marines seem like cheap stock icons ; you can check on the store page to know if it's a show stopper for you or not ; when it moves and you focus on the gameplay, it's more acceptable, though :-)
- Most campaign missions, especially the 1st ones, are simple and basic, and thus feel too generic
- Story holds little interest (personally, I think it's not penalizing for a RTS)
- Hearing non-stop the basic & repetitive firing sounds may give you a headache
- you can easily grind your way, as you can replay any mission as much as you want for extra cash, while the game lets you change the difficulty any time you want
- hardcore difficulty (3rd level out of 4 in the campaign) feels too easy, but it's ok when wanting a bit of challenge after a hard day of work, without getting even more exhausted :-p

Infested Planet is a decent Real Time Strategy game. The objective of the game is to usually to destroy AI controlled bugs and hives that come with different mutations.
Gameplay-wise, you control a squad of marines that can be upgraded impromptu. You have the standard military fare like the rifle marine, the shotgun, the officer, the minigun, the flamer, the scout and the sniper. Each role has their specialization and is meant to do a special thing. For those of you who miss the Bob-the-Builder aspect of RTS games, have no fear. The game allows you to build combat and research buildings. Combat buildings are your turrets and mortars while research buildings fall into engineering, teleporters and attack helicopter commands. Your enemy, the Alien Harvester, will simply be a host of hives spawning an inifite number of bugs.
Conclusion, do try this game. While it's not an epic game, it's simple to play and gets to the exciting parts of the RTS genre. There is little base building and more action. If there's anything really bad, it's that Infested Planet is another tropish game based on alien bugs.
