Okay, so I've been playing this game for a while. I was lucky enough to get into the closed beta, and have been playing consistently ever since.
It's very easy to learn, got simple controls and simple concepts. The characters are balanced really well; you can play any character effectively at any level of play. It's just a matter of skill.
The game functions around a system where every character has two possible weapons to pick up from the weapon drops. These range from a sword to a rocket lance, and every weapon has a couple characters that use it. The quick attacks on one weapon are the same across every character who can use it, but each character has unique heavy attacks with their weapons as well. In addition to the weapons, there are gadgets that will drop around the stage: a bomb, a land mine, and a spikeball.
Dodging is really well implemented and will be important to your play. Learn to use it and it can be an offensive weapon or a recovery tactic in addition to simply dodging. In addition, using your dodge in mid-air performs what is referred to as a gravity cancel, which allows you to use your standard (non-arial) attacks while in midair.
In addition to fighting with the weapons of the character, there are melee attacks, although there are no unique heavy attacks with the melee fighting. This can be very important, since throwing your weapons at your opponents can be a very useful strategy, and you can't always get back to the weapon to pick it up in time.
In couch party and custom online matches, you can utilize stances, which change the stats of your character. These are currently not available in ranked play.
In all methods of play, you can use alternate colour schemes, which are unlocked by playing with a character. These do not provide any change to stats or boosts, they are purely visual.
There is no pay to win. Playing succesfully earns you gold, and gold can be used to unlock your favourite characters permanantly, and a free weekly rotation allows you to practice with a few before finding the ones you like. It is possible to pay for "mammoth coins" which will let you unlock characters faster, but they will not do anything to increase the player's strength. In addition, mammoth coins can be used to buy visual changes which cannot be bought by gold, but like the colours, these changes are purely visual.
The community at low levels in ranked or in open custom matches can be... less than sparkling, but once you get to silver+ in ranked, the spammers and the people who will enter matches just to be annoying tend to be weeded away. In addition, the higher you get in the ranks, the nicer the people tend to be.
In my opinion, the best way to play the game is to find some friends and play with them. Custom online matches can hold up to eight players, so you should be set on that front.
Now that all the technical stuff I can think of is out of the way, I just gotta gush. I really love this game. Like... so much. It's like if Smash Bros was better balanced and spamming wasn't a viable way to match skill. Dodging is smooth and beautiful, and so many characters have really cool uniques! The lore that the devs have put into the characters isn't exactly important to the game, but it's fun to read anyways! The variety of the characters is amazing, and more keep being added! It's so well balanced that the win rate, last I checked, between the most succesful character and the least, was at an average of LESS THAN ONE GAME! It's SO well put together and SO smooth and SO fun, and I just... I really love this game. Go play it.
Tl;dr: Great game. Good balance. No pay to win. Go play. It's fun. Thank you and good night.

tl;dr it plays like a really basic city builder that delays construction when you've gotten into the swing of things. This should be early access at best, it needs loads of refining to be anywhere near what they have been showcasing.
It's 1960, my people are quite happy with my governing of the city, there's no water lines, sewage pipes or electric anywhere within the city. Despite this the Television business is booming, not sure how my people intend to watch the TV's, but I can't judge them.
The roads are still the same old dirt roads from the 1800's everyone is happy to drive around their cars on this with minimal traffic problems.
The communist party is quite happy for me to raise tax on the working class and lower it for the elite.
The game boasts having an indepth political system where you need to battle with different parties to make changes, but there's no point at all in picking favourites to buddy up with as all relations with these parties will reset back to 0 after a couple of years. So you can generally treat them how you want.
City expansion only becomes a problem if you have both a low income and low funds in the account, as then all parties will try to block all decisions you make. However if you're sitting there with a few hundred k in the bank, they will generally green light everything you want to do, like build an electrical power plant purely to export the power it creates.
The parties as well are not really sticking to what you think they would, you will quite often see the conservatives pushing for social equality with the progressive sides trying to block these movements, and as mentioned before, communists liking to tax the working class high.
The people in your city are quite happy to live with no water, electric or gas supplies. You can add these services to districts, but you get no return for doing so, people won't pay extra for them, so you're just throwing money away. They do claim to "boost companies" but again, increasing the sales of companies in your city doesn't actually do anything for your own income.
The rpg story elements hardly do anything for the game, you can choose one of 4 families with different back stories and ideas towards governing. All switching between these really does it decide which events you're going to get, and they will be the same ones each time at the exact same time, you get a few outside of this, like parties wanting to make you honourary members etc. but they're mostly meaningless.
Your character has traits, cruel, soft, opitmist etc. again, mostly meaningless. You might get the odd event pop up with a response option blocked due to lack of x trait, but refering back, your traits and what you say on these windows rarely matters.
Until elections come around, you don't need to make your citizens happy at all. No chance of an uprising due to lack of healthcare, policing, leisure or anything at all. You can quite happily ignore all the demands of your citizens until the ability to vote comes along, and you can even try to prevent that for an extended time.
Small aesthetic thing that bothers me. Why can I see loads of cars driving around my city when I've not even researched them yet. Also why do all the houses and shops have lights on at night if there's absoloutely no electrical grids in the city.
The game had some great ideas with the whole political thing, you can even blackmail parties, but they just don't mean anything towards running the city. You can spend the entire game never having to speak to any of them apart from suggesting changes to the city and waiting for them to agree on it.
And the fact that you can have a city with 0 utilities and everyone is ok with that bewilders me, but then you can't afford to give them to the entire city anyway.

Good game. An interesting political and economical simulator.
+ Reasonably difficult, you can be voted out in eras 3-5 if you're on bad terms with the political parties
+ Depicts the history in an interesting way, you can feel the world changing over time
+ Keeps you invested in the game, presents the player with challenges even in the late game (for me it was actually the hardest party-wise in the late game)
- Hard to understand the reasons behind what is happening at times (e.g. persistent low residential demand, constant influx of lower class citizens). Tooltips like the ones in Victoria 2 would be welcome. Many things may be not evident, like what exactly the tax rate does, I think at least an explanation would be good in such cases.
- Some things that you expect would happen, don't. E.g. people moving between the districts or preferring particular ones
- Watch your RAM and save frequently on the later stages, the game crashed to desktop for me around year 2010, for some other people too (8GB RAM)
All in all, I spent the weekend playing the game and had good fun, in my opinion that makes the game deserve a good recommendation despite some issues which may or may not be resolved later.

I'll mostly talk about the changes to the Special Edition version of the game (short summary for base game: amazing character action game). There's a few new cutscenes, a bunch of new costumes (the original game didn't even have any additional costumes), and three new playable characters. The three new characters all share the feeling that they're much stronger than Nero and Dante, so easier difficulties start to feel rather redudant. But anyone familiar with the game would wanna choose the higher difficulties anyway.
- Vergil is the focus of the three new characters and he plays similar to how he does in DMC3.
- Lady almost exclusively uses firearms so she feels like a very different but fun way of playing a character action game.
- You switch to Trish halfway through Lady's campaign and she's the least interesting out of the three characters. She features a lot of attacks with a very wide range of attack which makes me think she was specificially made for Legendary Dark Knight mode.
Unfortunately, there's no new music (even when playing as the new characters, you still hear the same music as you would with Nero and Dante), and aside for a couple of minor additions to the end of the campaigns, you run through the exact same levels with the exact same enemy layouts when playing as the new characters. I wish they would have taken this opportunity to find some new way to mix up the gameplay with the enemies or levels. That said, the new characters play very differently from Nero and Dante, so they represent a lot of new gameplay even if the levels and enemy layouts are the same.
From a technical level, the Special Edition is surprisingly inferior to the original game. The original game feels like one of the most optimized games I've played on PC, but this new version runs at roughly half the framerate. However, since we're comparing to an absurdly well optimized game from 2008, this doesn't mean this new version has performance issues. Despite the weird drop in performance compared to the original game, any modern PC should have no trouble running the game at 60fps.
Another technical downgrade is the resolution support. The original game would run at virtually any resolution you threw at it, but not only is the resolution support limited in Special Edition, the game will outright crash at startup if Windows is set to support specific resolutions (for instance, it happens with 5120x2880).
And one omission compared to console versions of the original game (this was also missing in the PC port of the original game) are the leaderboards.
The new content easily outweighs the weird technical flaws. It just feels like the game is one patch away from feeling polished.

Okay, so I've been playing this game for a while. I was lucky enough to get into the closed beta, and have been playing consistently ever since.
It's very easy to learn, got simple controls and simple concepts. The characters are balanced really well; you can play any character effectively at any level of play. It's just a matter of skill.
The game functions around a system where every character has two possible weapons to pick up from the weapon drops. These range from a sword to a rocket lance, and every weapon has a couple characters that use it. The quick attacks on one weapon are the same across every character who can use it, but each character has unique heavy attacks with their weapons as well. In addition to the weapons, there are gadgets that will drop around the stage: a bomb, a land mine, and a spikeball.
Dodging is really well implemented and will be important to your play. Learn to use it and it can be an offensive weapon or a recovery tactic in addition to simply dodging. In addition, using your dodge in mid-air performs what is referred to as a gravity cancel, which allows you to use your standard (non-arial) attacks while in midair.
In addition to fighting with the weapons of the character, there are melee attacks, although there are no unique heavy attacks with the melee fighting. This can be very important, since throwing your weapons at your opponents can be a very useful strategy, and you can't always get back to the weapon to pick it up in time.
In couch party and custom online matches, you can utilize stances, which change the stats of your character. These are currently not available in ranked play.
In all methods of play, you can use alternate colour schemes, which are unlocked by playing with a character. These do not provide any change to stats or boosts, they are purely visual.
There is no pay to win. Playing succesfully earns you gold, and gold can be used to unlock your favourite characters permanantly, and a free weekly rotation allows you to practice with a few before finding the ones you like. It is possible to pay for "mammoth coins" which will let you unlock characters faster, but they will not do anything to increase the player's strength. In addition, mammoth coins can be used to buy visual changes which cannot be bought by gold, but like the colours, these changes are purely visual.
The community at low levels in ranked or in open custom matches can be... less than sparkling, but once you get to silver+ in ranked, the spammers and the people who will enter matches just to be annoying tend to be weeded away. In addition, the higher you get in the ranks, the nicer the people tend to be.
In my opinion, the best way to play the game is to find some friends and play with them. Custom online matches can hold up to eight players, so you should be set on that front.
Now that all the technical stuff I can think of is out of the way, I just gotta gush. I really love this game. Like... so much. It's like if Smash Bros was better balanced and spamming wasn't a viable way to match skill. Dodging is smooth and beautiful, and so many characters have really cool uniques! The lore that the devs have put into the characters isn't exactly important to the game, but it's fun to read anyways! The variety of the characters is amazing, and more keep being added! It's so well balanced that the win rate, last I checked, between the most succesful character and the least, was at an average of LESS THAN ONE GAME! It's SO well put together and SO smooth and SO fun, and I just... I really love this game. Go play it.
Tl;dr: Great game. Good balance. No pay to win. Go play. It's fun. Thank you and good night.

Steam is home to an abundance of all sorts of games. Almost everything conceivable can be found there, from the latest big budget title to the most niche girls with cat ears hentai clicker game.
While some titles can slip through the cracks, Steam's major sales can always bring some interesting things to the surface for pretty cheap. The Steam bargain bin is kinda like a box of chocolates though. There's good, there's bad, and the doctors say if I have any more they'll take my foot. And sometimes, there's stuff like Revolution Ace.
Does your dad like to play the computey games? Maybe your grandpa? Do they talk about all the Japs they killed in The War? Are modern games too hard for them? Have them play this. They'll love it.
Revolution Ace is an old-school shoot-em-up, in the same vein as classics like Raptor or Tyrian. Or like Xevious, you probably know what Xevious is. Space Invaders. Pew-pew? The games they used to play on big ♥♥♥♥ing stove♥♥♥♥♥things. Not a hard concept to visualize.
You steer a ship around an auto-scrolling level and shoot incoming enemies. Sometimes you get power-ups, sometimes you don't. The communists would love to promise you power-ups guaranteed for everyone, but they're full of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Commie ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Revolution Ace is a decent shoot-em-up for a semi-modern take on MS-DOS classics, though somewhat slower paced than most.
Not particularly original, as most of it is a revisiting of elements from older classic shooters, shooters that are freeware you can literally just download for free somewhere. But people love retro, that's totally cool. Most indie games are just rehashed retro games anyway, right? They got the jumping, the shooting, and all the stuff you used to play on your old Nintendo computer game system. Same thing, right? Just like grandpa used to play. Only he played in real life, and killed real people. Ha ha, good old gramps.
Touting full 3D environments and all the marvels of modern graphics, complete with Unreal Engine power and real water physics simulation, Revolution Ace looks great. They put all those fancy words in the game description, just like a real AAA game. It definitely looks more modern and recent than any older shooter, which is really just common sense. It's not playing on a ♥♥♥♥ing calculator display. Of course it's going to look better. But there in comes the biggest gripe I had with the game.
None of it is necessary, none of it improves the core gameplay, and at times it actually detracts from the experience. You don't need to put a pound of sprinkles on a cracker with some whipped cream on it. They won't all fit, and you won't even be able to see the cracker. And who the ♥♥♥♥ would put whipped cream on a cracker in the first place? There's no reason for that. There's no excuse. It really feels like their priorities were a little backwards.
Bullets are near indistinguishable from the background on certain maps, the Call of Duty color palette melding together into a mess of movement that's almost dizzying at times. Sometimes entire enemies, or your own ship even, will get lost amid all the action on screen. There's just too much going on, everywhere, all the time. I don't mind the fancy backgrounds, but something to make the things you should actually be keeping your eye on more pronounced from the environment would've been really helpful. A more stylized approach probably would've went over a lot better.
Revolution Ace's odd graphical quirks don't stop at its overly obnoxious backgrounds though. There's multilevel enemy placement, with certain enemies in the air, and certain ones on the ground. Different buttons will be your ground attack and air attack, so you need to make sure you know what you're aiming at. Which is kind of a ♥♥♥♥♥ when you can't differentiate what is what.
Do you know the difference between a boat and a ship? Now imagine that same boat and ship, the exact same size, with almost no way to differentiate 3D space. That way, if you're fighting over a very plain ocean backdrop, they can still confuse you. Gotta make sure you're frustrated somehow. It's something you get used to, but a graphical oversight nonetheless.
The game's graphical issues reach their height of absolute exasperation in the multiplayer modes, which shrinks everything down for split-screen action. There's just too much happening on screen and not enough room to display it all, especially when the backgrounds make seeing interactable objects as hard as it already does.
I was able to work past the odd graphical design choices, but even then it's not a particularly great shoot-em-up. The slower pace is alright at first, but levels become a complete slog as you progress. The bizarre RPG elements don't quite fit. Upgrading and customizing your ship, I'm down with. Raptor had that, Tyrian had that. But the sluggish leveling and upgrading system in Revolution Ace almost requires you to go back and play older levels purely to grind for experience to unlock more weapon slots.
Enemies can take a surprising amount of bullets for a shoot-em-up, so you're gonna be stuck letting waves of enemies fly right past you because it's impossible to take them down without sitting directly in their line of fire for a few precious seconds. After the early levels, the enjoyment factor drops significantly. There's a substantial hurdle before the game becomes enjoyable again, and even then it requires a ton of grinding in a game that really didn't need this kind of system in the first place.
It's really not a bad game, just a significantly flawed game. It definitely tries its best, but ultimately falls flat and generally feels a little uninspired and dull. The multiplayer mode is a fun little twist, but suffers from the rest of the game's faults and can't really pull the rest of the experience up. Plus it's a game I bought for a nickel on Steam, the servers aren't exactly lit.
I can't help but feel like they really just screwed themselves over with the biggest market that would actually pay for that game, and that's old people. There's too many bright colors and that hurts their eyes, they can't play this. They're gonna drop this faster than folks drop at the retirement center. They're gonna go back to playing cards and staring wistfully out windows at autumn trees shedding their leaves, taking in the subtle symbolic nature of death and renewal. And how much they hate the kids these days.
Our view will pan to the lone leaf fluttering in the breeze, shaking loose and blowing away while they blissfully slip into a sleep they'll never wake from. They're dead. The caretaker will discover them in the morning when they go to sweep the dust off of them, and they will say "Oh well".
That's how I feel about this game. Oh well.

Enjoyed the game, played it to the end - I always like a "two games at once" game.
Despite the words "tower" and "defense" occurring in the description, this is thankfully not a tower defense game. It's primarily a match-three game (Bejewelled etc), with the secondary game being destroying monsters that are advancing towards your grid. Each rune (jewel/fruit/whatever) you destroy by matching shoots out a bolt towards the monsters, so you [sometimes] have to focus on matching runes that are on the same line as the closest monsters.
I was a bit surprised when things falling into a line of 5 does not have the special effect you get when moving things into a line of 5, but I think it's a good design decision, it makes the bonus effects more skill-based.
There's also a 'town' section for buying additional powers and tools, which further adds to the depth of the game. Unfortunately it takes a small leaf from 'social' games in having resources which build up over time in addition to resources you earn. Both kinds are needed, which means if you play the game through to the end in a few sessions you won't have accumulated enough resources to try out even half of the upgrades.
Missed opportunity; a boss battle in which you have to shoot the boss with particular types of runes would have been nice. I'd say wrong runes healing him 1/4 as much as the correct rune does damage, so that shooting wrongly is harmful, and the boss changing 'shield' color to the color you must hit with a second after each hit would have been a nice more-skilled touch. (Instead most of the boss battles were just "match threes as fast as you can, near the boss row, and it'll probably work out".) There was a boss that changed shield color and seemed to deflect shots sometimes, but it wasn't clear what the color meant and just shooting *more* shots protected you against the deflected shots so you didn't really need to figure it out.

I've played the DRM free version A LOT longer than what my "hours played" status above says.
This is a fun 'Match 3' puzzle game with light city building/management elements. You can research spells and items, recruit Citizens that help not only in combat, but improve your resource gathering and research speeds too.
You can recruit Citizens from the town and take them into the Match-3/Defense puzzle. Each Citizen has different abilities. There are 5 types of Offensive/Battle Citizens in total, and each has 2 tiers, making 10 in total, which you unlock by upgrading the Town Hall. For example, a Tier 1 Scout will run out into the field and pick up gold and scrolls that enemies drop when killed, but a Tier 2 Scout will not only run out and collect more frequently, but leave a bomb which explodes in a few seconds, damaging/killing enemies nearby.
You can also craft items that can be used in battle. To craft them you not only need to research them in the Armory, but have the resources too. A Dagger and Sword can be used directly on enemies to damage them to varying degrees. You can drop explosive pills on groups of enemies to kill them  all. You can drop barricades, training dummies, and oil to slow down enemies, and quite a few more.
And finally, you can research spells at the Academy and use them in battle. The effects range from destroying sections of the game board, which launches the elements at the enemies, or perhaps rearranging the board completely. There's quite a few more. You don't need resources to research or 'craft' the spells, they only need money and a bit(a lot) of time to unlock initially. Oh, and the Academy itself needs to be upgraded in order to research the various tiers of spells. So the Academy needs to be level 3 in order to research tier 3 spells. Once researched, you can cast it as many times as you want, with a cooldown of course. By cooldown, I mean '40 Matches' or '80 Matches'. And thats matches as in 'matching gems', not entire games. Matches made when gems are cascading count too.
When you actually go into battle, you're allowed to equip a loadout that can be changed at anytime outside of battle. You can equip 6 Spells, 6 Items, and 2 Citizens. Citizens and Items are depleted when used, so you need to craft/recruit them before running out. Spells aren't depleted, but you need to wait for the cooldown. All items and spells are hotkeyed to 'QWERTY' and '123456' for easy access, the Citizens are hotkeyed to '09'. All hotkeys can be changed.
The 'Conquest Map' is where you choose your battles. On the map there are areas, each with 4 towers initially, and when you beat those, a boss battle tower is shown. Once the boss is defeated, a new area is unlocked.
I really enjoyed this game, and definitely recommend it to anyone who likes Match-3 games and/or puzzle quest.

I'm not too good at writing reviews, but I'll say this:
RWBY: Grimm Eclipse, personally, is a really pleasing dungeon crawler made by Rooster Teeth (who I'm already a fan of). If you're a fan of dungeon crawlers, you'll like it. Enjoy it as you master and explore each playable character, all of which have their own unique combat styles and skill trees. Albeit short, you'll be able to demolish the campaign with your friends, or solo as all 4 (or 8) characters, and still find that it holds a fairly high replay value upon completion. Solo mode has changeable difficulty settings for an additional challenge, and co-op scales with difficulties based on the amount of players that are in the party. Alternatively, you can fight endless waves of enemies with your friends in horde mode!!
The achievements are pretty fun to get, and also aren't super ridiculous in terms of difficulty. That being said, to 100% the game, it does require you to buy $5 DLC package that adds four more unique playable-characters, coined the "JNPR DLC package", which within itself is worth it.
Voice acting is about what you'd expect from Rooster Teeth. Can get pretty awful, but a lot of it is reedemable in it's own way. All of the music is from the RWBY soundtrack in instrumental form. The visuals are pretty good - nothing over the top, but if you're the type that really cares about that kind of thing you won't be dissapointed.
I find the game to be absolutely worth the money. A lot of folks say that it's pretty short, and to that I can agree - you'll blow through the campaign in about 2 hours. That being said however, the game shines in terms of replay value. There are plently of achievements to go for, plenty of tasks to do, different difficulties, different characters to master, etc. Really, they should've included the JNPR DLC package in the base game and raised the price to $25 dollars to give the game more of an appeal, but that being said, yeah, the DLC is totally worth it, too.
All in all, I'd personally recommend it.

I am a big fan of Choice of Games, having enjoyed all of the games from them I've played thus far. Unfortunately, that streak of enjoyment has come to an end with "The Daring Mermaid Expedition". This is the first time I've ever played one of their games and just wished for it to be over. And, wouldn't you know it, my wish came true: it was over incredibly fast. Honestly, it feels more like a demo than a fully fleshed out game. Perhaps even a beta release rather than the finished product.
The premise of the story had me hooked. The thought that I'd be going through a lengthy and in-depth trial to prove the existence of mermaids along with my own skill. Sadly, the game itself was a let down. It's boring and disjointed, the way choices change your stats seems iffy at best. They really don't make much sense, you are given very generic choices that lead to long scenes that really don't seem to relate all that much to the choice you've chosen. There's very little to be done in order to research and the patron system, while intriguing, was not fleshed out. You're pushed into chosing your patron, who also seems to be your one possibility for a romantic partner for that playthrough, minutes after the game begins, without knowing anything but small rumors and hearsay about them.
It feels like a novel that was published with only the prologue included. Perhaps that's because they want to make it a series, but whatever the reason, it doesn't feel like a complete game. I might try playing it through again in the future and at $2 it's not like it's that much to chance on whether you'll like it, but overall I wouldn't recommend one way or the other. However, since I have to choose one way or the other, I suppose I don't recommend it. It's mostly a matter of taste, but in this case, it's a taste I don't enjoy.

While I enjoyed this game's writing and setting, it is extremely short, and I feel that the ending is very anti-climactic. I think this could have been a great game if it hadn't ended so abruptly, but as it stands, I unfortunately can't recommend this one.

Great release from CoG! I've only done one playthrough, but for $2 I already feel like there's a decent amount of material to make replays fun. I wish there was moe emphasis on the different routes in research you take as opposed to romantic and social opitons, but overall a lot of fun. If you like the CYOA genre, definetly a good game to pick up.

It's not the best nor the longest in the series, but at the heart of the game there's more than enough charm and fun to justify buying it. When you factor in the replayability that's inherent in a CYOA title, it's an especially good deal even at full price.
The length is a criticism mostly because it feels as if the game ends just as the plot's moving into gear. Almost as soon as you've started off, you're finishing up.
However, I found the game's core mechanic (patron system) interesting and there were choices that gave me pause- I'd like to see the alternative paths. I'll definitely play it again.

I'll give The Daring Mermaid Expedition a 7/10.
So...
Would I recommend this game to others? Yes, but I would recommend other Choice of Games' stories first!
If you're looking for something with a more complete story arc, and great plot branching...
Try "Choice of Robots" or "A Wise Use of Time". (Both of those are 'Great!' and every choice you make in those stories seem to have consequences, for better or
for worst, no matter how small of a choice it was.)
(The Daring Mermaid Expedition is just 'good', or maybe just 'okay', but the premise has potential. I bet they do another one similar soon or just expand based
on the world building that has already been done for a future title.)
I'll leave you with this thought: The most interesting part of The Daring Mermaid Expedition was a mechanic where you would report your findings via correspondence with your Patron and the Royal German Marinological Society. (This should have been played up more, and used to further more story bits. If a new "explorer guild" type of story game is written again, I would suggest focusing on these beats. It's a perfect wrap up to what just happens, and leaves you expecting fallout (both good or bad) from how you report it. Unfortunately, this never came to full fruition because 1. it didn't happen enough (needs more story), and 2. seemed like it was just used as a litmus test setup for if your patron would like you or not. (And not an ongoing journal of your findings or adventures, which is what it should have been.)
Buy it, Try it, and let me know what you guys think. I'm interested in reading other people's take with this game.
Much Love & Peace!

Far Cry 3 and Blood Dragon are both pies. One is smaller than the other, but tastes so much better.
Blood Dragon IS a late 80's game. Sure it runs on modern tech, but everything feels like an 80's cheese-fest action game. There are a few modern references mixed in with the nostalgia, but it's minimal to say the least.
But even for a guy born in the 90's, it's just fun. You can run faster, jump higher and be far more awesome in this game than in FC3. In this game, you can jump high enough to do an air-assassination from the ground. Ridiculous. Yes, it is exploiting the mechanics to make the game far easier, but who cares, its fun.
That's probably the worst aspect of the game. It's easy. That's the one shortcoming. Even if you turn off all the HUD options and put it on highest difficulty, the mechanics are so easy to exploit that every enemy, even the titular Blood Dragons, are just cannonfodder for you to blow up. There's no challenge. But it is still awfully fun to play, despite that.
If you enjoy humor, nostalgia and a bit of modern FPS action, and don't care too much about difficulty, this is your game.

Exemplifying the garish excess of the times, the action films of the 1980's and early 90's have become nostalgic artifacts from the youth of many of today's gamers. Far Cry 3's stand alone add on Blood Dragon capitalizes on this as an entirely ridiculous, self aware gaming experience that bathes in a pool of 80's action cinema staples. It's not exactly a new idea but since we are laughing at Duke Nukem instead of with him these days, it's safe to say there is room on the market for a game like this. Montages, a synth soundtrack, one liners, vicious weapons and colossal lizards that shoot lasers out of their eyes are central elements of this love letter to all things awesomely bad about 80's action flicks.

Blood Dragon takes the core elements of Far Cry 3 and grafts them into Blood Dragon's scan line littered world. It's landscape is dotted with outposts that look like GI Joe playsets which can be captured from enemy hands. These outposts have varying layouts and terrain that encourage you take take a new approach to each one. In these sequences the Blood Dragon's play their biggest role. These creatures have atrocious eye sight allowing you to sneak past them and can be lured with cyber hearts. Using the tools at your disposal, you can get the dragons to do your dirty work for you; though, if things go wrong they can become a much more formidable obstacle than the cyborgs that you are trying to clear out in the first place. Taking these outposts allows Rex to fast travel to that point and opens predator and hostage rescue missions. Predator missions task your cyborg hero with killing a unique creature or unit with a specific weapon while hostage rescues give you the job a saving a scientist from enemy hands. The wrinkle to these missions is that alerting the enemy to your presence will cause the guards to shot the hostage so some stealth is required to complete these tasks. Completing these mildly repetitive missions as well as collecting the various files, VHS tapes and televisions strewn around the island unlock weapon attachments. Being able to main enemies with a quad barrel shotgun with flaming rounds or a sniper rifle that uses exploding ammunition ensures that these side tasks are worth seeing through. The seven main missions can be completed in just a couple of hours so doing the side missions is highly encouraged.
Blood Dragon suffers from an imperfect upgrade progression. Killing enemies grants you cyber points which acts as experience. With every level he gains, Rex becomes stronger, receiving more health and special abilities. I wholly expected Rex to become a nigh invincible hard♥♥♥♥♥but the point at which he becomes a demi-god comes much too quickly. With a few levels and weapon upgrades Blood Dragon not only becomes unchallenging but most of the finer points of completing the side missions are decimated with a sledgehammer. It becomes unnecessary to rescue hostages stealthily when you can mow through a half dozen guards faster than they can kill a single scientist. Capturing outposts also suffers once it becomes feasible to stand toe to toe with twenty enemies using your mini gun.
With it's skies polluted by unicorn flatulence and flourishes of neon glow, Blood Dragon's aesthetic could be best described as a gay pride parade held in Gary, Indiana. The skies are hazy and red, the waters murky and black and colorful ruins dot the island. The terrain isn't as intricate as Far Cry 3 but there are enough landmarks and areas of interest to make it interesting to explore. Creatures with unusual color pallets and glowing eyes roam the island ready to pick Rex apart if provoked. Blood Dragon emphasizes artistic style rather than the technical prowess of the engine. The soundtrack, courtesy of Power Glove, is absolutely incredible and may be the single element that most sells Blood Dragon as a throwback to 80's action films.

I wish I could say in between for this game but unfortunately i can't. I have more negative issues with this game than positive anyway. For starters, it was assumed by everyone that this game was intended to be at least similar to SSB (Super Smash Bros.), and it fails to do just that. Sure, the concepts there and all, but what about competition? There's litteraly none. This game encourages button mashing, all things considered. Per suggestion: how about some DI? (Directional Influence), i mean it would help considering that the stamina system in this game is shorter than that of smash's. A shield. This is by far the most basic staple of a party fighting game genre. How about some diversity in the character moveset? this is what probably put me off the most. Every character's melee is quite literally, the same. I didn't feel any difference in playing Ada, than i did with any other character i could care to mention.
I take it back, the gadget/weapon system made me cringe beyond repair. Players literally must depend on these to do the majority of their damage, which is sad. Granted this was the one piece of data that differentiated characters from one another, except not really because there are characters that have the same item sets. Worst of all is ranked gaming. When playing against somebody, the fight starts out enjoyable, we trade blows and what not, but then come mid game and we each had a stock gone, the enemy resorted to what i like to call: cowardice. Where they prioritized throwing their current gadget away, and taking the next one until there were none left, leaving me with nothing to do without taking damage in the process. Honestly just get rid of the gadget system and have the characters come equipped with the said gadgets, it'd fix the game by a significant amount...
...Rambling and salty complaints aside, this game is visually beautiful. I never seen such a clear resolution in a fighting game on steam and it was a fun experience playing the game....against bots. I've been a gamer for my whole life. And I've played countless fighting genres. And each usually contained some form of fair, sportsmanlike competitive fighting format. This game has none. And it's resulted in the spawn of a toxic community that doesn't appreciate the game at all.
On a side note, if you could add an unranked 1v1 bracket too, that'd also be pretty cool.

It's a great "light" RTS. By light I don't mean difficulty, there's plenty of that to go around, I mean that all the base building and tech aspects have been reduced to a minimum.
Pros:
+ Simple yet hard to master RTS game.
+ Provides both a generic campaign and procedurally generated missions.
+ Completely asymmetrical gameplay, handle a squad of highly customizable marines against hordes of evolving aliens.
+ Settings menu with video options, rebindable keys and volume sliders.
+ Weekly challenges, lot of content in general.
Cons:
+ The campaign itself and its plot are very barebone.
+ While it wasn't a problem for me, I guess that the unlockable upgrades for your squad and bases aren't explained/introduced well enough and that could lead some players to lock themselves into using subpar strategies instead of experimenting with the new toys (at least that's what I gathered from many negative reviews).
+ Too expensive at full price.
All in all, it's a great coffee break RTS. It certainly won't steal starcraft's crown, but it provides a nice change of pace. I'm not sure I would pay full price for it, but at a discount or in a bundle, it's a must have for any RTS fan.

Very rarely am I as excited to talk about a game as this one - admittedly I did the standard impulse purchase of this very cheap game quite a few months ago during the Christmas sale and never looked at it again. I guess the art style of the thumbnail alone was enough to sway me, and when I returned to actually play it almost six months later, I was swayed yet again.
To begin with, let’s talk about the art style - it’s simplistic yet very nuanced, nicely rounded and soft. Lighting effects are used extremely carefully to create strong dramatic effects and during my playthrough (visible right here on YouTube) I noted that the entire game looked almost like a watercolour or ink painting, with strong blues and greens. Very much a fairytale-style piece.
Our basic premise is that we have two brothers whose mother died some time ago by drowning, as we can infer from the opening cutscene. This instils a pretty understandable fear of water in the younger brother which becomes important through the story. The older brother is stalwart and strong, as well as quite serious, in contrast to the more lively and mischievous personality of his younger sibling.
I should perhaps mention early on the rather unique control system implemented by developers Starbreeze Studios here - each thumbstick of your gamepad moves one of the brothers, with the corresponding trigger activating interaction with their immediate environment. You might be required to move a long object through a tight space or activate switches to allow each individual brother to pass an area - it’s masterfully done and I have no doubt that by the end of the game you will appreciate the level of understanding the developers had over this mechanic.
The game is split into very distinct areas, with an enormous range of atmospheres and designs explored over relatively small areas. While in other games this would arguably be undesirable, as in a roleplaying experience for example you want as much fleshing out for you as possible, you are left to infer what you can about the area around you from observation, in a manner similar to something like Dark Souls. Interactions between the brothers and certain environmental features can also give clues as to their feelings and explain more about just what is going on in each area.
And believe me when I say that this game does not pull punches. What begins as a bright and colourful fairytale type story does progress into something much more unforgiving and stark. The world out there is unkind, and you will certainly come to believe it. In the familiarity of the woods and fields around your home everything is safe and the only dangers lie in angry dogs. Progress into wolf-inhabitated forests and harsh tundra however and you will encounter very real threats that could mean the end of the brothers.
I’m almost ashamed of myself for having not bothered with this for so long - sale or not, you need to buy this and you need to play it today. It’s extremely short, taking me only about two and a half hours, but I’d have gladly paid twice what I did for it. In terms of originality and a narrative experience, you certainly won’t find much to compete with it, on Steam or anywhere else. Easily a 10/10 title in my book, and I hope Starbreeze does something similar in the future.

So. What is Infested Planet? Well, it's a tower defense... point capture... RTS... Nonono! Squad based colonization sim... That's not quite right either... Look it fills quite a few categories.
Lets get something out of the way quickly, I got this in a humble bundle for 0.89 Euro, tuppence, feck all, so would I recommend this at retail price, no. Not in hell would I, but for the price I paid it was a damn good game. This is excluding it's DLC which I do not have and probably will not get.
The story, well it's simple, humans want to live on this lovely planet, but the local wildlife doesn't really want that, purge the world and see what lies under the surface. That's your job as the mercenaries the army brought in, why would they get their boots dirty when you can do it for them. Needless to say you get stuck on the front lines pretty early on, nice way of hiding your difficulty curve there lads. Past that the story isn't that deep, characters are fairly one dimensional, stubborn general, Han solo, and science woman. Oh and the beasty of the deep of course. Honestly they're all pretty forgettable, though if you came to this game for the story you were mistaken my friend. No love triangles here, no remarkable one liners, nothin'. Flat dialogue from flat characters. It gets the job done.
Graphics are nice enough, simplistic but they certainly do the job. You won't be wanting for more when all hell ♥♥♥♥♥ the fan anyways. Handy dandy colour coded armor helps you pick out your troops and different enemy types. The fire animation is pretty enough and he explosions are... Well... Explosions. Nothing industry changing, nothing special, but it does the job.
Sound design is... There. Not much to say on that front, guns sound like guns, turrets like turrets, and so on. Not much music, and if there was I quickly forgot about it as I turned up my own battle music in the background. Something I highly recommend and the constant gunfire can get a little repetitive after some time.
It's a short game which is alright for the price I paid but past that it's honestly not worth it. I completed the game maybe fifteen hours in with ease, and got all the achievements soon thereafter. The additional missions you get throughout the game are entirely filler. They pad the games run time with maybe a paragraph of text to link it into the game world. The main reason to even do them is for cold hard cash, which I'll get to soon.
So, let's get into some more meat. As you progress you unlock new upgrades for your squad and buildings. So the game says "5 elite soldiers against an alien horde of 100,000", but you just start the missions with five people. Side point but I think there was one or two times I got over one hundred thousand alien kills in game.
You start a game with one base with five guys and you are tasked with taking all the enemy bases. You start off with some number of points you can spend on upgrading your troops, putting down defensive towers, or building auxiliary buildings with widespread effects. The defensive towers I've found to be worthless in the face of upgrading your troops (or just getting more guys). Most of the buildings are alright but all you'll really need it the air strike, munitions dump, healing station, and building upgrader. The rest are just not worth their cost. The troops upgrades are as followes, flamer, sniper, officer, and heavy, there are others but they just aren't good.
So, you got your guys, got your upgrades and are ready to rampage, and well then it's just telling your guys to go to the closest enemy nest and calling in airstrikes, rinse, repeat and there you have your game. Not much more too it then that, so if you think that'd be fun go ahead. Hmmmm... This ending sounds like it should be a negative review but hey, I had enough fun to justify the 0.89 Euro price tag to give it a thumbs up.

I'll just point out some of the more persistent issues raised over and over.
1. Unpredictable fps drops make this game a stuttering crapfest. servers will crash from time to time resulting in a loss of credits, xp, and the match.
2. Credit and warfunds system clash with equipment and vehicle balancing. Tanks are the weakest class in-game yet among the most expensive to deploy with credits or warfunds.
3. Match queue takes forever. Occasionally you have to wait in excess of 30 minutes to find a match, even in gold matchmaking.
3. Air is too overpowered, and for all the wrong reasons. Planes get the highest ratio of credits to kills/destruction with virtually no opposition or counter. A mediocre pilot flying a piece of junk can sweep up over 1000 points from a handful of kills and a few bombed jeeps. This leads into the next point...
4. Game lacks any credible AA threat vs planes. AA emplacements are present but nearly all badly placed, blocked by trees or buildings. AA is largely ineffective taking down anything past a Tier 1 plane anyway. Its too weak, too slow, and are usually destroyed by a head on plane attack. Any and all damage taken charging AA is magically repaired to 100% with a wrench, therefore rendering AA emplacements null and void.
5. Tanks are hard countered by just about everything. Even infantry can kill it in 2 hits with H3 explosives. Its a sad sight for a tank fleeing from a dude on a bicycle. Even the heaviest of tanks get vaporized into atoms by a few H3 or sticky bombs.
6. Game punishes people who get griefed rather than the griefers. No, I didnt type it wrong, its exactly as its written. People are penalized in some way or another for getting teamkilled on bikes, planes, tanks, mines, everything. People also get punished credit-wise by griefers detonating or running into their mines on purpose.
7. Game punishes generals for griefers trashing all of their resources in war mode. Its why few airplanes and tanks are ever fielded, among other reasons.
8. Typical game is a lagfest. Half the time you're getting shot around corners, bombed through walls, or shot through hills and trees. worse cases you actually see people and vehicles teleporting along. Lot of players who get reported for hacks are just laggers. some even try to lag deliberately to gain an advantage.
9. No matchmaking system whatsoever. Everyone from every rank is projectile vomited into a mish-mash of horrendously balanced teams. 4 light tanks versus 4 infantry, 3 tanks, and 3 heavy fighters. 8 infantry vs 15. Oh, and my favorite, zero people vs a full roster.
10. Almost non-existent spawn protection system. Spawn points are fixed, predictable areas. They are also badly placed. Planes farm these areas constantly, and tanks camp them from vantage points, sometimes across the map. Reminicent of the spawncamping from Bf1942.
11. Bugs all over the place. This game's a declared a release, but it plays like its still in beta. Here's a few of the more glaring bugs still around:
*Sound issues- Used to be really bad, but you still get mowed down by silenced mg42s and snipers. On some maps, you can hear mysterious explosions going off underground or random, unexplained vehicle crashing sounds nearby. Other sound issues include crappy gun sounds. PPS-43 is someone hitting bongos. PPD-40 sounds like chitty chitty bang bang. Mosin Nagant rifle is just a pitiful muffled pipe hitting the floor somewhere.
*Map issues- Vehicles get stuck on everything. Some maps have more boulders than the moon and random ditches that can easily ensnare tanks forcing you to ditch them.
*Collision issues- A tank hits a haystack hard enough, it can explode. A motorcycle going 100mph hits a chain-link fence, it explodes. Drive a pickup into sandbags or barbed wire, it explodes. You accidentally hit a picket fence going downhill on a bicycle...it can explode.
*Vehicle issues- Cars and motorbikes drive around as if the entire map (including roads) were a big sheet of ice covered in an oil slick. Even driving the same speed as someone runs is enough to cause a violent spin out. Now imagine combining this cartoon vehicle physics with previous nonesense related to collisions and map objects...
*Map glitches- This one isn't very common but its annoying enough to make it on the list. Some maps have areas that let you glitch through underground or on top of inaccessible areas. People can shoot you through the ground or through glitched buildings this way. They can get pretty gamebreaking.

I should have written something about this game a long time ago, but now that I beat the main game again(and also the dlc), I think I can give it a fair review.Trine 2 is quite possibly 1 of my personal favorite indie games. The main reason for this is that Trine has a full 3 player co-op campaign. Playing this game with friends is simply a blast. If you have any friends that wanna play it with you, I recommend that you do so. But hey, even if you don't have friends, you can always kidnap someone. The police will most likely be knocking on my door because I said that but oh well.
When playing this game, you can choose from 3 different types of characters, and each of them has their own unique abilities. The gameplay itself is separated into 3 parts. Platforming, puzzles, and combat, sometimes all of these at the same time. The makers have done a great job with the puzzles I can tell you that. They start of simple, and get more complex later on, but that best part is that you can complete them in many random ways. There is always a "right" way to do them, but in most cases, you can get through them in many random ways, which is something I really like. The game let's you be really creative, which many puzzles games don't do. The platforming is also quite nice, there is not much else to say about that. The weakest link here is the combat. You can be a bit creative with the way you fight, but mostly it turns into a pretty random mess.
Visually, this game looks absolutely gorgeous. It still might be 1 of the best looking indie games out there. The levels are also very varied, and the overall level desing is really good. There is also that goblin menace dlc that you get with the Complete story edition of this game. That does add few more hours into the game, so for new players it will propably take 8-10 hours to finish the entire thing. But what about the story you may ask. Well that does not really deserve a special mention. It's alright, but nothing more than that. Same can be said about the voice acting. I would not say that they are bad, but there is room for a lot of improvement.
My final verdict is this. If you like fun and good games you should totally give this game a shot. It's a bundle of fun and it only gets better with friends  And if you don't like good games then...I dunno...play something else I guess

The game has two aspect.  The city council politics play and city builder.  The city council part is shallow and incomplete.  The city builder part, however, does offer a lot of depth and novel ideas.  The negative reviews calling otherwise probably does not understand the game.  It is hardly their fault though.  This game is so poorly designed on representing mechanism information to player.  The shallow tutorial barely explains the UI and interface.  And even if you bother to read the game manual, it still fail to uncover mist on some of the most important mechanisms like how social mobility works.  The catastrophic failure of presenting mechanism information to player effectively made it more of a puzzle game rather than a sim game.
Rants aside, the game does have some novel design such as people's needs can be served by private sector or public sector.  And you can choose to collect a lot of tax and serve people directly, or use policy to guide the private sector to do that.  The two path apparently repesents two different modern political ideaology and was supposed to interfere with the city council politics system.  However, the mechanism behind this is more complicated than it sounds and, again, is barely explained, reaping all the potential fun off it.
In conclusion it is very hard to have fun with this game even if you are a veteran of city builder game and is willing to read the manual word by word.  But do take a look at the game manual to see if you think it is worth a try.  There is a lot in this game, it is just so hard to dig them out.

The game attempts to combine city building and politics and fails in both aspects. Both of these features lack proper depth and lack replayability after the first game due to their repetitive nature. The city building lacks proper customisability and when the city gets too large, the game crawls to a very low FPS.
The council is poorly implemented, parties will become defunct in the next era no matter how popular they are within the city. The only real interaction with the council is threatening or spying on them to pass a law.
The game can be summed up in three features: Place a district, change taxes and pass a very linear set of laws every game. The game has a good concept, but a very bad execution.

I want to really like this game; I expected a more indepth and political Tropico 3/4/5. Tropico's politics were tight but felt natural; if you worked at it you could make any voting block your reliable supporters and grow their numbers which also tended to anger their counterparts. Winning elections and not infuriating people into becoming rebels was a seemless part of the challenge of making a profitable island.
Urban Empire, despite being all about the politics fails to keep things are clear or as simple to grasp as that. In fact I feel that a political party's feeling about anything at any given time is up to luck. There is no way to identify a solid political party that will have your back and who will actually support your re-election seems random.
And let's face the elephant in the room, this game is heavily biased in the Liberal-Socialist wing side of politics since the State Laws are almost exclusively Liberal or Socialist in nature and are clearly railroaded to happen sooner rather than later. Let me return to Tropico; yeah it made sense that Tropico was more on the Socialist end being a banana republic under good old El Pres' but the Capitalists Faction would constantly tempt you to open up and if you didn't they would clearly and angrily oppose you.
I feel none of that from opposition parties in Urban Empire; once the Edict or Law passes it is untouchable and no one seems to care anymore. No one cares about anything! I feel no passion in anything! It's a dull boring march to becoming a Unionized Heavily Taxed Welfare State and no one in the actual city seems to care! There is no protest or fanfair, no one rallies around a party to counter my changes or gets angry when a bill is voted down! I know politics is dull and thankless but I struggle to believe there are living human beings in my city and not just buses!
Sadly, I knew this game would be a letdown. I had expected the lackluster city management but I always hoped the Politics would be interesting. It is just not.

20 hours and multiple victories in.
Urban Empires is an okay game. It seriously lacks depth once you bite into it and the developers didn't really put much attention into making sure that multiple play styles are competitive. At the end of the day the "best" move is to just go fully socialist liberal since almost all related edicts are totally positive anyway. I'm willing to bet that the overwhelmiongly positive effects that liberal and leftists edicts give is at least partially based on the developers own political opinions. There should be multiple feasible paths to victory even if you don't agree politically. Such a shame really.
Gay rights? Yes. Feminism? Of course! The bonuses are too good to pass. Same for child labor, women's rights, LGBT rights, etc. Rinse and repeat. I get that many of us support these things in real life but in a game each choice needs to have benefits and flaws. The game rewards progressive ideas by removing all flaws.
Furthermore the political parties are nothing more than a simple resource system. They have no agency or personality of their own. The other "players" in the game lack any sense of reason behind their choices. They don't have any clearly seen agenda and this hurts the game immenseley. Yes liberals are more likely to vote for more taxes and conservatives are more likely to oppose them but that's as far as the depth goes.
My last point focuses on events and the world at large. As you play, diffferent events come to pass on the world stage but ultimatley it doesn't matter what you do or how you react. It always plays out the same way with no real consequences for choices or outcomes of events. It doesn't matter if you support independence or not because at the end of the day it all disappears without explanation when you move to the next era. I didn't even realize we got independence until I saw some random screen with a reference. It didn't even matter. This happens with every event tied to the larger world.
TLDR: The developers hit on a great concept and if the game was 10 bucks I'd say they nailed it as far as liberal progressive SJW style games go. At 40.00 dollars we deserve far more depth and far more meaningful choices/options. Leave your politics at home and just focus on making a good game please devs.

I have mixed feelings about this game.  For the most part, it's everything I love in character action games.  It's got stylish, over the top action, ridiculous combos, and satisfying gameplay.  When it works.  So what doesn't work?  Let's talk about cameras and dodging.
For whatever reason, you can only dodge left and right while locked on.  Never in a forward or backward direction, as this will just result in a jump.  So then, you think to yourself "well, just dodge to the side."  Well, this is where the camera comes in to play.
Because of the game's fixed cameras, one moment you'll dodge in the correct and intended direction, the next moment, the camera will switch to a different angle, causing your next dodge to the side suddenly translate into a jump forward.  A jump forward that's right into the enemy's overhead smash.  And they've been winding that attack up for some time so you know it's gonna hurt.
For a game that encourages long streaks of combos without getting hit, it gets pretty frustrating having to fight the camera on top of the enemies themselves.  Couple this with a score at the end of each level that's tied to your combo counter, it felt like I was actively being both punished and handicapped by the game as I was not able to buy new abilities for my aresenal since I could never get my combo counter up too high until the eventual "oops, you jumped instead of dodged" moment that can happens way too often.
Is the game do-able despite this?   Totally, but I personally can't bring myself to finish it because of this issue.  If you can, more power to you.  If not, maybe look elsewhere.

Ultimately, this game deserves a thumbs up. The character generation, the incredible visuals and demon design, and better story than your average game all come together to make an entertaining package. It's pretty much classic, JRPG-style over the top story, fighting, weapons and fun!
But it does have a few flaws. And I noticed them a bit too much for my liking. Oh, it's still worth a thumbs up, just beware the little things that annoy. It suffers from the classic problem of third person games with beautiful cinematics that choose to cut camera angles all the time as you run - you OFTEN find yourself running in one direction, only to change camera angle and turn back again. You can accept this when wandering around, but in a fight it's really frustrating.
The other issue is the lack of real clues of what to do next. The best way to describe it is like this - a relatively 'on rails' adventure experience, but within the space you are adventuring in, they still leave everything open for you to wander around in. This is not good. Why? You complete a sub-component on that level, and then spend genuine frustrating time wandering around places you've been to already more than once, just to see if it triggers a new cut scene and progresses the story further now that you may have some new thing you picked up. The map is useless as it only shows exits and where you came from. No goals. No hints. If it was truly open world you'd have clues, trails, compass markers, a log book - just... something...
For example - Elder Scrolls series is open world. It has LOTS to distract and do, AND a compass, AND a log. This has no compass, no log, and NOTHING to do in rooms once cleared. So it's of no help to anyone to wander aimlessly in empty rooms over and over until you go to the right one you've been to before...
It's kind of a hybrid, and it will frustrate. Guaranteed.
But with that out of the way, it's a good game for three reasons. First, game play, visuals etc are all really polished. Big, over the top moves, lots of flashy stuff, and a decent difficulty curve, if nto perfect. Second, it just may have THE BEST monster design ever. I mean, seriously. Those demons!!!!! Just so damn well done. Third, the story is good. It's actually entertaining, rather than just a throw-away thing to pretend you are more than just a mindless beat-em-up.
It's good, but you'll have some moments of frustration.
Oh, and get yourself a controller. You will find it a lot better if you do!

I'm really enjoying this game -- managing relationships with political parties, begging/forcing what I know to be best for the city, trying to not burn so many bridges that I can no longer be re-elected...all while pushing for equal rights for all citizens, advancing technologies, etc.
I also enjoy the deep-dive you can do on stats.  At one point in the year 1914, I discovered that my town of ~3000 people had a whopping 22 movie theaters, and the number one employer of middle class citizens?  Movie production companies.  I'm a burgeoning Hollywood!
The biggest minus is that the game frequently freezes on my laptop, AND THERE IS NO AUTOSAVE ABILITY.  I have to remember to manually save every year or so.
Also, a lot of things are unexplained in the game...even in the tutorial...but I liked trying to learn as I went along.
I will say I was disappointed to see that things like electricity and plumbing didn't really change the look of my city.  In fact, the technological advances don't seem to actually advance technology at all.  People in my city were driving cars before we discovered the combustible engine which unlocks the automobile.  My entire city was on the telephone grid before we had electricity.  Perhaps most egregious, my character had to win re-election before citizens actually had the right to vote.
But all in all, this is a new kind of game and I'm fully on board with where it's going.  8/10.

I just got done playing this for like the last hour or so. I'm having a lot of fun with this game and it goes beyond just enjoying a match 3. In a normal match 3 you're focused on the board so you can discover opportunities for 4s and 5s or better, but there is a lot more to this game. You've got monsters creeping up to your base so you've got to make the matches that line up with them to destroy them and they might even drop some loot. Of course, you have to click on it to get it. Do you have time? What about that special gem you just scored on the board? Click it? The monsters are wailing away at your wall so you better decide fast! It's a lot to take in all at once.
That's just the battles. In between, you need to rule your kingdom with policies and deeds, improve the city buildings, train citizens, and much more. The improvements to the city result in the ability to earn even better weapons and spells for the battlefield. What more could you ask for? Troops? Got it! Now, you can deploy troops on your wall and I must say they are smashing (people who have played will get it). When do you deploy those troops? Do you take archers? Healers? Scouts? What about your equipment? Dummies? Swords? Exploding capsules? There are tons of combinations to let you deal with the battlefield and a great "RPG Interface" for improving them. The city is an absolutely awesome addition to this and really makes it a lot of fun.
Just when you think aww, man is this thing just gonna be a match 3 grin--WTF is that?! An enormous boss stomps onto the screen and the fight is on. This is no easy task and it gets harder as you progress to many different and interesting bosses. Luckily, the art is totally charming so the journey is enjoyable and it is really livened up with a solid soundtrack that sets the mood. The writing is fun and the game seems very appropriate for kids and adults alike.

I've been playing match three games since I was a kid, although we didn't have video games back then, so it was mostly matching small stones and goat knuckles.  The point is, I've seen it all.  Aside from the things I have not seen, of course.  So what does ReignMaker bring to the table, that makes it good, or even gooder?  Well.
There is the match three, of course, which is a very clear cut genre, but yoiu see, it is also a tower defense, as your matched blocks create magical bolts that fire upon the waves of attacking, um, evil things.  You can also learn spells that bolster your ability to blast molten death upon the deserving heads of the aforementioned evil things.
In between bouts of match three tower defense, you can return to your village, where you as mayor, or whatever, get to improve buildings, hire workers, research items and spells, and even respond to situations by creating government policies, which can sometimes give bonus items, or cause new items to appear in your town.
Overall, I find enough variety in ReignMaker to keep things fresh, and the only complaint I have is that lumber production is so slow it can actually slow your progress, as lumber is needed for anything you want to build.  That is fairly minor though, and the developers are actually responding to people on the forums, which is pretty amazing in this day and age where so many games are in early access, or simply released and abandoned, or abandoned in early access.
Anyway, good game, check it out.  Or not.  Up to you really, I have no stake in it :P

In the future, humanity uses AI driven machines to wage war, but this backfires when the machines turn on their masters. To combat this threat, your elite pilot takes to the sky in an old jet to retaliate. The machines are dominating the land, sea and air so your battle will not be easy.
At first I thought that Revolution Ace didn’t even bother with a story as the explanation for why you are piloting an old jet against futuristic foes is only revealed a few levels into the game. It doesn’t matter though, as no excuse is needed to engage in some old school, horizontal shooting action. Despite the Unreal Engine powered visuals, Revolution Ace looks like it was ripped straight out of a nineties arcade machine. It is clear that time has been spent on making the ground look interesting with effects like trees swaying in the wind and mountains that rise up into the screen but the overall effect is a bit underwhelming. It could just be my personal preferences, but the realistic style visuals just look a tad too drab for an over the top style game like Revolution Ace.
I can’t fault the diversity though, as the game takes you across jungles, mountains and oceans, with some levels shrouded in mist or covered in snow. There are definitely moments where the game does look good and there is certainly no lack of enemies to shoot at, but there is nothing that really sets the visuals apart from the pack.
Revolution Ace is a pretty straightforward shooter, but there are a couple of unique things that make it worth a second look. Firstly, enemies attack from both the air and ground and you use two separate fire buttons to engage them. Weaving through bullets while shooting on the correct plane can be tricky at first, but it soon becomes second nature. Completing levels reward you with experience points and shrapnel. Experience points are tallied up to increase the level of your jet, which leads to rewards such as more weapon slots, new weapons and a perk of your choice. The perks range from better armor to faster bullets or strong laser and there are not enough levels to choose all of them so you have to pick carefully. The shrapnel is your currency and is used to purchase the machine guns, missiles and beam cannons as well as shields and special attacks that make your craft so formidable. There are more than 20 weapons to choose from and the placement on your jet matters which makes it fun to mix and match to see what the results are.
The campaign mode felt a bit longer than what you usually find in the genre and upon completion you can start a tougher, New+ playthrough. There are also three difficulty settings to give everyone a fair chance at beating the game. Enemies attack in droves and on Normal or higher, the ones that you miss comes back for another go, but the fact that you have a shield and armor meter makes things considerably easier. Shooters with one hit kills can be frustrating, so Revolution Ace is a nice introduction to the genre that won’t scare away newcomers.
If you tire of the campaign mode or feel like you need some extra experience and shrapnel you can try out the Skirmish mode. In Skirmish you get to pick a level from any of the ones that you have already unlocked to practice or farm experience and shrapnel. Much more fun is the Versus mode where you play side by side with another player and can mess up their game by sending enemies to their side of the screen. The Battle Chains mode works the same as Versus but instead of playing against someone in real-time you challenge their recordings. If you complete the challenge you can send it back to the original player who then have to contend with all the added mayhem that you caused during your playthrough. The challenge ramps up quickly and this mode can become quite addictive, but finding other players is not that easy at the moment.
I had a lot of fun with Revolution Ace but this may be due to me playing shooters since the early days of the arcades. Newer players might be less forgiving about the bland visuals and rather generic audio. The controls however, are responsive and the game certainly packs a challenge, but apart from the versus modes it doesn’t really stand out from the pack. I really liked the concept so hopefully LGG can create a sequel, which really ramps up the production values.

With such fond memories of the first game, I honestly feel as though no sequel yet has matched it, problems;
The music, Alex Brandon did an amazing job on the soundtrack of the original which really added to the depth and immersion, since then the music has become dull, repetitive and very lacklustre.
Linearity, now. The first game was linear, there were a few sidequests, but you knew what the game was about, and why you were doing what you were doing. There is no sense of urgency when you can stop saving the world for a minute to save a damsel in distress.
Lack of locations, it took me a minute in Prague to realise that there are only 2 parts, not 4... I just completed the game, and it's only in the last minute it feels like Deus Ex.
Progression, remember that first robot at the statue of liberty, remember so many more at versalife, and how they were difficult to overcome... Hell, remember actually travelling to different places achieving things, seeking alternative routes to not raise alarms, or literally just bashing the same part of the game over and over to not die. Remember slowly unraveling a story, choosing allegiances, even Human Revolution had bosses, I spent the whole game gearing up for what?
I'm annoyed at myself for spamming everything right from the very start, I had raided the bank before the bank mission, why was I allowed to, almost every aspect of the story I'd already completed before it became relevant...
Where is the futurism, where are the riots, where is the action, why so many short stories and no real big one?
The game is VERY SHORT, I know the series is about exploration, reading about the story etc, but the actual gameplay was just samey and boring, i feel as though if I rush played it I could get it complete in an evening and still get a good nights sleep.

Torchlight II is a really good game, but not a great game. It has an endearing art-style that's easy on the eyes, and the gameplay is addictive enough to keep you playing 'till the end (I played about 50 hours by the time I beat it). However, there is nothing about this game that is exceptional or raises the bar. The story isn't deep or engaging, and the world lacks depth. Had the developers expanded the towns and added sub characters to strengthen the plot, then this game could have been a bench mark. The loot drops are well-balanced and look decent, the world is visually appealing, even interesting in some places, and the monsters are well-designed. But beyond the relentless grind, there's nothing much motivating you to keep collecting and throwing away loot 'till the next boss fight, except more loot and boss fights, that is. If you're just looking for a game to help you pass the time without being bored, then it does its job well, but don't expect an engaging story to justify the 50+ hours you may waste playing it. In the end, I feel like I got my money's worth, but only based on what I already kind of expected.
