The main "gimmick" of the game is the fact that you control the titular two brothers at once, using one analog control stick and one "action" button for each.
This mechanic, alien at first, quickly becomes second nature, letting you fully enjoy your travels through beautiful scenery following the brothers on a quest to find a cure for their dying father.
Talking about storytelling, that's another way Brothers sets itself apart from most other games, as the simple, fable-like story is told using gameplay and rare in-engine cutscenes.
You find out the personality and quirks of each brother by the way they interact with each other and with the people and creatures they encounter during the journey. You understand the power of their brotherly bond by the way they help each other out solving puzzles or getting out of difficult situations. All of this without ever having to read or hear a single word.
I would 100% recommend Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons if it wasn't already clear enough, as the way the game marries its storytelling to its mechanics is truly fascinating and definitely worth the 2 to 4 hours needed to complete it.

I don't speak Swedish, but without understanding a word, Brothers left me with lingering emotions long after I completed the game. Brothers is mechanically simple - the puzzles aren't very difficult and there aren't any complex gimmicks. The story is straightforward and progresses at an easy pace. The primary reason for playing this game is the story anyway. It's more than just the plot, I think, that made the largest impact on me and made it stick. The little details peppered throughout the levels tell stories on their own (i.e. complete the achievements!). The landscapes are utterly gorgeous (reminds me of The Lord of the Rings, actually), and vivid as well.
It's a game worth playing but don't expect to just casually burn through it like any other - this is one to savor for the details and the storytelling. Highly recommended.

You have five units under your control. You start at a base, and your goal is (usually) to destroy the alien bases, which spew out hundreds of enemies. You can build turrets, etc, which in some ways makes this like a cross between RTS and a tower defence game.
It's frantic, and quite engaging. It won't take long to finish the campaign, but the skirmish games will keep you coming back for more. Each individual mission doesn't take too long to complete.
Progression involves earning money for each mission which allows you to unlock turrets, boosts and reserve troops.
In-game you collect scrap, which you can trade to get shotguns for your troops, or make one of your troops an officer, and so forth. These reset each mission. Scrap can also be used to build turrets, mine-fields, medi-pods, etc.
Aliens will zerg you constantly, you'll have to juggle your turrets vs your troop advancement, and it will annoy the hell out of you when some of your own bases get taken, forcing you to regroup and start again.
Graphically it's nothing special. It has an old-school sprite feel about it. Audio is ho-hum. Where this game excels is with the full-on frenetic action.
I'll admit that I've had to take this game in small doses. It's a bit frustrating otherwise... but I'm definitely recommending it if the above sounds like fun.

This was one of those games I put off getting for the longest time because I didn't really like how it looked in the screenshots, and real-time strategy stuff only appealed to me in Starcraft and Red Alert games, so I figured I wouldn't like it. For me, Infested Planet essentially felt like Starcraft's combat and troop movement without base building, and I was okay with that. The game even has a story mode, and although it wasn't the kind of plot that was amazing, just
a storyline and putting effort into even having an ending that gave more information than most games' endings tend to give really delighted me.
There are quite a few levels to play through, and a selection screen shows where the missions branch from the main story line off to bonus/optional levels that are not story-based. These bonus levels are great for raising the cash needed to purchase persistent upgrades, which are something I tend to love in games. I was unable to complete 3 of the levels (got stuck when I got to levels with "Abyss" in the title), and while I normally take issue with being unable to progress, these tougher missions were optional with no story or one-of-a-kind in-game reward that I was locked out of. I'm fine with that.
The main game itself had some challenging moments, even on normal difficulty for me, and I managed to complete it. An easier setting is available, which I appreciate, since not everyone is as skilled at games or necessarily this genre of games. The developer clearly had intentions of making the game enjoyable for a broader scope of players than some developers care to cater to. Although I testify on the matter since I did not try a higher difficulty than normal, I will say that I imagine the highest difficulty would be pretty monstrous on certain levels, and would give players who want a challenge exactly what they are after.
Infested Planet's learning curve also deserves some praise. If all of the buildings/squad classes/abilities, etc. that you can use in a mission were available from the start, it would be pretty overwhelming to new players, and some might not get to try out many of the things you can build/use to strengthen your troops on the battlefield. Instead, the game grays out certain skills and gives you a few opportunities to use upgrades the game recently told you to use, so that you get accustomed to knowing when it might be best to use that upgrade. In the next mission, more upgrades are unlocked for you to try out, and so on and so forth, without it feeling too much like a tutorial past the first handful of brief levels.
These battles play out in a tug-of-war fashion, which reminded me of Defense of the Ancients. Aliens will frequently come at you in droves, and you must kill them before they can take out your bunkers and develop additional hives which will spawn more aliens. Pushing forward is necessary, but if you don't put down a turret or leave a troop behind, your bunker(s) will likely get overrun in your squad's absence. On most maps, taking out and capturing the land under all the hives results in victory.
The sound effects worked well, and I'll be honest: I cannot recall a single song from the game. It definitely had music and it wasn't grating or unenjoyable in any way.
Graphically, I initially didn't like Infested Planet's look, but upon playing it, I thought it looked just fine. It's fairly simple in appearance, but clearly a ton of work went into this game. By having a basic graphical appearance, a wider variety of lower end PC's are capable of running the game well, and tens of thousands of aliens can be killed (literally that many per mission, sometimes) on-screen in rapid succession, while showing the player when zoomed out everything relevant going on in the mission in various areas.
The last thing I would like to discuss about Infested Planet is one of my favorite features: FULLY refundable upgrade points. In many games, upgrading something is permanent, or you can buy an upgrade, but only get a partial refund when you refund it. In Infested Planet, you get 100% of what you spent back. Heck, if an upgrade structure I build gets razed by an enemy army, the game refunds me for that. Refunding is quick and easy, and encourages the player to try more tactics he or she might otherwise not try when a loss in points/funds is in the way. There are reasons to do partial refunds, sure, but I really enjoyed how Infested Planet handled this.
I do recommend Infested Planet and had quite a nice time with it. I hear there's a Planetary Campaign DLC for it, but I don't know if it has a storyline/characters like the main game did, and I don't know much about the mission/territory map or if I would enjoy that. I might check it out on a sale someday in a few months/years and remark on it then.

Great little real-time squad management games. Instead of hammering away at each other’s bases this game gives you a squad of soldiers to capture or hold bases.  It gives you a good balance of progressing difficulty as well as each level you beat the aliens "learn" how to better kill you.  Don't worry though you get money for each mission successfully completed where you can purchase upgrades, and for the really hard levels one-time bonuses.
Although I really enjoyed this game I did have a few problems with it.  I did tired of the story immediately and after the 3rd mission just found myself clicking past it.  It might have gotten better but I was not compelled to waste time on it.  Secondly, I found the point system for earning upgrades trying.  It almost is a puzzle game in finding the right purchases to win a mission.  The other problem is that it didn't seem worth it to build turrets.  It was easier to hire another solider and give him a flamethrower and have him hold the choke points.  This gave the game a very unbalanced feel and I didn't end up even using most of the upgrades outside of my formula (start with shotguns until you earn enough points then go to one sniper, one flamer, one commander to capture and a flamer for each choke point).
All in all, I would buy this again as it is a fun playthrough but not sure I am going to get much more play out of it after I complete the game.

Yeah, absolutely.
This is pretty much what it looks like: a tense, bloody battle against relentless waves of aliens.  In one sense, it's not quite a true "tower defense": instead of digging in and driving off invaders, you're generally trying to
territory - think of it as part TD and part real-time strategy - but it still very much scratches the itch.
Resources are scarce, and you can never get all the upgrades you want.  Picking and choosing is thoughtful and fun ... especially when the aliens mutate and the situation changes.  Rushing a "vile tongue" alien with a flamethrower didn't work?  Try falling back and setting up a mortar.  Shotguns not doing enough to clear a path?  Outfit your grunts with grenades.  Grenades and mortars not helping?  Use a sniper of your own.  And so forth.  But there is no "one true way" to win, either; you have plenty room to play with options and find out what works and is most fun for you.
The campaign seemed short but kept me entertained for almost 10 hours at normal difficulty.  Time flies I guess!  This is one I can definitely see going back to to challenge myself at higher levels.
Is this a $15 game?  Ehh, I'd say the production value isn't high enough to justify that price.  I got it for a buck from Humble, but would have been happy to pay around $8 for this.
Grab it.  It's good, it plays great, and there are no hidden downsides.  What you see is what you get.

It lacks flavor as the player can only choose a few families to play, three maps without much character themselves, and a lack of politic actions. It's just something small that I bet could be quickly patched in to allow the player to zoom out further.

Arguably the best hack & slash ever made, period. (Unless you prefer DMC3 with the StyleSwitcher mod, which is totally okay)
Devil May Cry 4 SE is a beautifully crafted spectacle fighter that possesses one of the best control schemes in the genre and a combo system that even surpasses most fighting games in terms of flexibility and creativity. The original vanilla DMC4 featured Dante and Nero, with the first 60% of the game spent controlling Nero and a switch over to Dante (who retains nearly all of his moveset from DMC3 and the added bonus of being able to switch between his styles during gameplay) later on. DMC4SE adds 3 entirely new characters to the mix (Vergil, Lady and Trish), and while they may not be exactly balanced with the game's difficulty levels, they're an absolute blast to play as.
Vergil: Possesses Yamato, Force Edge, and Beowulf, excellent mobility through teleports, and gains power by landing hits and NOT moving. The melee range god, his damage output is borderline disgusting.
Lady: Possesses dual handguns, a shotgun, and her Kalina Ann rocket launcher. Uses a full screen grenade explosion instead of Devil Trigger. Her gameplay is more based around spacing/zoning than style combos.
Trish: Possesses the Sword of Sparta and Luce & Ombra, her dual handguns. The queen of crowd control and multitasking.
Other additions to the special edition include:
-Legendary Dark Knight Mode (enemy spawns are ramped up to insanity, your screen will be full of enemies for most of your time in this mode)
-New costumes which were DLC in the vanilla game
-Japanese audio tracks
-Opening/ending movies for Vergil/Lady/Trish
-Overall graphics upgrades (might wanna disable the awful motion blur they added though)
Performance: Consistent 120-144FPS on all High settings with FXAA.
Specs: FX-6120 @4GHz, R7 370 4GB

I'm not too good at writing reviews, but I'll say this:
RWBY: Grimm Eclipse, personally, is a really pleasing dungeon crawler made by Rooster Teeth (who I'm already a fan of). If you're a fan of dungeon crawlers, you'll like it. Enjoy it as you master and explore each playable character, all of which have their own unique combat styles and skill trees. Albeit short, you'll be able to demolish the campaign with your friends, or solo as all 4 (or 8) characters, and still find that it holds a fairly high replay value upon completion. Solo mode has changeable difficulty settings for an additional challenge, and co-op scales with difficulties based on the amount of players that are in the party. Alternatively, you can fight endless waves of enemies with your friends in horde mode!!
The achievements are pretty fun to get, and also aren't super ridiculous in terms of difficulty. That being said, to 100% the game, it does require you to buy $5 DLC package that adds four more unique playable-characters, coined the "JNPR DLC package", which within itself is worth it.
Voice acting is about what you'd expect from Rooster Teeth. Can get pretty awful, but a lot of it is reedemable in it's own way. All of the music is from the RWBY soundtrack in instrumental form. The visuals are pretty good - nothing over the top, but if you're the type that really cares about that kind of thing you won't be dissapointed.
I find the game to be absolutely worth the money. A lot of folks say that it's pretty short, and to that I can agree - you'll blow through the campaign in about 2 hours. That being said however, the game shines in terms of replay value. There are plently of achievements to go for, plenty of tasks to do, different difficulties, different characters to master, etc. Really, they should've included the JNPR DLC package in the base game and raised the price to $25 dollars to give the game more of an appeal, but that being said, yeah, the DLC is totally worth it, too.
All in all, I'd personally recommend it.

Now I know this game isn't perfect, but it's got a bit of some sort of feel. I did get this game in the last of its early access, but since I didn't review the Early Access version I bought, I instead am just going to review the current version.
First thing I want to get in the way is story.... Okay.. there is a story, but how did they get to the first level? Where's a beginning cutscene explaining how they get to their location in the start of the game? Why is it only team RWBY, and team JNPR if you bought that DLC, that's going there? I need a bit of explaination!
Gameplay wise, though the game states that it had a Dynasty Warriors and Left 4 Dead inspiration, there's not a lot of enemies in the Dynasty Warriors inspiration. In complete honesty, I expected way more Grimm in the normal difficulty, with all moves having that AOE (area of effect) added in them. Instead, we have movesets that can only hit one Grimm, except some of Weiss's move set and ultimate. Missions are pointed out via, mostly getting from point A to point B, and defending an object of interest. It rarely gives the player(s) the ability to interact with something other than running around and defending objects of interest.
The game's DLC does seem a bit.... umm.... different. First of all is the first one, which costs about an estimate of $5. You get Team JNPR, that's it. The other 4 DLC is actually 2 DLC, but split between the two teams. Sounds a bit odd since people who want to play as Jaune Arc in a dress has to buy both the JNPR DLC and the Beacon Dance DLC for that team, leaving Team RWBY alternate outfit less unless they download pretty much the same DLC, but for Team RWBY. Same goes for the Beacon Academy costume packs. Those could've been just two DLC instead of 4.
Hoard mode is okay, but hard to do alone. I'd recommend you grab three friends though, since you'll be pretty much defending all bases, which is hard to do alone since a wave of Grimm can attack multiple bases. Adding turrets are very helpful as well.
Now back to the main gameplay. The character select is very limited. You get 4 characters in the core game. Add the Team JNPR DLC and you get 8. Add the outfit packs, and you still get 8. To be honest, I expected a lot more characters in the core game itself before being released. The game on screen controls show PS4 and XBone button layouts, leaving 360 controller users, like me, completely confused with there not seeing a Back button on screen, though the majority of the game controls for the 360 controller layout is the same as the Xbone controller layout. Control layouts aside, The two attack buttons are all Dynasty Warriors based, which is okay. You also have a ranged attack button which you can combo three shots, which the third shot is a powerful shot. I can't really talk about team JNPR since I don't have the DLC, but I can say that Team JNPR seem to be more of a carrier than that of team RWBY, with their little boost effects that is.
I can't really review the graphics of this game because the PC I played this game on is a bit more of a potato than what the game thinks that Potato PCs are. It starts lagging in the video a bit at certain parts, especially the bomb escort part.
The music's okay, though it seems that a bit of the soundtrack is just an instrumental version of the show's soundtrack. But that's fine since it's Rooster Teeth's property and all. I'm all for game companies using the show soundtrack in video games based on the show the game originates from, in this game's case, it's RWBY.
The length of the game is pretty short, which the length of the game makes it seem that I've bought too little, however, I bought this in a summer sale along with RPG Maker XP, so I can't really complain since I bought it during late early access.
In the Single Player Mode, especially in the released version of the game, I honestly expected Ally AI of the rest of Team RWBY. However, You pretty much do all of that alone. In the Multiplayer Mode, it's kind of odd that you can have two players play as Ruby Rose, or any of the other characters. I thought all players would only play the available characters that other players have not chosen, but I guess I was a bit surprised about that, even from the early access version of the game.
I think that's it. The game isn't that good, nor is it that bad. But this game does make me want to play in large gap intervals.

ReignMaker is an interesting take on the match-3 genre, adding a whimsical personality to a game-type of which many may have thught no new game needed to be made. Well, ReignMaker did. Matching tiles means something: you are defending a world from hordes of evil. And not only are you defending it, you will see it grow and care for its inhabitants, as you run your own little town in this world.
The town is a major part of the game. Here you train units to help you in your battles, create equipment and research spells. And you produce the resources with which to do all that. But more than that, you make decisions that will make the town feel unique: whenever you beat a new level, a policy decission will be presented to you, asking you to guide your town. How do you handle crop failure? Do you let that reknown berserker settle in your town? What do you say about theatrical plays that corrupt our youth?
All these decission will affect your town one way or another. You may get a free scholar to help your reseach. You may end up with more rabbits around your town or piles of purple fungal mold. And your citizens may live in a republic or end up in an oppresive tyranny. It is up to you. Either way, it will be cute and humorous.
Just don't listen to the random citizen who will want to move to Troj. There is always one person like that. Can't please them all.
One warning though: this game gets really tough.

"It’s a pretty hectic game and certainly not the “Match-3″ cut and paste product I was expecting.  The town management aspect is simplistic, perhaps a bit too simplistic for my tastes. It would have been better (in my opinion) if the resources were gained over time automatically as opposed to prodding the process along manually every few minutes…though this is a minor complaint.  I have to give the game credit though for trying something new…”ReignMaker” is unlike anything I’ve played up to this point.  For that reason alone, you should probably give it a go. When I first saw this released, I ignored it. It looked like a casual puzzle game that was a mobile port. And it was pricy for that style of game. Then I saw a friends review who liked it. I've been really hard up for ANY games lately due to the deluge of mobile crap, so I grabbed it. Yes, I know, counter intuitive. But hey, I can't hate on something Ive never experienced.
Normally I'm not a fan of puzzle games, but I did love and play the hell out of the Puzzle Quests (the first one was better than the second and Galactrix IMHO, but all are good), and also liked Puzzle Chronicles. All of those had some sort of strange addictive quality, even though without the RPG component, puzzle games are boring as hell and pointless in my eyes.  So I grabbed ReignMaker.
For starters, the graphics are appropriate. They are bright, colorful, and cartoony 3d images. It lends the game a good feel that fits well with the game style. The music is cheerful and the sound is decent, although the doo-do-DO-DOO (the typical "charge" horn noise) that starts a battle is annoying as hell.
Other than that, I laughed at the *very* badly narrated intro that starts the game. The images are cool, a stained glass style picture scrolling by and explaining the backstory. But the voice..oh god. It sounds like a wanna-be old man with a bad head cold attempting to do the stereotypical "fantasy world king" accent. And failing. I had trouble understanding some of what he was saying, and it sucked cuz there was no subtitles.
So the gameplay. Its like an *extremely* light city builder/resource manager, mixed with a match 3 puzzle that is also a tower defense game. The city builder is simple. There are places you can buy using resources and the places help you. Theres also policies, which are little events. You have 4 different choices of how to deal with the event, and the results of the choice affect your city. I have havent really explored too much of the city building aspect yet, so I will update when I do.
UPDATE: Its really simple. Half the buildings generate timed resources, the other half researches itemss. You can upgrade the buildings to get better battle items, spells, and troops. I hesitate to even call it a builder. More of a resource manager.
The other aspect of the game is decently fun. Its the battle. You start, and you can earn items from buildings in your city that help you. There are many of them all with different effects.
So its a tower defense meets match 3. On the left is your tower, filled with different elemental shapes and other icons that you match. Walking in from the right are enemies, many different types. They dont move up and down, but travel in a straight line towards your tower (at least at the stages im at now, dont know if they do later). When you match 3, a bolt of the associated element spits out of your tower and travels right, hitting any enemies in its path. Thing is, the bolt travels in the row you matched it in. So if theres an enemy in the 2nd row down matching an element in the 3rd 4th and 5th row down wouldnt hit it because the elemental bolts would be flying in the 3rd 4th and 5th row. There are also many other icons, both helpful and harmful/annoying. You can collect "scrolls". Each scroll creates an entry in a book where you can see the stats of each enemy and a brief description and images.
In addition there are little challenges you can do to gain resources, such as "match 4 fire elements" "use a heal icon" ect. All of this plus a ton of achievements and other little things makes this overall a fun lgame.
Its a little pricy for 14.99, but any fan of the puzzle quest type match 3s will love it. Get it on mobile if it exists there (Not sure, but judging by it it sure seems to be),

Give it a try. And get hooked. Excellent filler up. Best match-3  experience for me besides puzzlequest. And believe me, you need those extra power ups from your city. Kill things, gain experience, get loot and try to make your character as strong as you can, that is the core of the game. Fighting mobs of enemies is fun and collecting the loot from fallen foes, pots or chests is engaging and feels rewarding. Exploration is rewarded with quests, dungeons, unique mini-boss monsters and of course loot. The game really wants you to experience every dungeon there is, because going on a linear path and doing only the story dungeons will leave you extremely under-leveled and unprepared for the dangers ahead. It seems that going trough every optional dungeon will give the player enough gear and skills to tackle the main dungeon. This is also reflected by the size of the overworld, which starts relatively small and linear to huge and sprawling. And while there are only around 3 different environmental themes Runic Games made all the dungeons look varied and unique. Exploring every dungeon not only rewards you with loot but also a fun and colorfully designed dungeon.

With such fond memories of the first game, I honestly feel as though no sequel yet has matched it, problems;
The music, Alex Brandon did an amazing job on the soundtrack of the original which really added to the depth and immersion, since then the music has become dull, repetitive and very lacklustre.
Linearity, now. The first game was linear, there were a few sidequests, but you knew what the game was about, and why you were doing what you were doing. There is no sense of urgency when you can stop saving the world for a minute to save a damsel in distress.
Lack of locations, it took me a minute in Prague to realise that there are only 2 parts, not 4... I just completed the game, and it's only in the last minute it feels like Deus Ex.
Progression, remember that first robot at the statue of liberty, remember so many more at versalife, and how they were difficult to overcome... Hell, remember actually travelling to different places achieving things, seeking alternative routes to not raise alarms, or literally just bashing the same part of the game over and over to not die. Remember slowly unraveling a story, choosing allegiances, even Human Revolution had bosses, I spent the whole game gearing up for what?
I'm annoyed at myself for spamming everything right from the very start, I had raided the bank before the bank mission, why was I allowed to, almost every aspect of the story I'd already completed before it became relevant...
Where is the futurism, where are the riots, where is the action, why so many short stories and no real big one?
The game is VERY SHORT, I know the series is about exploration, reading about the story etc, but the actual gameplay was just samey and boring, i feel as though if I rush played it I could get it complete in an evening and still get a good nights sleep.
I personally feel like a naughty private detective robocop playing this game, fingers crossed (I'm at mission 14) it gets better. Hard to believe that what, 16 years after, and with god knows how many multiples of the budget and additional cast, a sequel can disappoint so much... Sorry to moan but... Wah!

If you played Human Revolution, you'll know what you're getting in Mankind Divided. Kind of.
First, the gameplay is better this time around. Shooting is tighter. Stealth is improved. The levels are bigger and you have more options to approach diffrent situations.
However, the game falls flat in the story. The game takes place two years after Human Revolution and I have absolutely know idea what's happening or who anyone is. The game poorly introduces you to new characters and the situation Jensen is in. Jensen seems to know what's happening but as the player you're just scratching your head. There is a really big disconnect with Jensen and the player which is really bad in an RPG. After ignoring the beginning, the story eventually gets going. This is where the game shines as you finally unravel the mysterious plot and go off to do a bunch of good side quests. But then, the ending just sort of happens and you're just left there wanting.
A lot of people think that the ending is a set up for you to buy the DLCs to complete the story. It's not. The DLCs are just padding. It's just going to add side stories and another cliffhanger. The story is going to be done when they release the second game.
3/5. I would not recommend the game at this point. Wait for the inevitable sequel, and just marathon the whole thing so you don't have to wait years for an actual conclusion.

Don't listen to all the negative reviews. I'll adress all the most hated aspects of this game:
- Small scope: True. Smaller then Human Revolution, but way deeper. Every room in the game is hand crafted to the tiniest detail. Every apartment you break in has its own story.
- Stupid story: False. The story is arguably better then the one in Human Revolution.
- Disappointing ending: False. Again, better then HU. You actually get to see the consequences of your actions, actions that are well distributed throughout the whole game. Not just choose your ending from A, B, C or D (D for depressing). You get a little bit of a sequel bait, but this is no cliffhanger.
- Ingame microtransactions: True. But wholly unnecessary. You will never feel compelled to use them. You are buying a full game.
Final verdict: closer to the original Deus Ex then Human Revolution, and that is all that matters to me.

Gameplay 8/10:
Each of the three playable characters comes with a satisfying and well-balanced kit, though after a few upgrades, synergistic puzzle-skipping patterns emerge. So, in a sense, levelling up is being punished by making the puzzle elements of the game less challenging. The same can't be said for the combat elements since the game offers two difficulty sliders that can provide a fair challenge to any team, pulling thus the genre shift known as this-is-a-great-platformer-oh-no-it's-a-beat-em-up.
Plot 5/10:
A scarcely noteworthy plot that should have been better, considering the craftsmanship that went into this game.
Character 3/10:
The heroes all suffer from caricature syndrome. The Trine is underdeveloped. The woman is what, a queen or something? The goblin king is a baddie. The other final boss likes to kidnap old ladies and suffers from asthma? I don't know.
Diction 7/10:
Though at some points it can ring false, it maintains qualities suitable to the characters.
Melody 7/10:
The only grievance one would have with the soundtrack is repetition. You got yer battle music, yer boss music, yer exploration music, and that's 'bout it, I reckon.
Spectacle 10/10:
This game is the absolute definition of beauty. Forget the gradual polycount increase you see in tech demos that add gameplay as an afterthought. Forget the pseudo-artistic vomit that comprises of nothing but dark silhouettes or blocky sprites that preys on the clueless hipster. Here is a very finely crafted and detailed game world that comes alive, despite only utilizing two dimensions of space.
Final verdict:
It's the quintessential 3-way co-op side-scrolling puzzle platformer/beat-em-up on PC. Do not settle for imitation products; buy Trine 2 today!

Despite some flaws I liked dmc4 more than I disliked it. The fighting system is second to none, it's super fluid and it feels great to tear enemies to shreds. You've got a broad arsenal of weapons and moves, but its gonna take some time and practice to master and chain them together. DMC is a skill-dependant game, I truly think the better you are the more satisfaction you get because performing those sick SSS combos feels immensely more satisfying than mashing the same button over and over. Graphics are surprisingly good as for a 2008 title even though this version is I believe remastered? (correct me if I'm wrong). The story is good, I was interested to see what's next.
Now I gotta point out some cons obviously: although its possible to get used to the camera its still very inconvenient and frustrating at times. I also thought the enemy variety was lacking and what shocked me is how many times the same bosses were reused... some of them were reused 3 times and not to say they are bad, vice versa the bosses are fantastic but come on... Last but not least what disappointed me was backtracking - you often have to run back and forth in the same area to figure out how to proceed further but then you revisit the same places again? Weird to say the least. None of that is game-breaking but kinda annoying.
Still DMC4 is a great game and despite the mentioned cons it's still worth playing at least for the flawless combat.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

One of the best HnS action games in one of the best if not the best HnS series of all time. Despite their missteps in recent years, Capcom manages to do this franchise justice and deliver an excellent SE upgrade at a reasonable price for both new and returning players.
- Preface: I'm a huge DmC fan, been playing since DMC1 on PS2. I actually bought a PS3 just to play this game and have clocked over 200 hours on the original release; S ranking every difficulty up to DmD and half of hell and hell. As far as core gameplay goes, nothing much has changed. Most of the good and bad of the original are still here and thankfully, most of it is good. This is a fairly old title, so I mostly just want to talk about what's new in the SE but I've listed some of the main pros and cons of the base game below:
Pros:
- Fluid and stylish HnS action that makes you feel like a badass even if you're new to the game.
- Good combo system that rewards you for understanding and incorporating different skills and attacks.
- Art design faithful to the DmC style.
Cons:
- Story is expectedly mediocre and predictable. It is decent in length but the latter half of the game involves a lot of backtracking.
- Enemy types could benefit from some variety.
- Occasionally wonky camera angles
Now for the SE:
- Presentation: I didn't play the first DMC4 PC release so maybe it was already like this but this game certainly looks a lot better than the PS3 version. Keeping in mind that this game is nearly a decade old, it looks great at 1080p. Uncompressed textures and new special effects do a lot to make the game feel modern.
- Characters: The SE introduces three new playable characters in Virgil, Trish and Lady.
Virgil feels like a faster version of Dante at first as they share some melee move sets. He does however, have a unique playstyle of his own. Equipped with the legendary yamato as his main weapon and summoning swords which can be used for defense, offense and as a targeting gap closer, Virgil is easier and a lot of fun to play but quite overpowered.
Trish is my favorite to play of the three. She is fast but doesn't pack the same punch as Virgil. Unlike other characters, she doesn't have to swap weapons and her moveset allows her to incorporate her two "weapons" (One of them is bare fist) together flawlessly which allows for some crazy combos.
Lady is as OP or as challenging as you want her to be. As a weapons specialist, she breaks one of the fundamental rules of DMC's game design which is ranged weapons can only deal limited damage. You can very easily get through the game just spamming her bazooka but if you want to get a high combo, she can be challenging to use.
Overall, the three characters feel distinct enough and are all fun to use. They obviously don't fit into the story but the extra cinematics Capcom made for each is appreciated.
- Game modes: I believe turbo was included in the original PC release but it really is a fun option to have once you're familiar with the game. Speeding the game up by 20% makes the gameplay feel faster and the combos more fluid. Legendary dark knight mode is interesting as the extra enemies let you pull off SSS combos left and right. However, the game is obviously not designed around this mode which can lead it to feel cluttered and difficult to see in tighter areas.
- Technical: This I'm sure was in the original DMC4 PC release but it needs to be mentioned that this game supports up to 120HZ refresh rate. While it's not exactly a technical feat considering the age of the game, the fact that it's included in a console port (and from Capcom of all companies) deserves recognition. I dug out my PS3 for comparison and the difference is night and day. The game runs buttery smooth at max settings, never dropping below 120 FPS.
- Unlocks/DLC: Almost as a hallmark now of all Capcom games, there is a lot of paid DLC for this game. However, all of it can be unlocked via playing the game. They also increased the orb gain by a fair amount so the progression feels much more natural. The orbs are independent of each character, so you don't have to worry about acquiring them again after spending all of it on upgrading one. If you've already played the game like me and don't want to go through it all again, pick up the DLCs on sale, it's worth at least that much.
- Closing remarks: I've been on something of a Capcom boycott after all their anti-consumer practices and ♥♥♥♥-ups in recent years with games like SF5 but I'm so glad they didn't ♥♥♥♥ this one up. There's a good amount of additional content and fun for returning fans here that warrants a recommendation even at full price. If you've never played the game before, now's a good of time as any to experience it. Overall a 8.5/10 even by today's standards.

First,  let's make it clear, this is NOT a city builder like Cities Skylines. It is closer to Democracy 3.
The concept of this game is a great one in my opinion, though the execution is somewhat questionable:
1. Grab that Cash and Make a Stash. The biggest issue is value for money, $43CAD is a bit steep for the amount of content you get, compared to the likes of lets say Facturio, which is $25CAD.
2. Same Day Different Ruler. I'w done playthroughs with all the different families and all of their events are scripted and always the same, there is no variation to the outcomes of the same options when you decide on an event. Furthermore the different families play pretty much the same in general with little variations.
3. Click and Wait, Click and Wait! The Council is more of an annoyance than a great game mechanic at this point. It lacks any depth whatsoever. There is little consequence in♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off your rivals. If “good will” goes negative the only thing is that your pleas/demands/threats have less of an effect. As opposed to, when threatened, causing massive opposition from them, this seems to not happen. Furthermore there is no interaction with the parties on the council other than the voting.
4. Information Boogaloo...Though the game has a myriad of info screens, it somewhat lacks the ability to give you necessary information. You have no way of knowing why businesses are doing poorly or why there are problems in certain areas. The game has lots of visual cues that tell you something is wrong or happening, but nothing to indicate why or what. This is a problem since now you have very little info to figure out how to solve it.
5. Flash Ahaaa, Fastest in the Universe. The pacing seems to be a bit off, you can breeze through the 5 eras in 2-3h or so. This makes the game more of a race to the finish rather than a sit down and rule your city type of deal, if I were to compare it to Crusader Kings II.
6. Rule and Drool. Since all the events seem to be scripted and there is no randomness or variety in the outcomes of your decisions, the ruling aspect of the game gets old quite quick. Which is a big problem since the ruling mechanic is the main focus of the game. To add insult to injury there is very little to do: plop down a district, raise/lower taxes and pass a few edicts...that's pretty much it. There is very little political intrigue. You can spy on parties, but the result is the same, you get dirt and use it to get the party to vote in your favor...again not a lot of depth.
7. Mayor the Useless. Your character is a bit useless, though you get some bonuses here and there... there is again no depth or necessity for it, unlike Crusader Kings, where your ruler has a major impact on your country's well being.
In conclusion the idea is great, but this game lacks any sort of depth whatsoever. Couple it with the $43CAD price tag and value for money isn't there! It's sad, as these types of games are my forte, was hoping for a more complex city RULER rather than a mobile esque clicker.
The game has a lot of potential, it just needs to be taped. Maybe with steamworks support and a lot of DLC this could evolve into something great. We shall see what becomes of it.
If you want a city builder - this is not it.
If you want a city ruler - this is not it...Yet.
If you want a simple niche game...if the price doesn't concern you - give it a shot.

I will start by saying that I am having a lot of fun with this game. I love the concept, but the execution is a little... off.
Most of the reasons for this have already been stated. The interface should be improved dramatically, it takes too many clicks and submenus to do things that I should just be able to do with one click. I have experienced my fair share of graphical bugs that have caused me to restart the game. The tooltips are not as helpful as they should be in explaining the effects of what's going on. For instance, it will say +1 Change in a certain area. Sounds good, but exactly what change was made? It just says change. That's not helpful at all. I also believe certain things are overpriced, and what exactly does upgrading your infrastructure even do? I've been using dirt roads forever with no problems. What is my incentive to spend all this cash on upgrading then? Speaking of overpriced, $39.99 is a bit much to charge for a game that should be considered early-access at this point. I feel like I am test running a beta version. $29.99 or even $34.99 would be more acceptable to me, and give me more realistic expectations for the game. As it stands, I cannot reccommend the game, however, in a few months when all the bugs are worked out and the interface is improved, I will absolutely recommend it.
TL;DR Great concept, poor execution.

I really thought I could write this game off as being mediocre, yet overall fun. By the second or third level, I could almost convince myself that I'm used to the controls.
Yes, THE controls. Not the DEFAULT controls, the ONLY controls. Because someone in current year thinks it's okay for a PC game not to have control options. I thought we solved this back in the 90s. Worse yet, the controls make no sense for the game.
Now, I don't consider myself as having small hands by any stretch of the imagination. But there's only so long I can stretch one hand over Shift, Space, and R, while doing WASD with the SAME HAND, before my wrist gives out. Why would you put all the important keys on one hand? Well, mouse aiming, of course. Mouse aiming in what is essentially a 2D game!
On more than one occasion, I was able to get a slight high ground, which basically made the game a shooting gallery, as the enemies get stuck on STAIRS. You're clearly not supposed to do that. And it's not as if you actually AIM with the mouse, either. There's a forced auto-aim which will gladly shoot into the camera if it feels like it. In fact, I could barely reason some consistency from it, as it will often ignore an enemy that's center-camera and right next to you, to shoot at something completely unrelated and miles away. The only reason to move the camera is just to see where the enemies are before they hit you. Having an automatic per-scene locked camera, or target-locked camera, or even just the ability to zoom out a bit, would have all solved the problem and made the mouse redundant completely. Heck, given how irrelevant the 3rd dimension is, just buttons to turn the camera left or right would have done the trick.
And speaking of target-lock and auto-aim, it would have been REALLY nice to be able to pick and lock targets. Especially during the boss. Now, the boss isn't hard by any stretch of the imagination. I brought it to the last hit on the first try, and every try since. But it has instantly-respawning helpers which seem to exist simply to draw away shots meant for the boss. Or break your attack. Or do the actual damage, since the boss sure as heck doesn't. Add to that the fact that the boss can just choose not to be vulnerable to attacks whenever it wants for as long as it wants. And it seems that the whole point is just to prolong the battle until either your wrist gives out, or one of the helpers gets a lucky hit.
Because, really, one lucky hit from any enemy is all it takes. Until the boss, I felt this was nice, as it meant you have to either kite or counter, rather than go straight into the enemies. But when you fight for 30 minutes straight, only to die to a pure random hit, you have a very different perspective.
Again, not that the game is hard by any stretch of the imagination. The difficulty setting only changes the number of enemies, not their strength. Which, really, just allows you to charge up the ultimate or level up faster. There are only a couple of spots in the first two levels where you have to defend something else, where the enemy numbers really work against you, instead of being in your favor. From level 3 onward, I see no reason to play on anything less than Eclipse.
As for fan-value, if the lack of verticality for heroes which, in the series, run up wall or propel themselves with gun recoil isn't enough, how about the fact that all of the characters are functionally indistinct? Sure, there are some mild changes to the skill tree order and hitbox sizes, but ultimately they all have the exact same moves and unlockables. There's no change of playstyle, there's no clever use of semblence, if you've played one, you've played them all. Before I played, I was wondering if I should get the DLC characters, so I can play with my favorite. After playing with all the existing ones the answer was an unequivocal "Nope".
As a final saving grace, I tried to see if the "ranking" system gives this overly short and feature poor game the replayability or content it lacks. NOPE. If the low level cap wasn't enough, here's a chance to reset all of your progress AFTER you've grinded everyone to the cap, for nothing more than bragging rights. No new cap, no new abilities, not even increased difficulty. NOTHING. At least MMOs dangle some nigh-worthless reward in exchange for my grinding. But not this game.
Overall, this game COULD have been a platformer with crazy parkour and individual character abilities, such as air dash, whip swing, and wall run. It COULD have been a Koei-style MOBA where you run from one objective to the next, through an open map, cutting your way through a mountain of Grimm. It could even have been a fighting game, covering the tournament arc. But instead, it was a cheap cash-grab where you fight wave after wave of same-y low-challenge enemies in a small flat box.

My rating: roughly 3/10
-    Bought during Steam Sale at a price where selling all the cards in the current market would actually profit by a few cent. (Now I see that as a a marketing strategy)
-    At the moment, I am at +3. The real game started when I was around something-teenth level where all equipment slots are unlocked, and I got to get past x5 combo. Things gets harder and my weapons seems to have hit their limit and I can only rely on Perks.

-    Various weapons and builds to choose.
-    The scenery is nice, and the graphic is good. So good that I sometimes fail to detect enemies' bullets or the enemies themselves standing right there.

-    Level. It makes this game seems grinding. (I know it's not quite but...) It also makes the early game so slow that you couldn't defeat many enemies.
-    Perks. They come so early in the game that I didn't know what to do with them. They also matter so much that I want to reassign them without having to restart the game. Is there a way to do so, or can you maximize them all eventually?
-    Scraps. They are harder to find at the beginning, where you will want to try out various weapons, but once you get all elite ones, they don't really matter anymore and just pile up.

It's not that I don't like the idea, but it is just not right with number of players who are still playing and participating. Also, from my experience, Battle Chain is still a little buggy. TL;DR - This mod, while short, is very sweet!  It is amazing and I would highly reccomened it to any Half-Life fan or even to none HL fans, since the mechanics in this are very interesting and fun, in a sort of tech demo way.
Full Review:
This was an amazingly well done mod!  I have to stress how well put together it was and just the overall quality both in mechanics, level design, atmosphere, and of course gameplay.
The Mechanics are a really cool concept and very original (to my knowlegde no game/mod has ever had the lighting based mechanics with enemies before), and the idea of the gravity jumper is pure awesomeness, and totally something I could see in HL3!
The Level Design was also really really well done, particularly the last level, which I won't spoil here as it's something I highly recommened people expereience for themselves!  The puzzles also felt very Valve like and once again would fit perfectly in say, HL3.
Atmosphere.  Oh the atmosphere.  I have to say, this felt JUST like playing through HL2 for the first time, and once again I could totally see this being the introduction (or mid point "re-introduction") for HL3.
Gameplay was SOOOOOOO much fun!  Like really, don't take more word for it, download this RIGHT NOW and try it for yourself!  Again, the Gravity Jumper was great to use, and worked really well.  I was a bit concerned about fall damage, but it seemed to always know when I had jumped and didn't take any.
Overall this mod is great!  It is pretty short, and honestly felt like a tech demo, but it wasn't so short that it was pointless.  It was short.  But very very sweet!  My only complaint is I want more!!!
I really want to stress my respect and appreciation to this mod team!  Your guys work here is amazing and highly deserving of attention!  As someone with a very basic understanding/low level experience with coding/programming, I am actually very curious to know how difficult a lot of the coding for this was, cause I can imagine it might be quite tricky, which just shows how talented and skilled this team is!!!
P.S.  Tin-foil-hat time!
So, what if (and stay with me here, this is going to sound crazy I know!), this is actually a tech demo for HL3?  What if Valve released this under the guise of a mod to get a feel for what people thought of the mechanics and get some feedback from the community?  What if this actually a glimpse of Half-Life 3?!?!  I know that's crazy, just a wild thought that popped into my head (I am writing this at night while fairly tired...), but how amazing would it be if that were actually the case?
OK so joking conspiracy theories aside, this is a really amazing mod and I don't want anything I said above to in anyway detract from the makers of this mod.  But yeah, IMO, this could totally be something made by Valve, so that just shows how truely awesome these modders are!!!  Keep up the good work Shokunin, Thomas M. Visser, and Vincent Thiele!  You guys are awesome!

If you like Match-3 games you'll probably like ReignMaker. The meat of the game is in the battles, where you play match-3 on one side of the screen while monsters attack on the other. The matching is pretty straightforward (you get some spells you can cast to shuffle or destroy tiles, you get bonuses for matching 4 or more at once, there are locked and frozen tiles, etc) but the combat side is pretty interesting - at first I just ignored it and focused on making matches at the bottom of the screen so that matches on top would happen automatically, but it's actually worth paying attention to where monsters are and trying to line up matches in the right place, especially against later bosses when you need to keep them stunned to avoid being hurt. Also, items can be used on the battlefield side to deal with monsters, and they drop a lot of loot and collectable scrolls that are worth getting.
The town part of the game has good parts and bad parts. Resource production happens in real time, so you can just leave the game running and make as much ore and wood as you need (though money only comes from battles). This is where windowed mode would have been nice. After every new level you beat, your town faces a new dilemma you have to choose the outcome of. The dilemmas are well written but don't seem to have any actual gameplay consequences.
Steam says I've played 4 hours, and I've beat almost half the levels, so I'd guess the total playtime will be 10 hours for one play-through. There are different towns you can play as but they have only minor differences so replaying with a different town wouldn't be too different of an experience.
Update: Frogdice thoughtfully contacted me and corrected some screw-ups I made. The big one is that there IS a windowed mode, it's the last option on the options screen, and I managed to completely miss it. Another one is length: I've now done 34 levels (out of 50) with 8 hours played, so the game could end up being around 15 hours in one play through, not just 10. There's also an infinite tower after beating the game, but I can't speak to that.

I've been playing this game since it was in Beta.  I'm not normally a big Match-3 guy (more into MMOs and FPS, etc), but one of the reasons I have stuck with ReignMaker is that it has a lot of extra elements around the Match-3.  The lite citybuilding is fun, and I like seeing how my citizens are going to look different after I make several policy decisions for the city.  And making matches to have spells shoot out and kill guys attacking my tower is a lot more interesting to me than a puzzle game where I am making matches just for score.  I'd recommend this to anyone who wants to add a little more strategy to their Match-3 game.

I'm a sucker for a good Match 3 game. Everyone needs a little casual in their life, right? ReignMaker is a fantastic choice if you're looking to scratch that itch.
To start, the game has some light city-building mechanics from the start. Pick a city with a passive bonus and then use resources such as wood, ore, money, population, money, and food to build and upgrade buildings that provide magic, weapons, defensive units, and extra resources to help build up your city.
Once you go into battle, you can use up to two additional troops you have trained to help fight. For example, you can use an archer and a stonethrower to help deal damage while you take care of the rest. Every battle has rows of enemies coming down the line (think Plants vs Zombies). It is up to you to match different elements to deal damage to those enemies before they deal damage to your tower. Every so often quests will pop up such as "Match 3 fire elements" that will reward additional resources. You can also use magic and items that have been researched/purchased to help get the upper hand. You will want to ensure you use EVERYTHING at your disposal. While the game starts out very easy, the boards become more complex and new mechanics get thrown in such as corrupted elements that will make it so nothing it cast once the match is made.
Post battle you are presented with an event that occurred while you were at battle. These events allow you to choose a policy or a method for dealing with the particular issue at hand. While some policies have an immediate effect, others have a small or a slow growing effect that become more apparent the longer you play. So far it has served as an interesting piece of storytelling and each policy is complete with an outcome once you make a choice so you are never left with a feeling of "so what?" Some events have be humorous, and others have been tales of love lost and found (and some deal with poop because who doesn't like some good ol' fashioned toilet humor?). There is a definite variety to the policy portion of the game.
Rounding all of this out is a thorough Bestiary (as FrogDice games are known for) that lets you see your foes up close and personal and a pretty decent soundtrack. The voice acting isn't anything to write home about but it serves the purpose. The graphics are, again, nothing to clamor over but they are charming and the purpose is served. This is a game that is all about the gameplay and it certainly delivers in full.
If you're familiar with other FrogDice games and have enjoyed them, you can expect more of what makes a FrogDice game worth playing in ReignMaker. If you are unfamiliar with FrogDice games but enjoy a good Match 3 game, definitely pick this one up. There is a level of depth in this one that I haven't seen in a Match 3 in some time. Icing on the cake: you can sit back in your chair and just play with the mouse; no need for the keyboard (other than to put in the name of your city in the beginning). Doesn't get much better than that.

The game is easy to learn, though I do wish there was a quick runthrough on controls. (Especially the signature mechanics having direction based inputs) The art style at first is a bit weird and to be honest I'm not as huge of a fan of it, but the backgrounds are great and I think they're very good at the level design. My favorite stage is probably Big King's Pass for it's aestetic and unique platforms. There's a good variety of game modes, my only complaint is I wish there was a team quickplay mode because I would absolutely love a non-ranked 2v2/3v3 mode.
My biggest problem in the core gameplay is probably the light attacks not having much variety in between characters, the stats and stances help this problem a little bit but I do feel like all the characters sharing similar attacks does feel like you're kind of playing the same thing. Keep in mind Blue Mammoth is trying to alleviate this by introducing new weapon times, but I guess I would just love some alternate light attacks per character. The signatures are fine, but I would love to see some more variety in the items because most of the time you're going to be using the Bomb over the Horn or Spike Ball. The prices for the skins are just a bit steep, but it's optional and support the game dev so it's nothing serious.
Ranked seems fun, when I get come practice in I'm going to get one of my dumb jerk friends and play 2v2's with him and see if we can hit gold together.
Their release cadence is pretty good and they try to put their fingers on the pulse of the game and balance quite often, I just feel like their biggest focus should be on making all the characters feel a little more specialized, but regardless, it's a fun game and absolutely worth your time.

I rarely like to post negative reviews for a title, instead liking to offer encouragement and critical appraisal for developers. However this title was a serious disappointment to me, and coming from a big publisher behind the likes of Tropico, it really needed to be better.
In short Urban Empire is a political simulator, but the sad fact is it never really lives up to that in any meaningful way. All the parties I encountered, despite being placed in what seemed to be a realistic way upon the political spectrum, ended up having little to differentiate each other. With enough bargaining ( the game lets you plead, demand or threaten to change party member's stances on a vote) every party could be persuaded to accept a vote. In two hours of play I lost one vote, and that was because by that time I couldn't really care less about pushing any harder.
This game has potential, but currently it feels highly random. I played for two hours and in that time I rarely felt like there were any major differences between the political parties, other than the fact that the game's scripting told them how they should vote on an issue. The social democrats always seemed to disagree, and need to be persuaded, where as the physiocratics always agreed whole heartedly. By the end of my two hours I was sadly bored stiff.
You might say two hours is a short time, but I saw the second era and I put through quite a number of votes and city infrastructure changes, but by the end of those two hours I felt distinctly like I was (to quote someone else) 'pulling levers and watching how it changed things'. Between votes I would just sit and watch the city, and in the long run it all came down to budget, and a procedure of picking edicts to increase income and forcing votes to up the taxes.
I just couldn't be bothered to force any more votes or try an more edicts because I simpky felt like this 'balancing act' was all I'd be doing for 4 eras. Then, much to my annoyance, I tried to save my city only to find the game wouldn't let me. It appears that unless you have finished all tutorial missions then you can't save. I'm sure that's a bug that will be fixed, but it didn't improve my first impressions of Urban Empire at the time.
Urban Empire is a nice idea, but I feel it lacks too much depth to make it a game I'd recommend to people. I watched much of the game on YouTube before release, and I pre-purchased based on my thoughts. It had looked fun from watching, but playing was not the same experience.
If Urban Empire only had half the humour and detail of Tropico it may have allowed me to get past the monotony of the political system (yes, I do feel it was monotonous), and indeed the only attempt at humour was a reference to Tropico (which I won't spoil). It was a nice touch, but didn't improve on things.
For the first time I feel inclined to refund a title, and for that reason I can't recommend Urban Empire. There is a game here should the developers act to add in a layer atop the political bargaining. An ability to design the layout of your city would be a start, and frankly that is another thing that stopped me finding any real enjoyment in the game. If I could have done a mayor's job and planned the layout of my city, then I might have had something to do whilst waiting for votes to pass and balances to improve. But for some reason the city builds itself, or you at least have no say in road layout and rci placement. You can determine how much industry, commercial and residential is built, but not where. It's almost as if you're playing the role of a mayor with lots of helpers turned on to leave you less to do. You're just public relations for the mayor, really.

Overall, a good game. Had it since beta (and the fanmade version before that), and still has some issues but I'll note those later.
First, the good things:
-Characters are modelled nice
-Eclipse difficulty (hardest) is fun to play solo
-Interesting story
Then, the bad things:
-Levels feel too large with too few enemies on lower difficulties
-Paid DLC for skins and another team that SHOULD have been included with the game for free considering...
-The story is so short, you start to wonder how, exactly, it ended when you get put back to the title screen.
Things that would have made the game better (for the Devs if they're listening):
-More levels! Maybe another 12 levels on top of those currently in the game with similar length would have been nice, seeing as it only doubled from beta to release when normally games give you ~90% more after release.
-Longer battles, tougher opponents, etc. to make the game more challenging (60 cream puffs are still just cream puffs, you know).
-Would have liked to see a bit more involvement with the characters during and between battles, such as an equipment screen, health potions, buff items, etc. (think back to the fanmade one. That was pretty awesome.)
-Horde mode shouldn't have to be a base defense game. I honestly just want to kill grimm, so give me a "zombies" style infinite horde of increasing difficulty to decimate.
UPDATE: JNPR and RWBY DLC
So I bought the dlc packs for team RWBY and unlocked team JNPR and there's a couple things I wanted to point out for those who are thinking they might want to buy either.
-The outifts are actually quite nice (my favourite is Weiss's dance outfit), but nothing over-the-top amazing. Supposedly you could (in theory) do a better job with mods (that apparently exist according to the guides).
-Team JNPR doesn't change much about the game except if you want to play as Jaune.
-Starting with Jaune, his super gives your team a buff, which makes absolutely no sense for single player but... whatever. Due to his play style, it makes the game easily twice as hard without touching the difficulty setting (not more grimm, just more difficult to kill the ones that are there). Also, his ranged is replaced with a short charge that does almost no damage.
-Nora can't hit the broad side of a bard with her ranged, so hope the AOE works for you.
-Pyrrha is actually on par with team RWBY.
-Ren is also not bad, but I haven't really played too much with him yet.

Can you say "conflicted"? This game will make you say "comflicted" in review. On the one hand, this is one of the very few modern shoot-em-ups that take its inspiration directly from Raptor - my most favourite shmup of all times (you may love Tyrian more - I forgive you, but I don't understand you). Not from R-Type, Gradius or other Japanse games which I mostly disliked, and which eventurally evolved into bullet-hell genre, which I avoid at all costs.
On the other hand, while Ravolution Ace takes a lot from Raptor, it does not always succeeds in copying, and additional elements sometimes seem to make matters even worse.
Firstly, this game is very hard. On Normal, it plays a lot like Raptor on the highest difficulty. Even the basic enemies can take a lot of punishment, and your weaponary is not up to it. You WILL skip a lot of enemies, even in the first levels, and you will probably fail to complete on of them. The solution, unfortunately, is grinding. New weapons cost a lot, but they matter. While they will never make you feel like an invinsible super-hero, they will, at least, make it possible to get to the next level's boss with enough shields and armor to take it down.
Grinding is a cornerstone of this game. I don't like to grind, so this is a huge minus for me. Fortunately, there are a few ways to grind, which make it more interesting. Boss Attacks are the quickest: pretty soon, you can manage to grind Boss Attack I with your eyes closed. But they pay not very much. Replaying levels you already completed in Campaign also is not very lucrative. But Random levels can bring you a lot of cash! At 20 level, a pass through "Random Skies" will get you about 80K credits - about 1/3 of money you need to buy _any_ top-tier weapon. Also, since enemies (but not landspace) is randomized, it's slightly less boring to grind those.
Another big problem with this game is enemies and bullets. In a way, this game deserves the name of bullet-hell much more than any Touhou title: in a lot of levels, the screen will be filled with bullets, but they will not be flying in any disernable pattern. It will be utter chaos, and you will NOT be able to eavde them all! Also, many bullets, especially from ground vehicles, are VERY hard to see, especially with all the explosions happening in the sky. You will often take a lot of damage from unseen sources before you understand what is going on.
Enemies also do not have obvious patterns. Memorizing a level will only help you a little, this is not a game about memorization.
The need to switch between firing at ground or at air enemies is sometimes frustrating. I'm not sure if it is a good idea at all. In Raptor, some weapons only worked on ground units, and some only on air, and that was enough, really.
So, in the end:
Pros:
+ Raptor-inspired shmup
+ Nice visuals
+ Interesting, if somewhat unsatisfying weapons (it gets better at the top tier, it really does)
+ Level-up system (Perks)
Cons:
- Very hard, probably endlessly frustrating for a novice players, but a bit too challenging even for me sometimes
- Requires a lot of grinding (but grinding can be varied, so it's not as boring as it could be)
- Bullets lack patterns and hard to see on background
For some reasons, it also has a multiplayer mode. I never wanted a multiplayer mode in a shmup, but I guess some people enjoy it...

For $1 from the Humble Bundle, Infested Planet was unexpectedly fun.  I initially overlooked the serviceable graphics, but noticed that the game runs really smooth with tons of aliens on the map. The easy parts of the game are a soothing bloodbath, and sheer chaos in harder scenarios forces you veer from initial plans. A first impression that this game is a twist on tower defense isn't that far off, but the execution is really fun and frenetic.
On paper, the RTS base attacking and tower defense elements aren't all that new, but I really like how you can focus your attention on attacking an enemy hive, then zoom out and realize that one of your control points is being flanked.  The enemy pathfinding is pretty good, and the dumb swarms will avoid your kill zones, taking a long way around to one of your far off bases. Balancing both offense and defense meant that I was never waiting around like in typical tower defense gameplay loops.
Some of the best moments in game involved deciding whether to let a base fall to continue wiping out the edge of a map, or to rush a single guy over to build a turret. The game's generosity with refunding your build points, on destruction of assets or when you recycle your mistakes, really helps with the dynamism of the game flow and lets you recover instead of immediately restarting the missions.
The marketing of this game is unimpressive, but overall, I'm glad I gave it a try.

Themed like the strategy game someone should have made using the Starship Troopers license. You’re fighting on an alien planet against millions of chitinous bugs. It mirrors some of the film’s plot beats, like discovering that the race has brain aliens who do the species thinking.
Your side is more than just your five soldiers, first of all. As you progress, you purchase unlocks using money gained by fighting in missions. Depending on which you choose, these new tools allow you to swap one of your regular grunts out for a sniper or a flamethrower guy, or to give your soldiers the ability to place buildings which offer battlefield boosts like extra ammo, strength, or the ability to call in helicopter bombardments. The aliens also evolve, tweaking themselves in much the same way as your own buffs.
You’ll clear out a base, destroy its spawning pods, turrets and main structure, and then stand on the point to capture it for yourself. Then you’ll move on. Later, as enemies become tougher and advancement slows, you’ll spend a moment at each point you capture establishing a fire base. You’ll recycle old, now redundant turrets, and place a new set on the front lines. You’ll grab your health pod, which can be dragged behind one soldier to provide area-of-effect healing to anyone nearby.

Once you have finished the story and even the side missions you can still do things in the world lile the many Easter eggs, actaully go hunting as there is wildlife such as deer in the forests or explore and create chaos and destruction. The online is next. Online brings all the chaos, guns, cars, missions and world of GTA and let's it go wild with regular updates that give more missions, vehicles and weapons like a yatch, tommy guns, the latest cars and even the ability to create your own business empire or biker gang. These are all done with the chaos of other real people around you! Finally modding. Modding has now been kind of unbanned now thanks to Rockstar telling Take Two to basically calm down so you can mod in single player. Interesting Match 3 game. Basically you build and upgrade a village to provide power-ups for the Match 3 combat game.  Then you use the money from the Match 3 game to purchase upgrades for your town.
Occassionally you'll get popups in town about a random event and you have a multiple choice decision you can make. Depending on your choice you may unlock other power-ups.
Several of your buildings are for gathering resources - ore and wood that you use to build and upgrade structures. A farm to feed your people. A blacksmith to research new weapons and an armory to store them in.  You use the weapons as power-ups in the match 3 game.
You can build and upgrade an Academy for spells to use in the match 3 game, A City Hall to hire workers for your buildings or as power-ups such as an Archer or Boulder tosser to fight off the encroaching enemy. And finally a Grainery to bring in more settlers.
Combat is a road map of towers on the continent. Once you win a match 3 game in one, you can advance to the next tower or redo a battle at a solved one to grind money.
In the combat sequence you have enemy forces coming at you randomly in rows. As you make matches in the match 4 game it sends out energy beams from the matched gems out into the enemy ranks of those rows. You can also use your archer/boulder tossers/loot gatherers/healers as power-ups to help defend the walls or keep your troops healed.
As you defeat enemies, they may drop piles of money that you can click on as you're  making your matches.
All in all it's an interesting twist to your standard Match 3 game. All the standard Match 3 obstacles are there - as are the power-ups. Just that now they have to be researched from your village before use, and some unique power-ups like archers and such running around shooting the approaching waves of enemies as you make matches to send out energy beams to blast them away from your ramparts.
Other than that nothing terribly unique from any other Match 3 game - just its presentation.

Overproduced mess with only the minimal improvements to the formula and a slog to get through. Questionable microtransactions (which don't carry over to different saves) are already reason to protest enough, but even without them, the game just isn't very good.
Optimization is all over the place. The story has a beginning and it ends before it properly reaches the middle. The choices provided in the game rarely have any effect of significance, in that the game changes just a little, but you don't feel involved. There is only one, big, hub city and the changes that happen within it are dictated by the plot, cutting out the player completely.
Most importantly, Eidos Montreal still hasn't realized that Deus Ex is not a stealth series. Human Revolution made the same mistake, but it was at least functional in its linearity. Mankind Divided goes out of its way to force the player to engage in sneaking missions and, the irony is, the developers don't know HOW to make a stealth game. The mechanics are stealth-but-not-stealth-enough and the thing that many seem to forget when it comes to stealth games is that level design is paramount in making them work. Some of the side-quests are kind of fun and interesting, but the story missions are badly paced and offer no surprises.
In the end, the cardinal sin of Mankind Divided is that it doesn't offer anything. It feels like a waste of time from beginning to end. Its metaphors about racism are paper-thin, its conspiratorial approach is infantile and in all that exists a game that's just... boring.
If you LOVED Human Revolution and you need a bit more, you may want to give it a shot; but only when it goes on-sale.
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is, effectively, the worst things about Skyrim, Dragon Age: Inquisition and Metal Gear Solid V combined into one. Too loud, too long for all the wrong reasons, entirely pointless and ultimately a major disappointment on all fronts-- and there is a special place in hell for people who make games with loading times that can take up to 2 minutes.
