An incredible title, marred by typical publisher interference and penny pinching schemes. While it's easy to blame Square-Enix for all of this, you really can't. It's true that they control the purse strings, but any artist with even the slightest bit of integrity and pride in their work would dig their heels into the floor over the laughable features that were added, and if refusal to co-operate then results in the game simply not being made, then so be it.
Since they obviously didn't fight them, some of the blame will rightfully have to go their way, and that's the end of that. There's really nothing more to discuss.
If you ignore the phone game quality Breach mini-game, the DLC items that are phone game-tier one use consumables (as in one use across ALL SAVES YOU EVER MAKE, EVER), and some rushing here and there, you'll find an exceptional title. I mean, this is the sequel to human revolution, which is one of the best games ever made, so anything less than that would be a failure.
Despite being the sequel to the third game in the series, DX: MD draws heavily upon the first game, which was a welcome surprise for yours truly, but made  the average teen gamer confused, lost, and feel out of his depth Naturally, despite the many coolbacks and homages, it's Adam Jensen II: first blood part II. Yeah, more on that 'confused teens' comment... While people have been begging for what they perceive as a return to form, it turns out a large portion of the playerbase actually can't handle exploration, somewhat limited ammo, less resources in general, somewhat rougher choices and consequences, and more of a cerebral experience, balanced weapons so all guns have a purpose. Now the latest news on the street is that HR was better because reasons. If these people would actually do more than follow quest markers and impotently attack riot armor cops with shotguns, flashbangs, and tear gas, when said player only has an issue, I don't know what to say to these lost souls.
Prospective buyers shoul disable all the casual feautres, which includes quest markers, and simply pay attention. At no point does a quest giver tell you to go to X, instead they give you the street name, number, and full address - unheard of since HR's time, Without slavishly lemming training the quest marker, you'll find yourself explore an incredibly meaty game, (expected, considering the series' pedigree), but a lot of love and care has done into art. This is one a handful of titles through history that have gone with hard brutalism and succeded. No joke. A 69 dollar dell monitor, that shows black as purple would naturally kill this experience, so please get your colors adjusted and corrected iv possible.
The biggest change, by far, is combat. Combat has always been the weakest of the DX pillars (stealth, social, exploration, combat), but with MD, it's been upgraded. If you're a fan of the crysis series, you'll instantly feel at home with everything, right down to the quickchange weapon mod system. Also rather than the traditional 400 billion trash guns, there's only about a dozen really useful and thought out guns, with some quirky 'uniques' on top, like a full auto shotgun that only shoots armor piercing slugs, or the mega high DPS combat rifle variant that only fires EMP ammunition. You also get a wide assortment of augs that double as weapons, and Adam somehow incorporated nanosuit 2.1 technology, now sporting the new MAXIMUM ARMO- I mean titanshield aug, which does exactly what it says on the tin.
As for the other pillars, no other deus ex game has had this much of a focus on exploration. You're gonna miss a lot of little things, and even some big things, on your first two or three playthroughs.
The only gripe is really the system requirements. Much like how combat is very inspired by crysis, so too are the system requirements. You need a beast machine, or at least beast computer knowledge, if you want to play with eye candy and technology turned to 11. People who got suckered into the GTX 970 3.5 gig meme card are at a distinct and crippling disadvantage, as their 3.5 gigs of VRAM just isn't quite 4 gigs, which is the requirement for a lot of cool stuff, so prepare to lower some settings if you're on one.
While many are citing poor optimization, there's only so many ways to 'optimize' 4 gigs of textures to make them fit into 3.5 gigs of space.
Overall, and aside the awful launch debacle and publisher/developer meddling, this is an amazing game that you really should play, but may not have the hardware to enjoy fully.

Hands down one of the best games of this current generation of gaming (so far). Like its predecessor, it dives into real-world issues and it does it in such an addicting multi-faceted manner that it boldly stands out as one of the more unique RPG experiences.
Pros:
-STORYTELLING: Similar to DE:HR, DE:MD takes a similar approach to the 'PLAY YOUR WAY' mentality, but expands on it in a BIG way. Jensen doesn't really lose abilities like most RPG sequels force you to do for some reason at the beginning of the game. INSTEAD, he gains access to NEW abilities very early on, and his new abilities aren't even "oh yeah new game new abilities" NOPE, they're actually tied into the story and there's a whole side-quest that spans a big chunk of the game length all about the new abilities. Speaking of side-missions, you now have side-missions that flow in and out of the main narrative and some being very lengthy multi-tiered side-missions that have arguably better plots than the main story. The game almost ALWAYS gives you something to do and by simply exploring the various open-zones you always have someplace to go. This game doesn't feel overwhelming like some RPGs because its locales are very condensed yet very detailed. But at the same time it's not small to the point where there's no content. The game has a very, VERY thorough lore woven throughout it and it's very noticable how much attention was given to developing the world and atmosphere for this game.
-COMBAT: If you choose the loud and proud way, combat is MUCH more intuitive and fun this time around especially with the TITAN Aug, Slow-Mo Vision, and Nano-Blades. In DE:HR, Combat existed but in a very wonky way. Combat in this game is much more fluid and guns are fairly customizable.
-STEALTH: Stealth gets MUCH harder, but you also get more cool toys to play with. The Tesla Aug and the Remote Hacking Aug make fine new additions into balancing the Stealth aspect of the game, but stealth in this game challenges the likes of MGS when it comes to late-game stuff.
-VISUALS//PERFORMANCE: Here's where the game lacks. The game LOOKS good, however animations are fairly stiff, lip sync is WAY off, almost all other non-main character models have super generic lifeless faces. Conversation animations are borderline abyssmal (they look like they're from a PS2 game, most look like recycled assets from DE:HR) and in this day and age for a game like this to have animation as its one-off is kind of a let down. However, don't let this turn you away from the game. As much as an importance visuals and graphics have nowadays, they do NOT pull away from the experience as much as you think. I'm running the game on Ultra with every possible setting on (GTX 1080) and the game runs very smoothly. I only see hiccups when moving between locations (loading assets) and have encountered the game crashing once (failed to load a save after moving up the graphics settings).
-OVERALL: WE DEFINITELY ASKED FOR THIS. 9/10, DEF GoTY contender for me.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

First of all - this game SHOULDN'T be compared to city builder games because it has a completely different approach to the city management with more emphasis on the family, politics and different era characteristics.
You actually kind of macro-manage districts with not much room to manipulate like you are able to in typical city builder games. The game leads you through some of the most interesting eras of modern history, with all the global crisis affecting your little city as well. You develop technologies to boost your industry and commerce, propose edicts to balance out some of the issues you might have in your city, you make taxing changes etc. In my opinion, it all feels moderately complex although it has quite a lot features.
Now the biggest problem that I personally have with the game is the transparency. After a couple of play-throughs I still have no idea why some of the issues appear in this game and I cannot pinpoint the source of the problem in order to find a way to resolve it. I feel like the game is missing more clear UI, explanation of the various stats that your companies have that affect their success, and so on. There should be a lot better advisor system in my opinion.
Overall - the game is fun and it has a kind of a fresh approach to the city game genre. It does make you play it a couple of times which I tend to value the most in games. However it does not justify the price. It should be priced at about 20$ at most because it lacks the complexity to be valued more.

Fun game ideas, decent execution on some of them, not-so-good on a lot of them. And then there is the performance problem, or the complete lack of performance.
If the performance wasn't so god-awful it could be a fun game, if a bit silly and random in its political simulation... But if I can't actually play the game, well, not much fun to be had.
Let's take it step-by-step:
1. Politics.
Fun idea. Fun when it works properly, but often it doesn't. The political compass doesn't translate into sensible parties (sensible as in resembling reality to some degree), and there is no way to tell how you are being placed on that compass... you might think you are a left-leaning liberal, but when mayoral elections come along, all the right-wing centrists support you, and the progressives are the ones that vote against you. Why? No way to find out.
Nevertheless, if you suspend your disbelief, and have don't expect the compass to be anything remotely realistic, it is an interesting barrier mechanic you have to work your way around... Devs should just throw out the realistic names and connotations, and just run with the underlying mechanics.
2. UI and useability
UI itself is decent, if a little action heavy (too many clicks to accomplish some things) not too hard to use, or learn. The problem is there is a big lack of feedback and general information about what is gonig on in the city, and what the consequences of your actions are.
*Why is the restaurant industry making more money than the next 10 combined, while not having a sales boost or booming demand? No clue.
*Why are the elite and lower classes unemployed? No clue, the industry tabs only shows middle and working class jobs per category.
*Why are all these businesses bankrupt in this one district, but not in the one next to it? No clue... I can look at all of them individually, but it only tells me the current situation, not any of the causes.
*Incomprehensible tooltips galore, where figuring out if the +5% figure on a red downwards-arrow accompanied icon is a good thing or not is a matter of trial-and-error.
*Some decisions in events have no tooltip, but if the previous choice had one, it remains displayed, confusing the player.
3. Variety and replayability:
Barely any of either. Game is fairly linear, with far too few choices.
*A grand total of 3 maps are present currently, but since the maps make no difference in how the game plays, there might as well be 300. One of the maps states that the mining industry would be a defining economic force, due to mountains and such... well, that does not in any way translate into game mechanics. I tried all three maps, and had pretty much the exact same industry composition on all of them.
* The 4 families are fun additions, they can make you play somewhat differently. Good idea, expand upon this.
4. And the big bugbear, Performance:
*Specs: i5-4670 @3.4GHz. GF970, 16GB-1866 RAM, 256GB SSD.
*Scenario 1: max quality 1080p, 1914, city of 45K people, era 3 techs all unlocked.
*Result 1: 2-16 FPS on 2x speed, 5-22 on 1x speed, 10-15 second freezes every 3-4 months. Unplayable on higher speeds (freezes every couple seconds).
*Scenario 2: lowest quality 1080p, 1914, city of 45K people, era 3 techs all unlocked.
*Result 2: 15-25 FPS on 2x speed, 20-30 on 1x speed, 5-10 second freezes every 3-4 months. Barely playable on higher speeds.
Having taken a much smaller city (15K people) to 1936, while still having 30-40 FPS on 2x speed, it seems that population increases and number of districts severely limits performance in the game.
This is the one that kills it for me, if I'm doing well, the game becomes unplayable very fast. Until the performance issue is solved, I can't recommend this game.
This game should've been released to Early Access, and sit there for a couple months until it is fully baked, then release it.

1820年，皇帝赐了你一块地，给了你500k的个人起始资金和1000k的城市资金，作为城市的创建者，从下手划分第一块行政区起，你将要开始你的市长生涯。而这个城市的名字，你把它叫做“Kaisershafen”（要是你没改名的话）。
在最开始的阶段，只能建造一个低密度、仅有最基本的基础设施，甚至连分区比例都无法自定义的行政区，开始走向小城崛起的道路。
Kaisershafen的繁荣发展与别处是不同的，他麻雀虽小，但确人才济济——什么热力学、流行病学、炸药、电子游戏等等，都将在这里被发明。不要怀疑，是虽然表面上是发展云，但是研究完成一个之后会让你选择下一个“发明”，想来诺贝尔、开尔文这样的人物都蜗居在这个小城，这样一个小地方何愁不兴旺发达。甚至将来自己发射个卫星，也不是不可以。更难能可贵的是，这里还是人权斗士的运动基地，什么劳动法、女权、环保、动保，在这里都可以看到他们活动的身影，性爱革命、消除歧视这样的运动也是说“发明”就“发明”，端的是“世界何其大，发展靠我家”。虽然Kaisershafen在地球上占据了这么一个举足轻重的位置，但是也不固步自封，世界之大，我市伸出友谊之手，堪堪选出了6个未来入得了法眼的城市：牛津、旧金山、悉尼、圣彼得堡、上海、仙台，虽不是首都，
但先不急，先把眼下这个小镇子经营好吧。
城市发展之本，便是资金了，如何让运营城市的成本低于带来的收益，便是发展首要的问题。
每建立一个行政区，都需要额外的成本，而人口的增长和行政区数量的关系尚不明确，所以要慎重创建新的行政区，在有需求的时候再建岂不稳妥得多。发展的步子也不能迈的太大，不能将无法承担的基建一股脑儿的往城区上般，而要走一步看一步，先找个试验田看看带来的收益能不能值回成本，再考虑是否将这个推广。
这本是一个城市发展的应有方式，然而UE内部经济循环的不明确导致就算成本一时没有把握，城市入不敷出眼看走向崩溃，依然可以靠不断提高税率来弥补漏洞，而此时本是用来制衡市长行为的议会，居然也会用脚投票，只要不结余太多的提税提案，通通通过。
也尝试过降低税率来观察是否能通过刺激消费带来收入的提升，但结果是虽然有略微的提升，但是效果远不如直接调节税率来的明显。虽然高税率之下随处可见破产企业，但是城市收入还是稳步提升，人民也过得幸福如意，简直匪夷所思。
压榨人民制定高税率，虽然日子当下过得有些紧，但在研究完一项科技、时代更替下，收入能实现稳定的增长，日进斗金不是梦。正所谓“降税容易提税难”，赶早变着法从市民手中抠钱才是硬道理。
既然提到了议会，那就不能不说说这个游戏的议会系统。
由于前几个时代皇帝钦定了玩家来做这个市长，完全不怕被弹劾，也不怕有竞争者的出现，本来用来制约玩家用来改变法案支持率的“政治货币”党派好感度，尤其在不能跌破下限-10的情况下，其本身意义也然无存。在好感度为正的情况下，恳求非常有效，一旦跌到负值，那么胁迫反而变成了最容易的途径。议会便犹如一个玩具，任由玩家揉捏。
就算是后期出现了竞选也无妨，只要城市发展良好，每两个月去稍微胁迫一下每个党派，市长位置还不是手到擒来。每6年一次的选举，也不过就是消耗我“政治货币”的途径而已，和之前已经不同
至于与经济相关联的提案，只要城市日进斗金，财务无忧，不管有什么政治诉求这些党派都会无脑通过。
随着城市的发展，城市密度需要由低向高发展，来容纳更高效率的住房、工厂和商店。然而，在此之前已经建立的建筑物无法自动更新，于是中后期拆迁（需要科技解锁）就变成了一项很常见的工程。虽然看着一座座房屋轰然倒塌是一件很爽快的事情，但是一个区域那么多建筑，一个个点过来确实非常的累。在没有框选和快捷键的条件下，一个个选中建筑，移动到右下角摧毁，在到屏幕中间确认选择，然后一片区域重复几十次，是一件很傻B的事情。
虽然拆迁需要付出一定的代价，相应建筑物带来的利润也会随之失去，但是之后新建筑慢慢拔地而起，带来的利益也是明显的，只是太繁琐的操作容易让人失去耐心，所以我都是在区域比例分配那里先全选成住房，确定改变区域后，再全选为工厂，提交改变，用私人资金改后，再手动分配比例，反正改变区域比例不要钱，所以用自己的钱也就不需要提案，区域人员的安置赔偿都不用管，虽然也要动好几下鼠标，比一个个摧毁省力多了。
关于人权的问题，一直以来都是现实生活中争议颇多的地方，在这个游戏中也是。琳琅满目的提案，有些就算放到当前来看也是尚未实现。比如同工同酬、同性婚姻合法化等等。非常的pc，倒是我喜的部分。
最后说说这个游戏其他方面的质量。
游戏汉化不易，但是这个汉化的质量确实有点垃圾。比如前文提到的“发展”和“发明”指的是同一个东西；比如“少数名族”的同性恋问题；再比如将LGBT翻译为“同性恋”；再比如本段标题的“退化完成”，而英文原文是“Downsizing done”。而只在科技完成时出现的原本就不多z中文语音中，我竟然还在其中听到了一条英文语音，不过我倒是忘了记下是哪一段。没玩过游戏就翻译，以及缺少统筹校对，是很多已有汉化的通病，这个游戏汉化该有的也都有。
游戏本身其他的硬伤也不少：
1.流程单一，一个家族就是一个既定的事件，没有重复玩的价值。三张战役地图大同小异，也就是地形稍有区别，反而是三个挑战还有那么点意思。
2.优化烂，游戏进行到后期卡的不行，载入及保存时间长，常常未响应让人以为程序崩溃。玩着玩着程序崩了的情况也有发生过。
3.内部经济逻辑不清前面已经提及，进入下一个时代只不过就换了个接班人，收入却猛的增加，着实让人捉摸不透。
4.成就系统混乱不堪，目前成就各种张冠李戴。
5.画面，嗯感受一下高楼大厦吧（？
同样的一句话，送给这个游戏，这游戏内容看似丰富，实则浅尝辄止，壳子只要有现在的一半就够了。当然如果你是乐观者，可以玩一玩。

So, I watched Quill18 play this, and decided I wanted this game. Pre-bought it, and have not regretted the decision.
This is sim city meets civ meets democracy in a sense.
You build your city like in Sim City, you research like in Civ, and you pass edicts (laws) like in democracy.
I love how you need to pay attention to the political parties, and how the politics work. Do you try to find a middle ground, or do you try to get one or two parties more popular so you can work with them?
Do you implement all the laws, or do you move your city in a specific direction?
So, the city council does not want to build another city district, well maybe if you place the new tech'ed radio tower there they will.
Decisions, decisions.
I have found no major issues with this game, however there are the odd spelling mistake, but those are far between and very easy to work with, and most likely something that will be patched sooner rather than later.
If you expect this game to be a pure city builder where you are all powerful, you will be disappointed, but if you are looking for something where you have to balance the various needs of the city, you will not be disappointed.

A shallow attempt at making a MOBA-inspired hack'n'slash. It's chock full of bugs and other issues that've been in the game since launch day, none of which have been fixed in over a years time.
They've replaced the decent in game art and models present at launch and replaced them with ugly, and very creepy porcelain doll models. After letting the ugly things sit there for some time, they eventually fixed it by adding new models that have the body of RWBY characters, but the faces are weird and off-character. At this point they also replaced all ingame art with crappy deviantart pieces. Just look at how horrible Yang looks, must I say more?
Instead of fixing broken and poorly designed levels, they just tacked on more equally shoddily made levels. At the beginning, this game was NOT worth the price. And now, after over a year and it sitting at $20, it's BARELY worth $20. If the work put into it was decent at all, it MIGHT be worth $20. A reasonable price for this game would be $7 to $9. I wouldn't pay much more for such a game, knowing it's a bug-riddled cashgrab attempt.
Combat, abilities, and characters are so watered down they're pitifully weak and underwhelming to play. Guns USED to be decent, they're so weak now, I don't even see the point in them existing anymore. Even though they may visually look different, all characters play very similarly, and the fact they all pretty much do the same damage with the same attacks and really no differing playstyles or attackstyles is just sad. The addition of Counter is a cool concept, but it doesn't always work, and it's the only good point of combat after the initial fake shine wears off, which is quick for something so mundanely boring. And I love games like this. So that's saying something. I get the feeling characters were "balanced" to be pvp characters, since they're so samey and so weak and pitiful. But the game has no PVP whatsoever, so who gives a flying flip, it's a stupid, stupid screw up. It's PVE against AI, against a TON of AI at times, and it feels more rewarding and fun when the characters aren't crap. They may LOOK like RWBY characters, but they don't play, look, or even feel like RWBY characters.
They're idea of difficulty is purely more numbers, more health. Which the most despised, cheap, and pathetic way to make something more difficult in games. Padding numbers doesn't make it more difficult, it only makes things take longer, and it's boring. I'd be way more interested in an enemy with normal health, cool moves that can be dodged that don't have padded numbers for damage, and same with bosses. Enemies are just mindless weeds for you to mow down in a boring, unfun, monotonous way.
My concern is now that this game was never MEANT to be a full, decent, fun, and enjoyable game. It was never MEANT to improved and have it's issues fixed.
So what is it ACTUALLY supposed to be?
A low effort, poorly made attempt to make money. An overpriced game with little to no content, still broken, watered down and poorly gameplay, and instead of FIXING anything....
They add DLC to try to get more money, because it's got the RWBY name, and that 'automatically' makes it all okay.
My recommendation? Don't buy any of it, don't buy the game, and never buy any game from RoosterTeeth ever again.
That includes to poor looking Tabletop game they just announced, it's gonna be a repeat of this mess of a game.
And if you don't believe, explain why RoosterTeeth stopped playing this game extremely quickly. They know how crap it is, even they don't wanna play it. But they'll play it a LITTLE bit, just to help sell it.

"Revolution Ace" is a great indie shoot 'em up similar to the classic "Raptor: Call of the Shadows". You fit your ship with a number of weapons to battle hordes of air and ground targets. Collect scraps to upgrade your weapons and gain experience to level up and learn perks for additional bonuses.

Infested Planet is a deceptively simple, surprisingly challenging, and shockingly well-balanced action strategy game.
The main game involves a pulpy and thin, but well-written story in which humans are attempting to take over and control a planet infested by aliens. In order to do this, you must wipe the aliens from existence. Missions are broken up into three different types, although all of them are variations on the same theme in which you control a squad of marine riflemen dropped in an arena, and your goal is to stem the endless flow of aliens from their hives, destroy their hives, and capture the control points they sit atop, gaining experience points with which you can upgrade your units, build technology to improve your quality of life, or build defensive placements to protect your strongpoints.
This is an oversimplified description, but you get the idea.
The genius of this game, and what makes it stand apart from other similar games is the beautiful balance that allows for a free-flowing and dynamic pace, and the wonderful customisation options that allow you to change and adapt your team to the evolving circumstances. In most games of this type, if you're losing, you've lost, and the back-end of such battles mainly involve you delaying the inevitable (think Age of Empires when you've only got civilians left). But Infested Planet is so well-balanced that even losing doesn't mean you've lost, it simply means you've got an uphill fight to win. There are certain points at the highest difficulty levels that you can find yourself in stalemate, but the next match you play will never take place in the same space, so it's rare that you find yourself in a truly unwinnable state.
The simplest missions involve you taking enemy emplacements one at a time and shoring up your stongpoints so they aren't overrun while you turn your back. However, most maps will have a randomised series of channels and conduits through which the aliens can travel, meaning that while you may be able to defend one path, the enemy can often flank from a different junction, or split themselves into two streams of attack and overwhelm your defenses. You only have a limited pool of points to spend, so in deciding whether to place defenses or to upgrade your men you're inadvertently deciding the enemy's course of action in the game to come. And it's all well and good to be on top of things, but the game reveals its secret genius when you're slowly being beaten. Even if the enemy destroy your emplacements and set up a new hive, the ebb and flow of the game allows you to retreat and regroup, scraping back from the verge of defeat to overcome the challenge with the right decisions and skill. Even if your last control point is destroyed, that's not to say that you can't move elsewhere, take an underdeveloped enemy point and start making your way back up the map again. The genius of the game's balancing is most notable in the raid missions (repeatable, randomised side-missions that you can complete to earn cash and buy more upgrades). Raid missions are set to a timer that increases every time you take a strong point. These games reward quick initial action and displays of brute force, however, in this blitzkreig style of play you inevitably leave a trail of undefended strongpoints that are soon attacked by the enemy. These battles are often desperate, and I've played single games that have lasted 20-30 minutes and have led me all over the map, creating new strongholds on all sides as the old ones are destroyed, and taking and retaking control points that are gained and lost in equal measure. Unlike traditional RTS games, no one point in the map is 'your area' or 'their area' - you must take what you can and build from there, be opportunistic but tactical, because in Infested Planet, you haven't lost the battle until you've lost the battle.
To be honest, I can't believe I have so much to say about this game, because it doesn't look like much before you play it. But I'm greatly surprised by how good it is. I got it in a Humble Bundle and it was incredibly good value, but I recommend it for retail price if you're into action-strategy, or dynamic capture-defend/RTS type games.

Free to play done right (and no it's not pay to win either :D ). Don't listen to folks who have one or two hours logged, you really can get a lot out of this game if you can put in some time and a little money. After all we all put time into games and some are bloody expensive!
LoTRO is the least frustrating free to play experience I've had as Turbine gives you a taste of everything. They don't lock out 99% of the game. Completing 'deeds' (challenges like kill X amount of goblins) will earn you Turbine points for micro transactions in the LoTRO store. With enough time and patience its possible to buy several store items from in game rewards.
If you spend even the minimum on Turbine points (£5) you get upgraded to premium account status. That gives you two more character slots per server and removes the gold cap.
However if you're aiming not to spend anything at all you can't have a job or life and do that. That is some serious grinding. You'll also HAVE to spend time grinding the Turbine points if you don't even want to spend a fiver to remove the gold cap, as two gold is not nearly enough in game currency later on. Good thing is that before you remove the cap all money you earn gets saved in an overflow wallet ready for when you do gain access to it.
WHAT FREE TO PLAYER'S GET
The epic quests that make up the main story line are mostly free (to continue it you need to buy the expansions).
Player housing is free. Some items used to decorate can be bought in the store but most you get for free.
Some trait slots are free. These are different to trait trees (the skill trees you spec into to get your abilities). You gain most of these by deeds and they can be slotted to give either passive buffs or more skills.
Steeds. Getting your horse/pony/goat (can only ride goats in Moria) is a free option but the riding skill itself is not free. Don't throw your arms up in protest yet. With small effort you can get the 95 Turbine points you need to purchase this skill. Most deeds that award Turbine points (and most of them do) are worth between 5-10 points. Some deeds are worth more. It's easy to get (VIP's get a free quest that grants the skill). Some steeds are available in the store. With the Rohan expansion you can ride a war steed for mounted combat and customize it's appearance but that can get bloody expensive.
The Shire, Bree, Ered Luin, Lone Lands and Celondim areas are free. Free, Premium and VIP players all have to buy the expansions, there are five in total. There are quest packs for other regions you can buy in game from about 595 Turbine points. You can travel to the areas you don't have the quest packs for, you just can't do quests there. It's important to note that free content (excluding skirmishes) drys up around level 35-38. Moria, the first expansion is best entered around level 50 so you'll be needing a quest pack to fill in the gap.
Some skirmishes and repeatable instances are free.
Joining a crafting guild is free but you need to pay for full access to it. You don't need be in a guild but it gives you access to far more recipes than you'd have otherwise. Having full access is a distinct advantage as there is far more choice.
All but the Warden (one of the tanks) and Rune-Keeper (DPS and healing, not the only DPS or healing class in game) classes are free. The Rune-Keeper is well worth it, lots of ranged DPS magic fun. The Warden is more of a secondary tank with combos (called gambits) and other tricks thrown in.
The fishing hobby (the only hobby) is free. You can catch fish to display in your home or to cook if you or any of your alts have the right crafting profession.
The in game mailing system is free and is very useful to post items to your alts, not just other players.
Creating a guild (known as a kinship here) is free (well it would be stupid otherwise lets face it).
Free daily silver hobbit present.
WHAT VIP's GET
If you go the subscription route you become a VIP. VIP's pay the following:
$15 a month
$29.97 for 3 months
$59.94 for 6 months
$99.99 for 12 months
For your chosen cost/sub length you get:
Mailbox field access
Access all character trait slots
500 Turbine points per month
Access all quest packs and skirmishes that are not a part of expansions
Unlimited chat
20 Slots of shared wardrobe space (this enables you to cosmetically equip gear on any character)
Additional inventory slots
Custom character portrait frame
Daily +100% XP (for 30% of a level)
Free weekly gold hobbit present
Access all monster classes (Monster play is mostly PvP)
Access all crafting guilds
No currency cap
Maximum auction house listings
The most major benefits are the quest packs, skirmishes, 500 free Turbine points, crafting guilds and monster classes. That gives you a ton of extra content.
PLAYING THE GAME
Choose race of men, hobbit, dwarf or elves, then pick your class. The usual DPS, tank and healer classes are present, along with the squishy pet class (Lore Master, that does more than just use pets). Next is the choice of where your character comes from. Choosing this region doesn't determine more than a preset skin tone and hair colour (which you can change). Choose your hair style, facial features etc, pick a suitable name and away you go. The level cap for characters is 100.
The tutorial is easy and makes it clear how to use your abilities. A nice touch is the tutorial skip option available at character creation if you've already done it before.
The usual MMO type features are here. Choose a crafting profession to make useful items along the way, level up and upgrade your weapons and armour, collect type quests, kill type quests, quests in instances as well as those in the open world. Most are set in the open world. There are also repeatable daily quests in certain areas. The interface makes it easy to see who is in your area if you want to start a fellowship (team). There are different instance quests called skirmishes. These can be repeated and are a bit more entertaining than the usual quests as they have a few different objectives and ambushes. You gain 'marks' for successful objectives as well as completing the skirmish itself. These can be completed solo or in a fellowship. Turn the marks in for rewards.
When you start to level up you'll be getting trait points. Each class has three trait trees that will determine specifically how your chosen class plays and what skills you gain. Some skills however are not determined by which trees or how far into them you spec as they are standard skills. The Guardian (one of two tank classes) for example has a tanking, DPS and two handed tanking tree choices. You can choose to specialize in one tree or spread yourself a bit thinner into others as well.
Being an MMO the graphics are not top notch but they are beautiful. Water effects are nice.
USEFUL INFO ON CRASHES
Many players have suffered from constant crashes. Check out post #11 in this thread;
That may solve your issues. Also if you have Pando Media Booster installed get rid of it! Not only is it pointless it can slow LoTRO to the point it crashes. Both these solutions worked for me and my wife.
Yet again this is one of the vast amount of games these days that has annoying bugs. Hopefully you won't suffer them or at least be able to sort them with the above solutions. Also some of the store items are far too pricey (extra bags and anything steed related in particular).
There's a lot of nice places to explore and plenty to do once you have a stable game. There are many more features I've not covered such as raids, PvP and monster play, not to mention the legendary weapon system and your free hobbit present you get each day. Have a bit of patience and you'll love Middle Earth. :)

Probably like many people, I first heard about this game through Totalbiscuit and his high praise of it as his favorite game of all time. I don't always agree with him, but I do respect his critique, and I figured anything he held in such high regard was at least worth a look (especially during a sale). I was not expecting the game to become my own favorite game, and... it didn't. But what it did become was a defining experience that I will always remember playing.
For the vast majority of the game, I thought that it was just going to be a cute puzzle game to me. There were narrative sections where I knew I was supposed to be invested, and to some extent I was, but it wasn't hitting me at my core. The puzzles were clever, the setting was interesting, and I wanted to see how things would turn out, but I wouldn't have called it amazing. I would have called it good. Not great. Something that I didn't regret playing, but wasn't going to be something I came back to when I thought of my greatest videogame experiences.
But then the last twenty minutes of the game happened.
Suddenly everything that the game had been building up mechanically and narratively tied together. Simply put, there are very few games that tie together story and gameplay mechanics and use them so perfectly like Brothers did during its epilogue. That is when I was geniuely touched by the narrative. That is when the game won over my heart. Usually mechanics are simply used to make the story move on. This game turned the very act of pressing the buttons to play the game into a major narrative point. It fused watching the story and interacting with it by utilizing the very things the player had been doing the whole time playing it. This is when I saw a great game.
It's not perfect. Some of the systems could use more explanation in the early-game and sometimes the puzzles can get borderline repetitive. But by the end you'll realize that they always knew where they were going. I truly wish that all games could access the depth that this one does. This game stands as a flagship of what videogaming can do at its best. It should be a game that others are compared to. It's not my favorite game, but it doesn't have to be either.

Don't waste your time with cash grab sword and boards, this game is infinitely better (if you can stand dated graphics.

I'm a huge fan of Deus Ex, and given the initial mixed reviews, I was worried. However, having finally finished the game, I feel like I can really give this game an overwhemingly positive review.
MD is in no way a perfect game. It improves on Human Revolution in many ways but suffers from issues of its own.
The good:
* More Deus Ex. I seriously love the series, and this game didn't feel like a cash-grab. Its well polished, and Eidos obviously took a lot of care in crafting it. That being said, the DLC system *is* a cash grab and leaves a lot to be desired.
* Level design. Very well thought out levels. As always, stealth is the way to go, and is a blast. Lots of information and interesting bits hidden in the sidequests and random locations
* Music. Maybe not as memorable as DX1 or HR, but extremely well done. Even the main menu music was epic.
The bad:
* Denuvo. Seriously, SE get it the ♥♥♥♥ together. Denuvo is horrible, and you shouldn't be required to be online to play a single player game
* DLC system. The pay2win dlc microtransactions are trash.
* Story. Obviously cut to allow for another game. Story was not as strong as previous installments, but still gripping and epic in its own sense. Enjoyed cameos of characters from previous games. However, some characters weren't very fleshed out and by the end I still wasn't fully sure of their role or purpose.
* Performance. I'm not expecting to play it on ultra-high, but the game just didn't feel completely optimized. Nixxes did a good job, but the day one CTD should not have happened. Post-patch, crashes and low framerate drops are only an occasional annoyance.
Overall I'm happy. There are some inexcusable issues with the game, but DX:MD is a game I see myself playing again and again, and it rightfully earns the Deus Ex title. The unfortunate issue now is that we must wait 4-5 years for the next installment.

That's really the only word to describe this. It's a severe letdown, and honestly there isn't $60 worth there.
Everything is far less memorable overall. The art direction is far less distinctive and inspired, and far harder on the eyes. Whereas HUman Revolution really did let you feel engrossed in a cyberpunk world, for whatever reason this world just felt a lot less immersive and worth caring about.
The plot and storyline are a step down. Events, characters, and dialog are less memorable, and it just feels plain shorter too. You travel to fewer distinctive locales, a vast majority of the time is spent in the main city, and the other locales you travel to are pretty short and small on their own.
The game as a whole is short feeling. You'll look at my 44.5 hours at the time of posting this review and say "That's pretty long for a linear game!" No it's not, that's mostly just loading saves up again.
The side quests are easily the best and most interesting parts of the game.
The graphical fidelity is pretty dang impressive, but without the art direction to back it up.
Optimization is terrible. There is nonexistent SLI or Crossfire scaling. The game frequently uses 50-80% of all cores of a i7-6850K while failing to maintain anywhere near 60 FPS at 4K on a GTX 1080 (or two). On top of this, there have been various well known progress-stopping crash bugs in the game too, hopefully they have been fixed by now.
The gameplay itself is the only thing improved over Human Revolution. Things are more streamlined, intuitive and the maps themselves are generally pretty nicely designed with lots of alternate pathways and secrets to uncover.
The trend of big AAA letdowns continues.
Verdict:
Wait for a sale. ($30 recommended)
EDIT:
Oh, and a cliffhanger ending. In a Deus Ex game. That might have something to do with their intentions with this.

Okay wow this is an unexpectedly good game. Bought it randomly for $0.25 (ironically like inserting a single quarter into an old timey arcade machine).
First of all my background: I played ~300 hours of Raptor Call of the Shadows when I was growing up (shareware version from a magazine, then I bought the full version that Apogee mailed to me on floppies).
If you loved Raptor you'll love this.
If you saw screenshots of Raptor without understanding it, or prefer Japanese-style bullet hell shooters, or side scrollers, you might not like this.
The tactical combat is almost exactly like Raptor, right down to most enemies shooting yellow orbs at you (and the "wave" gun and auto-targetting laser). You will take damage, that's unavoidable, so shield/armor management is an important part of each level (just like Raptor). You can equip multiple weapons with vastly different weapon patterns. Target priority and order is very important, as is deciding between air and ground. Lots of neat enemies and some fun levels with your plane flying higher/lower or the view rotating.
First some complaints I read, but didn't experience. Not sure if the dev just fixed them over time or if the original issue was wrong. Either way:
- Grinding - There was grinding in Raptor. If you don't think so you didn't play Elite difficulty, where you had to farm the lower difficulties for money and upgrades. Even before the final Outer Regions waves you'd farm the earlier levels that dropped shields to have more than the max. So redoing some missions or a bit of skirmish here shouldn't be unfamiliar or unfun.
- Performance - Ran fine for me. I didn't have an fps counter on, so maybe the framerate dropped, but projectiles were still dodge-able and there was no visible stutter. When playing the graphics actually look better than the screenshots.
- Slowness - For the screen/view size the plane is almost exactly as fast as Raptor. Again, expectations.
- Anemic Weapons - Depending on your loadout you might have to stay on a target for a bit. There are few one shots here. No surprises considering how long even late-game Raptor took to kill some enemies. This means you need to get used to how many shots it takes to kill an enemy, and not waste more than that.
- Hitboxes - Your plane/ship seems accurately represented, and I've dodged shots by what felt like pixels. Sometimes enemies have deceiving hitboxes in regards to their shape, but that's pretty rare.
- PhysX - Someone mentioned needing older Nvidia drivers for this game. I ran it fine with the latest drivers at the time.
So basically a lot of the complaints can be explained as: that's how Raptor did it.
If I DID have a complaint with the game it's that incoming enemies don't have shadows, which makes it a bit hard to be pre-firing at the right area. The backgrounds can similarly be a bit distracting/overwhelming at times. And the weapon and equipment could use better ordering or sorting in the shop. Not anything game breaking though.
But that is balanced but a dozen pros, a few of which I'll list here:
- Random Levels - I would have killed for this feature as a kid. You can choose a seed and get a random level complete with a boss. So fun and so replayable, and really adds enjoyment to any "grinding" aspect. In addition the campaign is 20 levels, plus another 4 unique plus 8 types of random for skirmish.
- Shield Recharge - Shields have a recharge delay and rate which kicks in once you start shooting. Managing this is a lot of fun and adds a new dynamic.
- Enemies Return - If you don't kill an enemy they come back later (and reward less scrap on death). So levels quickly spiral if you miss kills.
- Ground and Air - Very fun switching between the two, and it's a bit more seamless than Raptor where you'd have to swap active weapons. Here you just hold "Shift" to fire any available ground weapons.
- Builds - With perks and such varied weapons you get a lot of choice to each playthrough. You could focus on Plasma, or maybe go for rebounding missiles, or rapid firing machine guns.
- Modes - Some really unique and imaginative modes outside the main campaign, such as competitive "Battle Chains". Great amount of content for such an inexpensive game.
In summary the best way to describe this game is an underrated gem and spiritual successor to Raptor. I'm sad for the dev that it didn't get more initial praise and seems to be misunderstood by the majority of the community.

You're not a god, you're a mayor with your hands tied who has to answer to the city council and the citizens. It's a challenge. Good luck!
Urban Empire has elements of Democracy, Banished, and a little bit of SimCity. But with a lot more variables.
Yes, you can create districts, plop train staions and ports, or turn on the gas and electricity. But you're not doing any of that without the votes. You need to make decisions that gain you support of the councillors. While making decisions that are prosperous for the citizens and businesses. It's a balancing act.
Although there are several pages of data to ponder while planning your decisions, the feedback is not explained very well. However, after playing more than two or three hours you start to see how it all works together.
The graphics and sound are very nice. The UI is well organized and easy to navigate. I have experienced no bugs and it runs fine on my four year old laptop.
So for those who are patient, with an interest in politics and city planning, give it a try!

By far the best story-telling in a game I have ever experienced. The game mechanics are simple but innovative, with the player using only 6 buttons to control both characters and the camera. At first controlling both brothers feels unusual, but by the end of the game it's second nature.
A variety of landscapes are presented with incredible beauty. It's a game that will certainly provoke your emotions, with moments that are both heart-warming and heart-wrenching. It's this balance between joy and tragedy that makes the story so compelling.
For a game without any intelligable dialogue, the story is told effectively thorugh more subtle means. Without revealing any spoilers, the ending of the game in particular finds a way to present an incredible depth of character development given the short length of the game, and does so directly through the game's control system. This is one of the many highlights of a very artistic and unique game, and I can't think of any other game where the player feels such an emotional connection with the story simply by pressing a button on the controller.
I don't think I've ever cried playing a game before. This game however, was an exception...

I often find myself disinterested in strongly story-focused videogames. If I wanted to read or watch a story unfold, I would pick up a book or a movie, respectively.
But I completely adored Brothers.
Why do we love stories? Personally I think it's because we look to stories for reflection of our experiences, and we love to be emotionaly manipulated. Brothers will make you feel all kinds of emotions, leading you to associate your controler's sticks and buttons with it's characters. I felt commited not to let my fingers slip in dangerous situations, even though I have hand problems and it hurt my wrists.
Brothers is also fundamentally a classic fairytale - it's magical and grim; it's characters are confronted with hardships that are often unfair, and everything it has to say about human condition feels very true. You will encounter all kinds of situations that hint at the wider world and what it is like, but without explicit lore, you can only guess at what is going on. After all, your characters are children and even the older one barely understands how the world works.
I would rather end the review here, than risk spoiling this amazing game for you. Let me just reiterate that it touched me deeply and I honestly would recommend it to basically anyone.

If you're fan of the 1980s, you won't be disappointed in this Farcry 3 spinoff. In this game, you'll experience chessy, but great one-liner dialogue that are actually movie refencres of the 1980s, explosive action-packed storyline, dinosaurs that shoot lasers from their eyes, and play as an badass cyborg that is the best of the best... Sergeant Rex Power Colt!

Awesomesauce!
Set in 2007 but with an 80s look and feel, you are Rex Power Colt, a Mark IV Cyber Commando (best guy in the universe), whose mission is to stop his mentor gone rogue, Sloan. The story is silly and fun, full of jokes and references to 80s movies and modern video games such as Alien and Assassin's Creed. The humor in the game is so cheesy it actually is pretty funny.
The game's mechanics are built upon the already great Far Cry 3 mechanics with a few twists of Cyber Powers and Sci-Fi stuff which is pretty cool. To run faster than a car and jump from the top of a mountain only to hear your Cyber legs laughing at the laws of physics :)
The game has a huge map (roughly 40% of Far Cry 3's map) filled with outposts to overtake, many collectibles, and Dino Dragons to fight (Dragon + Lizard beasts that shoot lasers)
The soundtrack is easily a 10/10.

This game deserves every glowing review it has ever received. The quality of design here is absolutely mind-blowing. The character design, the voices, the 'script', the music and all of the ambient sounds and world design that bring this beautiful fantasy planet to life; everything is knitted together so tightly that you will fall in love with this game within the first 5 minutes.
This is a short game, but it does more in 3 hours than most games can do in 10. It is an emotional ride with some humour along the way. All of the puzzles are simple and the controls are surprisingly intuitive, so the pace of the story is never interrupted. I can't think of a single negative comment to make about this game, I cannot recommend it enough.

Let me start off by saying this is an amazing game.  I'm a harsh critic and if this game sucked, I would be the first to complain about it trust me.  I've read through some of the reviews and I'm confused, which game did you play?
- There is one city in the game, ok but its a rich environment, not a giant cardboard contentless city claiming to be open world like some other games I won't mention here where you have miles and miles of vistas you can't interact with.  This is a smaller city but its truely an open world.  There is allot going on.  There is allot you can interact with.  Sometimes quality is better than quantity.  They put allot of detail into it.  Occasionaly you will be sent out to do missions in other maps and return to the city.  Although there is one city, there will be times when the city takes place at night and it will become a different environment, also very detailed and rich with content.  They even give you a cool apartment with some storage.
- There are story elements everywhere.  You can follow missions and side quests or just explore on you're own and run into the situations anyways. Example, hear a conversation about some criminal activity or read it on a computer or a note then follow the clues and solve the crime.  Or, explore a random location and oops, walk into the crime situation anyways and deal with it on the fly.
- You can play this game anyway you want which I love.  Go in like terminator tearing apart anyone in your way or go in like Sherlock and talk your way through it.  Do a side mission, solve a murder mystery, bust some drug dealers or don't.  Stick with the main mission.  Solve problems in multiple ways, not linear.
-  You will not beat this game quickly unless you cheat with trainers.  It is designed to be played without cheating.  If you do, the game will suck for you and you won't experience the story.  I strongly recommend no matter how much it hurts, don't go in with unlimited ammo and blaze through the levels or you will be disappointed.  It's like fast forwarding through a movie.  The point of this game is to follow clues, listen to conversations while sneaking, hacking emails and finding your way around.  You can snipe your way through, smash your way through, hack your way through or talk your way through most situations.  Stop and think, delete the trainer and stay off of cheat engine!  It's more fun when you play as intended.
- Forget the micro transactions.  Square made them do it.  The developers put plenty of items in game all over the city.  There is stuff everywhere, in the buildings, outside, in the sewers, and on the missions where you leave the city.  You can craft items.  You can sell the tons of loot you will find at shops.  You can buy in game what you need from the credits you will earn from selling loot.  You can buy praxis, find praxis or earn praxis by leveling up.  They made sure you would never need the micro transactions.
This is not grand theft auto.  This is not watch dogs.  This is you in a small town in the future fighting oppression and solving a main mystery as well as several smaller mysteries at you're own pace.  Enjoy it because games like this are rare.

I love city builders. However, games like Cities: Skyline gave you complete unilateral rule like a dictator. Tropico was almost the same replacing certain buildings with the idea of zoning that are prevalent in the other games. What I truly wanted in a game as complex as Cities: Skyline was a council that lorded and hounded at every decision I made through the giant political machine hovering over my fair city.
Urban Empire was supposed to bridge that gap between city builder and political simulator. Marketed as “Be a Mayor Player”, whatever that meant, you had to develop the city through different eras and leaders through both physical development and the political challenges. You had to develop the city’s society through services while balancing the budget with the city council’s eye on your every move.
Oh, what fun I will have!
Or, was it a disappointment?
Barring you the description of how the “Wheel of Life” (supply/demand for societal expansion) works, let me tell what worked and didn’t.
I love the idea of a city council. Frankly, the only reason for me to get this game is because of the idea of city development through voting in a city council. The simulated cityfolk are still allowed to partake in the city’s market economy, but certain services in the Wheel of Life requires the city council’s intervention. Services like fire stations, parks, clinics, opera houses, schools and workshops require that the council vote over the improvement.
I also love that the city council has era-appropriate parties occupying the council. My personal favorites were the existence of three parties: The Freedom Party (aka the Nazi Party), The Pacifist Party (super left-wing and liberal), and the Green Party (same like Pacifist Party, but more environmental). Political maneuvering with various parties with different ideologies isn’t a walk in the park. Liberal policies will be unacceptable to some parties, but with the correct development and policies placed into the city early in the game, you can have conservative parties agreeing with leftists liberal policies. The game’s city council rewards players who know how to political maneuver themselves through the era with the easement of passing legislation.
However, even with such “coded rewards” written into the game, it suffers from a very counterintuitive user interface. My anecdote is with the idea of banning prostitution and the failed revocation of that law. While the game works on a dual axis binary of conservative/liberal and left/right which works to describe a political ideology, binary shouldn’t be used for your mayor’s decision on certain laws. Like real life, a law passes or fails through the vote of the city council.
However, your mayor can only push for a law ahead. If you were to personally revoke a law and convince political parties, they will not push for the revocation. What needs to be worked on are the clarification for the poltical choices of Pleading, Demanding, or Threaten a political party. The developers need to add an additional button to show whether a mayor is pushing to support or oppose if the player makes a mistake.
Speaking of mistakes, the performance of this game slows after building a lot of districts. As my trams in some districts zigzag their way through town, the scrolling speed to and fro the city is hampered as building textures load slowly or having serious graphical glitches. The performance has been problem since Tropico 4. Kalypso and the development team at Reborn Games need to calibrate and fix these issues if they were to create sequels. I understand the simulation games are the ones to usually suffer performance issues (like Cities XL), but albeit the game being playable, it becomes an absolute dread as the game stutters dealing with new simulations to compute. Mind you, I was also running my Performance Monitor next to my game and it is a RAM-eater, taking up 7 GBs of memory to run this game, even after adjusting graphic qualities to its lowest.
In conclusion, the only reason I am recommending this game is due to its uniqueness of it being both a city-builder and a political simulator. However, I would love the developers to start thinking of this game like a Paradox Interactive game, giving us greater freedom in creating a character and the political situation around the player. I would like them to solve the major performance issues that made this game somewhat unplayable in future eras of the game. Personally, I would return to this game again once they have patched some of the performance and UI issues.

Unfortunately for me, the day before Urban Empire released, a problem with my graphics drivers was uncovered. This means that I had to play Urban Empire using my crappy integrated Intel graphics card and was unable to get more than 10 FPS at the lowest settings.
Despite this, I played Urban Empire for 6 hours on release date with no more than 10 FPS. I have thoroughly enjoyed my time with Urban Empire and I am sure that I will put many more hours into this games (regardless of FPS).
If you have played the Tropico series, Cities: Skylines and/or Democracy 3 then you will probably like this game as it is essentially a combination of the three.

Urban Empire  is, unfortunately, not what one could expect from a city management strategy/simulation title of its price. Gameplay is incredibly shallow and repetitive, decisions and mechanics seems trivial, and the narrative is far too simple and sparse to compensate. In general, there is a painful lack of objectives or feedback from the game for any given strategy or outcome- just a quick blip of an event that adds or subtracts stats that have little to no bearing on your experience. You can run your city into the ground, or meticulously balance your budget by hand, but either way, nothing changes in terms of challenge or reward.  A sandbox without the toys, if you will.
On the whole, the game feels like a very early release, minus the performance issues.

Really loved the depth in this game ; lots of choice and a lot of political realism ; what I would love to see for an expansion would be more scenarios such as the WWI period and the revolutions that followed.  Maybe stuff in response to the Great Depression and World War Two.  Also I take it the early game is based on the Austro-Hungarian Empire.  Historically the Austrian Social Democrats were Marxists until they were crushed by fascism.  BTW I'm only up to the 1920s so far - so I don't know what comes after.  Sometimes I think I'd rather a scenario based on leading a Party rather than a single Mayor ; But who am I to complain?  This game fixes lots of the problems I once associated with the Genre.  A progressive welfare state is viable without ideological assumptions in the scripting which rule out social democratic strategies.  I really hope expansions and mods follow this ; Its really good so far - but I'm sure it could be better.  One last thing that annoyed me:  I hung on as Mayor in the 1920s but I can't seem to shake the right-wing parties ; I'm still getting good legislation through ; But it would be nice to have strategies capable of turning the tide in favor of the left-wing parties...  BTW the Communists also often play a spoiling role early on - which is not historical...  The self-proclaimed Communists parties arose in response to the split in European social democracy on account of World War One....

Hello and welcome to Scraps, a project I´m following since a year or two and I actually bought today because I forget everything that comes in my mind in 2 minutes. And compared to its state two years ago, this has actually taken pretty big steps. Only the good parts didn´t change at all, e.g. the gameplay itself.
wot is dis?
This actually is one example of a yet unnamed genre, I call it Build and Fight, call it how you want. So the genre of Robocraft and Homebrew (since they added guns now with the latest update). Gameplay is simple: Build stuff, destroy stuff, collect stuff and repair and build stuff with your collected stuff. ez.
build stuff?
Yes. You get a nice range of parts and then you just build a vehicle out of it. How it´s used and built is up to you, whether you want a lightweight ram with dozens of engines doing 400 km/h or a giant a55 tank with dozens of cannons or something rather normal, depends on your imagination. Building itself is really easy, but also depends on physics.
Remember: Even though you can put enough weapons on your vehicle to eradicate complete europe within seconds, you can´t expect your vehicle to do 150 km/h, like in Robocraft. The limit of how much you can put on your vehicle doesn´t depend on your player rank, but on the servers scrap limit. So, compared to Robocraft, this is balanced very well. Also, you can tune the suspension on your vehicle to edit the handling and center of mass.
range of parts?
You start off with a chassis and a cockpit. You can choose between three chassis yet, a small lightweight one for cheap and light vehicles, a normal one and a big one with enough space for at least 3 million engines and cannons. Then you build on energy generators (because guns need energy to work) and batteries, cooling parts  (because guns get hot while firing), armor to not die the second you get out of the garage, engines, guns and extensions to get more space you need for another 1 million engines.
can i play dis on my potato?
YES YOU CAN. JUST DO IT. (sry)
If you compare this to other games based on Unity, this game has excellent performance and looks fairly nice.
Any cons?
Except having almost no players, not really. This is Early Access, so you can´t expect this to be 100% bug free, but so far In the last year I played the demos of Scraps, I haven´t encountered one bug.
The End?
In my opinion, this is the greatest example of this Build and Fight genre. Robocraft is nice, but these idiotic rank limits and nonexistence of balance are really unnecessary. And to be honest, no one knows how long it will take until Homebrew gets into a well playable state. Buy this. Please. We need players here. For real.

♥ You can do anything.
Want to have a polygamist family? Want to roll around in money? Want to travel to Egypt, steal treasure from tombs, and have an affair?
With Sims 3, you can. If you only have the base game and none of the DLC's, you can easily get mods for the game that will add an endless amount of things: instant money, incest, custom jobs, etc. With Sims you
have the character live the life you imagine for them.
♥ Relationships.
This is by far why I've played Sims 3 for as many hours as I've had. In Sims 3 you can find a boyfriend, marry him, cheat with his brother, and divorce - all in the same day. Sims 3 doesn't have morals and doesn't want you to have them either.
For that reason, you can cheat as much as you want, have as many kids as you want, or embrace the single, celebrity rockstar life. If you want to have an arch nemesis and revel in kicking their trash can, you can.
Or you can be the seemly modest grandmother who writes erotic tales at night and takes care of her grandchildren, plays chess with her husband at the park, and bask in your retirement during the day.
♥ Everything is up to you.
From the design of the house to the look of your Sim to their likes and dislikes, you control anything and everything. You aren't limited in any area for even their needs you can control. If you use a cheat code, you can easily make their needs (hunger, sleep, etc) to 100% meaqning you'll have more time to focus on the fun aspects of their life.
With Sims, the character is entirely in your hands.
✘ This game lags.
A lot. It's known for crashing without warning, freezing at any vital moment, and can be quite fussy to run. I've learned that when you first launch the game - DON'T DO ANYTHING. Just let it play through the cutscene and go to the main menu. Don't try to skip it, don't try to rush it.
The same goes for when it freezes and lags.
Otherwise it's going to sulk and quit on you just when your Sim becomes famous or is about to have their baby.
✘ The base designs are...bleh.
I used to think they were amazing - the blocky hair, the ill fitting clothes, the ugly looking earrings. However once I discovered the world of mods, I learned how awful the base items are. Brawlhalla is Smash Bros. with all of the excess mechanics and stage randomness removed.
The goal of the game is the same as Smash: knock your opponent off the edge of the screen. However, it has taken out a lot of the things that made Smash so difficult to learn in recent years and what is left is an elegant game that is easy to understand but hard to master.
: The first thing to notice is how accurate and precise the movement is. The movement in other games of this style is often very floaty, making it hard to position your character correctly. In Brawlhalla the movement is 1:1 and easy to predict.
: The controls are mercifully simple: weak attack, heavy attack, jump, throw item, and dodge (and taunt). The key difference between Brawlhalla and other games of this type is the weapon system. When unarmed every character has the same moves, but when you pick up a weapon powerup you will get one of two weapons (randomly). These weapons are set per character, and the light attacks are the same for every character.
There are combos, but they are limited to strings of three attacks at the absolute most. This places more of an emphasis on positioning and correct skill usage - though to be fair, there are a few difficult combos that are essential to very high level play.
: The differences between characters come down to three "signature" moves per weapon, and different stat configurations (armor, speed, etc.). While this probably sounds like a negative, what this means is that it is very easy to reach a point where you can play almost any character, because all you need to do is master the basic attacks of each weapon and then test out a character's six signature moves. Even better, the signature moves often function in similar ways: no direction + signature is usually an anti air, for example.
: Apart from the weapons, there are exactly four items. The bomb detonates on contact, the landmine sticks to a surface and will blow up when a player approaches, and the spike ball is a projectile that is reusable and does a high amount of knockback. There is also a horn, which can be blown to summon a fireball and carry in a weapon for you, or it can be thrown as a projectile.
All four of these items can be caught out of mid air if your timing is good, and most of them can be used to set up elaborate traps or combos; bounce the bomb against the ground and then kick your opponent into it as it arcs downward.
: If you do want to grind out hours in training mode, this game offers you lots of data. You can see the hitboxes of any move, and even slow down and replay each frame of a move to see where the hitboxes and hurtboxes are at any given point. There is the standard combo and damage counter as well.
: All of this is to say that this is a simplified game in all of the best ways. Sticking to a small set of items and reducing the control barrier makes Brawlhalla a joy to play and improve at. The complexity comes from learning how its design elements interact, more so than grinding out hours in training mode.
This recommendation is really for people who are not a fan of the increasing complexity of Smash Bros. Fans of that series may be reading this and thinking that all of my positives sound like negatives. If that sounds like you, try it out anyway, it's free.
Lastly, I want to say that the way the developers interact with the community is great. Their patch notes are delivered with good explanations for why they made each change, and they take both game feel and win ratio into account when balancing characters. They update weekly, or nearly weekly, the servers are usually good, and new characters come out regularly.

A really great game. I may not have a lot of time on Steam but I beat the game on GOG a while back and because I got a key for it from the Humble Bundle, figure I may as well give it another playthrough. First off, I love the theme of the game. It lets you feel like you're fighting in the movies of Aliens or Starship Troopers, fighting off the seemingly endless flood of bugs. Personally, it seems to feel the game is still a little too easy even on hard, so I'd suggest you play through the campaign on that to start. The HB doesn't say it, but it also comes with the Trickster's DLC which helps boost up the gameplay, but not the PLanetary Campaign, so you won't have the deep replayablity.
The gameplay itself has lots of options you unlock and because you're never just fighting down a single hallway, you have to plan out your path. The Swarm will constantly evolve new things to try to stop you and you're often going to have to adapt to what the evemy is throwing at you, be it stronger defenses, longer range, new enemies, and so on. The AI is also pretty good at finding flanks as well, if you try to defend a direct path from the swarm, expect them just walk down a different path.
Now you may find it a little hard to find $15 worth of game here, I'd base it more around $10 for the base game. If you can get the game and all the DLC for $10, you'll get good value out of it. If you're going to grab it from the HB for 1$, expect the cops to show up because it's a steal at that price.

This game can only be appreciated by fans of the show. Unfortunately, I have never watched the show. The character models are very basic, as to be expected looking at the source material, but the UI, combat system, voice acting, enemy design, and map design follow suit.
The sound effects sound like stock ones and often are reused or dont fit the purpose they were selected for. The voice actors are mediocre at best and they recorded very few lines in the first place, leading to certain, commonly used moves only having one line used making them grating to use.
There is a major jarring difference between the low detail in character and enemy models and the decently clean and detailed world textures, making the people in it feel even more plain. This is especially bad when the enemies are only really differentiated by the few different details.
The maps are not just linear, which is not in itself a problem, but they LOOK linear, often being hallways made by fences or canyons connecting empty or mostly empty circular areas for wave based combat.

All in all the game feels like an alpha for something else. As a matter of fact, this seems like a very similar game to the new Nier, granted that game has a bit more focus on the bullets than the melee. If your absolutely desperate for more RWBY, then go ahead, but otherwise its a waste of money.

With the WB's reversal, and their new decision to release KP2, MKXL, and further support for the PC version, I am restoring my original review of the game from December of 2015.  It may be edited later, when I obtain KP2, to detail further information within:
Yes I recommend this game, for the very simple reason that I enjoy it.
Now, you have to bear in mind that I give little care for online multiplayer in fighting games. In my experience, it has always been a lag filled waste of time. So I am basing my opinion largely (not entirely though) on the campaign mode.
I thought it was fun. After the previous game retread the ground from the first three games, bringing the series back to its roots (which was sorely needed), this game was allowed to take things in a whole new direction. There's several new characters, a good thing to add to the series, which lets a new generation continue the fight twenty five years after the previous game. And, of course, it sets up for a sequel.
There are things to dislike. Not the least of which is the excessive amount of DLC. Even if you buy the premium version, which includes the Kombat Pack (which I did), you will be missing Goro, and several costumes.  [Edit: It appears that these missing packs will be part of Kombat Pack 2.  I'll amend this when that pack is out.] Now, we are no longer paying full premium price anymore, but even when the game recently went on sale (it is currently the holiday sale as I write this), the DLC did not. On top of that, there are plans to release another Kombat Pack, with more characters. While I don't have anything particularly against continuing to add content to games, I do think the pricing is a bit steep. $30 for just a handful of characters and some outfits is a tad much. Likewise, $5 for a character alone seems steep. There's also the option to simply buy all the Krypt unlocks, so that you have the whole game ready to go right away. There's nothing inherently wrong with letting people who just don't have the time or inclination go ahead and unlock it all, but I feel that the price point of $20 is far, far too high for such a feature. This is where the $5 price point should be, if it should be a price point at all (this is PC we're talking about here, mods or cheat codes should be able to do the unlocking for you).
On top of that, I was saddened to see a few characters, such as Sindel and Baraka (the latter a personal favorite of mine from MK2) are available to fight against, but not as. It's understandable, given that the characters have various styles, but I still would have liked to see them playable. A roster of 24 (initially) is actually fairly impressive overall though, and more characters have since been added. And the characters that are there have some good variety. A few fatalities, some brutalities, lots of special moves and some variations. Looks to be at least a few costumes as well.
As for the smoothness of the characters, I have found a few that did not seem as responsive as I'd hoped. A lot of characters seem to have a huge wind-up for their specials, that usually opens them to quick counters, particularly from the AI. This can make them difficult to play as. But if you play around enough, you'll be able to find a character and variant of your liking.
The graphics are a big step up from the previous game. Both in game and in the cinematics. The fight choreography in the cinematics has been substantially improved as well. This game looks amazing, if your machine can run it.
All in all, the game is not without flaws. But I would say, yea, it's worth picking up. If you're a fan of Mortal Kombat. And if you can get it on sale. Though I would also suggest that if you really want to get the most for your money, hold off a bit and see if they release a true "complete" version.

Devil may cry 4: Special Edition is an action game focused on combat. This is virtually the same experience as DMC 4 safe for the 3 new added characters, a new difficulty mode and a few graphical "improvements". It features one the best combat experiences available, along with a cheesy/whacky story that you’ve gotten used to, if you played any of the previous games.
Pros
-Great combat system with a plethora of combos, weapons and styles that gives you many options
-Skill based with a high skill ceiling
-Even if cheesy, story and characters are enjoyable and generally likeable
-Bloody Palace, a wave based mode increases the game’s longevity and so do the multiple difficulty settings
Special Edition Pros
-3 new characters with distinctly different styles. Vergil plays similarly to DMC 3, Trish has plenty of area of effect moves, Lady focuses on firearms, something unique in DMC.
-New difficulty mode “Legendary Dark Knight” provides an extra layer of challenge with a hugely bolstered enemy count
Cons
-Campaign is clearly unfinished, as you end up replaying half the game, in reverse order, once you take control over the second character
-Enemy variety ends up lacking, as you near the end there are no new enemies
-Even on “hard” difficulty, if you don’t care about your score, it’s not that challenging to finish the campaign, even if you do a poor job at managing your combos and especially if you use healing/revival items
Special Edition Cons
-The new 3 characters end up sharing the same campaign as the old ones. With Vergil you go through the entire game and with Lady and Trish the game is divided between the two as it was between Nero and Dante. This wouldn’t be much of an issue but considering the repetitiveness of the original campaign, this means that if you go through it with all characters, you explore the exact same levels 3 times, not counting the fact that practically half of each campaign, as I stated, is essentially backtracking. This is by far the worst issue brought upon by the Special Edition since no new levels were made taking these characters into account.
-New graphical “improvements” don’t exactly look good, in my opinion, but they also affect performance considerably. It’s a good thing there are unofficial ways to disable some of the features.
-New Characters might have a few unbalances and be overpowered in certain situations, especially Vergil, who can clear the entire screen with certain special moves.
Conclusion: DMC 4 was a great game held back by its unfinished state and the same can be said regarding the special edition, since those issues remain. However, the outstanding combat system should be enough to convert any fan of the genre. The new characters may be overpowered, but they’re still a lot of fun to play with.
It is important to note that I think it is CRUCIAL to edit a few of the settings as they affect performance considerably and don’t look all that good, you’ll find guides to easily do it in 5minutes with no issues. For reference, I had 30 fps on 1080p and the fps doubled with those changes.

If Torchlight is a game that has a specific thing it does very well, and Diablo II has a lot of things it does well, Torchlight 2 is their beautiful, beautiful love-child. It takes the strengths of both games and fixes and improves upon the weaknesses and core mechanics of Torchlight.
Cash has a purpose in mid-to-endgame besides endless gambling (an issue that both Torchlight and Diablo ran into), the levels are much, much more non-linear and dungeons can be re-run without having to exit the game (improvement on Torchlight and Diablo mechanics), there's more familiar choices, and you can choose between male and female characters for each class, and the female characters wear equipment that actually looks like equipment as opposed as fashion.
I loved Torchlight, and still occasionally play it as I work towards getting those last few achievements. Torchlight 2 had big shoes to fill as the sequel to Torchlight and the spiritual successor to Diablo II, and it filled them magnificently.
