It's a technically great game, and when friends are online, is fun to mess around in. The story mode is great and tells a great story, but it's surprisingly short, and has an ending that leaves a lot to be desired.
Graphics are outstanding, mechanics are outstanding (gun play, car handling, etc.), but it gets stale after awhile. We were promised a single player story-centric DLC and we never got it, and that's disappointing coming from Rockstar, a group that's normally good at community relations. Michael, Trevor, and Franklin are great characters... iconic even, but they got brushed under the rug in favor of GTA Online. The same thing every other gaming company is doing... focusing on online play when the community is asking for a good story mode.
GTA Online is incredibly boring. That's an understatement, too. How is it that we have one of the most detailed world in open world video game history at our disposal and we're still left with an overwhelmingly boring online game mode. It makes no sense. And yet, Rockstar still focuses on it, even though story modes are obviously more their strongsuit. It's baffling.
On top of that, modding, a big, and dare I say important part of PC gaming was, for lack of a better way to put it, banned completely, and while I understand why it had to happen on Take Two Interactives part (legality and copyrights and all), it's a big hit to the game, especially once you 100% it.
TL;DR
If you haven't played it yet, experiencing the story mode is well worth it, as it has a great story to tell. Progressing through the story is a lot of fun, but savor it, because it'll be over long before you're ready for it to be over. If you're going to venture into GTA Online, do it with friends, or you're going to be bored.Cinema mode is a great mode if you're into filmmaking.

This is one of the most frustrating games you will ever play. If you have tons of money, have no life other than to play the game, like to find loophole cheats that don't ban you, or all of the above, you'll do well here. This is one of those games where there are so many brilliant features, you want to play. It's one of those games where you hate it, a lot... but you can't stop playing it. It's the only progressive WW2 leveling shooter on this scale. However- everything is expensive, and as you're struggling to 'get good', progress to earn enough in-game currency is incredibly slow. I played casually for a year, dropped a little bit of money into it many months ago, and still.... just getting a scope for a rifle so you can compete with getting instantly sniped almost everywhere you go... well, I still don't have a scope. And I was trying. However if you dump a bunch more money into the game, you can start a character with a scoped rifle. Simple hand grenades can destroy the tank you took months to earn, with one grenade. Also, you have (believe it or not) cost per shot. Yep. And the more you mod your rifle or tank or whatever to try to compete with the obsessive players/rich players/cheaters/basement virgins... the more you have to pay per shot/per spawn of your vehicle, AND you have repair costs too. After a while, it becomes impossible to save up money very quickly, and you find yourself having to play even more obsessively to just get money for the next thing (and let me remind you- that next thing will cost you more per shot/spawn/repairs). You will get the drop on someone, from 10 feet away, and shoot them twice in the back, but before you can fire a third shot they turn and instantly shoot you dead... with one shot. You'll work really hard to stealth around, flank, try to use tactics, be sneaky... but someone always seems to know where you are, and they will one shot you, or bunny hop around you with a shovel (yes, a shovel), and hit you once with it and you die, after expending a magazine to try to hit them just a few times, and you do, and they don't die, *you're* dead. It's laughable. I'm a huge WW2 buff, this game has so much promise, but it's horribly tuned to the COD crowd, the troll crowd. I wish I could have written a good review about this game, but after four decades as a gamer, and trying it off and on for a year, I'm sorry... not worth it. Trolls and flamers save your usual crap. Save the 'you just suck', 'cry some more', bullsh*t. We've all heard it before, and I won't listen to it, and anyone with any brains and maturity has heard it all before too. I hope they fix this someday, the content and art deserves not to be a worse version of COD.

It's definitely more fun than it has any right to be. The game is pretty simple and starting the story made may actually make you believe that there isn't much substance here, but oh boy.
Basic gameplay is a sort of endless spawn horde mode. You take control of a bunch of marines and fight the alien horde...it's really just basic attack move and use some special abilities like helicopter strikes, etc. The core gameplay is less about micro and more about macro. Things start out pretty simple:  You have five riflemen and the enemy spawns simple aliens. You march bravely forward into the jaws of hell and finish the first nest to replace it with a base of yourself. Later on in the story at least there are upgrades to turn that base into a fortified healing bunker...and even later on you can outfit it with a little cannon. For each captured point you earn points, which you can spend on buildings, abilities, defensive structures or weapons for your marines. Add an officer to the squad, outfit someone with a shotgun or a flamethrower, or simply hire more marines, etc.
But wait, that's not it, now your enemy gets to mutate and up his arsenal as well, i.e. the more nests you destroy and take over the more advanced enemies will spawn and try to overwhelm you. This makes up for the fact that the enemy has less spawn points now and can really cause a lot of trouble. And that's basically the game...the "story mode" takes about 3 to 4 hours on easy maybe. On harder difficulties I can imagine it to be more of a tug of war, until you get the upper hand. Some missions pack quite a punch and the persistent upgrade system has enough room for you to complete some random missions as well to earn more money. I got this in a humble bundle and was not disappointed. Would I pay full price for it? Eh, maybe 50%, but there's also weekly challenges and leaderboards, so if that's your thing...go for it.
Why they decided not to add an asynchronous multiplayer mode is beyond me though.

If you'd like to sire a legion of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and take over a town, play this game.

If you ever wanted to become best friends with the Grim Reaper, play this game.

If you have a decent/recent PC, it should run fine -- a little laggy, but nothing that destroys the experience.

This is a game for you if you like platforming and lite puzzle solving. The game also features very stunning visuals throughout the entire playthrough. Most of the level backgrounds are impressive and give the platforming layout a nice sense of depth.
Hard difficulty is recommended as the various traps can be run through in easy and medium difficulties without taking much damage. In hard difficulty you usually die instantly if you try to run through the traps like a headless chicken.
Online co-op is available for maximum of 3 players which I highly recommend as every character has their distinctive (and important) roles to play. The character roles also become more apparent when you play co-op as you can't swap between the characters (like in offline) as you please (if you disable the option), but need to work together to overcome the obstacles. Plus, it's always funny when someone screws up and as a result the whole group dies instantly.
The three playable characters are wizard, knight and thief.
Wizard can conjure various metallic platforms to jump on and is especially useful to reach some of the very hard to reach places. He also has a cute wizard's hat which usually flies off hilariously when he dies.
Knight has a shield + sword combo for defence, and to assist the wizard with platform creation he can magnetize the shield. Knight can use the shield to glide through the air like Mary Poppins.
Knight also has a big hammer which he can use to bash enemies and break wooden objects.
Thief is the nimble one as she can use grappling arrows to swing from wooden surface to another. She also has few stealth tricks to confuse the enemies, and can create low gravity bubble which comes in handy from time to time in co-op. In addition to normal arrows the thief can also shoot ice and fire/explosive arrows.
The levels are scattered with experience bubbles and vials which are used to unlock all the abilities of the characters. In addition the levels feature treasure chests in various secret places which unlock poems and concept art that can be viewed from the main menu gallery.
Checkpoints are frequent throughout the levels. Characters are healed (amount depends on difficulty) and resurrected at the checkpoints.
Enemies are mostly goblins with various equipment like shields, spears and armour. The enemies drop experience and sometimes health pickups that heal every member of the party. Levels also have themed wild life which can both aid and hinder your progress.
As a negative point the cutscenes cannot be skipped in multiplayer which isn't a problem in first playthrough, but can become tedious if you're planning to play it through more than once in co-op.

This game is visually stunning, the soundtrack has grand emotional depth but doesn't overpower, and the story of these two brothers on a journey to acquire that which will save their ailing father is incredibly moving. The single player "co-op" style of gameplay was a little brain-bending, but the game is not very challenging - it doesn't give you too many chances to die. However, this game isn't about technical gameplay; it's about the story. And it's a beautiful, heart-wrenching story told essentially without any dialogue (the in-game speech is in a fabricated language). 10/10 would recommend. :)

- Beautiful scenery (seriously, the character models might not be so impressive but the environment is stunning)
- Nice music (a great atmosphere is created in conjunction with the scenery)
- Fun and non-frustrating puzzles
- Interesting controls
- OK story
- Game is relatively short (perhaps 2-4 hours)
- Controls can be tricky to get used to (especially if you're playing alone)
- Not much of a challenge
- Story is not as fantastic as other reviews seem to make it out to be
While the storyline is nice and tear-jerking, the scenery, music and game-play is what made this game for me. The world created for the Brothers is the major selling point! The story is OK at best, unfortunately. Not the most creative or mind blowing, but not mediocre either. Furthermore, the controls are creative but also confusing at the same time.
When playing with a controller, you control each brother separately using the two analogue sticks and trigger buttons. Sounds simple enough, right? Yes, until you mistakenly let go of the wrong trigger button and one brother goes plummeting to his death. No biggie. However, I played this game twice: once alone and once with my girlfriend. When playing with a friend this becomes a much more enjoyable experience. Each player can take control of one brother by sharing a controller: one analogue stick and trigger button each. This basically nullifies control confusion. So grab your significant other and buckle down for a pleasant few hours!
If you want to spend a few hours playing a very casual puzzle-platformer with great scenery then this is the game for you! Having said that, I would
pay full price for this game. Wait for a sweet deal and grab it then.

I really like management games, just like I like games involving means of manipulation or sneaky means to achieve your goal. I will actually start with the Cons on this one:
Cons
- The praised 1000 events are boring with very minor (if at all impact). It's just a popup, you choose an option and get a mostly useless bonus or harmless malus. I had hoped for some event chains, something requiring action and something refreshing now and then. Nothing.
- Economy often makes no sense whatsoever. The income drops and increases A LOT rather randomly and you don't even get a hint of why. The statistic tab is abismal. Most stuff you can't really read out of it.
- The family choice is bland and rather meaningless. I usually approve roleplay elements like this but this is VERY basic and not fun.
- I really hoped for more of an impact of the world's events on the town. There is (close to) nothing there. That makes absolutely no sense.
- There really isn't much point in optimisation. At times the most profitable districts are the basic ones without any costly upgrades.
- Based on my observations there seems to be only one real way to be financially successful (not spoiling it). All attempts to use other playstyles that based on the data given (demands for residents, commercy, industry) would have made way more sense ended horribly bad.
- I see close to no replay value. The events don't offer any.
Pros:
- The approach for science is nice and refreshing.
- Living through the changes in history e.g. the rights of women, the privileges initially reserved to few yet opened up over time is quite fun.

TL;DR: Imagine that you have a large amount of candy. You do your best to maintain that amount of candy, while also giving some out to people in need. One day, a man comes up to you and threatens to falsely accuse you of a crime if you don't give the people more candy. Naturally, you give in to his demand, and resolve yourself to producing more candy in order to keep up with this demand. A month later, the man comes back and demands more. You oblige him again. This cycle continues until you have no candy left and all of the people in need are fat and unhealthy. The man approaches you and asks for more candy. When you explain that you have no more candy left to give, he kicks you in the balls and throws you off a cliff. The people that you gave everything to eventually starve to death, cursing your name for not giving them enough. Now imagine that you gave that man $35 to do this to you. That's what this game is like.
I was very excited for this game. So excited, in fact, that I pre-ordered it despite my normal policy of never pre-oredering a game. The concept is very intriguing and I've always loved city-building games, so naturally I thought that this would be a good pickup.
Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥was I wrong.
First off, you walk into this game knowing pretty much nothing about its mechanics because the tutorial doesn't tell you how every action interacts with your city, so you're pretty much blind walking in. In addition to this lack of information, the game punishes you harshly should you ever do something "wrong," so when your profits tank and your citizens start complaining you have no idea why it's happening or how to stop it. Companies go bankrupt for no reason, citizens don't work efficiently or buy things when they're not completely satisfied, and everything costs so much to maintain, so you're either forced to load a previous save or start a new campaign if something goes wrong. A "wrong" action could be as simple as adding street lights to your city, because they will inevitably bankrupt you while not doing a damn thing to help.
The citizens are also extremely finicky and hold way too much influence on how the city fares. If *GOD FORBID* you don't give them enough areas to entertain themselves, they'll tank your city in minutes. You are also forced to pick tech trees that don't really have any real benefits other than that they allow you to place a "small park" or a "theatre" in your city, just so you can play the game for more than an hour without losing $50k a month because they can't ♥♥♥♥ing deal with dissatisfaction. Oh, and another fun bit about the buildings  that you're forced to place in order to keep them happy is that they cost exorbitant amounts of money to build and maintain, so you're pretty much doomed to go bankrupt eventually either way. I also can't seem to wrap my head around the fact that a town with less than 2000 people in 1892 needs *AT LEAST* a university, a hospital, several schools, several police stations, 5+ parks, a dedicated seaport, their own train station, electricity, subsidized water/sewage systems, and free ♥♥♥♥ing mass transit in order to not complain and ruin their city's economy.
Also, the whole "politics" aspect of the game is essentially useless, except when you really want to save your city (because in that case they'll all ♥♥♥♥ing rally together to block you from making any positive change). You're forced to beg and demand that these city council members give you clearance to satisfy your citizens or save your city from bankruptcy, even though you've been granted your position by the ♥♥♥♥ing Emperor himself and should be completely free to ignore them. Another fun aspect of this system is that your ♥♥♥♥♥y citizens will vote for opposing parties in the next election if you don't completely satisfy their needs, so one party will carry half the votes in the entire council and can block any one of your political moves at will.
Eventually, you're forced to hike up taxes to >20% in order to stop the bleeding for a while, but even that will only be a temporary fix. There's no real way to guarantee success in this game, even if you're only prioritizing profits and minimizing funding on the 10+ public safety buildings that you need in order to keep your town with 2000 people in it from feeling dissatisfied.
New technology doesn't seem to help with any issues, either, because your citizens will still find a way to screw up your city. Edicts don't work, spying on other parties doesn't work, and frankly, the game itself doesn't really work. You'll suddenly be making $100k a month and you have no idea why it's happening, so you don't know how to keep it from inevitably tanking. These grace periods last JUST long enough for you to propose building up your city's infrastructure and spend most of your saved up money, but almost immediately after you spend some of your security cash your citizens will realize that they only have 3 theatres when they want 4, so they'll stop going to their jobs, all of the businesses and factories in your city will go bankrupt, and you'll be sitting there wishing that you hadn't bought this game or even attempted to succeed in it.
This is the most frustrating game I have ever played by far. The thing that makes this hurt so much is that I was really looking forward to it, and that the devs completely botched the execution of this game when its premise was so good. I'm not going to recommend buying it until it's been fixed, or if it's $10 on sale and you're a masochist.

Deadly traps is a hardcore platformer in the vein of games like super meat boy.  There are 3 worlds with 10 levels each, each level is one screen and filled with lasers, cannons, saws, spikes, and other various things that kill you.  Controls are simple and very responsive, you can move left and right and jump/double jump.  Your character moves at the perfect speed, fast enough to be able to get through the traps, but not so fast that he is difficult to control.  In order for a game like this to work the control has to be absolutely perfect, and it is, you will die a ton in this game but it is never the fault of the control.
Level design is good, you can see everything as soon as the level begins.  There are no cheap deaths in this game, every trap is clearly visible and you know exactly what to expect as you progress through the various stages.  This game is difficult, but there is no annoying trial and error stuff here, in theory you can beat every level on the first attempt, in practice that will never happen.
You can start the game from any world, all 3 worlds are playable from the get go so it gives you some freedom in how you tackle the levels, the downside of this is that the difficulty curve is basically non-existent.  The game starts out tough and staysthe same level of tough throughout the entire game.  I also don't know if this is just me, or my skills increasing, but I felt like I died hundreds of times in world 2 and barely died in world 3.  On world 2 I was averaging 30-50 deaths per level, in world 3 I died less than 10 times per level.
The only annoyance of the game is that the traps don't reset on each death, which leads to a few annoying spots where you need to wait for the right conditions to progress, it is not terrible, but when you are on your 30th death on a level and feeling frustrated it throws off your progress and adds an extra layer of frustration to the level.
Bottom line is this game is a dollar and for that price you get an excellent platformer, with tight controls, and great level design.  If you are into these types of games that buying this should be a no brainer.  The game will make you rage for all the right reasons and is a very satisfying experience, that took me about 2 hours to finish but your mileage may vary based on your skill in these kinds of games.

This is a great game. I have played the original gunz as well and in that one you can master the kstyle which takes a lot of skill but this one has a different flair to it. (Although their are some similar aspects like reload shot with wayne) It takes some getting used to if you are used to playign gunz 1 or new to gunz in general. There are six different characters with their own melee weapon, they have 2 different gunz and eath with their or r e and q moves. (this uses an zbar which is similar to mana). This game can produce some extremely intense battles when you reach a decent skill level which is highly entertaining. The community is very small so you will run into a lot of the same players which i think is kind of cool because u develope friendships or sworn enemies. The normal mode matchmaking search is kind of dying but just go to practice game section of the game. The lobbies are created by players (you can create a deathmatch yourself and start the game and wait for people to join as you warm up flying around the walls.) The practice game is where the good players join and get ready for some intense battles. I will describe the characters. Ivan- he uses a sword he also has a smg to spray if needed and has a sniper (his most valuable weapon) His e move is a whiring kick that sends his opponents flying.. His q ultimate is a quick samurai slash that is a one shot kill Rena - She uses 2 daggers she has a smg for spray and duel pistols for bigger damage. Hes e move produces a clone of her that will explode in a couple seconds but while this happens you become invisible and confuse the opponent. Her ultimate is a spinning  dagger attack that does extremely heavy damage. Elana uses a bat has an assault rifle and a grenade launcher her e scans for enemies revealing them and her ultimate is her slamming her bat on the ground creating an explosion whihc is almost a 1 shot kill if your in area.. A well-made combat system brought down by its rushed development. The Special Edition hasn't made efforts to fix the issues present in the base game. The extra characters feel like they were added to distract players from the repetitiveness of the levels but end up highlighting that flaw even more. In fact, Special Edition is more like a character pack with some graphical improvements.
Some of the locales are neat in principle and aesthetic, but fall short of their potential. Fortuna Streets, Castle Fortuna, and HQ were some of my favorite areas but weren't all that interesting as far as level design goes, save for being fancy backgrounds. It feels like a squandered opportunity.
The new characters are pretty generally obscenely imbalanced: Vergil's concentration gauge combined with Distortion and Heavy Sword Rain makes bosses trivial, Lady is similar with Shotgun Charge Shot 3, and Trish feels more appropriate even if lightning-Straight and lightning-Volcano (whatever those are called) can handle pretty much everything.
Although, DMC4 is a game that's really only as good as the player; its quality feels more appreciable once you start to utilize what your character has available to them. Each character has their own, distinct moveset (even if select attacks are reused across charcters), thus causing them to play quite differently from each other. I actually don't even like Vergil or Lady (even if I was hyped to play them when SE was announced), but the character variety is appreciated.
Anyway, the game's main selling point is the combat system. I'd recommend it because I've had a lot of fun with Dante and Nero's moveset (and the other characters to a lesser extent). If you want a more complete game with a better story and locales while keeping the combat depth, try DMC3 and check the forums on how to fix it up.

Sorry, this is Fantasy Gameplay with Functional Problems. You can't acctualy play the game without finishing the Tutorial. But the Tutorial does not allow saving the game. This forces you to finish a Tutorial which may last for hours. But the Tutorial has functional problems. Scrolling and zooming does not work well, and not far enough outward to see the big picture. So to see your whole town and important locations around it, this game fails. Tutorial arrows cover information you need to read. Double pop-up screens occur with ghost images over each other. Loading between different sequences takes a long time. Scrolling any menu makes it "bounce" at top and bottom of the menu selection list. Trying to place the rail station while using the mouse to scroll and zoom disconnects the placement of station command many times. After much trial and error in this Tutorial, you find there is only one fixed location for this station on the map but this is untold to the player, so it is not necessarily near where you placed the town at the start. So you can memorize where this was on the map, and then restart the Tutorial to restart the town closer to this station location. When finding it and successfully placing the station, the town council now votes "against" the station. This makes no sense. Why can the player not be aware of this "opinion" before researching and trying to build? And Why did they vote that way? The council does not explain their objection. Poor game design and mechanics. Also the Game as "history" makes no sense. A proposal for Womens Right to Own Property has approval of all parties, but a train station does not! It is the 1820's. Town development does not follow real town development throughout history. Even when using the Dense Grid the town grows like modern suburbia, not like tightly packed houses around a core or town square. Inventions are not historical. Political viewpoints are ahistorical and the Council disagreements on each invention makes no sense for city development. What does this leave? Pretty graphics and a contrived storyline, and you must always use the same contrived player characters. Besides being technically buggy, when the Tutorial does work it has a strange idea of "history" that borders on "fantasy" in gameplay. Not acceptable all around.

Within Five minutes of my starting I said out loud, "Good f#@k this is beautiful". 20 minutes later I was still saying, "Good f#@k this is beautiful." As such, this review is really going to be me gushing about a 50 minute experience that I recommend to everyone despite my wish that it was much longer.
This game is very open, and while some people criticize it for being extremely vague with its narrative, I was able to collect a good sense of what was happening even without finding all of the journal entries. the game takes place after the uprising in Half life 2 in a city in a vastly different area from City 17, as the architecture is generally different. It feels more American than European this time. It appears that the Combine either remain in the city or are trying to take it back from the rebel forces and that you are almost entirely alone with the Zombies, Headcrabs, and Combine Soldiers of this new city. To top it all off, the game takes place at night, and darkness is actually used as a gameplay mechanic when underground and pitch black lighting levels can be obtained. The atmosphere is absolutely perfect in every way, bringing a perfect mix of eerieness and action to the forefront. When I started to play through this game I was immediately reminded of how Valve wanted to get back to the horror vibe when they put out Episode 3. And while this game doesn't actually contain any genuine horror moments, I kept thinking back to that quote the entire time I was playing the game.
Another Quote that kept creeping back up was how Valve supposedly wanted to make the next Half Life game an open world game. I always had theories about this could work, going as far as to map the entire concept mapped out inside my head, but this game, which isn't even open world, is essentially the proof of concept that an open world Half Life game could work. The levels are so intricate and nonlinear that it felt more like exploring than pushing forward, very reminiscient of the original 1993 Doom, but somehow managing to erase the maddening maze wandering feeling that comes with levels with multiple paths. There are a couple of open areas in this game as well that really show what can happen when you keep one formula and apply it to something larger. It feels like a genuine Half Life game, despite its large and relatively open areas, something that Half Life isn't really known for until Episode 2 comes into play (and even episode 2 is a stretch).
This game feels more like a genuine Half Life expansion than Opposing Force did, which many still regard as their favorite Half Life game. There is a disclaimer at the bottom of the store page that states that this game is not a Valve product, and that the Half Life ip was licensed out to the developers. That being said, That disclaimer really only shows the quality of work done by an excellent team of THREE PEOPLE. If Valve hired this team today to work on Episode 3 or Whatever it will be called, I would not lose a wink of sleep knowing one of my favorite game series of all time was in the hands of these three people. If you like Half Life even a little bit, this game will rustle all of the right jimmies for you. Even when the game lasts for under 50 minutes, I still cannot recommend it enough. If this game were full length I would have no trouble at all paying for what is essentially professional level work, but the team has decided to release this glorified mod for free. If they held a kickstarter or something that would put money toward making a full game, I would definitely reserve my copy early. This game is just that good, so good that I call it a game instead of a mod.

Very inventive and fun. I love the new Concussion Gun and mechanics that are introduced with it. If I didn't know any better, I would have assumed this were a demo for a new Valve game. There is so much creativity and potential here; the idea of blast jumping in the Half-Life universe is great, and this game really runs away with it. There are so many new things that you can do with the Concussion Gun. Destroy the environment, send enemies flying, send yourself flying. It's really hard to put the weapon away. When I first fired the Concussion Gun and played around with it, I couldn't help but grin.
The destructible environment was very impressive, and the developers really paid attention to detail. Combine Striders can blast apart walls you are using for cover (including in buildings you think are safe), forcing you to use the Gravity Jump mechanic to dodge bullets, rather than boringly hide in a building and fire a rocket out of a doorway every now and again. You can also shoot shipping containers off from their cranes and onto the Striders, making room for some creative gameplay. It's like being re-introduced to the original Gravity Gun all over again, but this time things are far more interesting. A few battles take place in large environments, and really take advantage of your newly augmented mobility. Gravity Jumping away from bullet fire, onto roofs, and around the environment is exciting and fun. The scale and verticality of the environment takes full advantage of your new weapon, and has you wanting to climb higher and higher. This game feels like a mash-up between Portal and Half-Life. You get Portal mobility and Half-Life combat. It's insanely fun.
I was very disappointed when the game ended so soon, but since this is a free mod I understand that it couldn't be helped. I'm itching to play more and I really want to see more of this, it's way too much fun. If you have 40 minutes to kill, check this game out, it's loads of fun and will have you wishing for more. This game is great to try up until level 20. Once at level 20 however, you have the option of becoming a premium or a VIP. Although the game is set up as free to play, it's quite difficult to do much if you aren't at least a premium up to level 20. Your currency is limited, a lot of your inventory is limited, the vault is limited, and you don't feel quite free.
What I find troubling about this game is that there is a strong suggestion to pay money to advance. Not even to beat others, but to just advance further into the game and level up. They highly recommend you to use real life money to exchange for their currency (turbine points) or to subscribe monthly for VIP status.
That being said, the monthly payments aren't too bad, roughly $10-$15, which is about normal. The quality of the game itself is quite fun. There is quite a lot to do, and each character feels really diversified. It does feel cluttered at times though, due to the high number of repeatable quests and lack of structure for quest taking (grab whatever quest you see, run to it). The main quest doesn't feel too prioritized, but it is a decent story line. At times, it feels like you are just being led around by your quests, rather than pursuing them. They feel really one dimensional, but necessary.
The largest appeal of this game is the characters themselves, and the level of customization for your abilities, play style, looks, and classes. I really enjoyed this bit. There are specific skill trees you can specialize in, and they're diverse enough that they don't feel like the same class with different specs. Another thing about skills and abilities is that there is the Deed Log, which keeps track of achievements. This is a great concept of the game that rewards you well for doing specific achievements, which feels very rewarding. This adds to the customization appeal, where you can pursue an achievement to get a skill and be satisfied.
In short, I would suggest playing this game at least up until level 20, and to really investigate the skill trees, the deed logs, and traits. Also, experiment with different classes, each class feels very unique, and within each class, is a sub-class that is also unique in a sense.

Review:
The Lord of the Rings Online as an MMORPG is one of the more polished one and has kept up with the times visually. The gameplay is very similar to you if you have played MMORPGs like World of Warcraft and Everquest and does not offer anything on this front you could not find from another game. Where LotRO shines is the lore, story and world design.
The Lore stays true to that of Tolkien's works for the most part and, usually, what deviations exist usually are still in the spirit of the professor's works. The story follows the Lord of the Rings book trilogy's story mostly, with lot's of additional content that portrays events during the War of the Ring which are not delved into in detail in the books. The world design and art direction is great, what the game lacks in pure fidelity it well makes up for in design.
Lord of the Rings Online offers an unrivaled experience when it comes to exploring and immersing yourself in Middle-Earth, from the burrows of the Shire to the plains of Rohan. The game will hit home with Tolkien fans who enjoy exploration, roleplaying and solo/small group oriented adventuring.
Pros
-Great Story, that follows the books faithfully and explores additional lore friendly events.
-Good solo experience, the games focus has during the years switched to cater to solo players.
-For fans of the Middle-Earth Legendarium
-Very friendly to Roleplayers.
-Gorgeous world.
Cons
-The game feels somewhat dated by now.
-Lack of raids and traditional instances in later expansions. ( which might be alleviated if you are interested in alternative instance types, like the Skirmishes and Big Battles.)
-Weak PvP-content. The PvP has been relatively stagnant and there doesn't seem to be much improvement on the horizon

Is this a bad game? No.
Is it fun? Debatable.
I wish I could give this a neutral review, but I can't--hence I'm sticking to a positive one with some caveats. If you're like me, you should probably avoid this game.
Runs are procedurally generated and this does not work in your favour--especially since the title claims to be tactical. There's no strategy that can save you from not being able to find food; pften times, you won't find enough to feed your tribesmen and they'll die. Even after thinning out your numbers in order to provide for the remaining members, it's still near-impossible to maintain enough food.
You can switch between bare hands, holding spears or torches, increasing your tribe numbers if you have enough food to sustain them, and even sacrificing members in order to create more food in a pinch.
Your run ends once you reach the other end of the map. Time passes when you run, so the next map will be played during the night if you first ran during the day and vice versa. There's the option to wait out the night, but this will cost more food than you'll likely have.
Unfortunately, night time is fraught with dangers and increases your risk of going hungry. In order to see what's in front of you in the slightest, you need to hold torches. Torches scare off animals and burn berry bushes, which means acquiring food will be even more difficult still. If you don't hold torches, however, you'll easily run into obstacles and predators and your tribe will die.
I have yet to see the tactical aspects of this game. There is resource management, sure, but the procedural generation makes it so that stockpiling anything is nigh impossible. Predators and other tribes will kill you on site and herbavores will run off unless you spread out your formation to groups of only a few spear-toting tribesman. Changing formation is often stilted by the environmental hazards, so I found it difficult to hunt if only because I'd smash into something shortly thereafter and kill half of my tribe.
There are no upgrades at all--none that can be earned during your run nor ones that carry over and make subsequent runs easier. As such, the procedural generation will continue to screw you until you're too frustrated to bother.
The game is presented in pixel art, which I'm a fan of. I also like the prehistoric theme. The music is a constant loop of tribal beats and I muted it after the first few minutes.
.Pros.
.Cons.
.Bottom Line.
For the price, you can do better. Runners are meant to be challenging, but typically you can memorize obstacles or you're given upgrades to make it so that you get a little further each time. Tribal Pass does neither and so it just becomes an exercise of frustration.
Kept me entertained for a couple of hours. Nice simple fun but not a great deal of depth.

With the WB's reversal, and their new decision to release KP2, MKXL, and further support for the PC version, I am restoring my original review of the game from December of 2015.  It may be edited later, when I obtain KP2, to detail further information within:
Yes I recommend this game, for the very simple reason that I enjoy it.
Now, you have to bear in mind that I give little care for online multiplayer in fighting games. In my experience, it has always been a lag filled waste of time. So I am basing my opinion largely (not entirely though) on the campaign mode.
I thought it was fun. After the previous game retread the ground from the first three games, bringing the series back to its roots (which was sorely needed), this game was allowed to take things in a whole new direction. There's several new characters, a good thing to add to the series, which lets a new generation continue the fight twenty five years after the previous game. And, of course, it sets up for a sequel.
There are things to dislike. Not the least of which is the excessive amount of DLC. Even if you buy the premium version, which includes the Kombat Pack (which I did), you will be missing Goro, and several costumes.  [Edit: It appears that these missing packs will be part of Kombat Pack 2.  I'll amend this when that pack is out.] Now, we are no longer paying full premium price anymore, but even when the game recently went on sale (it is currently the holiday sale as I write this), the DLC did not. On top of that, there are plans to release another Kombat Pack, with more characters. While I don't have anything particularly against continuing to add content to games, I do think the pricing is a bit steep. $30 for just a handful of characters and some outfits is a tad much. Likewise, $5 for a character alone seems steep. There's also the option to simply buy all the Krypt unlocks, so that you have the whole game ready to go right away. There's nothing inherently wrong with letting people who just don't have the time or inclination go ahead and unlock it all, but I feel that the price point of $20 is far, far too high for such a feature. This is where the $5 price point should be, if it should be a price point at all (this is PC we're talking about here, mods or cheat codes should be able to do the unlocking for you).
On top of that, I was saddened to see a few characters, such as Sindel and Baraka (the latter a personal favorite of mine from MK2) are available to fight against, but not as. It's understandable, given that the characters have various styles, but I still would have liked to see them playable. A roster of 24 (initially) is actually fairly impressive overall though, and more characters have since been added. And the characters that are there have some good variety. A few fatalities, some brutalities, lots of special moves and some variations. Looks to be at least a few costumes as well.
As for the smoothness of the characters, I have found a few that did not seem as responsive as I'd hoped. A lot of characters seem to have a huge wind-up for their specials, that usually opens them to quick counters, particularly from the AI. This can make them difficult to play as. But if you play around enough, you'll be able to find a character and variant of your liking.
The graphics are a big step up from the previous game. Both in game and in the cinematics. The fight choreography in the cinematics has been substantially improved as well. This game looks amazing, if your machine can run it.
All in all, the game is not without flaws. But I would say, yea, it's worth picking up. If you're a fan of Mortal Kombat. And if you can get it on sale. Though I would also suggest that if you really want to get the most for your money, hold off a bit and see if they release a true "complete" version.

And as far as not explaining, the tutorial is horrible (I will give credit that you can now disable it, which you couldn't for a time) and drags on for ages.  The tooltips are vague at best and just don't work at worse.  The council will always oppose you, just so you have something to compete against, and even if you cater to their needs you still have to burn your goodwill to get votes through.  And if you city ends up stable and making money you are just sitting waiting for the next tech to roll around so you can repeat the same cycle of picking a district upgrade and/or edict and spending your goodwill to get it passed.
All told, if you want a city builder play City Skylines.  If you want a politcal simulator, play Democracy 3.  And if you want more Tropico, just go play Tropico, because Urban Empire fails to be a good game in any of those cases.

While "waiting" for that overwhelming cliffhanger in "Episode Two" to emerge from the ashes almost a decade ago for a much needed continuation (now, that's an understatement), this absorbingly short
mod is creatively impressive in the puzzling presentation of level design as well as engaging in its minimilistic setting.

The alteration of the enthralling Gravity Gun is an interesting feature that distinguishes this mod from others; instead of pulling and discharging objects, you perform high jumps and shooting deadly shockwaves to make progress. As for the rest of the weaponry, many of them return but not without a sense of redundance, since the Gravity Gun alone would basically suffice while adding further creativity in combat strategy and problem solving. That crowbar is quite handy though...
Taking place at night at an unspoken location in the same universe as Half-Life, the vague narrative of
appears favourable in heightening the great atmosphere that unfold at a solid pace. The enhanced lightning is also nicely done and the stirring soundtrack is faithful to the source material. The conclusion however - instead of de-escalating the pace and obtaining some kind of closure - is rather rash and too elusive which in a way undermines the overall impression of this otherwise recommended and well-made mystery.

Brief review of infested Planet.
+ : Good control grouping
+ : Changing and challenging mutations
+ : Short but well written story mode.
+ : Skirmishes for further play, with varying difficulty.
+ : End Mission is quite a spike in challenge, took a couple attempts even on normal difficulty.
+ : Game implements strategy nicely, what building you want to go for (aircraft support, grenades) or try turret rush, or create more marines, or upgrade your few marines with stronger weapons (shotgun, flamethrower, sniper, officer, etc).
+ : Automation of structures being built with closest marine, can also simply right click on resources (ammo, 'points') on map. Then if you have all marines selected and move click afterwards, it won't stop that single marine from constructing or going to gather the resource. Noob friendly.
+ : Can micro a bit.
+ : Sharp and clean UI on menu and in-game.
+ : Skirmish mode, Weekly Challenge, Story is available.
+ : Easy to get into and understand.
+ : AI is pretty good, didn't feel like another player but it got challenging. Generally when you captured your first base, that would be the trigger for "hives" to start sending out units from all directions.
- :  No Macro shift movement when pick up 'point' resource boxes. Have to wait till marine gets to it and then select him and click to go back to a controlled node to deposit.
- : Short campaign story, but there is DLC..
- : When starting a map, doesn't give you time to assess what is going on or which strategy you will implement for victory. So starts ad lib or you will have to strategize and then restart the game.. which restarting the level is quick and easy though. (or press space.. doesnt tell you can do that though).
- : Default hotkey setup not very good, recommend to setup to your liking. i.e Changed "buildings menu" from '...' to B. And turret from 'W' to T.
- : Difficult to see the marines health for quicker micro movement, as it is a ring around them and when have them bunched up can be visually overwhelming.
Replayability : This is subjective but it does have replayability, definitely would if had multiplayer included. Me personally, i've had enough just going through the campaign, it is too generally the same to bother with harder difficulties or other modes.. while the concept remains fresh the gameplay can become mundane.
Optimization : The game runs smoothly on my computer and it isn't a complete beast pc. Even with 100's or 1000's of enemies on screen, i think many computers can run this cause is optimized nicely.
Subjective Review/Price : Alot of it goes back to replayability, as i have 4 hours on it after messing about and beating the story on Normal, that is really about it to the game for me. I got it for $10 and even with that price it leaves a sour feeling on the wallet, and on steam it is actually $15. Personally i feel it can be worth $4.99 - $7.99.
I hope you got some insight from my review, thanks for reading.

Pretty original game. Very simple concept: you control a running tribe, being able to:
- split it or gather it to cover particular grounds
- equip it with lances, torches or bare hands
- grow the tribe (increasing its food consumption) or sacrifice tribesmen (to get food when you ran out)
And with this, you must deal with various dangers and bring as many tribesmen to the end of the level. Sounds easier than it actually is ;)
An advice for beginners: don't overgrow your tribe. Actually, I found that the easiest way to finish a level was to play with just a few tribesmen: this way at least you can hardly starve out.
But the more people you bring to the end, the higher your score, so eventually you'll have to put that into the balance if you want to score high.
My main criticism would be the lack of a detailed guide or tutorial. There is a tutorial, but it's far from covering everything, so you'll have to also learn from game tips that appear occasionally or from experience. For instance:
- rhinos won't kill you if you don't have a weapon equipped
- flies will eat your food

I wish I could give this a positive, because it is a good game and I do enjoy the graphics, the concept, the watching of my city as it grows, the budget juggling and politics of this story that you play...

This is supposed to be a game, though it ends up feeling like a story that you're watching. The political parties in this game can be held back and resisted for a while, you can't control the population to influence the elections, so you're at the mercy of the games random mechanics which are poorly explained, the horrible lack of tooltips giving you -Any- information, about anything and everything, you can't even find out a why business went out of business, or why it's bankrupt, or who works where, or how to help citizens improve...
and the political parties, eventually you can't do anything but accept their utter rule over you and the policies "You" enact for your city, even if you're highly opposed to them and have been for the entirity of the game.
I respect that democracy is showcased here, but that's exactly what's wrong with this game. In the hours I've played it, I did have fun and I'll probably continue to have fun, but I don't feel like I'm a part of the game or my city or my leader, I feel like I'm merely watching them play their story.

I had really high hopes for this game, it looked like an intriguing twist on the city-builder genre. Unfortunately, the twist, i.e. the city politics, is one-dimensional and totally lacking in interaction with the other factions. Your family choice seems to have no bearing on the gameplay, other than the odd event which pops up every couple of years, and the lack of customisation is a shocking misstep (perhaps when basing a game around family dynasties, Kalypso could have looked at the success seen by Paradox with their Crusader Kings II series).
Then there's the gameplay itself. It is completely impossible to run a city at a profit if you want it to grow, or if you want it to have even basic amenities, like schools and police stations. You find yourself raising taxes to ridiculous levels, which has no impact on businesses or people, or begging the Emperor for a loan. For some reason having a port or train station actually loses you money, as if those two crucial pieces of infrastructure were unable to make a profit. Wholly unrealistic.
If those basic things can be changed (i.e. the entire economics of the game), and if the politics can be made interesting, rather than repetitive (i.e. the entire basis of the game), and if more options for customising characters were made (i.e. the entire plot of the game), then this would be worth some money. This is the first time I've every bothered to write a Steam review, which in combination with that blue thumbs up icon should tell you something right away.
I was quite late to the party with this one, since it was first released over three years ago. A seemingly simple yet tactically varied experience, that uniquely blends elements of RTS, Tower Defence and the best parts of the Starship Troopers movie.
Only in Total War games will you encounter a similar number of units on-screen at once, but here the balance is skewed completely towards the aliens, of which your handful of marines will easily face tens of thousands in a single mission. There's something extremely cathartic about seeing your tiny squad shoot and burn its way through such a horde.
The real draw here though is the mutation system, as the aliens respond to your advance by coming up with new and interesting ways to kill you. Some of these may seem much worse than others, which can be frustrating at times, but ultimately they can all be countered through some combination of items from your varied arsenal, it's just a matter of experimenting and finding it. There are still one or two buildings available that seem pretty much worthless, but almost everything has a use in some scenario.
Your main introduction to this game will probably be through the Story campaign. The story itself is rather meh, mostly serving as a framework for the game's tutorial and the selection of unique missions that follow. I had a blast playing through it, but after getting all the achievements I've not really bothered again since, spending most of my time in either skirmish or the planetary campaign modes.
The skirmish mode provides a bunch of preset mission options on randomised maps, but also provides a whole host of custom options for you to tailor almost everything to your preferences. There's no way of saving these settings as custom presets, but it's not much of a hassle. And at least once, you have to play a custom mission where all settings are turned up to maximum.
No multiplayer, but I've never really been bothered with that sort of thing anyway. If you're the competitive type though, there are weekly challenges with leaderboards where you try and beat other players' high scores in a variety of missions.
Make sure you get the 2 DLCs as well - Trickster's Arsenal introduces a host of new abilities for your marines that I couldn't imagine playing without anymore. Burrowing Hive pops up far behind your front lines? Use Teleport Jump to get some marines there quickly. Tower Spawner approaching a bunker defended by a lone marine? Drop a Cluster Bomb on the eggs before they can hatch.
The Planetary Campaign DLC breathes new life into the game. By restricting various techs, while needing you to unlock others, it forces to you to try out new strategies, using buildings and abilities that you never would have bothered with otherwise and giving you new a new appreciation of their effectiveness. The added strategic layer acts as an extension of the tactical game, with your forces in a constant struggle to push back the alien swarm as they evolve new mutations to counter your tactics and grow in strength right up until the final stronghold.
tl;dr Hands down my GOTY of 2017 so far.

runner is really good term to describe
. It has unusual game mechanics for this type of game. They are really simple when you look at them on paper; but when you start your run it is not at all rainbows and cupcakes; and it is prime example of game that looks easy, but is really hard to master.
You not only run forward to reach your goal, but you have to take care of your tribesmen in order to survive harsh environment they live in. You need (most then anything) food to feed your tribe.
No food = your unstoppable army of prehistoric people starts to die pretty quickly.
Food can be obtained, by setting up the right formation so you can pick berries from bushes, killing a moose or other tribes ... in worst case scenario, you can degrade yourself to cannibalism with hope that you will survive until next level. Harder it is due to obstacles in your way. Rivers, quick sand; flies that will eat your food; bloodthirsty sabertooth, extremely tough rhyno - both can be killed (apparently), but with them in my way I found only death of my people. Easy ...
And doing this when night settles in and the darkness cover the whole world ... easy peasy.
*stares into the wall, reflecting on many, many, many deaths, and failed runs*
is for me really frustrating, because I am not skillful enough and patient enough to get good in this game, and complete it. I make a lot of mistakes by missclicking, wrongly evaluating situation ahead of me ... and all of this is only my issue. Game itself runs well, controls well, there is nothing wrong with it - something is wrong with me, obviously.
Technically is pretty alright game, nothing stands out really - negatively or positively - that would need special mention.
Overall it is a nice, little, neat game, where you can get easily lost and kill couple hours, if it fits into your wheelhouse.
I encourage YOU to give this game a fair chance. It might surprise you.

This games is insanely fun... for a little bit. It might be THE brawler game for PC when it's finished but it's lacking much in... substance. I've had a lot of fun trying it out and playing with friends, but as a big fan of this style of game since the N64, I have to say: this is NOT the PC successor to any of those games, not yet. But with a bit more work and feedback, it could be.
There's a crisp freshness to it, and nice simplicity in setup, matchmaking, micro-transactions, and many others. Nothing feels forced; it's not a money-grab, it's not an e-peen contest. It's a healthy young game. But it's not there yet. It's overly simple and feels like it's missing some small but key element to the battle system. Right now it's way too smash heavy and lacks adequate counter-play and strategy but the basics are there. For now, everyone should find it fun for a while, until you don't. It gets old fast, but it will bring you back again tomorrow, it's that kind of game.
If they can take it to the next level, this will be the next big thing. Complete the combat system, add finesse to the attacks and defenses, take a look at original ideas, and make this the game to beat. It's possible, just not there yet

This wasn't really what I expected. I don't blame the game for that at all. I wanted a more intricate mechanic based around complex relationships with the city council and citizens that reflectedin votes and decisions. This game isn't that and again that's not the game's fault.
The concepts in the game are amazing and will probably carry the game for awhile, but after I played for a few hours I wasn't having any fun and didn't feel connected to anything in the game.
The economy was probably the biggest turnoff for me as it is spiradic at best. It appears that the only viable way to offset costs is to constantly raise taxes. I've been a part of city government for many years and it simply doesn't work this way. Several things, including state and federal funding, for infrastructure and services have been left out. The early eras are understandable in this regard however. Though adding sewage to my districts shouldn't cost me 50k per month for 2,000 people. Wtf are they eating that requires that kind of cost for sewage?!
All in all I'm sure this will be an awesome game for alot of people, but it just wasn't there for me. I wish there was a "meh" recommendation on Steam. Maybe Paradox will take a stab at something in this ballpark eventually. Ended up refunding.

So, I know that this isn't a city builder but a city ruler blablabla. However, the gameplay is incredibly shallow in most aspects. The concept is amazing and I think the devs wasted some potential with this game. The main issues I have with the game are, as I said, shallow city sim related gameplay you might be used to get from other games - which in itself wouldn't be a major deal if other aspects of the game would be more interesting. However, there is no real roleplaying aspect other than the occasional trait points you get (or lose), flavour text for characters and houses.
Then there is the "political" side of the game, which is pretty disappointing. You basically have a bunch of political parties that shift in power. Wanna pass a law and parties that support it are in the minority? No problem, just tell the leader of an opposing party that you'll ruin his career or straight out threaten to murder him and there you go, vote passed. Zone out a disctrict or build a police station? Threaten people. Increase taxes, funding for something, strenghten LGBT rights from horrible to kinda horrible or get ♥♥♥♥ing elected? DO THE EXACT SAME ♥♥♥♥ING THING! Why is there no campaigning for elections? No political intrigues, managing your own party or whatever else politics could have been implemented in this game?
A price tag of ~20 bucks would be acceptable for this game. I'd say factoring in the current price of €45 for me, I'd give it a 4/10. Disregarding price, a 6/10.

The game is kind of fun, but gets old really quickly. You burn goodwill to get votes. The only time its difficult is a change to the taxing. Other than that I don't have to do anything, and the vote simply goes through. The political system, the main selling point of this game, is super simplistic. It's cool for the first three hours, after that it gets boring fast.
I kept trying to like this game, I really did. I just couldn't.
Also, there are some typos and some placeholders in text left over, like when you get re-elected it says "You are the mayor of [city]. Congrats!" (or something to that effect). Thats right, instead of having your city's name, it says "[city]"
Hoping some new content gets released, cause I'm kinda stuck with this now.

A Refrishing Swim in a Shallow Pond
Pros:
+ Very few titles in the genre
+ What it does, mayoral simulator, it does well
+ Peaceful, layed back gameplay
+ Runs well and looks as good as it needs to be
Cons:
- Not a lot going on, there are times where you're just waiting for the time to tick by.
- The game's politics definitely tend to lean one way moreso than the other
- Difficult to tell what choices makes what changes
Neutral:
o Shallow gameplay. You make choices and hope you have enough clout to sway votes to your side. That's pretty much it in a nutshell.
o There definitely seems to be an optimal way to go about advancing your city and districts.

SCRAPS has basic graphics which are likely to improve in later development. This means that you don't need  5 processors, 8 fans, 2 PC cases or anything alike to run this game with 60fps or more. I actually like this style of art, it's simplistic and easy, so your computer doesn't get burned down! Anyway, the models are very high res, they're also pretty bad*ss whilest  being made by a developer who knows what he's doing. The SFX are basic, the textures are quite basic (the ground probably has the best texturing in the game) but the game runs just fine. Hopefully you get my point, this game is for gameplay but not for graphics.
There's tons of parts to build from, such as tank cannons to energy generators. Your vehicle will have its own needs, such as head income and outcome, so you'll need to slap a block or few to tackle  them. However, your vehicle has very limited space, even the large category is quite limited. You can even change how high up the suspension is to alter weight! The building is quite in-depth, but content is still lacking. The balance isn't that good at all, I can take sacrificing speed for more cannons, but the other bots always get me from behind ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) So I can't really kill them without placing a cannon that rotates 360 degrees and hopefully can aim low enough to kill them. But I guess it does make some sense, the Overly Powered builds can be strong going head to head since it's the place of the most firepower, but weak in the back. So I guess it has many challenges waiting to be found out about, you can even make a car that goes 200mph and falls all the time. So this game is fun for the player being able to make crazy builds.. as long as the player has the scrap required (scrap is the game currency to fix, upgrade, or add more parts to a vehicle).

One only has to look at the numbers to see that Runic Games really struck gold when they released the hit sequel Torchlight 2 as a follow-up to their original action RPG game, Torchlight. While it may not give anything new to the genre and it didn't win a bunch of awards like its predecessor, it still sold over 2 million copies in less than a year of its full release date. Impressive. The reason is quite simple: everything Torchlight 2 does, it does well.
All of our favorite features from Torchlight return and have been improved, such as pets and fishing, in addition to some new features being added. Some of the changes you can expect to see include: an expanded crafting system, a longer campaign that spans across various maps, the user interface has been improved and made simpler, mods are openly welcomed, a Multiplayer co-op mode has been added, and now players have two choices to continue gameplay even after finishing the campaign with New Game Plus and Mapworks. The graphics and sound are really nice and the special effects are superb. With Torchlight 2's random map generator for dungeons, replay value is even greater. Loaded with action and filled with loot, this game is sure to entertain.
Probably the best thing about Torchlight 2 is the seemingly endless customization possibilities. Players can choose their character from four different classes, each with their own unique abilities and specialized equipment. There are countless armor and weapon variations throughout the game, most of which add additional bonuses or power-ups to your character. Then of course, sockets can be added to the equipment which will allow you to insert gems into them, giving even more bonuses and special abilities. And don't forget that while journeying through the expansive dungeons scattered across the maps, players will come across furry little critters that offer an assortment of enchantments that can be added to each item for a fee. With the right combinations you can turn your character into a demigod and that's before you ever begin experimenting with the almost limitless crafting system where players can create stronger potions, better gems, more unique items and armor, etc.
Of course, no game is perfect and players have their own tastes and preferences. So while the game is a lot of fun and highly recommended, there are a few things players should know when deciding on whether to buy this game or not. There is no controller support included with Torchlight 2. Players who prefer controllers over mouse will need to add in their own mapping or download one. The good news is there are several already out there and can easily be added, so its not a really big hassle. Don't expect a deep storyline in this game. While there is a story that plays out across the campaign trail, its not fleshed out very well and is less than enthralling. While it is lacking, this shouldn't be an issue for the most part because the game keeps the action moving at a steady pace so most players probably won't even give it a second thought anyways.
Also, expect a few random bugs. Fortunately none of them are game-breaking and not of big consequence but they do exist. From fishing holes not being accessible to loot being hurled out of the player's reach or even characters occasionally being pushed onto a ledge by a charging mob with no way to escape (other than using a port scroll), know that on occasion something like this may happen. Players aren't really going to miss much of anything as a result and aside from these minor nuissances the game runs very smooth and never crashes.
While Torchlight 2 isn't ground-breaking and its not going to blow your socks off, the game is still very entertaining and offers numerous hours of gameplay. There's a reason why its one of the most popular and liked games on Steam and can be found in most game libraries. This game has a lot of features included and all of them are packaged extremely well. If you don't already own it, I definitely recommend picking up a copy.

If you enjoyed Torchlight, you'll find more of the same in Torchlight II - and 'More' is pretty much the theme.
Whereas Torchlight was a very concise game with one central hub and a very deep mine to explore, Torchlight II has expanded with several 'base hubs', themed areas and a whole host of new enemies to turn into gibblets. Personally, I found this to have it's positives and negatives.
There were times that I missed the simplicity of Torchlight, of just digging down deeper to find tougher and tougher enemies the deeper I delved into the mine. I missed how all your essential services were kept together at the mining camp, and it was easy to navigate. There were times in TL2 where I had to bounce between several hubs to get back to the original base camp where the shared stash and personal stash was based to retrieve gems and items I had stored for later. While this isn't anything major, it did add up to what I felt was a lot of down time between turning monsters into blood stains.
However, the expanded features of Torchlight 2 do add several themed areas which are you able to explore to a point (and in some cases contain hidden quests & secret rooms), and probably more important to some - hosted coop. Coop mode is fairly stable and somewhat easy to setup and join when it comes to finding a game. The game provides an in-game text box to allow for people to communicate.
The main addition that I find as a huge bonus is the integration of the Steam Workshop, which has enabled several add-on mods and 'fixes' to things you might not like (such as mods which bring back classes that were removed from the original game).
In short Torchlight II is worth playing, as it does enough to be different from the first Torchlight (like it or not), and it's one of the more polished dungeon crawler/loot games out there. Have a good look through Steam Workshop to see if there are any additions you'd like to add to the playthrough, and you should be able to create an experience you'll enjoy.

Update: A year and a half later after I wrote the intial review...well, my appraisal hasn't changed.  In fact if anything it's improved - the devs continually update the game with meticulous attention paid to balance, while also seeking to move the game forward with new mechanics that enhance and deepen gameplay, along with releasing a new character every month, which continually keeps things fresh and interesting. Take the words of any naysayers with a grain of salt - as with any game like this, people will balk at any change.  Here's to the game's continued success!
A solid PC replacement to the nonlinear fighting game genre, currently dominated by the Super Smash Brothers franchise. Brawlhalla is also unique enough to present new challenges to seasoned veterans and to stand on it's own merits both artistically and mechanically, accessible enough to introduce to your friends or siblings who are desperately looking for a game that you all can play together, but with enough mechanical finesse and nuance to present an engaging deep game for those that desire it.
Featuring easily set up online and couch-party play, Brawlhalla doesn't mince about with getting you straight to the point, allowing you to get straight to the game while still presenting you with the charm, artistry and finely tuned gameplay required to give you a solid fighting experience.
More well balanced than most fighting games, the initial appearance of a lack of variety is both deceptive and allows the game to avoid tier bias and gameplay that strongly favors one style or character over another.
The online mode is great to play on short breaks, or if you're looking to be more engaged, there's a highly competitive ladder mode for extended competitive play.
Great all around!

The Tribe has some cool ideas in it and tries to take the runner genre in a cool direction but it has some major issues that have only been partially address since Early Access. I think it's worth $5 but only if you're into the specific twist it's offering.
The basics are that you're a tribal leader who is trying to lead your gaggle of cavemen to a mountain on the other side of the world. You have to go through a number of levels to get there, each of which is randomly generated and can be made up of several environment types with different risks and benefits. The randomness of the level generation can sometimes be very unfair but that's the nature of the beast. Your tribe is always running and you can spread them out to various different pre-determined positions and retract them using the mouse buttons. You have to acquire food and grow your tribe as you go but the more tribesmen you have, the more food you burn. However, the more tribesmen you have, the more dangerous creatures and situations you can handle.
You have several abilities you can trigger and retract using the number keys. You have spears which have to be out to hunt animal food but will destroy fruit and scare the animals away if you have them out when on the same row as them. You also have fire which you'll need to scare some bigger creatures away and light the way at night, which you'll sometimes have to run through if you don't have enough food. You can also spend some of your food reserves to grow your tribe or cannibalise some tribesmen to get some emergency food. Yep, there's cannibalism in this game. You'll also encounter other small tribes and if you're big enough, you can recruit them or kill them for food as well.
Unfortunately, you're never really told how many tribesmen are needed to deal with the various threats you'll come across. This requires a lot of frustrating trial and error and will cost you many runs as you try to figure it out. The patterns your tribesmen take with different mouse clicks is also not made clear and this also takes a lot of practice and memorisation. Beyond this, not much needs to be explained to you, which is good because what English is in The Tribe is very poorly translated and some of it just makes no sense. There were larger, largely text based encounters that took place in between missions in Early Access that have been removed, I assume partially because of these translation difficulties.
The music and sound effects are fitting of the era being depicted in The Tribe. I originally didn't like the art style but it grew on me with time and I think that will come down to personal taste. The game runs fine, though its leaderboard implementation is not especially great.
For $5, I do still recommend The Tribe, even with its faults. It's a good take on the runner genre with a unique setting and mechanics to match. If you don't like runner games and learning and adapting on your feet, this probably won't be for you. But if you like a challenge and something that rewards quick reflexes, definitely give it a shot.
