Eurofighter has only tenuous claims to realism. The actual Typhoon is a collaborative effort whose design and production are shared among Germany, Spain, Italy, and the United Kingdom. It hasn't seen combat yet, but there are several operational models, and it's doing the rounds at air shows, so this game isn't so much outright fiction as it is early speculation. The German consortium that manages the actual plane's development has endorsed Eurofighter Typhoon, but that isn't saying much--considering that Lockheed Martin endorsed Novalogic's completely unrealistic F-16 Multirole Fighter. Eurofighter isn't quite as simple as F-16, but there's still a lot of silliness going on, and it will turn off hard-core flight-sim fans. This silliness includes broadly modeled sci-fi weapon systems, a simplified damage routine that uses hard-coded hit points, an overpowered flight model that will leap off the runway like Tinkerbell and glide forever if you shut down your engines, enemy aircraft that blatantly violate their real-world capabilities, and even the ludicrous equivalent of a boss battle that's waiting for you at the end of the campaign.
Although there are some dynamic elements, the campaign is worth playing through only once. It's driven mainly by a sequence of scripted events that slavishly repeat each time you replay the game. Russian forces invade Iceland, gaining ground when you fail a mission. Successful missions beat them back one territory at a time. Unfortunately, as a single-player game, Eurofighter is entirely closed off behind its campaign. There are no single missions, skirmish modes, quick-action options, and scenario editor. There are some interesting multiplayer modes beyond simple deathmatch, but without a matching service or a stronger online presence, you won't have an easy time finding other players. Also, it won't work on a LAN unless each player owns a copy of the game.
Although it uses the engine from DID's Wargasm, which played down close to the ground, Eurofighter's graphics look every bit as good as those of DID's past flight sims. Iceland's green hills and rocky snow-covered mountains are nicely drawn under a lowering gray sky layered with cloud cover. The pyrotechnics and aircraft have been given a lot of attention, and it shows. You'll see some spectacular battles with planes letting out streamers of contrails, bursts of chaff and flares, and bright glowing missiles on columns of smoke. Not many post-World War II sims model flak guns, but you'll find them here sprouting deadly airborne flowers of smoke and fire. The aircraft models are particularly impressive, from lumbering transports to Harriers with camouflage paint and the Eurofighter itself, lovingly drawn down to every last "No Step" decal on the wings.
From its previous games, DID has carried over the "smartview" concept, in which a camera jumps around the entire map and shows the highlights of the war in a series of cinematic cuts and sweeping views. This is a great way to make use of your downtime (when you're waiting between missions), but it's not as flexible as the smartviews from DID's previous games, in which you can choose what you want to see. Oddly enough, the external views aren't very flexible either. DID has created a gorgeous game, but it didn't allow the full freedom to admire it.
From inside the plane, the game doesn't look quite as good. The internal cockpit graphics are blurry and low-res against the detailed terrain. Because the Eurofighter uses an advanced "glass cockpit," it is flown almost exclusively using multifunction displays, represented here by configurable inset windows that pop up along the bottom of your monitor. Many of these displays are too cramped (you can't zoom out far enough) or too cluttered (there's too much brightly colored information competing for your attention). Because the controls are so streamlined, it can be an ordeal trying to target the enemy you want. To Eurofighter's credit, there's a lot of friendly activity in the skies around you, but it's not easy to decipher. You can't target friendly units, and there's no theatrewide airborne radar, like the AWACS in DID's previous sims. This means a lot of the activity in Eurofighter feels like an unknown jumble instead of an actual war effort. What are all those MiGs doing swarming around those green contacts 20 miles from your starboard? Is it a helpless C-17 being jumped? Is it a dogfight with local friendlies? To find out, you have to go look for yourself.
Although Eurofighter supposes a lot of new technology, most of it is given to the Russians, who wind up fielding magic cruise missiles and the functional equivalent of UFOs. Your weapons are common to those of most flight sims, but most of them are woefully underdocumented. Pity the poor newcomer who doesn't know how to lead a laser-guided paveway to its target.
Some of the weapon modeling is suspect. Since countermeasures such as chaff and flares are fully automated, it's hard to get a feeling for how effective enemy missiles really are. At any rate, they seem much more accurate than your own supposedly state-of-the-art meteor missiles, which are inclined to lose their target lock at the drop of a hat. Then there's Eurofighter's version of the hellfire air-to-ground missiles, called--get this--brimstones. These nearly useless weapons seem to be outfitted with a dirt-homing seeker head, because they're more likely to plow into the ground beside a tank rather than actually hitting the tank itself. It's aggravating enough trying to plink hard-to-see ground units without worrying about your useless brimstones. It's a sad state of affairs when you'd rather have a rack of dumb rockets rather than the latest hi-tech guided missile.
Because of its streamlined gameplay and suspect realism, Eurofighter isn't going to appeal to hard-core flight-sim players. But considering that it's locked into a campaign that's more about pilot management and cockpit juggling, Eurofighter also won't appeal to casual gamers who just want to blow things up. Rage has done a far better job combining pilot management, a scripted campaign, and graphics-intensive action in Hostile Waters. And DID has done a far better job creating accessible flight sims in its EF2000 series. Eurofighter Typhoon is stranded somewhere between these past efforts, and consequently brings together the least of both worlds.

GunZ the Duel was a very interesting and fast paced experience. Instead of being bound by classes, you were free to experiment and customize your character as you see fit. Your main limitation being weight, your loadout would usually be quite balanced. If you wanted to carry a rocket launcher, heavy machine guns, and a sword for maximum DPS you might have to head out without armour, for instance! You could go full melee, full ranged, or anything inbetween. It was a beautiful system that encouraged you to try everything it had to offer.
As time went on, players also adopted K-Style. Using animation canceling, players could perfect a complex series of keypresses that'd allow for seamless traveling across any given map - and unrivaled combat prowess limited only by a K-styler's skill level and dedication. Both K-Stylers and the more average vanilla-gameplay style worked hand-in-hand and made for amazing and intense matches.
Questing was a bit confusing, but entertaining and challenging all the same. So much freedom, new gametypes and updates every so often, it was fun while it lasted. Near the end of its life, GunZ the Duel introduced an almost MOBA-style gametype that allowed players to get better gear than the real-money store offered. This killed the sales and "forced" them to shut the original GunZ down before GunZ 2: the Second Duel was released. It seemed like the timing was a little too perfect and on-purpose, but I digress.
GunZ 2: the Second Duel changed some things up.
Movement was made to be more accessible. They moved away from the steep learning curve of K-Style, opting for a system where you can run up walls and get around with but a few taps of the spacebar. This seems alright. Where I think it begins to fall apart, is the addition of classes. For me, this destroyed much of the experimentation and customization that made GunZ so balanced and fun. With these classes, at times it almost seems like a rock-paper-scissors scenario. Everything feels clunkier than the original GunZ. The first game had very tight controls that were beyond responsive. It was built to be that way. This one isn't as quick and generally feels a little sluggish and off for one used to the old style of gameplay.
Nowadays, the servers for this game are barren... With no community to even play with, this game simply needs to be avoided entirely at this point. I'd say give it a try if you were still interested, but I can't even offer that much anymore. Just avoid it.
If you're like me, and very much enjoyed the original GunZ, look into something called Freestyle GunZ. It is a fan-run version of the original game with a bunch of fan additions. It isn't the real deal, but it's the best we've got now and has a decent playerbase. Way easier to find a match there than the mess that is GunZ 2: the Second Duel. Old veterans and those new to the series alike won't find what they're looking for here.

I was really hyped about this game when I first saw it, but it turned out to be disappointing and overall I don't think it's worth 40+ euros. My recommendation - play Tropico instead, it has better music too.
1. The tutorial doesn't quite help in instructing what to do. I was asked to create a new district, but the proposal didn't go through, so I had to wait some time to create the said district. All peachy, but now what? I've played for 20 more years, but no other pop-up to tell me what else to do. And of course there was no goal mentioned anywhere, however, I couldn't fully utilise all the features, because the institutions were locked (even though I've researched both the port and train station). So I had to start over the campaign.
2. The map is not fully displayed, not even as a minimap, nor can you move around by moving the cursor to the edge of it, so creating a new district or placing a service turns out to be quite hard to do, since you have to right click+drag to have visibility.
3. Things get repetitive after a while - All you do is plead the council to approve your proposals and select choices on random events.
4. Technology vs city approvals - Ok, you have the electricity, water and gas unlocked, but your council is constantly REFUSING to adopt these technologies in the districts. No matter how much you plead, demand or threaten. So what's the point of having them, if you can't use them?
5. No clear explanation on how the economy works. You are just told in the tutorial that you can see the city data. But that's all. So you end up with bankrupt companies without explanation and the point mentioned above doesn't help either, since the companies can't expand/function due to the lack of resources.
I wish they had released an early access game, at least to have the satisfaction of knowing they'll improve it.
Think twice before you buy it.

There's bad games and then there are games with absolutely no positive quality to them at all.
Sure, it's hard.  It's also stupid.
You don't have any checkpointing or saving system, so although you can probably get through the first terrible level in a couple of tries, the 2nd level will probably be a little tougher to get through, but each time you fail on the 2nd level you have to repeat the 1st level.  That also means listening to a sound clip of R.Kelly's "I believe I can fly" every time you need to make the jump at the end.  Be prepared to hear that sound clip a lot, because the 3rd level is tough, and you will have to repeat that first level almost every few seconds.
There's no models, textures, or anything else.  Just platforms that slowly move and try to make you fall, so you can go repeat all the prior levels, without any reward.
There's also another sound clip, I assume it is the developer's voice saying "you win".  It's a rather crude sound clip, probably his first take, and it wouldn't surprise me if it was recorded on a cell phone from the mid 90's.  You get to hear this sound clip when you reach the end of the level, even if the next level is virtually identical to the one prior to it.
Not to mention the non-installer issues where you actually have to manually install the game into the Steam folder.  Or how it says "SpeedRun" in the game's blurb but speed in this game will get you killed instantly, and you have to hear R.Kelly again.  Actually, not hearing the R.Kelly sound clip is the reward of beating a level, if there is one.

As someone who rarely plays fighting games I was surprised how amazing this game is!
Brawlhalla is a 2D fighting game similar to  Super Smash Bros Melee, very fast paced which requires quick reactions.
Just find a game, choose a character and you are set for your match!
Every character plays differently regarding the 2 weapons it gets and what kind of "signature moves" you can do. Every few patches a new character is introduced to the game.
You can choose between different game modes:
Online Free for all - 4 players are battling against each other. Every kill earns you points, every death you take takes points away. After 4 minutes the player with the most points wins the match.
Custom games - Invite some friends, you can customize the gamemode, time, bots, teams...
On to the competetive ranked modes
Ranked 1v1 - Battle against another opponent, everyone gets 3 Stocks (lives) and whoever takes all of the opponents stocks wins the game. If you win, you earn rankpoints which add up over time and rank you in different "divisions". If you loose, you loose points, which can get you downranked
Ranked 2v2 - In this mode you can battle with a friend against 2 other opponents and get rankpoints for your team and for yourself exclusivly for the 2v2 mode. Be careful though, you can hit and kill your teammate, which can lead to amazingly funny moments. :D
And thats about it. This game is free to play and you can play every aspect of it without spending a dime. There are some legends (characters) locked in the beginning, but you earn ingame gold over time, which can unlock the remaining characters. Every few weeks, after the patching, the legends rotate, so you can play the previously locked ones as well. The only thing you spend real money on are cosmetics or purchasing all legends at once.
One counterpoint though, but it's not related to the game directly. The community tends to be pretty toxic. A ton of guys call you a cheater, hacker or spammer if you win, or a noob if they win.
On the other hand, I met some pretty cool dudes in the game and we are playing ranked 2v2s a lot. :)
Do I recommend this game?
Yes, absolutely! Its very fun and easy to pick up and just messing around. If you like the competitive aspect of it you will very much like the ranked modes. Also, to mention it again, the game is free, just try it, you will not regret it!

DISCLAIMER: The game described herein is a free to play multiplayer game. Your experience will vary. This review is based on infantry and paratrooper gameplay for reasons which will be described below. Because of the inherently subjective nature of this sort of game, no scores will be attached.
IMMERSION: The game is a first person perspective shooter. Environments seem reasonable for immersion purposes visually. Audio is also reasonable for the purpose. Players have the opportunity for agency, but it is limited to uniform colour and loadout. There is a caveat to this though, agency comes with high costs in time spent unlocking and earned currency or purchased currency. Combat tends to be fast paced and close quarters instead of methodical slow advancement. There is a possiblity of that sort of engagement, but it seems to be an exception, not the rule.
DIFFICULTY: difficulty is not adjustable. The user interface unfortunately contributes to difficulty. This is mainly because some functions are not obvious at first glance. Players must be in a match to access a keyboard layout or rebind keys. While these are mostly common across the genre, there are commands specific to this game.
LASTING APPEAL: If the game seems to have a stumbling block it's here. Time to enter a match varies by faction, matchmaking group (a stat derived from gear level, class, or account ranking, this isn't clear), and class with under represented factions finding matches quickly. In my experience this could be as little as 10 seconds and as long as 7 minutes. Servers are random luck, there is no server browser to address this. What seems to cause the most frustration though is the slow pace of unlocks combined with the high costs of upgrading. Additionally, and this is extremely subjective, the progression curve ends up being inverted, high ranking players will often have heavily upgraded fully automatic weapons, new players will have semi-automatic rifles with seemingly unhelpful sights (apart from the M1 Garand). While to a degree this is historically correct, there are weapons in game with dubious claim to historical correctness. What all this means for new players is there is a high frustration curve, and it will last for a good while. Still the game is worth trying because none of the issues are unfixable. Maps can be account level locked, co-op matches can be implemented, a weapon rental system can be added, etc.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

The game brings aspects of politically-driven and city-building games that come together to create a unique experience. Utilizing a district zoning method with other controls (such as adjusting the density of the district to be sparse or tight-knit, or changing the amount of lots dedicated to residential, commercial, etc.), you are able to plot out the literal squares of your city. However, the thing that caught most people off guard is that you don't manually place buildings except for municipal services (like schoolhouses, clinics, or fire stations). Most of the changes that impact the city and change the outlook of things take place in the senate where you propose tax hikes/cuts, adjust funding, and issue edicts for approval. Depending on the relationship between the mayor (player) and present political factions and their spot on the political compass, they will ultimately decide if you are able to carry out your plans. The game is mostly a balancing act where you try to weigh it to your side. From time to time, the game will pose events that impact your contstituents and need your input, like if you support or want to abolish child lavor, support alcohol liscenses, or if you should enstate anti-pollution laws.
I for one enjoyed what the game had to offer, and would recommend this game to any individual who wants a game to simulate real political functions and to also revel in making personal decisions about the citizens you reside over.
If I had any critques about the game, I'd say that a neater user interface would be better, and to make alerts to the player more visble and last longer. Secondly, have the tutorial go more in depth about companies and how to make revenue.

I'm a student in Land Use and Government Law (among others) and I've been waiting for a game that makes you less of a "God Mayor" simulator where you design a city without limitation, but more of a "county supervisor" simulator, where even small actions are political and costly beyond just the bottom line of the city. TL;DR This game is a indirect city management game with politics that takes some time to figure out and is deceptively complex.
This is a fairly unique management simulation.
You are a mayor who is one of several stereotypical dynasties who has been granted control of a city.
You take no direct hand in building it but must manage the city indirectly though successful political maneuvering of the council.
The game has a very familiar city-builder-esque cycle:
1. Choose and Object to build
2. Wait for budget to be positive enough to sustain it.
rinse, repeat
It adds a few other things to the cycle:
Petition the council for funding of your project or fund it yourself.
Intorduce laws and get them passed.
In between all this you must regularly make decisions on various events both random and othewise presented to you. These events can have bigger consequences than they first appear.
Early on in this game; I felt like all the options they give you in manageing the political parties were just different shades of the same flavor but the political system is actually much more subtely complex than I thought.
Another thing that ended up being more interesting than it first appeared is the economy.
If you enjoy games like Crusader Kings 2, Victoria 2 (really any paradox grand strategy or grand strategy games in general) You will probably like this game. If you want an outlet for your creative outbursts this will probably end up frustrating and boring you.

On top of that, after you place a "ward," it's then broken into different zones, residential, industrial, etc.  From what I can tell, it just randomly assigns these zones, depending on the terrain.  Again, totally annoying and screws up the building process.   30 minutes in, and I still can't figure out how to place the Train Station.  It really shouldn't be this difficult or clumsy.
Tutorial is a joke.
Luckily I a got a refund.
So TLDR:
Clumsy, complicated building and planning
Control taken out of players hands/ distributed by random assignment
Politics not really engaging
All we needed was a polished and engaging build-off from Tropico ... but they threw the best parts of Tropico out
Music and sound, meh.

I really don't know what to say about this game.... A part of me likes it, and a part of me doesn't.

Instead what I got, was a boring "don't worry about this we'll do it for you!" type of game. No challenge at all, hardly anything to do, and things become repetitive quickly. I also noticed the graphics of the buildings degrade a lot when you're not zoomed in on them, they literally become white squares with black windows (played on ultra).
I'll list some of my Pro's and Con's.
- Game was fun and intriguing for the first hour.
- Feels and
different from other city management/builders.

- Graphics could be better.
- Price tag is drunk, even the 35€ pre-order price I paid for it.
- Game becomes dull quickly.
- The AI is as dumb as me.
- The UI is confusing, and the "benefits" from doing things are poorly explained. 5% Sales demand = ?.
I wish Steam had an option that was in between "Yes" or
.
If you like really easy city management/builders with close to no manual control over the layout with political implementations, this might be for you. If you're willing to pay 45€.

For now, I'm going to give this a no. I'll probably try to get a refund.

Devil May Cry 4: Special Edition is a hack and slash, created and published by Capcom. It's a remaster of Devil May Cry 4, same boring plot, same universe and this is the worst PC port I have ever played. It's horrendous, I regret buying this game. It has some performance issues like running this game on 30fps capped on your playthrough (I think this game is CPU intensive). You cannot turn off the motion blur, light shafts and godrays. I did perform a stress test before doing my playthrough, it was running 60fps solid but right now, its running on 30 fps. I was really disappointed about it. Special Edition added 3 new characters, Vergil, Trish and Lady. But they don't have their own unique cutscene, story and their own battle background music, it's just borrowed from Nero and Dante's BGM (Background Music). I want to point out that how the hell Nero introduced in DMC4? I want a backstory about him but like I said, it's a boring and unexplained plot. I am going to defend that the combat system is amazing, that's what it's known for DMC franchise. New features added like Legendary Dark Knight Mode, it's a game mode where you are facing against an overwhelming numbers of enemies. Turbo Mode to increase the gameplay speed up to 20% (So, it's 120% speed of gameplay). I was having fun playing LDK Mode as Vergil. I don't know why Capcom added so called "Time Savers" DLC. It's just a garbage DLCs that you will get 200,000 Red Orbs, Blue Orbs to increase max health and Proud Souls (I easily get 1,000,000 Red Orbs and over 500,000 Proud Souls from LDK Mode) and Super Vergil, Super Dante and Super Nero costume (Infinite Devil Trigger).
In this game's overall, I am so disappointed about this game. The performance issues, boring storyline, recycle levels and character's own storyline made me feel like I got scammed (It's Capcom, what do you expect from the corporate?). It's a 5 out of 10, not recommending this game, EVER. God, I'd rather play DmC Devil May Cry than this PC port.

First of all great game. There are however, a few glaring issues that may need to be fixed in an upcoming update of some sort.
1.) Scarlet's attacks have a MASSIVE amount of range, especially the lance. This does not mix well that she is tied with being the hardest hitting character from the get go, along with having decent other stats makes her a very cheap character to play as [regardless of whether she gets the hammer is besides the point]

3.) Some of the characters [almost all of them] require little to no skill to play. Hattori and Lucien are the notable exceptions, as their attacks don't have absolutely massive ranges and high amount of damage. This is a fighting game, but most attacks rely on huge ranges instead of actual skill
4.) A lack of invincibility frames KILLS this game. Having your♥♥♥♥♥beat off the screen in the middle of performing what should be a killing blow makes no sense at all
5.) The jumping mechanics. Enough said on that front
6.) The light attack do next to nothing. It would make a lot more sense if lighter attacks were easy to string, but there is virtually no stun time for hitting an opponent, and the range is normal for a fighting game compared to heavy attacks' range
7.)The characters need more moves. The amount of moves a character has is extremely basic, and makes gameplay repetitive and tedious as opposed to fun to play. In addition the only stats that matter are attack and defense. The other two don't seem to do much
8.)The online is full of kids who will spam the same attack over and over and over and that massively removes and playability of the game

Great game.  Short, but cheap.  You'll only get about 3 hours out of this game (more if you do collectibles) but it's a great 3 hours with an amazing ending.
As far as gameplay, imagine that Far Cry 3 got a lot less buggy, a lot less tedious, the combat got a lot more stable, and was injected with a heaping, healthy dose of FUN.  Fall damage was removed, as was the need to breathe while underwater, and you can sprint at about 30 MPH.  Everything has been given a neon tint (to emulate an old 1980s sci-fi movie) but it's never really distracting.  Overall, the dialogue and combat feel very Duke Nukem-ey.
On the negatives, the game is VERY short (3 hours on my playthrough), but it's an extremely enjoyable experience for those 3 hours.  By the end of it, you'll be feeling like a super-powered monster, able to kill almost anything in one or two hits.  I found this to be pretty boring, because then the combat just got tedious instead of challenging.  Still, I loved this game, and I can't wait for the sequel.

Before I start to try to write a review, I want to give you two points that may give you a better approach to this game:
1) It doesn't really need a controller. Keyboard works fine and, probably just for this game, is better than a controller.
You'll understand why, I'm sure of that. Basically, don't use the controller.
2) It is a short game, so I recommend you to buy it at 75% or 90% discount.

Before you read (As my review could not appear as interesting nor helpful) Buy it, while keeping in mind those two points I wrote.
Shall we start now?
This game is enchanting. A fable. Entrancing landscapes reminds me of paintings, a game of lights, strong yet soft colors that you probably dream about when listening to yes, a fable.
The music is another turmoil of emotions that blows with the story, the hills, the water, the grasslands. It's the wind itself that lifts leaves and sighs, smiles and tension.
Their own language doesn't need to be truly understood. You won't need to understand their words to bond with their footsteps and their story.
I used the word "Fable" Because is what I truly saw and wanted to believe to when I played this game.
As such then, it has a moral: how harsh is not life itself, but living.
You'll see how places of sadness and slavery can't suffocate hope and love, you'll live while the past haunts you, growing over a guilt that shouldn't exist.
You'll see how mischiefs and purity of a child, even when on a journey to save your father's life, wins against all odds.
You'll see that the bright life of your village is a deep contrast to what lies behind its gates, among rivers of blood and vultures.
And you'll understand that the only way through everything is to keep pushing forward: it doesn't matter if you are half of what you were when everything began. It doesn't matter if you were a bit spoiled; because life gives and pretends you to give her the same and a bit more, even if you don't smile anymore. Even if you're alone (Although you never are truly alone).

Urban Empire is not a city building game.
In Urban Empire your main goal will be to stay in control. If you want to place something as trivial as a police station, you have to be able to pay for it, pay the service costs, have your political allies and enemies approve it during a vote and be sure that the running costs don't kill your city long time.
Personally, i didn't have any technical issues but there's some reports in the Forums you might wanna check out. The overall gameplay is fine but feels lacking in some aspects and now and then it's not exactly clear how some things play together until you've done some trial and error. However, overall it still makes for a good and unique game.
If you're looking for a relaxing city builder, there are better options available. If you're looking for something you have to work into but is quite rewarding this might be for you. It's certainly not for everyone - but that's what steam refunds are for.

City builder with the political aspects of games like Democracy 3, and a Penultimo cameo.
I rather enjoy it, because with the political aspect, you need to pick and choose your battles. Always strongarming the council into getting your way WILL backfire on you.
Build new districts when the economy is booming, increase taxes when it's in the red and always keep at least 10X the city's income in the treasury for cases where the economy turns around.
The council is remarkably reasonable as long as you don't strong arm them. They will go against their own political compass if the economy is threatened or if it's booming and play to the approval of the public. If your city has high education, even the conservatives are likely to vote yes on progressive matters to avoid loosing approval.
And if you have trouble getting something trough the council, like expanding infastructure in a district? Do it in steps as it's much easier to get trough.
However if you try to play it like any other city builder and constantly strongarm even your political enemies.. you're going to have a bad time. So don't do it. Go with the political flow and try to focus on a healthy economy with your own ideals for the city being secondary.
Doing as described above, I was able to expand the city into 6-7 districts before the first era was over and with a few 100k in income, which I managed to expand into over a million by the third era. As a result I only ever had to persuade or strongarm the council in 1 or 2 matters so far, and where the vote didn't go my way or I needed to get it trough despite the council makign it impossible, I just overturned it instead of trying to strongarm every party and move them into negative approval as i seemed to take a much lower hit from overturning the vote and the good will bounces much faster back from a 1-2 hit accross the board than from a 5-8 hit on a few parties.
Also if you have trouble starting off and expanding, then start out by raising taxes 3-4% and as soon as you're in the positive after building the first district, zone another before you start adding services. It'll give you a bigger starting population & industry which will help keep your economy strong and make it much easier to continue expanding after adding services.

This review will be updated as more information is gathered. [Updates at bottom]
TL, DR: In a game espousing political wrangling, manipulation, and development there is only one political path available and it will happen whether you pursue it or not; the other parties will eventually pass every edict that is beneficial/required (unions, child labour laws, etc.) without any need for input. There are no significant historical decisions to make, as history is single-tracked (so no alt-history fun), your decisions are irrelevant and coercing the political parties is pointless anyways because there is only one outcome no matter who you play as. Tropico had more political influence and shaping than Urban Empire does.
The Tropico from the 1990s.
=====Normal Review Follows=====
The citybuilding element of this game is simplistic (not bad) and a little awkward at times (having to modify/improve infrastructure on each small district individually): it's serviceable, given that the game is focused on the political landscape.
Unfortunately this is where the game (from what I've seen so far) falls flat. Playing a technocratic mayor I found that the only social progress I would ever meaningfully make was towards the ideals of the modern left; nearly all of the conservative ones seemed to have drawbacks whereas liberal ones were purely beneficial. Why would this bother me, given that I am (for want of a better term) liberal? Because there was no teeth to the opposition. There was no temptation. The populace inevitably voted left-wing and thus all edicts were effortlessly passed to support their policies, while the conservative groups languished, ineffective, in the background. Was it because I educated my populace that they so overwhelmingly supported such efforts? It's impossible to tell, since education is required just to keep the population content.
To compound matters a selling point of the game is marching onward through the eras with the political tribulations that followed. Unfortunately these matters seem to have almost no impact on anything you do in-game. A recession hit and I lost some income but recovered regardless. The Emperor was deposed and fled to my nation but no apparent benefits, drawbacks, or gameplay mechanics followed. Russia gets invaded by bloody France and there is no evident impact on my city. There's no alt-history, as has been confirmed by others, and there doesn't seem to be any way to influence politics or even be influenced _by_ politics, at least from what I have currently seen.
Next playthrough we'll see if a nationalistic luddite will actually change the way the game goes, or if it's all just kicking and screaming into the mundane future without regard for the possibilities that would emerge from quirky alt-history antics.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So far, so bad. Only way to progress is through unions, rights, etc. Spent the entire first two parts of the campaign resisting Unions (despite them having no mechanical downside and, I believe, being absolutely necessary to upgrade your economy/income), but ultimately it's futile.
While you can use underhanded means to usurp other political parties there doesn't seem to be any reason to do so. Over time they'll want to pass various laws that will only improve your society/income/etc. As previously stated, these edicts are almost exclusively left-leaning and there are no means to, say, create a human rights abusing society like China.
In a game where the entire draw is the political wrangling and manipulation, why is there only one political route to pursue that offers any success and is met with minimal resistance regardless of which parties you court? Hell, the conservative (or just abusive) policies I try to set offer me little but political gain with the party I already associate with, while the liberal/human rights ones give political capital, popularity, and economic advantages.
I feel like I'm railroaded into playing the game only one way. Despite having four "Dynasties" a tthe start (which, too, are preset) and the tagline being the option to influence decisions such as womens' rights and child labour, there is literally no reason to oppose any of it. Whether you pick the human rights advocate or the tech-hating luddite conservative it all ends the same way and trying to change it does nothing but prolong the inevitable.
Urban Empire espouses choices that matter but so far... none of my choices matter.

PvP comes in the form of "Monster Play," where you choose to fight as one of Sauron's minions or take your character into battle as one of the Free Peoples of Middle Earth. Ignore the push from other players to get to the level cap. This one is all about the journey, not the destination.

If you're a fan of the Half-Life series, Transmissions: Element 120 will make you have a really good time. Despite its short duration, the impact it leaves is very positive in my opinion. The game manages to captures the essence Half-Life and at the same time be something unique, which is not easy to do. First things first:
As for the plot (if there's any), it is very vage to actually say something about it. You can interpret it the way you want because there is no obvious argument elements in this game. This is not a negative thing in my opinion since it's a good way to catch the interest of the player.
Gameplay is the same as Half-Life 2 and its episodes (Which is really good in my opinion) with some small differences. You get a brand new weapon in replacement of the Gravity Gun. This new weapon, contrary to the Gravity Gun, emits repulsive forces that allow you to jump higher and push object that you can't physically reach. This helps you go through most of the game. Enemies also aren't able to see in darkness. This creates several situations that make the pacing of the game not feel heavy.
The graphics, despite not being an exponent in the industry or the best, they do fulfill their purpose. As you progress, you will see some awesome views, that along with well placed effects, great lighting, and awesome sounds generate an incredible atmosphere.
As mentioned before, the new ambience sounds are a great contribution in this game. They are well selected and well placed, so they have the best impact. You'll also hear the classic Half-Life 2 sound effects through the game, either enemies or objects. The most important thing here is that the devs know how make to use of the sounds, thus creating incredibly atmospheric scenarios.
In conclusion this is a game that provides a very good experience to anyone who plays it, even more if you're a fan of the Half-Life series. Its duration can be a positive or negative depending on the person, but to me personally it isn't a problem.

RWBY: GE isn't a terrible game, but it isn't the best game either.
Pros:
- Gameplay: While there isn't a tutorial or anything, the gameplay is actually kinda fun once you figure out how everything works.
- Level Design: I appreciate the large battle areas as you tend to have to run around to let your aura regenerate and shoot your enemies back while waiting.
- Characters: The character models are well-done, and their voices are the ones from the anime so I can't really critize them there.
- Graphics: Even though I have it at the lowest setting due to my weak graphics card, every looks pretty nice.
Cons:
- Story: I don't think game developers realize that most people tend to ignore conversations of characters that aren't in any sort of cutscene. And even you do pay attention, this story doesn't make a whole lot of sense and feels like it's there just to hang out.
- Gameplay: Even if you switch between characters, the fighting can get very repetitive regardless of what enemies you fight.
- Sound: The music is so quiet sometimes, and half the time there's no 'battle theme.' Also sometimes the voices sound really weird when you use the heavy attacks.
- Characters: The 4 dlc characters actually feel somewhat different than Team RWBY. Team RWBY is only minimally different amongst themselves.
- Level Design: Half the time the large areas that you think will be a battle are just an empty are with maybe a couple breakable boxes or a secret.
- XP & Skills: While I'm okay with a level cap of 10 (although the cap being like level 15 couldn't hurt), it's disappointing that xp orbs are the only obtainable items in the standard game. The skill upgrades also feel bland, and certain ones feel like their requirements are to high for the benefits they give.
Overall, RWBY: GE is a great concept of a game, with a lot of incompleteness that couldn't really be handled unless you watched the anime and were really interested. If they would smooth out just about everything in this game instead of making useless costume dlc, then this game could actually get a lot more players (whispers* especially if they had 2-player local).

This game is a masterpiece.
It is huge fun, very accessible, challenging, unique and fairly deep. If you love WH40K, Starship Troopers, RTS and/or strategy games, you will love Infested Planet.
The game is simple but not simplistic. The interface is clean and effective, controlling your units is intuitive. Despite being a strategy game, the balance of action and decision-making is excellent. The complexity of the game comes from the way the various systems (simple unto themselves) combine to provide a wide variety of situations to which the player must adapt. Despite the apparently simple gameplay, there is real depth here.
It is very easy to get playing. The story campaign starts with short easy missions, but ends up with massive slogs with full tech trees and hundreds of thousands of enemy casualties. You earn money to unlock new troops, techs and advantages along the way. You can emply many kinds of tactics from airstrikes to small high-tech squads with flamers and miniguns to large Imperial Guard-style meatgrinding charges.
The release of the dynamic "Planetary Campaign" DLC has greatly boosted replayability. The campaign will have you saying "just one more turn" and before you know it, hours have passed. The player can choose from five map sizes and five difficulty leves. Map layout and available techs are randomized. Part of me hates this (when I don't have my favorite tech available), but part of me appreciates that this forces the player to try new things, further extending the replay factor.
The graphics are fairly simple but very evocative, the sound design likewise. There are very distinctive aural clues to certain enemy types appearing, your bases being attacked, etc. When you close your eyes after a long gameplay session, you will see hordes of aliens in your mind's eye.
The developer is active on the forums and responds to the community. He has continued to support and expand the game.
Infested Planet is a master class on how to make a single player PC game. A clear vision, refined mechanics, trust in the players to understand and enjoy the game, customization and technical proficiency. I have not encountered a single bug (other than the millions my troops have splattered).
The one thing I would wish for is mod support.
Buy this game and all expansions, you will not be disappointed.

Drain's full LP of the game:
Infested Planet is a highly addicting RTS, which innovates in countless ways vs your typical RTS titles. While the campaign mode is short and won't provide many hours; its value will return tenfold in its customizable skirmish mode, which now includes a DLC for a map conquest campaign. This game was short and sweet.  I'm decent at these games so I started on the second hardest difficulty, but after just two rounds I stepped up to the hardest.  At that point, it was challenging enough to enjoy.  There's enough variety to keep you busy for at least 20 hours at that rate.  Worth it.

- Random alien mutations appear during the course of every mission, requiring your strategy to adapt as the aliens start deploying spiked barriers, shields, towers, spitters, and even evil clones of your troops.
- The story mode missions have a fun mix of objectives which can vary from protecting convoys to racing evil clones to drag crates to your own side of the battlefield.
- Solid selection of tactical options and upgrades in all modes, with the best one for the situation varying by the battlefield shape and alien mutation path.
- Simple, forgiving economy system inside the mission, with rewards for killing hives and finishing secondary objectives, and instant refunds if you regret a purchase or the tactical situation has changed.
- Excellent context-senstive commands.  You can run most missions with your whole team selected.  Ordering a building constructed or crate pulled automatically peels a squad member off to do the specific task.  And the grenade bombardment command is smart enough to avoid wasting ammo on overkill.

- You'll need to crank the difficulty up to hard or harder for a real challenge, but it's definitely there once you find it.
- There was one bug during the campaign that resulted in an escort target getting frozen in place. Resetting the mission fixed it.
- Occasionally hard to keep track of where allies respawn. The game seems to aim for the nearest control point, but that's not always clear with a highly mobile squad.
- Final boss battle was too easy compared to the lead-up mission.
- Once enemy clones appear fielding a scout is suicide, since the paralysis ability is overwhelmingly lethal in the hands of an evil clone.
This is a very solid real time tactics gane game with a slick interface and satisfying variety of missions and challenges.  I wouldn't blow full price on it, but if you see it on sale for $10 or less, it's  good for several hours of alien liquifying.

I think just about everybody is going to say this is a SSB clone, and while I won't entirely disagree, I have to say that this game is still vastly different... and it's not all good.
Pros:
* No pay-to-win
* Fantastic controller support
* Interesting character designs and art style
*Hit/collision detection is very excellent
Cons:
*Very simplistic fighting mechanics - Even with the weapons, there isn't much in the way of combos.
* Every character fights pretty much the same way - While this might partially be because of a person's play style, even characters with seemingly "long range" weapons like guns don't have any range. This essentially makes every character a melee fighter, and with the movesets and combos being just about the same, this gets boring pretty quickly.
*Lack of items - While I can understand not wanting to have dozens of items like SSB, 3 items isn't very fun either, especially when coupled with the previous issues.
*Lack of a full roster - Something else I can understand, you want people to support the game. At the same time, only having a handful of fighters to choose from (especially with the other issues) without being able to just play and unlock them... bad, just bad.
Overall: The game is alright. I know it isn't fully developed yet, so there's plenty of room for improvement, but even looking forward, if it's anything similar to what I see now... I'd stick to SSB.

This game is mildly buggy for me, and looking at the other reviews, it appears systemic.  That said, it's a pretty fun game.  100% worth getting if it goes on sale.
This game is easily doable with just a mouse (make sure to enable "Mouse Move"), and is good for running campaigns.  I tried to figure out a way to get the precision of movements with the mouse, with the long-distance movements of a keyboard, but it ended up a mess, so I just stuck with mouse-only.  However, when you get into Battle Chains, you'll either want a very big mousepad, keyboard controls, or a handheld controller (most recommended).
The beginning is pretty boring and sucky because you have crap weapons, and the good stuff doesn't appear towards the end of the first campaign.  My recommendation is to put it on easy and push for level completion asap, as gear and perks are locked by level.
[BEGIN SPOILERS]
As a side note:  Play through the first campaign once before going back and picking your perk/equipment.  Some people like the auto lasers, some people like homing missiles, some like chaingun spam, some people like the "death ray penetrator", etc.  Your build depends highly on what's available, and only until you have all your slots and weapons will you be able to form a solid build.
The most useful weapons for you early on will be your machine guns.  Because you only have two slots, and you're given missles which only hit Air-To-Air (ATA), you lose half your effective power against ground targets.  Because machine guns can hit both Air AND Ground, you don't lose your effective power using them (and because you only have a few slots available, you need to make the most of them).
You should be able to unlock **First Purchase and **Perky within 10 minutes.  And then **Unleash the Power and **Rejected within 30 minutes.
After the end of the first campaign, you should be close to, or have just unlocked your last weapon slot (everything is unlocked at Lv16).  Once all your slots are unlocked, you can choose/tune your build.  Completing the first campaign will unlock **Victory is Mine.
After you play around a bit with what you want to play with, create a new profile and start over again, picking the perks pertinent to your buildpath.  The new profile will also help you unlock achievements  **I Am Superior and **Long Running Series as you can play Verses Mode and Chain Mode between your two profiles..
The campaign can be played through 3 times on a profile.  The first time is normal, next time is called "+1", and the final time is "+2".  After that, the option is locked out, and you are forced to skirmish or battle chain.  At the end of +1 Mode, you will get **I am the Master.  You should also have completed **Powerful, **Super Master, **Ace, **Spam This!, **Careful Planning, and **Elite.  Possibly even **Millionaire, though I didn't unlock that until I started doing battle chains against random people.
Now that Campaign Mode is locked out, it's on to Skirmish and Battle Chain Mode.  Soon you should unlock **Catch 'em All with the new powerups.  Also, depending on your superpower, you should be able to drain/black-hole the red ship to get **Seeing Red.
After you chain a few times against yourself (I would suggest hanging around the last boss and letting your score surpass the other's by just a little bit), you'll get **Long Running Series.
The last two, **Just Too Giving, and **Combo Master, will require you to kill a *TON* of spammy things; I was finally able to unlock them by doing the "Random - Sky (+2)" level with 2 chains.
Also, as a side note, you can set levels to +3 after +2, though I'm not sure what the difference is.  Possible bug?
[END SPOILERS]

I think just about everybody is going to say this is a SSB clone, and while I won't entirely disagree, I have to say that this game is still vastly different... and it's not all good.
Pros:
* No pay-to-win
* Fantastic controller support
* Interesting character designs and art style
*Hit/collision detection is very excellent
Cons:
*Very simplistic fighting mechanics - Even with the weapons, there isn't much in the way of combos.
* Every character fights pretty much the same way - While this might partially be because of a person's play style, even characters with seemingly "long range" weapons like guns don't have any range. This essentially makes every character a melee fighter, and with the movesets and combos being just about the same, this gets boring pretty quickly.
*Lack of items - While I can understand not wanting to have dozens of items like SSB, 3 items isn't very fun either, especially when coupled with the previous issues.
*Lack of a full roster - Something else I can understand, you want people to support the game. At the same time, only having a handful of fighters to choose from (especially with the other issues) without being able to just play and unlock them... bad, just bad.
Overall: The game is alright. I know it isn't fully developed yet, so there's plenty of room for improvement, but even looking forward, if it's anything similar to what I see now... I'd stick to SSB.

Capcom’s year of upscaling its formidable back catalogue continues apace, this time with Devil May Cry 4: Special Edition.
It was originally released in 2008, and was the last of the so-called “white haired” Devil May Cry games before British developer Ninja Theory’s 2013 reboot. DmC received a mixed reaction at the time – somewhat harshly, in our view.
Fans of the franchise will be glad to hear that, as with Capcom’s current-gen revisits to various Resident Evil games of yore, it breathes new life into a game that's as reassuringly familiar as a comfy jumper or a family pet.
Apart from the much higher-resolution visuals, the chief attraction of the remastered Special Edition is the addition of a plethora of new characters. These include Trish and Lady, who had cameos in the original game, and Vergil, Dante’s twin brother who also featured in Devil May Cry and the rebooted DmC. You can play as each, slightly disappointingly, through the original collection of missions – although they do all feature different beginning and ending cut-scenes for each campaign.
Their differing play-styles add new depth and subtley to what would otherwise be uncomfortably repetitive proceedings. As does the cleverly conceived upgrade system that brings the in-game currency you earned playing as one character to all the others.
You also get the fearsome Legendary Dark Knight game mode – pitting the hardcore against a veritable maelstrom of demons – and switchable costumes for each character, which gratifyingly persist into the cut-scenes.
For the uninitiated, Devil May Cry is an agreeably typical Japanese action-adventure, which concentrates primarily on spectacular fighting with swords, guns and, in the case of Nero, an extending demon arm. It throws in a hint of platforming, some rather variable puzzle-solving, and a few of the most ridiculous, overblown and satisfying boss-battles you'll ever encounter.
As is often the case with games of its ilk, it also sports some of the most risible dialogue imaginable – even Terry-Thomas would have baulked at voicing the sentences uttered by the cartoonish baddies.
Visually it’s pure Gothic, with a mainly incomprehensible plot that revolves around angels and demons. In other words, its aim is to entertain at the highest level, rather than carve out a historical niche as a piece of serious art.
And entertain it most emphatically does. In the original game you start off as Nero, whose demon arm can grab and pummel enemies, and who also has a gun and a sword, which can powered up in various ways.
Devil May Cry 4: Special Edition rewards you handsomely for stringing together stylish combos of different moves, and you can cash in those rewards for increasingly arcane new moves. The points you earn for upgrading each character are carried over, so if you're trying out a new character, you can instantly upgrade them considerably.
This is an exciting prospect for big fans of the franchise and novices alike, and although it takes a while to get to grips with upgrading, you'll soon discover how important it is in the general context of the game
One feature of the original was its extensive and imaginative re-use of assets: you essentially play a campaign as Nero, followed by the reverse as Dante. It ought to be a major issue when you’re invited to play through the same campaign-of-two-halves with two different characters. Luckily, the variation in the style of play adds freshness to proceedings.
Nero is a good all-rounder, whose demon-arm “grips” are particularly handy. Dante is slower and more powerful, with better guns and a selection of swords. Trish and Lady are agile, gymnastic and more sword-centric. And Vergil benefits from an interesting Concentration mechanic that, if mastered, can lead to some really spectacular demon-demolishing. You do end up slightly jaded going over the same levels repeatedly, though.
The upscaled graphics help, though. We always thought that the original’s graphical ambitions outweighed the capabilities of previous-generation consoles. This proves to be true: the hike in resolution renders several busy sequences – previously incomprehensible – more clearly. And we never experienced any issues with frame rates.
Devil May Cry 4: Special Edition is something of a guilty pleasure – it’s an archetypal mix of the sublime and ridiculous. It’s great fun and offers plenty for those who played the original. And if you’ve never played a Devil May Cry game before? You, too, will find its considerable charms difficult to resist.

I'm a big fan of the devil may cry franchise, but this one is the worst!  It lacks the charismatic characters the series is known for, and the level design is downright lazy.  You will go through the same levels TWICE.  Then you'll fight every boss THREE times.  The one upside, is that the combat is downright fantastic, as expected.  Even if the bosses can seem really unfair, the combat is still what holds this game up.  The story is pretty lackluster.  Your basic, bad guys capture protagonists girlfriend, protagonist tries to rescue them and finds out the villians are out to release the demons into the world (shocker!), protagonist stops them.  Seriously...that's it.  Dante is in it, but he has such a minor and cliched role.  The reason he's in it at all (to recover Virgil's sword) is laughable.  Trish may as well not be in it.  She just walks around every once in a while...that's it.  The villians are just typical sword fodder with no believable motive and are not interesting in the slightest.  They make me really miss Virgil.  Nero is really front and center in this game, but he is no Dante.  He doesn't have any charm, he isn't funny, and he doesn't really feel very badass.  Just a bummer really.
Then, there's the camera...It's really really bad.  You might be in a fight when suddenly, the camera angle changes.  Because the perspective changes, that move you wanted to execute just got screwed because now you have the controller thumbstick pressed the wrong direction!  This is even worse during the platforming segments when you are jumping from one location to the next.  When the camera angle changes in the middle of maneuver, moving left is now moving right, and then...fail.  You get up and this time anticipate the camera angle change so you won't fall again...  This doesn't make the game challenging, it's just poor design.
This isn't a bad game, it just the worst in the series.  Hands down.  It would have been much better if it were half the length, instead of artificially extending it by making the second half literally the same as the first half.  Oh, and the dice boardgame segments are really terrible and frustrating.  DMC has always been a game about mastering the combat, fine tuning your skills.  Then they throw in these dice segments that are pure luck, just doens't make any sense.

A hauntingly beautiful story that reduced me to tears (both happy and sad) several times. The visuals were fantastic, and the way the controls were linked to the narrative was probably the best I've ever experienced. Controlling both brothers at the same time made the puzzle solving more interesting, as each brother could produce a different result from interacting with the people and the environment, and you had to figure out whether both brothers or only one was needed. It's easy to play in one sitting, but the story will stay with you for a long time after you're finished.

It's amazing how you get used to the controlling system. At first it's a bit confusing, but after a while it comes almost naturally, controlling both brothers smoothly. The game is really beautiful and very deep emotionally, the views and landscapes are breathtaking. It's a short game, yes, but I would totally experience it again.
The game was all about death and being able to cope with it, though. Beginning with their dead Mother, the journey is to save their dying Father. There's a lot of disturbing imagery regarding the hanging bodies in the forest, the man who you find hanging himself next to the burnt down house and... dead bodies. Then there's of course, the valley of dead giants that you basically need to mutilate to get through.

This game is really fun!  Sort of a small squad-based RTS mixed with some minor tower defense elements; mostly it is you just killing hordes and hordes of crazy aliens.  With some obvious nods to Starship Troopers, of course.
There is a decent progression system with lots of upgrades that unlock over time.  And the Story campaign lets you choose which missions you want to take on after the first few intro ones.  I wish there was persistence with my soldiers from mission to mission, though.
There are a few different mission types, from quick raids to defense to all-out-slaughter, which mostly determines how you want to spend your initial deployment points.  The maps are randomly generated, so even if you replay to do better or earn more money it won't be exactly the same every time.
The graphics are serviceable but definitely don't impress in screenshots (or even videos).  However, once you see swarms of hundreds of aliens moving across the map that all kind of fades away.
Another downside is that the game doesn't do a great job of explaining how some things work.  For example I can't figure out how to use some of the upgrade buildings, and the missions quickly turn so frantic that I don't have the time to mess with it.  Apparently there is a spacebar decision pause mode, which it didn't explain at all and I only learned about from other reviews right now.  :/
I got this in a cheap pack with all the DLC, but haven't even messed with the DLC stuff yet and it has been completely worthwhile.  Frantic, well balanced, just-one-more mission gameplay.

Great indie gem that is easily worth the price. While the strategies to win the game aren't especially deep, it is fun unlocking more advanced tech as you go and reaching that point of having access to the best weapons, buildings, and abilities.
A great strength of Infested Planet is how adaptable your forces are. You can swap the weapon type / class of a soldier (or even dismiss a soldier) at any time without losing any permanant resources (if you swap to a cheaper weapon you get a refund for the difference, etc...). This applies to auto-turrets, mine fields, buildings, etc... as well.
Often times the aliens will spawn a mutation that forces you to react by changing your squad loadout on the fly, so it is great that the devs allow you to do just that. It is a game that rewards both light strategic thinking and quick tactical decision making on the fly.
The only thing that would make the game better imo is some kind of RPG system where your squad members could carry over between maps. With proper management they're no more likely to die in this than they are in XCOM (abuse that teleport!). As it is your squaddies are entirely generic from map to map and even death to death. If nothing else, a neat touch could be keeping count of how many aliens a specific marine had killed in a battle / campaign :)

Revolution Ace is a Horizontal Scrolling Shoot'em Up game in Retro Style. A good comparison with one game of the 80's may be Foundations Waste, because of the similar setting in terms of story, enemies and landscapes. But, of course, a game that occupies 2000 times as much space should be claimed as an evolution compared to the games of former times. This is possible and justifiable. Speaking of the ship with its guns and shields, the game modes and the graphics, it's a pleasure to be part of the action. The sound is a mixture of patterns of games of the past and the difficulty levels allow the player to challenge his/her limit.
Not so special for games of nowadays, but nevertheless interesting, is the battle chain competition mode, where two players fight against each other by creating a battle chain in sending more and more enemy units to the other player, who is obliged to destroy them quickly to counter strike his opponent. All in all, it's a solid evolution of a classical game type.

I'm gonna repost my original review edited, with an addition for the most current state of the game.
Let me preface this by saying I have played more fighting games than any game genre out there. I love fighting games I always have, I'm not here to say Brawlhalla isn't a fun or good game, just that it is not a good "fighting" game.
It simply does not fit the genre. It lacks the one thing that makes a fighting game so competitive and functional; consistency. Myself and my friends have played hours upon hours of this game since it was in early closed beta. I took a break for a while due to some of the systems just not functioning the way they should in a fighting game. I came back after one of my friends became very competitive and they added a 2v2 ranked mode, so we started to play together. We're a platinum rank team despite having half the wins and half the hours of most other platinum teams.
The game however has some serious technical flaws:
One of the biggest issues I've found are the hurtboxes, they don't make sense. You can actually view these in the training/pratice mode and they are god awful. They are at most times an egg shape around the sprite of the character you choose. That itself seems like sloppy and super lazy approach to hurtboxes, but it gets worse. There are moments when your character will be outside of the hurtbox, sometimes with a noticeable gap between you and the hurtbox. The direction the hurtbox comes off your character does not have to make sense for a blast or meteoring at all sometimes it's just random.
Secondly, the hitboxes (yes the hitboxes and hurtboxes BOTH need work) why are the weapons not the outline for the hitboxes? I don't understand how that could not just be the easiest approach. There are times when using a character with a spear that the spear hitting your opponent is not enough, you have to get in to where your chests are almost touching for the spear to connect. What is the point of having a spear then if I still have to get within punching range?
The inconsistencies are a big issue for me, as I play some of the more consistent fighting games such as the Street Fighter series or KOF. Moves are not assigned to definite outcomes should they clash, based on hours of trying different approaches to set up moves it appears as though it is randomly determined not preset that one move should beat another given a certain collision.
EX: Four times I attempted to grab an opponent out of their down "sig" or heavy with my character, Baraza's, neutral sig. Three out of four of those attempts failed. Why did the fourth one work? He should've hit me just like he did the other three times. I ended up killing him and winning the game for our team and I'm telling you he should've hit me.
UPDATE 2/16/2016: This game is still trash, and has actually gotten progressively worse as development goes on. The community is one of the worst I have encountered in a game at all (and I used to play COD and LoL), on top of that the developers seem to encourage this negativity with their scumbaggy taunts they sell in the store. They are feeding the community to be one of the worst in the business. That's poor leadership. When we talk about "salt" in other fighting games it's a negative thing, it's meant to be something that we shouldn't be pushing for to happen, this game's devs seems to want all the salt they can get from their players.

Anyone can build a city - not many can RULE a city.  Fair warning, this isn't another SimCity or Cities: Skylines - this is the political game BEHIND the running of the city, with a little smattering of city building and planning mixed in.  Where you would plan to build a police station, and how to route roads was the bread and butter of city planning games - how to get the city to run effectively through city councel politics is this games focus.  This also means that you have to learn the political game of schmoozing, pleading, walking the fine line between love and hate - and not making enemies.
Pros:
+ Different approach to a genre that has recently enjoyed an upswing
+ Making friends and influencing people really has an impact on things, versus just making money the primary factor in something failing or succeeding.
+ Different political families present something to latch onto as the player - you are playing a role, not just some invisible semi-god making decisions about things affecting everyone else.
+ The different eras allow you to see how progress affects decision-making.
+ Tool-tips on many concepts allow you to grasp the games concepts without digging out a PDF manual (or printing them off, if you are 'pen and paper' kind of ruler...)
Cons:
- Some of the random events seem to not be well described - so choices seem arbitrary.
- Difficulty lacks granular controls to allow you to ease into this new hybrid genre of a game, you either catch on and succeed or you don't - and you end up restarting when it all goes to ****.
I think the game would be worthy of a good 70-78% approval rating.  Good roots, but needs some smoothing over in spots to really make it a knock-out.  Definitely worthy of the pre-order cost, a good choice with a small 'wait-and-see' recommendation at full retail price.  Kalypso always seems to iron out the wrinkles in their games, and they will likely do so with this one as well.
Just remember - ruling the city requires politics, politics is playing nice with others, if you don't play nice with others - this game is going to be really hard for you.
That gameplay is just boring, I like games with politics but this game really really bored me.  If you want a game with this style that is fun, play Tropico.

When speaking in terms of style, Super Blue Boy Planet is definitely a unique game, albeit mixed with some troubles cannot be overlooked. Thankfully, it is not that the premise is overly clichéd in that said hero tries to save WORLD from aliens and the like. Instead, the focus is set on the Hero going on an adventure to try and save from Aliens an INDIVIDUAL, whom in this case is his girlfriend. And so, it was only a tad bit clichéd, but unfortunately does not give a whole lot to its credit. Going on to the levels aspect, its The Twenty-One Levels are undoubtably where the majority its uniqueness lies, however, they just were not long enough. The "Four Bosses" were mediocre at best, being poorly constructed, both in color and motivation; substantial improvements, certainly and no doubt surely. The third and fourth fights are simply reenacting the first and second bosses, again and this was not a creative factor, whatsoever. A solution I present is keep the first two boss fights, different third boss and fourth boss, but if fourth must be kept, then maybe, "Boss Ufo's Revenge" would suffice, even something else entirely. Also, six hits per boss wasn't quite enough and not very fun; a minimum of eight hits would suffice and increase only up to four from there. For Example, first and second bosses would take eight hits, ten hits for the third boss and twelve hits for the fourth and final boss. These aspects to give them a greater sense of creative feeling. Also, one boss every five levels would be enough and NEVER out of order like 4, 3, 6, whatever it was I cannot remember, sorry lol. When speaking in terms of bosses speed, they were likewise not very fast for they should be to increase their speed the more and more as the player gets closer to defeating them. Finally, something about the title SBBP seems out of place and in dire need of some obvious originality. What's quite obviously shown in-game by the game's creator is that the adventure is still in the early stages of development - hopefully the Alpha Stages - which is understandable and completely necessary. My feeling is that SBBP should had been put up for download as a demo because of very early developmental stages. There is exists the potential and ability for the game to become a much better and smarter accomplishment than has been played so far, quite honestly. So, improvements, really vast improvements are a must. With these things being said, so far so good to the creator. Now go and do an excellent job!

I've been playing this game for 2 years or more and though I do not consider myself a connoisseur of Tolkien's writtings, I know enough of the lore to interpret whatever artistic agenda the developers included in the game.
Many of you might ask,
"Is the world size on scale with the books ?"
Answer is yes and no, if any of you know the technicalities of a (MMORPG) PC game, then you'd prolly understand what it means to host a game world(with decent graphical features)  that has hundreads of kilometers in all directions. The game has a classical MMORPG outlook of Middle-earth but the walks between Bree, Shire and Blue Mountains aren't as tiring and long as it would be if the game was 100% canon.
Mind you, there's a very complex process in recreating scenarios and plots when you try to make a game or a movie from events of a book. Likewise, to make a movie after a very complex game. While not impossible, the quality won't be the same, and from a fan's point of view, might as well burn the whole thing...
No no, I'm not going to start a discussion about what the Tolkien society thinks of Peter Jackson's works or any of the other bs.
My point is that you will encounter some artistical improvisation in the game that might confuse most of you Middle-earth fanatics. Bear in mind that making a balanced game world, even with Tolkien's ideas, requires some improvisation here and there.
As such, you will encounter areas, monsters, bits of unknown lore, either made from scratch or continued from the bowels of all speculations.
"Does that diminish my gaming experience as a die hard Middle-earth junkie?"
That depends on you  really, while the atmosphere is very canon, you have to delve into the game to feel whatever charm it has.
Try the music system of the instruments you can find and learn, go fishing, explore areas that aren't too dangerous. Do you feel dwarf-ish today? Go mine ore to make armour, shields, swords and axes for your kinsmen. Feeling like a greedy dwarf today? Go mine jewels and make amulets for your...self.
The game is F2P mind you, though you will need to pay a monthly fee to have acces to advanced areas to quest around, though you can make micro-transactions in the store and just buy the quest packs you desire. Want Angmar, Evendim, Forochel and Moria quest pack? Sure, knock yourself out.
Also, bear in mind that the main Epic quest is free to all players.
Too frugal?
Just do slayer and exploration deeds where you receive Turbine Points which you can use in the store to buy game content you desire, traits, unlockable craft guild traits and so on. There'll be a bit of work to be done through that method but there's no hurry either way, especially when dem discounts are lurking on the horizon ;)
