Fun gameplay, with the kind of stealth and non-lethal options we've come to expect from Deus Ex. It in fact expands on the non-lethal options, including even a Typhoon mode which is nonlethal.
Many Deus Ex games up to this point have been better at disguising the linear nature of their respective stories; this game doesn't perform that particular bit of prestidigitation as well as some of its forebears.
You may find the obvious linearity as opposed to subtle linearity upsetting. It didn't bother me, as I've found all Deus Ex games tend to exist in a model of the illusion of choice. I've never had a decision in a Deus Ex game have any impact on the next game, and rarely am I faced with a extremely serious, diametric choice within the game either. In fact, in this game, there are three distinct points at which you must make what are rather significant choices in the game, resulting in life and death consequences (beyond simply lethal vs nonlethal gameplay). I won't share the details beyond a very broad comment of how you have to weigh some rather serious ethical theories at least three different times. There are also sufficient side-quests to fill out your experience moreso than I found true for Invisible War, for example.
The game ends... Abruptly. It seems as if there were some very strange choices made at the publishing end of the process, or perhaps a deadline encroached and hard decisions had to be made. I didn't expect it to end when it did, and I was rather disappointed by it.
A disappointing ending does not a bad game make, in my opinion, and even in being disappointing it was still not terrible. I'd give the ending a C, maybe a C+. Not awful, not great, just average. In my opinon, the rest of the game deserves a B or B+. I wouldn't fail a research paper for having a poor summary, I won't fail a game for having a lackluster ending.

I finally finished this game after a year. I started in October 2016 and started again this October. This gave me a rather unique insight. The good: ambiance, art direction, and aesthetic. If I could use one word to describe this game's visual style it would be "sexy." I hope Cyberpunk 2077 draws some inspiration here. The bad: everything else. For example, after one year I could actually remember nothing about the story itself after starting the game again, which is a sure sign it's a bad story.
I'm actually surprised now how bad this game is. I would still recomend it for the points above and just to experience it once -- it is a Deus Ex game after all. However, everything from the characters to the story is just confusing. Other than the basic premise of augs vs. non-augs, which only makes sense because it's flavored by contemporary events, all other story elements are either irrelevant or confusing. I mean, looking at the story literally, well it's not like anybody in the real world is in a hurry to turn themselves into walking toasters. It's a non-issue. The other stuff about the Illuminati just got downright confusing. You'd have to read the wiki to make sense of it all. The gunplay itself is less satisfying than Fallout 4 to be honest. The guns don't have a good feedback or recoil simulation to them. Towards the end it honestly felt like shooting Nerf guns or something.

Cyberpunk world with huge amounts of potential completely fell short. Really expected there to be more here. Dues Ex acts as though it wants to give you big choices on how you handle things in the way of augmentations (speccing Jensen) but ultimately, i saw very little use for anything but a stun gun and the aug vision. Shooting was clunky and not even worth a second lethal playthrough. The end boss was boring and weak. The ending came about where I think the MIDDLE of the game should have been.
It took me about 20hrs to beat and I poked around QUITE a bit. (60+ hrs logged i left it on a few times and left the PC). The main setting was boring, not really interesting, and gives you a ton of different nooks to explore but for what? Just to find some extra crap you dont really "need". The character development and relationships are just not there? I didn't feel connected to hardly anything in the game. To be honest, I was kind of happy I could move on to another game. This saddens me greatly as the graphics were fantastic, the stealth system was super smooth and enjoyable. I want to play it again, but the thought completely bores me so I wont.
Ultimately to me its a 6/10. I did not feel connected to the cast. The aug system presented a bunch of augs that were useless. Hell, I barely ever punched someone, let alone investing in the aug that lets you hit 2 at one time. I literally used it ONCE. It was cheaper to just pop them real quick with a taze and move on. It was faster and more efficent. Too many ways to do one thing and only one is really the best. Its worth a play, just not at full price. This is a $25 game to me. I hate giving this game a poor review...hate it.

While the game was fun for maybe the initial hour or so, it became painfully obvious that it either wasn't finished or it released before the developers had finished.
Combat quickly grew monotonous as you'd find the only two ideal solutions to dealing with enemies are mashing left mouse/parry while you wait for your abilities to ready up, or kite enemies around in a circle and move in for chip damage every now and then. The ranged weapons, while nice to have, usually don't server any purpose in combat, and are vastly outweighed in regards to effectiveness by melee. There was virtually no dynamic in dealing with combat situations whatsoever.
The objectives were boring and repetitive, much like the combat. It was either kill everything or protect something, while maybe a couple of times throughout the game you'd find yourself doing something different, like the bomb pushing, for instance.
It's worth mentioning I have no familiarity with RWBY's story whatsoever, so there is possibly a LOT I'm missing here, but I'll still speak what I got out of it. The story is lame, simply put. As far as I'm aware, according to friends, it doesn't really pose any significance to the actually plot of RWBY. If anything, I actually found the story hard to follow. It feels very... scattered, I guess. Characters just kind of kick in right after or before combat, and usually say something that really doesn't catch my attention at all. By the end of the game, I sort of just had a fragment of a clue on what was going on.
The game is especially lacking in content and replayability. Besides team RWBY, the campaign and the horde mode, the other team and all the costumes are locked behind DLC barriers, when they should have been available in the game from the get-go, be it unlockable or not. These issues don't even take into account the lackluster length of the campaign, which I was able to complete with a friend in roughly three hours.
While entertaining initially, it doesn't take long for the average player to take notice of this game's shortcomings and the fact that this game probably left early access WAY too early. Maybe it's just me, but I feel like 90% of these positive reviews come from die-hard RWBY fans who overlook the game's severe flaws for the fact that it's just RWBY.
It is certainly not worth twenty dollars.

First and foremost, I would like to take a minute to mention the
behavior of slamming a game in steam reviews purely because it has optional micro-transactions that aren't needed in the slightest to complete the game. The game is extremely easy.
You cannot, in any shape or form defend your behavior and review when you've played 0.7hrs.
It is appalling.
Review the game on how you feel it comes together as a whole, not just targeting the publisher at 20 minutes played.
You think you are high and mighty sitting there like your internet review carries amazing weight, but all your doing is screwing the game developers out of a job and possible sequels....did you think about that on your Ivory tower?
No. Sometimes, the publishers screw the devs by making them include these things in the publishing deal, and it is a well known fact now that Square Enix are moving out of the full priced games to pushing DLC and mobile content. So make sure you are circle-jerking the right people.
I do however get the frustration behind not knowing pre-order items and microtransaction items were single use. In that regard, SE and EM should have had better communication with the community.
Now for the actual review
- Personally, I loved it. They ramp it up as it goes on and as the credits roll it leaves you wanting so much more Deus Ex. Great way to build up a possible sequel or DLC story pack. The story, it's characters and the way the plot evolves leaves you never knowing quite who to trust, which is perfect for this kind of games.
It's very conspiracy filled. And very Deus Ex.
There is throwbacks to HR which I enjoyed, and while I would have liked the mystery behind what AJ was doing between games more fleshed out, I am happy with that they gave. The main part of the game could have been a tad longer. I clocked in 20 hours with most side missions completed.
The ending is quite abrupt and I can see how it would have thrown some players off, but I enjoyed the dread and tension the ending scene built up.
- Visually this game is a treat. I run a very old computer with a fairly average Graphics card and the game benchmarked and ran it at optimal settings for me. I played on High with shadows and such things on medium to low and the game still looked incredible. On a powerful machine I can only imagine how good it looks.
The world is alive with vibrant neon and murky sewers. The devs did an amazing job at making Prague look beautifull and menacing at the same time.
The sound quality is fantastic, the musical score that runs through the game amps up at the right moments. Plenty of little details about as well, and great sound effects.
I played using a keyboard and mouse with no issues. The controls are responsive and slick, with augmentations and items very easy to hotkey. The game works fantastic for both Keyboard and Controller users. This is a good port. They patched out most launch issues within the launch week.
Wether you are going full Solid snake or full Rambo, there are some awesome options for you. The abilities all fit nicely, and if you are going for Rambo, you can turn into a death machine. The abilities are fantastic and the crafting system a neat little addition. Turn your shotgun into a rapid, multishot firing death stick.
Hacking is back, and while I find the games RNG can be brutal in some situations (you may fail 5 simple hacks in a row because even with a 10% chance of detection you can trigger the firewall very easily).
Alternatively, you can often find ways around any situation that require no special abilities. I would often find myself sighing from not looking at all my options, after finding secret routes to places where I'd just had intese shootouts.
The game is incredibly easy on normal and I would recommend going on the hardest difficulty you can. You can purchase additional Praxis through micro-transactions but the game gives you experience and Praxis quite easily so you will never need to spend an extra cent.

Story writing: 7/10
Story length:  7/10
Graphics and
sound quality: 8/10
PC port and
controls:      8/10
Total score   8/10

Revolution Ace was an interesting attempt to build a shmup in the Unreal Engine, which was not at all designed for the purpose.  The resulting game isn't a disaster, but neither is it a compelling success.
The appeal of shmup games typically comes from hectic action; your weapons are typically devastating, killing the weakest foes in one hit, and your fire rate is intense.  Challenge in a shmup typically comes not from any deficiency of your avatar, but the sheer numbers of enemies it sends at you, the intensity of their fire, and the speed at which they move.
Revolution Ace departs radically from that standard shmup formula.  You and the majority of your foes move slowly, even sluggishly.  Your weapons are uncharacteristically weak, requiring a good second or so of concentrated fire to take down most normal opponents, who are comparatively few in number.  Instead of a hyperkinetic frenzy of ducking and weaving through enemy fire while opponents explode in dramatic fireballs all around you, Revolution Ace feels more like a slow, stubborn push through the enemy forces, hoping to make it through to the final boss before your armor is depleted.
The addition of true 3D modeling, switchable air/ground fire and recharging shield to the genre are interesting, but don't really make up for the loss of the speed and destructiveness that is the hallmark of this style of gameplay.

For the entire review, head to
"Revolution Ace attempts to breathe life into a stagnant genre and, for the most part, it does. A quick check on its Steam page shows almost 400 reviews with a “Mostly Positive” rating. However, this genre resurrection is paid at a high price as most of the systems that made the genre popular in the first place have been sacrificed in favor of grinding and a generic power fantasy mechanic. There is obviously a market for this type of gameplay but I don’t see much intersection with the fanbase of the older style of sidescrolling shooters."

When I was little, I used to play those aircraft shooter games at the arcade machines. Those can be fun, just moving the joystick, rapidly tapping on the 1, 2 or 3 buttons, destroying everything and picking up everything. Then when you die, you just insert more coins and continue the game. One simple playthrough. No headaches.
Some may like it that way, but some might find it boring. How about this: an aircraft shooter game that you can play in the comfort of your home, with elements of customization; change weapons, upgrade armors. Gives you all the more reason to pick up drops than just aiming for the highest position on the highscore board.
That is what Revolution Ace is. It is an arcade aircraft shooter. But it isn't just any aircraft shooter. It is 30% shoot anything that moves, 30% strategy and deciding what weapons to use for which mission, and 30% grinding for experience, levels, and the currency to upgrade stuff. The other 10%? Oh, that's reserved for the multiplayer capability.
So if you like all the elements that make out the 100% of this game, get it, but only if you're a fan of aircraft shooters. It's not the top notch game in the market, but it's not all that bad either. I can definitely recommend this.

Another issue that I see with this game is the armory/money system. I'm not a fan of the pricing in the game, and the whole store just doesn't feel all that right. Now that being said I was using a gamepad, as this is the type of game that I feel SCREAMS gamepad, but perhaps I might be wrong.

I just think that this game has this unfinished feel to it, and maybe there's a lot yet to come, but as of right now this is a game that unless you are a DIE-HARD top down shooter, have to have every top down shooter known to man, type of person, this is a game better off left alone. Interim review after about 2 hours.
The game is not unlike Xevious.   Other reviews mention other games like Raptor, etc.   The last time I played games like this was either in the arcade or with some DOS games.  It does provide some nostalgia.  You can mount weapons that are air to air only, air to ground only, or universal.   As you earn points from killing full waves and also total number of kills, as well as the fortress or bosses, you gain both a chance for perks with your level and also you earn credits to purchase newer weapons or older weapons to swap into your various mounts.  You can store some in your inventory once bought, to be swapped in as the mission, in your opinion, dictates.  You can replay any mission via Skirmish, there is a campaign, and there is co-op, and a believe multiplayer.  I simply played single player through the first 4 missions or so and via skirmish.
This is not exactly my sort of game.  Although I did play some of the earlier DOS games like this, enjoyed Galaga at the Mall, and especially enjoyed Xevious.  This game is not unlike them.   That's the main positive.
The negative is that it is not that responsive and given that it takes a much larger footprint to accomplish the same thing, I think you might be, in some ways, better off playing older/similar games.  The graphics are not astonishing, nor are they necessarily better.    In defense of the game, I'm simply playing this on an Intel HD 2500 gpu, with an i5 rated around 3.4 GHz.   Still, this is not the most efficient program, but then, DOS and even Win95/98 were much more efficient to run on a computer for this sort of program.
So, it is fun, but it is not all that responsive.  I found that, for me, the main issue, is that the keyboard response for the airplane is a bit less responsive than I like.  I had expected it to run more efficiently.
If you have a decent video card, which I'm sure doesn't have to be that modern, you probably won't mind.  But I caution that this is a greater slowdown than I found in Skyrim, Bioshock, most FPS games in my library, and the like.   But games vary.   Where I had no problem running Dead Island with consistently good framerate, there is no doubt that Dead Island Riptide runs sluggishly, at least during the tutorial.
Still, I'd expect better from Revolution Ace.
Other than that, the game is similar, although it seems a bit less fair than Xevious.   It seems you are challenged more from the lower part of the screen than Xevious and the like.   Nonetheless it is adequate, if you have the time to learn the patterns and have good responsiveness.  It's relatively fair, looks ok, and is enjoyable.
I got the game on sale for a mere $0.19  , that's an incredible price.   For now, I'd recommend those with laptop integrated graphics to be prepared to be disappointed, although my set-up is a desktop.  But for others, the game should be adequate in performance.   It's nothing revolutionary or stellar.   But it does take you back to the arcade when you want it to.   If you have other arcade like games, reconsider before you pay much for this game.
On sale for the price I got it at, it's impossible to complain.  If you have a decent video card, and you don't have some arcade game in the vein of Galaga, Xevious, Raptor, or Zone 66 -- it's worth giving it try.  But if you had already one of those and are happy with their look and responsiveness, I'd say so far it isn't worth adding to the library unless you simply want something new to fill in the gap in that genre.
I'm going to recommend it, but again, this is a rather lukewarm recommendation.  If you see one of the older games and they look good enough for you, chances are high they'll be more responsive.

Runic Games, creator of the award-winning Top-Down, Action-RPG
, further the Torchlight franchise with the second rendition in the saga,
commences with you, the protagonist, in hot pursuit of the Dark Alchemist, the inevitable villain. The Heart of Ordrak, which he has taken, has imbued him with inconceivable powers & a clear purpose. Will you be able to stop him before his mental blight sets Vilderan aflame?
The game takes place in Vilderan, a vast continent, sub-divided further into different areas. Vilderan’s areas are diverse & unique to each Act, from lonesome deserts to dense marshes. It invariably exudes an open-world adventure unlike its predecessor.
There are four distinct classes – Engineer, Outlander, Embermage & Berserker. Each class has three different skill trees, which enable mixing & matching different skills to maximize efficiency and/or enjoyment. All weapon types can be used by any class, further adding to the sheer variability of play styles.
The character creation screen has a small selection of different aesthetic options. The option to choose between genders is also present. There is a wide variety of pet companions to choose from.
There are four distinct difficulties – Casual, Normal, Veteran & Elite. They pleasantly suit a wide array of gamers & scale in difficulty at a fairly even pace. Hardcore mode – a defining proponent of the genre – is also present & available at any difficulty. Enable at your own risk, of course.
The co-op in
boasts of a user-friendly system that enables up to six players to play together. Either join a band of adventurers or start your own adventure & wait for others to join in on the fun. From showing your friends your lackluster DPS while a werewolf teaches you a lesson in face-to-paw combat to trading your wares to better your gear, the co-op experience is not to be glossed over.
Steam Workshop enables the use of a sheer endless amount of mods to suit almost every whim. Mods may also be used during co-op sessions if users have the same mod(s) installed.
The graphics and universal interface in
are reminiscent of its predecessor but overall feel refined & improved upon. The graphics while marginally cartoony bring the world to life & does the game its due diligence. Brawlhalla is like crack and its hard to get off.
The game is a multiplayer 2d fighting platformer which closely resembles Super Smash Bros, though obviously possessing it's own unique characters and some augmented mechanics. There are quite a few characters and at first glance they all appear relatively the same, until you start using them. The other game I would say Brawlhalla lends inspiration from is Soul Calibur. Routinely, (in SSB style), weapon pickups appear throughout the battlefield.
Each character can use one of two weapons and the weapon you get upon picking up the weapon drop is one of those two. Within that mechanic, each character utilizes each weapon in a slightly different way, resulting in some very stylisticly different fighters. You can also of course duke it out with your fists as well. It's always fun to throw your enemy for a loop by throwing your weapon at them then rushing in and giving them a haymaker to the face.
The game is still in beta and there are very few 'miscellaneous' items on the battlefield, tho it's hard to say what will come as more content is added to the game (just the other day they added another new fighter) but at the moment the combat feels very solid and fair (maps are also quite simple, though there are many variations). I'm going to be giving this game a lot of attention, and several fellows of mine have organized a small tournament for which I am eagerly training up for. This game is awesome.

There's quite a few reviews that describe this game the same way. I think the primary reason behind that is The Legend of Dark Witch 2 is 100% an homage, if not a 'love letter', to the Parodius and Megaman franchieses.
It starts with the base mechanics... You have in level upgrades that you can select as you accumulate 'Tres'. This is the Gradius/Parodius mechanic. A bar along the bottom of the screen grows as you kill enemies, the farther along the bar you are, the more powerful (relatively) the upgrade is. You can activate the power-up at anytime with a button press (B on an XBox controller). 100% the Parodius power-up system.
Each level has an end boss with a specific weapon that you learn once you beat them. To get to them it's a side scrolling, run and gun platformer. You can play the levels, for the most part, in any order. This is 100% the Megaman modality.
The two styles mesh perfectly together. Playing through on Casual, the game was simple enough but it had sufficent challenge and I'm looking forward to tackling the harder levels.
I do see this as more of a Parodius X Megaman than Gradius based on the beautiful, charasmatic and cartoony characters and environments. Several of the stages are just full of detail and really harken back to the 32-Bit console days. TLoDW2 feels like a Sega Saturn game.
Even better, the mechanics aren't limited to just choose your power-ups and choose your path. There is also a light RPG mechanics where the Tres you accumulate is carried over. You can then exchange Tres, and the hidden Syega crystals, for upgrades to your weapons and power-ups. I horded Tres probably a lot longer than I should, mostly just upgrading the increased Tres drops by enemies (always take your XP multipliers when offered) and increased base damange. I strugged a bit on the final boss until I really committed to increasing my overall health (which was a mistake to hold off on) and unlocking at least the recovery magic item.
I was enjoying the game up until that point, but I realized I loved this title when presented with the new game plus and mini-game options. For New Game+ you unlock the bonuses you want with another form of the Syega currency. Things like higher jump, simplified blocking and increased health. Even better, you not only earn Syega by completing the game but by playing the mini-games! Spending some time with the video poker mode, I was able to unlock more bonuses. And while it's just video poker, I loved having a way to unlock power ups in a relaxed, low key manner.
Clearly a ton of thought and heart went into this game.

This is not a bad shmup by any means. However, there's one critical issue that is holding me back from recommending it: energy.
In my opinion, a good shmup NEEDS to have energy. You must be the last hope for humanity, maybe witnessing your allies die in the opening cut-scene. The music needs to be pumping through your blood non-stop. Basically, the feel of the game MUST be energizing and insanely epic. This game just sort of says, "Fight the bad guys if you want to... it's really not that big of a deal. The war isn't that important anyways. And I wouldn't even say 'war' since it's pretty much just a small 5-minute conflict between some American soldiers and a crazed Jihadist somewhere in Afghanistan." What I mean by this is that there really isn't anything driving you to PILOT YOUR CRAFT THROUGH THE SWARMS OF ENEMIES, ANNIHILATING THE ENTIRE ARMY SINGLEHANDEDLY, SINCE YOU ARE HUMANITY'S LAST HOPE. It's just... boring.
There are a bunch of cool game-modes (most of them multiplayer in some way) that I REALLY dig, but the lack of energy prevents me from enjoying the game. Tacking on some cool game-modes doesn't make the game exciting when it's in reality, pretty bland.
The moral of the story is that you should just pass this one up. There are so many better shmups in the world, many of them right here on Steam. Crimzon Clover, the Tale of Alltynex, and, of course, the legendary Ikaruga. Those all have an insane amount of energy- play those first, and then you'll understand what I'm talking about here.
There are definitely some good parts to this game that I have never seen before (and, consequently, highly respect the developers for) like the graphics and game-modes, but Revolution Ace just isn't worth your time. I went into this expecting a niche shmup that would satisfy my shmup-craving soul, but it isn't quite that. Shmup fans, look elsewhere (seriously, get those shmups I mentioned above NOW if you haven't already). If you aren't a shmup fan... don't let this be your first voyage into the amazing genre.

I had been eyeing this game for a long time; it looked like a lot of fun but I was a bit put away by the cost. When I finally saw it was on sale, I got the Deluxe Edition right away.
Oh boy, it is fun!
I think the closest comparison to how this game feels is the film Starship Troopers. The core of the game is as follows: on each randomly generated map, there are several capture points. One of them is yours, and the rest are the aliens'. You have to send your small team of marines to capture these points. However, there is a hive to destroy on each one, protected by automated defenses, not to mention the ENDLESS stream of bugs that will go after you. By capturing points and collecting some crates spread around the map you get resources that you can spend on more marines (dead ones respawn), new weapons for your marines, turrets, robot medics, global abilities and more. However, since these resources are limited, you will have to decide and eventually recycle your buys because...
... the aliens aren't static either. For each point you capture, they will get a permanent mutation according to your strategies. For example, using flamethrowers might cause their poison turrets to have a knockback effect, or have a much longer range. Their hives might start to spit acid themselves. Their critters and spawners might enter frenzy mode after you capture a point. They might start to spawn hardened critters, living bombs or even clones of your marines! As the aliens adapt, you'll have to adapt as well, by recycling upgrades (for 100% of their cost) and reconsidering your strategy. There are a lot of mutations and upgrades, so the game never gets old.
The game has a campaign, random skirmishes and "weekly challenges" where you compete with other players for a place on the leaderboard. The campaign is quite varied, and serves both as an introduction and as a way to play special missions, like escorting a convoy or testing a new lifeform. You'll earn credits by completing these increasingly difficult missions, which you can spend on unlocking all these cool upgrades for your marines (I guess in Skirmish mode all of these upgrades are already unlocked). The story is cliché, but enjoyable.
I highly recommend getting the Trickster's Arsenal DLC. It adds new toys for both your marines and the aliens, among other stuff, giving some nice additional variety to an already varied game. If you can, get the Deluxe edition!
I must mention the dev is making another DLC that adds a conquest-like campaing, where you would be capturing regions of the planet via regular missions, and unlocking upgrades as in the current story campaign. Since he announced he was working on it on March, I'd say we can expect this new DLC to arrive soon...
Finally, the simplicity of the graphics means it will probably run super smoothly on the vast majority of computers. Units and effects are simple but pretty, and retain a lot of detail if fully zoomed in. It does look and sound nice to me.
Oh, and one can't review this game without mentioning the HUGE bodycount. On the post-mission summary, it's normal to have killed tens of thousands of aliens and having lost tens of marines. A nice reminder of the scale of the battles!
To finish my review: a game that is genuinely fun to play, that will make you think to overcome the AI's reactions to your own strategies, with a lot of ways to play, and space marines vs bugs, plus continued dev support. Do I recommend it? Hell yeah!

I'm a big fan of StarCraft and science-fiction in general. I like the idea of survival and holding out as long as possible against overwhelming odds. So I was immediately sold when I read the game description. During the 20 hours I've played this game, I kept wondering to myself "how did this game get 95% good reviews?!"
Regardless of what you may read in the description of the game, there is only one survival mission in the story campaign. In the rest of them, you're wiping out the aliens on the map, and with more than 5 marines. Including air drops, you can easily get to 15 or more.
The campaign isn't "lengthy" as described in the store page. You can beat it in less than 10 hours without rushing it. Overall, the game can be 100% finished in under 20 hours.
I was expecting so much from the storyline. It ended up being a bad rip off of StarCraft and Starship Troopers, in my opinion. Felt like the dialog and plot were written by a teenager, and the very small number of characters (4 in total) are so cliché. One of them, the "Sarge", actually talks (well, there's no recorded dialog...) like Raynor from StarCraft and basically plays the same role.
If you are used to playing RTSs, then this game is way too easy for you. Your soldiers don't permanently die, they automatically respawn. Everything you build, including units, is 100% recycable, meaning you can't make any permanent wrong decisions that you have to compensate for. Just recycle everything, fall back, and restart. You would think I need to play a harder difficulty? Well, sadly, there isn't really a difficulty option in the game.
I didn't feel like the game was able to teach me about my units' strengths and weaknesses. I ended up using pretty much the same combination during the whole campaign. You can actually beat this game while only using 25% of all unit and building types at your disposal (I still have no idea what the grenade upgrade does and how to use it...). The balancing of the game is a big problem.
Some missions are quite long to beat, yet the game lacks an in-game save feature. I've had to keep the game running in the background to not lose my progress. Music is repetitive, art is very simplistic...
I think the worst part of the game is the level design. Though it boasts a "procedural map" system, all levels feel the same and can be beaten pretty much the same way. Not much diversity in objectives. The game tries to hide this fact by calling missions "raid" or "capture". But in the end it's just about killing alien Hives (another rip off from StarCraft...), the only real alien building of the game.
That being said, I don't consider this a very bad game, but just not worth the price. And I don't think it should be considered an RTS, but rather a casual game with tower defense elements.
It's a bad experience.

This review might be somewhat scattered, but it is as spoiler-free as possible.
According to old rumors and recent developments, MD is supposed to be the first part of a trilogy, so the story mainly focuses on setting up many plot-lines for the future games. And has a smaller scope compared to HR. While not a bad thing in and of itself, it does make the story seem shorter and the ending will probably make you go "oh, that was it?", despite the fantastic final sequence.
Perhaps the worst part of it all, Eidos are still pushing the silly augs vs normies conflict. I didn't mind it the first time around, but why go through the same thing again? This isn't Deus Ex.
What stands out however, in my opinion, are the background conspiracies. Things that you can only piece together yourself from terminals, pocket-secretaries and throw-away lines. The game is rife with them.
Sidequests of the game's second half really shine as well. Old-fashioned murder mysteries, tin-foiled conspiracy nuts, bank infiltrations and touching reunions - what's better, right?
And you'll find plenty of references to the original Deus Ex. Mostly done tastefully.
The main and side characters are a bit of a mixed bag. The Council of Five is in their prime; King Bob, as usual, steals every scene he's in; Eliza is always there to provide you with fair and unbiased news reports, quite like this review.
Embracing what he became and no longer driven by revenge and his ex-girlfriend who may or may not be worse than Hitler, Jensen is given more characterization. As well as something else.
But the new support cast is not quite as likeable as it was in HR... which can be viewed as a framing device. "Everybody Lies" is more applicable now than ever - and the characters that you can't trust fully are quite outstanding and well-written.
Unfortunately, some other completely secondary characters happen to be old, used tropes or just painfully bland, like Vega. Vega was a mistake.
Gameplay is outstanding all around. Non-lethal playstyles got new tools to make them more fun than restrictive, lethal ones have found new ways of causing carnage. CASIE has introduced a couple of new dialogue features. Stellar level design makes actual, proper stealth (as in, avoiding the enemy, instead of quietly taking them out) far more fluid as well. Multitools make a comeback, adding to options, without breaking anything.
Prague as a hub is filled to the brim with nooks, crannies and sassy home security systems that are simply begging for Jensen's attention. In a single hub you will find more content than in both Detroit and Hengsha combined.
Performance is crappy, just crappy. FPS holds up fine, but the hubs tend to stutter for me, sometimes pretty badly. I suspect this has something to do with the new engine. PC version in particular has a couple of rather unique issues, at the moment, like the save limit nonsense. The release has been messy, even if it's nothing that can't be fixed in time.
Microtransactions are in the game. There can be no excuse for pulling this crap, especially in an AAA title. From what I understand, this is on Squeenix. I didn't ask for this, the players didn't ask for this and I certainly hope Eidos didn't either. Thanks a lot, Squeenix. At the very least, the game isn't designed with them in mind.
It's not perfect, and the suits at Square-Enix are trying really hard to sabotage it, but so far they haven't succeeded. Overall, a 8.5 /10 and a good contender for my personal GOTY. Eidos did a fine job.

If you loved Human Revolution you'll love this. Basically the same thing, but much prettier, with some slightly tweaked gameplay. The world is full of rich little details, difficult decisions for you to make, and vents for you to crawl through. It's the kind of game you sit down to play for a bit, and eight hours later you realise you have work in two hours. I definitely did ask for this.
There seems to be a lot of negative reviews, and I guess this is because some of the decisions Square Enix have made. I don't like the fact that microtransactions exist in a full price game (why can't these just be cheat codes), or that the season pass has single-use items, and the way that a mission that could've been included in the game was split out as day-one DLC is pretty awful. But it doesn't really distract from the fact that it's a really good game. I guess there must be enough people pre-ordering things / using microtransactions to justify this. Not me. Don't be part of the problem, people.

The level design and gameplay overall is a huge step up from Human Revolution. New augs are awesome and fun to use, especially in the lethal run, which always felt lacking in HR. Prague hub is densely packed with various "show, don't tell" things laying around that present the stories about living in that period, as well as numerous side quests and lore stuff. Side quests are the true gems in this one, with many ways to find and complete them, some of which can be done with pretty unconventional methods. The Palisade Bank especially is a treat to break into or to raise hell with hacked security systems. Golem city looks amazing both aesthetically and in terms of level design.
Music is again great, but it doesn't stand out very much, probably due to there being only one hub, but there are some very solid tracks on there. Didn't like the changes to the CASIE aug, makes the conversations way too easy now, hacking is harder (and prettier) which is nice.
The setting is made to look believable enough and is executed nicely, the story in the background is more interesting than what you get hands-on, which again is the staple of Deus Ex conspiracy stuff which I enjoy. I just hope they won't retcon too much of the original, but for what they had shown in MD, it seems promising enough.
Didn't care much for the new characters except for a couple, although they did a pretty good job of making you doubt their true intentions. Of course, I appreciated the appearance of characters from the original game, with Bob Page's original VA on board. Shame about Sarif's VA, I doubt the truth about him not returning for MD will ever be revealed, but you can look up this great article by the lady named Xen about it, called
.
So the biggest controversy is the game being supposedly split into a trilogy and you'll feel it once you get to the ending, which is a bit sudden. It fills the role of an ending to the "first act" and it ties up the main plot, though it lacks that sense of completion of a fully priced title, then again - the side quests and hub stuff filled that hole for me nicely, so your mileage may vary.
Microtransactions system is the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing any publisher could think of for this game and it's pretty self-explanatory. Breach mode is not as bad as I expected (I would prefer more of the bigger maps, packed with drones and stuff), but still, it shouldn't even exist.

The Legend of Dark Witch games have been my favorite games of all time ever since I've played them on the 3DS Version. But what makes the steam version so unique? A returning character from the first Dark Witch game, who also just so happens the be the main antagonist of the first game: Riva!
With hidden Syega pieces to find, moves to customize, and entertaining bosses, this game is really fun!
Overall, if you're a fan of 2D Action Platformers, especially those that play in the style of Mega Man, this is the game for you.

As with The Legend of Dark Witch 1, this plays like a mix between Gradius and classic Mega Man. Collect experience from defeating enemies and redeem them to power up your player character, to make them faster and stronger. This game was released on the Nintendo 3DS eshop and, like the first game, has been reworked for a PC release. I worked on the beta release of the game.
I enjoyed this game very much on the 3DS and I am very glad it made its way to Steam much like the first game. Dark Witch 2 is a huge improvement over the first game in many ways, feautring more customization, more stages, more bosses, and more playable characters, including the Steam-exclusive Riva. There are shops to buy items to help you in stages or increase your power. There is much, much more content than the first game.
Among the best changes to the gameplay are customizeable upgrade slots and a new "ammunition" bar for using your boss skills, so your experience is not depleted when you want to use boss weapons. This is a very welcomed change for those who became frustrated with the ammo system in the first game. Additionally, collecting 4 crystals per stage allows for the player to choose which attributes they want to upgrade, as opposed to getting very specific ones.
The sprite work is fluid and cute, and the music is fantastic.
I have put lots of time into this game on the 3DS version. If you enjoyed the first Legend of Dark Witch game, I very highly recommend this one.

Edited due to popular demand.
The Legend of Dark Witch is a action series originally developed for the 3DS, but has been brought to Steam with HD artwork and redesigned UI to make everything fit into one window.
The gameplay is very similar to the clasic Megaman games. You jump, shoot, fight bosses and gain their powers.
There's another gimmick though. While fighting enemies they will release tiny butterflies called Tres, which builds up a meter at the bottom of the screen that you can consume for a temporary upgrade for that stage or until you die. It works just like the upgrades in the games Gradius.
There's also a shop where you can use your collected Tres to buy passive upgrades, to give yourself more life, attack power or extra lives.
Overall a very fun game. The music is great, the controls are very responsive and can be customized to your liking.
My biggest issue with the game is that even though there's a lot more stages than the first game, they all have very similar design. Most of the stages are just a straight runway.

Okay... Since I've played all the previous GunZ games, I'll let you guys know, in my own opinion, what has been improved on and what has made this new game worse than the first one.
The Good Stuff:
1. I like how you can continuously run on the wall, this is a good improvement from the first GunZ where you'd have to continuously slash against the wall in order to keep climbing. (Even though it would be nice if you could still slash against the wall and climb that way too like in the first GunZ)
2. I like that the rolling-dash has been replaced with regular dashing when having weapons equipped. (Although I think that optional maneuvers for dashing would give the game more diversity, or maybe having another key for special maneuvers like a backflip f.ex)
The Bad Stuff:
1. The host (the player with H on the ping) has complete advantage over other players in the game, when a player is the host, that player will always hit the other players without any delays while shooting or attacking with melee weapons, while all the other players will have a hard time hitting the host.
The host will change _WHILE_A_MATCH_IS_RUNNING_ most of the time more than once in every match. Now you can imagine how frustrating it is to get used to 999 ping for 5 seconds, and then having the ping suddenly drop to 50, and then back to 642, etc, all while a match is running. And also; when the host changes the ####### status menu is forced in the middle of the screen while you are still playing the match.
This is a seriously game breaking mechanic, it should be improved. IMO the player with the lowest ping should become the host before the match starts, and it should stay consistent throughout the match, changing the host in the middle of a match is the most ridiculous thing I've ever seen. (Not that this would change the fact that the host still has a huge advantage, because the host experiences no lag at all, apparently- this game should be played via LAN connection)
2. Specific weapons are locked to specific character classes. This limits character customization, why even include customization if you're going to make specific weapons limited to specific classes, this is ridiculous IMO. (GunZ - Now limited to specific classes)
3. There is no way to play the regular Deathmatch (all vs all) in Normal mode to gain exp and in-game currency. That's another thing that I don't like about GunZ 2, at least at the moment, not sure if it's ever going to change.
4. The campaign. I don't feel like it is fair having to pay real money just because you died too many times. I think that this mechanic is making most people leave the game. Everytime I have paid for something in a game it has been because I have wanted to, not because I have been forced to. If any developers are reading this then please take that into consideration.
----------
That's about all I have to say for this review. I don't recommend the game because of the issues, if it wasn't such a pain to play the game then I would recommend it to everyone. It is free to play after all, and it's a GunZ game, so it would have all my support if it wasn't for all those issues I mentioned above.
I'm still going to play this game from time to time, I love the structure that GunZ has to offer. I'm just disappointed that this game has so many issues, otherwise I would completely love it and recommend it to everyone. You should still give it a try though because it's free and at least you can enjoy it for a little while before the annoyance kicks you in the butt.
Rambling about GunZ 3 ideas:

Incredible game. Pretty simple on the face of it. You kill alien hordes that look like gigantic insect colonies. Imagine one of those solo Starcraft II missions where you're a small band of marines going around and killing bases. It's like that but a full game built around it.

Infested Planet does a good job of slowly introducing new gameplay mechanics and features. The variety of missions is pretty enough. Infested Planet:
Short version: this game is gud.
(See: so short that I even managed to save a character while conveying “good”.)
Short, interesting RTS. Small squad takes on infinite bugs.
I find the most interesting of strategic decisions are the ones I’m forced to make after the situation changes unexpectedly. The core mechanics of Infested Planet build those situations into the game. Every success of mine as a player is met with a random twist on the part of the AI. This creates a set of situations which are at once familiar to long-term players, but also interesting even with the repetition.
Also, this mutation mechanic helps avoid the core pain of many single player RTS campaigns: these maps aren’t puzzles, but rather are a constantly changing set of challenges.
The other important bit that makes this game enjoyable: single mistakes are usually recoverable. As a player, I found it easy to create a stalemate that would allow me the space to think and breath and plan. And if I tried something that didn’t work, it was usually fairly easy to get back into that stalemate situation while I something new. Mistakes were usually punished just enough for me to know that I’d made one, but not so hard as to cause me to restart my entire attempt. Clever, clever system.

After playing the Demo, I just HAD to get it. Torchlight II, in my book, is one of the most well-made "Diablo-Killer" since Sacred 3 destroyed it's franchise. Aside the 3 original classes being replaced by 4 new ones, pretty much everything you loved from the first opus is there... and more. The Steampunky world has expanded from the former village to a vibrant and cartoony-like large world. I haven't gotten that far yet (barely beyond the demo) so I don't know if the "Random Maps" merchant is still there (I sure hope this features is still effective for the sheer replayability factor it gaves to Torchlight 1). And now you can play Torchlight with friends (mp was the only thing missing in the original game). And the game runs great on older rigs (see how the requirements are forgiving), so if you can't run Diablo III because your pc is a bit old like mine (I settled for the 360 version for D3), give Torchlight II a go, you won't regret the alternative at all.
Torchlight II offers you a world you WILL want to fully explore  and not just for the mob xp, there is secrets everywhere, and lots of referencing (counting one about my favorite movie as a child: *Spoiler Alert* The Goonies; find One-Eyed Willy's other eye on "Chester Copperpot" - yes the corpse of the treasure hunter is there as it was in the movie- Then duke it out with Willy and his undead crew... Awesome!!!). The world is FULLY randomized, I've started all 4 classes, and I haven't been on the same map twice even tough the starter quests were the same... Just like Diablo 1 used to be.
Easy to learn and master, Torchlight II will entertain you and your family (there is violence, yes but it's pretty much Looney Tunes kind, so you can let younger kids play it safely without having to comfort nightmares, lol) for hours. Maybe not a must-have for everyone, but it is a sound purchase that won't waste your gaming money.
I love it so much I bought a 4 pack to give copies to my older teens and my best friend. It's good, it's fun... It's Torchlight II!
** Update** After completing a first run and then starting New Game Plus, I've discovered that the map vendor does indeed still exist in it's own pocket dimension: The Mapworks, you can unlock this upon defeating the Alchemist... Along with the storyline, this gives Torchlight II tremendous replayability... without any dlc purchase involved. Would be nice to see this kind thinking setting a standard in the gaming industry. Great Job Runic! **

TL;DR: It's fun, buy it. Lady/Trish highlights the most frustrating parts about the game, but Vergil gives you what the game should have been.
If you are looking for a recommendation, I say go for it. The gameplay is awesome, and the addition of 3 new characters is absolutely incredible.  If you are new to the series this is probably the best game you can get on steam if you want to see what all the hubbub is about (DMC3 is a better game, but the port is.... well terrible)
If you are wondering why this game got terrible reviews back in the day though, allow me to explain. First of all, and this is something that this new game cannot fix, is the game has the worse pacing pretty much ever because of character switching and environment reuse. Roughly 50% of the way through if you are playing as either Nero/Dante or Lady/Trish you will change to the other character, and then on the last 2 levels, during the famous Capcom boss rush and final boss you will switch back.
The Nero/Dante switch was considered annoying back in the day, but the 2 characters play somewhat similarly, so it was annoying but not the end of the world. However, the Lady/Trish switch, although I love both characters, is the most jarring and confusing mess ever, because the 2 characters aren't even remotely close. By the time I got used to how awesome Trish was, I was playing Lady again, and had to relearn everything to fight bosses. Super Annoying.
But if you play through the game as Vergil, that doesn't happen. Since he plays by himself, the pacing seems way better, despite of all the backtracking and dice games (shudder). This is how the game should have been designed, imho.
I like the new characters, and if Capcom needed people to buy this in order to make more, I'll gladly throw money down. All I ask is next time, allow us to use whatever character we want for the duration of the story and switch, or have each character have their own complete levels that are independent of the others. Action games like DmC are about unlocking new abilities and getting better over time, when you interrupt that process via forced character switching you damage the natural pace of the genre. Don't do it again! :P

I remember the '80s. I remember the weird, disjointed remains of the CCCP as a collapsing threat, and the last vestiges of the terror of nuclear war. I remember thinking that corporations were going to soon be able to own people, and I remember those last, fleeting touches of a dead future.
Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is more than just a parody. More than simply a mockery of an age, a tribute to ten mad years when we were trying to leave the past behind with lasers and robots. It is possibly the most cathartic experience I have ever had playing a video game. It's simple, yes. It's linear, yes. It has all the flaws and laudable elements of the initial release of Far Cry 3.
When most games want to build up to a climactic fight, they present you with a challenge. I see now that this is the wrong attitude. There should be no challenge. No huge game-topping boss battle where you struggle hard to apply everything you've learned and done throughout the game.
You should be an invincible sociopath with unlimited ammo. You should mow down waves of those who stand before you, cackling madly at their ineffectuality. You should play the end of most games like you play all of this one.
I was at the right age in the '80s to imagine myself as someone not unlike Sergeant Rex Power Colt. I found that the experience did not disappoint.

I guess technically I was so young in the 80s that calling myself an 80s kid would be a bit presumptious, but I definitely got enough experience going through the history buffer of movies during the early 90s that I can easily appreciate the nonstop tongue in cheek parody that is Far Cry 3- Blood Dragon.
If you're not afraid of neon lights, are a fan of the terminator soundtrack and enjoy being a cyborg, riding a giant eye-laser shooting dragon lizard, then you should definitely pick this up.

The thing about this game is the sense of humour – retro parody - it’s something you going to love or, like me, find really irritating right from the word go. I was bored to death and hitting the esc key during the intro and ten minutes in to the game I was looking for the uninstall button.  Youtube has some videos that detail the first fifteen minutes of play. I would check those out first to make sure that this is the game for you.  I am afraid I can’t recommend it at all, but it may be your type of humour. God help you if it is!! Check it out on Youtube and decide for yourself.

Have played this since open beta.  Graphics are phenomenal.  Tolkien lore is throughout the game.  Great story, even better graphics.  Awesome play!
Edit:  Now it's end of March, 2017, and the 10 year anniversary is coming up...the following is what I posted in response to a negative review of this awesome game....
Those are comments from someone whose played about 10 hours....now hear from someone whose played LOTRO for about 10 years....
--The graphics are freaking awesome!  Very realistic.  You can lose yourself in it.
--The former person had no idea how you can play this game for free and get most of the perks.  You can get a horse without paying real money, you can swift travel long distances after you get the ending hub, which you will get after you travel to the next zone of quests.
--The music is pretty dang awesome too.  Different for each zone, and matches the landscape theme of the area.
--If you love, or even like, Lord of the Rings, or JRR Tolkien, you will find Easter Eggs all over the game, matching places and people and occurrences in the book.
--The story is pretty dang awesome!  You quest and explore and go about Middle Earth in parallel to the story in the books.  The epic quests these are called, and there is the fighting of good vs. evil, seeing the virtues in characters as well as their failings, seeing your character up against the odds and being able to triumph.  There are side stories that abound, including love stories, and fellowship stories, and all kinds of additional characters that supplement Tolkien's masterpiece trilogy, along with some Hobbit lore as well.
--The "map" is immense...it now includes everything from the Shire to the gates of Mordor.  Many of the areas came in free expansions, though some areas like Moria and Rohan are paid expansions that doubled and tripled the "map" at the time they came out.  If you want to see the Shire, Bree and the Prancing Pony, Weathertop and the LoneLands, Angmar of the Witch-King, the Trollshaws, Rivendell, Moria, Lothlorien, Mirkwood, Isengard and the Twin Towers, East and West Rohan, West and Central and Eastern Gondor, Osgilliath, Minas Tirith, Ithilien, and the Black Gate as we go into Mordor (next expansion), then you have come to the right place.  TONS and TONS of quests in each area, including the epics.
--Cosmetics!  You can have from 3 to 7 slots of different looks that can be cosmetically slotted....using armour you have found from drops or quest/instance rewards, from gaining reputation from the npcs in each zone/region, from Lalia's Cosmetic Shop (an ingame store with ingame currency and you can try on the stuff before you buy), and from many, many other sources....not to mention that there are over 20 colors that you can dye each piece of "armour" (head/shoulders, back/cloak/pack/quiver, chestpiece, pants, gloves, boots)....just tons of possibilities.
--Music!!!! Besides the ingame music that comes with and matches the feel of each zone, you can MAKE YOUR OWN MUSIC using ingame instruments (over 8 different ones) and can team up with others using ABC files (many created online already by past gamers) and have a BAND playing in the Prancing Pony, on top Weathertop (they call it "Weatherstock" ingame! on the server Landroval) as well as many others.
--Crafting!  9 professions to craft weapons, armour, food, woodworking, scholar, explorer, tailor, jewellery, prospecting, etc.  These can be made for your toons or sold.  In fact, you can level up while JUST CRAFTING.  I have leveled several toons to at least level 45 without questing after the intro instance.  Very easy to do.
--Free to Play!  You can earn ingame currency to buy quest packs by deeding, or by buying a la carte.  These are not hard to earn with a bit of time, or you can get them quickly with about as much real money as you would spend on a phone app.
--Even Better!  With one month's subscription, you go from F2P to Premium which gives you quite a few perks that are PERMANENT, even after you go off subscription.  Obviously, subscription is the way to go with tons of storage, housing, shared storage, wallet, and free 500 Lotro Points every month....quite an advantage for just 10bucks a month.  But if you don't want to pay a mere 10bucks a month for VIP, you can go Premium with one month's sub, or stay F2P and EASILY play like a truckload of people do ingame already.
--PvP....Want to play as a force of Sauron instead of one of the good guys?  You can!  There are two pvp areas that you can do this.  If you play the good guys (the Free Peoples) you can enter and leave the pvp areas freely.  Will have to pay for it if F2P, but totally worth it.  I've played both sides, and both are fun.  With a 5 minute wait, you can even flip sides and fight for the other guys (if you want to, ya "flipper"!)
--Challenging Instances...Tons of instances, and you can replay them as often as you like, and half of them are scalable so your low level toons play too....just set the level at the original level or higher, increase the tier of difficulty up to 3 times more difficult than normal, and even go for Challenge Mode!  3man, 6man, 12man, and even one 24man instance.
--Skirmishes--can also be played at solo, duo, 3-6man, 12man....these also include a personal soldier pet, and can be used to level up between quest packs, earn Lotro Points, earn ingame currency, do deeds, teamwork, or solo.  You can choose between 6 soldiers to assist you and level them up along with you in the skirmishes.
--Legendary Weapons and Items....with Moria expansion, you get a weapon and item that level up with you and can be enhanced with additional stats and skills as you level it, with three different tiers per Legendary, and at every level after lvl 45-50 (with Moria..totally worth it).  TONS of different ways to level these.
--Essence gear....upper levels have slots where you can customize your armour with "essences" which are basically stat mods that modify the armour and jewellery with whatever stats you insert.
--Kinships.....aka "guilds", which have their own Kinship houses, chat channels, typical stuff....you can also have your own
--Housing....own your own house and customize it, be it a hobbit house, a house of Man, and elven house, or a dwarven house....and now they've added Gondorian housing (called Premium) that you can own as many as you want to buy (real currency) that triple the sizes of the regular houses and kinhouses.
ALSO....you can customize each class (9 classes, 1 more on the way) with one of 4 races (1 more on the way) with three different skill trees, 2 of which you get free.  These skill trees (you choose which two, and can change any time) will allow you to solo easier in one line which is more dps, or you can choose one of the other two, usually that allow you to either heal better, tank better, buff better, or mixes the other two lines, depending on the class.  You can even mix and match skills from each line, though it will limit you from obtaining the "capstone" skill or skills, but doable.  VERY CUSTOMIZABLE.
I could add a TON more stuff, but this game is GREAT!  Fantastic game, fantastic fun.  And even MORE SO if you like Lord of the Rings.  If not, it's still a good vs. evil knights and lore-masters and nukers and tanks kind of game that you can solo well or team in a "fellowship" quite well too.

I could not recommend this game more. The game is unique and it saddens you when it ends. (I'll get to that in a moment.)
The main draw of this game is the new "Concussion Gravity Gun" and let me say, nothing like this has ever been done in Half Life, or in any Source game before. This is a completely unique weapon that shoots out an orb (Element 120, an element that bends space and time and all that fancy stuff. You shoot it, it throws sh*t around.) that feeds off of your AUX Power from your Suit. This is a really good mechanic, as this allows you to use it repeatedly without the worry of never finding ammo for it, but also forces you to not spam it. I really like this, as it allows you to not spam a VERY powerful attack, but still use it a lot.
This game can also be quite scary at a certain point, not in a jumpscare fashion, but in the fashion of you are in the middle of danger, and shooting or attacking, could get you killed. You are in the middle of a horde, but they won't attack you unless you're in the light, or you shine your flashlight at them. This is very well done as your mind is telling you constantly while it happens, "Danger. Danger! DANGER!" Constantly while you're in that situation, and I almost wish more was done to make these, honestly terrifying moments happen more. Sadly this is only tied to one place, but it is done, VERY well.
Scattered in the game, are little clipboards that the game refers to as "Journals," and gives some backstory on the people who created the Concussion Gravity Gun and Element 120. These are interesting, and if you like backstory, definitely try and find them. They aren't in plain sight, and they may take some hunting, but I think you'll find it worth the hunt.
Now let me talk about the ending. This game's ending, p*ssed me off. This is for so many reasons, as this game, with me taking my time, and dying once or twice, took me 45 minutes to complete. I get that this is a free-to-play game, but it leaves you out of no where. This game's ending is one of my few gripes, besides the god awful load times, which are needlessly long.
This game could be a full release, and if it were to happen, I would buy it. The new Concussion Gravity Gun is awesome and I wish there was more to use it for in the game as it has so much potential. I feel that this game deserves a seven out of ten.
The game is fun, and it does a lot of good to make the source engine fair to you and the weapon you are given. The load times were long, but I feel like this is just because I wanted to continue playing. The game can be a challenge but not unfair. Please, play this game. It's very worth it.

I'm going to address the main complaints I've seen about the game and relate my personal experiences with it. Hopefully this helps some people decide whether or not the game is for them.
Performance:
I haven't had too many problems with the performance. There have been a couple of weird graphical glitches (maybe a total of ten minutes throughout all of my playtime so it's not that bad) and the load times can be fairly long at times. Occasionally I have had some drops in FPS (usually for a few seconds immediately after an area loads and then it is fine). Considering that I have only 4GB of RAM and the minimum required is 8GB, that may very well be part of the problem I am running into. For the most part though, the game runs great for me and certainly better than Fallout 4 or Dark Souls 3 ever has. It's impossible to make sure the game will run perfectly on every possible hardware configuration, but the fact that there have been so many performance issues for others is inexcusable. Hopefully they manage to patch whatever is causing it if they haven't already.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is very similar to Human Revolution so if you liked that game, you will probably like this one. It is much more open than HR was much earlier so you can basically just go exploring right away. Some people like that and others don't. Personally I enjoyed it as there was a lot to do and discover.
Story/world:
A lot of complaints I have seen is that the story is too short. This is just going to be a matter of taste. Some people just want to have the whole story front loaded to them, but I actually vastly prefer a story that takes its time to build the world. The storyline itself probably does feel short if you just rush through the main missions. However, I think they did a fantastic job building the world. As with the previous games, you can find computers, notes etc. that help flesh out the world and give you information about individuals and their everyday lives. They do an excellent job of giving enough information where you can figure out what probably happened to these people or how they are related to the story, but it rarely just tells you anything. Overall, I think they did an amazing job setting up the world and actually making it feel alive. I never felt any connection to the world in the first game because it just sent from one place to another without taking the time to give you a feel for what was happening to the average people in it. Here, I actually cared about what was happening. The story may feel short or incomplete to some people, but I think it was perfectly fine. Remember, it is part of a much larger story and we already know where it all eventually leads. It is also clearly setting itself up for a sequel and I guess some people think that because the story isn't completely self-contained like the others that it must be incomplete.
Tl/dr: I thought the story was quite good and accomplished exactly what it tried to and the fact that they did such a good time fleshing out the world made your choices actually feel like they mattered unlike the previous games (especially the first two)
Microtransactions:
I completely agree that microtransactions, especially in a $60 game, are generally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. However, a lot of people seem to have the reaction "It has microtransactions, therefore it must suck". They are so unobtrusive in this game that I wouldn't have even known they existed if I hadn't read reviews complaining about them. All you can buy are praxis points (basically level ups for your augments) and more credits to spend at vendors. However, at no point in the game does it ever feel like it deliberately limits your progress to encourage you to buy anything. If anything, I actually feel that you level too fast and get way too much money. By the halfway point, I had all of the augments I cared about fully levelled and there was nothing else I wanted from the vendors. It feels like they made the game without microtransactions in mind and then tacked them on at the last minute because they knew some people would pay more money to avoid actually playing the game they paid $60 for. I can't really fault them for putting them in because they can make money for doing essentially nothing. It has absolutely no effect whatsoever on your game if you don't purchase them so I don't get why anyone actually cares. Honestly, if all microtransactions were like these then my guess is nobody would care about them. The fact that the weapon DLC is only good for a single playthrough is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, mostly because they do not make it clear that this is the case, but again they don't add much to the game so it doesn't really bother me.
Overall:
This is one of my favorite games in the series. It does an excellent job of making the world, and the people in it, feel alive and even though I'd have loved for there to have been more to the main story, it still feels perfectly fine the way it is. The gameplay, like the previous game, is great and a lot of fun. There are some performance issues, but they have not been nearly common or problematic enough to interfere with my enjoyment of the game. Of course, this is all my opinion. Whether you enjoy the story, world, gameplay etc. is obviously going to be largely based on your own preferences.
Since this is the internet and people can't have different opinions, I'm going to respond to the fanboy accusations now. If you don't like the game, that's fine. If most people don't like it, that's also fine. However, that doesn't mean that I am wrong to like it nor does it mean that I am somehow deluding myself into thinking that I like it. I genuinely enjoyed this game and the fact that others have not is completely irrelevant to that fact.

If You don't want to read every point I labeled what the each paragraphs covers
Let me start out by saying that when playing this game I really wanted it to be good.  Before buying Mankind Divided I had heard of the despicable DLC/pay2win policy and some issues in the game but it was single player so I didn't view them as a problem and I doubted the Bugs could be that bad since Human Revolution played great on PC from control scheme to performance.  My first Deus Ex Game was Human Revolution so I can't compare to the original Deus Ex series but when I first started playing I didn't know too much about Deus Ex so I was blown away when Human Revolution surpassed my expectations completely.  I enjoyed the ability to go in guns blazing or explore more and find multiple alternate options that were more stealthy or even allowed you to circumvent obstacles entirely.  The cherry on top was the story that explored transhumanism and how advanced prosthetics might impact society while unraveling the mystery behind the Sariff Industries attack.  So all things considered I figured if this game was half the Game Human Revolution was the $60 price tag was worth the cost.  I was so wrong.
from what I
seen Mankind Divided is a continuation of what made Human Revolution Great which is why it pains me that the game in it's current state is unplayable past the most introductory sections.  In the first Mission you have most your previous game's augmentations which I enjoyed being able to use to their full extent and the level design encouraged creative solutions, exploring and encouraged choice in playstyle.  I took great pleasure in outwitting my enemies ghosting my way through the the entire level.  The Augs I did mention, however, are not permanent and serve more as a trial to see what you enjoy.  After the strong start you are crippled and have all the augs you have come to enjoy again ripped away from you for the sake of grinding skills which while annoying was not too unbearable since new augs are opened up in return for those you lost and it probably had to happen at some point so as to not be too easy a game.  After that I figure I would explore to earn back xp.  The building Jensen lived in had many apartments you could break into learning about the personalities and lives of your fellow augs. I have put a sizable chunk of my 8 Hours exploring, trolling npcs, snooping around apartments, swindling arms dealers and reading as much as I can which I enjoyed immensely until I decided I had explored enough and was ready to move on to the third mission.
Previously there were random moments where the game would considerably lag but reloading a save would easily fix the problems so at that moment in the game I assumed the everyone on the Internet was simply overreacting to minor problems like they always do.  That was until I tried to move past the first area of Prague.  Going into the subway The lag became unplayable  I literally dropped to one frame per second and the pause button wasn't even guaranteed to work.  Despite turning the settings down restarting and multiple updates the lags still persists.  If I reload a previous save and walk to the subway again the lag comes back stopping me from doing anything of value.
Ignoring the bugs the game itself is awesome, the gameplay is an improved version of Human Revolution and is incredibly solid with good gunplay, variety in weapons (I already have 6 different gun types), customization in the form of mods and of course weaponized augs if you like those more along with the range of choice levels provide that I mentioned earlier. As for the cons while the cover system still is great it doesn't seem as smooth as Human Revolution but that is admittedly probably due to my loss of experience with it.  The AI can be dumb sometimes for example guards move in predictable paths and the arms dealer I mentioned ripping off earlier, I stole from by stacking objects in front of him Skyrim style so he wouldn't see me stealing right in front of him.  I then proceeded to sell him back his own weapons for a profit without him questioning anything.  This can actually be a good thing to you as outwitting the AI in creative ways can be fun and truly intelligent guards would make non-cloaked stealth nearly impossible.  It is important to note I was playing on one of the harder levels (but not the hardest) so really the only difficulty comes from your squishiness in combat which is easy to avoid if you play right.
The worldbuilding is top notch with stories behind almost every section of Prague that are revealed if you wander off the main path.
(Some minor spoilers ahead that might spoil discovering some interesting tidbits or pathways I found but no major plot points)
(Some basic information about the world that you may want to learn about yourself but will not detract in any having learned from here)
I haven't downloaded the Deus Ex app so there are still some collectibles and that are completely inaccessible to me which I am disappointed in considering how much I like to explore the world of Deus Ex, although what I have been able to read is interesting.
If you read this far and didn't skip past kudos to you, but if you want a summary my advice is that there is a great game here but to wait until more effective patches are made and hopefully Square Enix changes their stupid policy of requiring an app to view content. Still if you really enjoyed Human Revolution and think the chance of wasting money on an unplayable game is worth the risk of possibly being able to play an awesome game then by all means buy it now but know you are risking an unplayable trainwreck of a game.  For most I advise to wait until the game is more polished and on sale so you don't make the mistake I did.

Normally, I could agree with Heroes and Generals, with their FPS optimization update/fix in one of the recent updates though; in-game performance has declined for me and becomes less and less enjoyable. In the past, even on the larger maps, I could play on High Graphics at 120-150 FPS and that includes during intense firefights and high-object battles. With the FPS patch update, I can no longer breach 100 FPS and during intense fights I tend to drop to 40 FPS, that in which, if you are like me and have grown accustomed to playing games at 100+ FPS, you will understand just how terrible the recent update is for people experiencing the same issue.
Even if you play at just 60 FPS, you can still recognize just how bad it feels to drop to 40 and below.
It is a horrible experience and I am very disappointed in how they have tweaked their engine, the game is still good; albeit essentially a B2P game, still offers an enjoyable experience through the difficult leveling system and availability to grind for currency (if you like that sort of play-style). Overall, the game has improved much since the intial stages of release. The customization options for your weapons are simple yet very effective. The one downside to this game, I would say, is the fact of how expensive in-game purchases are for equipment; such as weapon attachments. Vehicles I understand the cost of seeing as having 1-3 tanks on a battlefield can completely shift the tide of the fight. Weapon attachments like scopes, barrels, and even a few of the weapons themselves are completely over-priced in accordance with how difficult it is to earn in-game currency.
This game would probably attract a much larger player-base if it wasn't so difficult to obtain good weapons and vehicles.
Pros -
Excellent and immersive playability-
Great vehicle and vehicle weaponry mechanics-
Excellent and semi-realistic movement system-
Goofy physics-
Effective and simple weapon customization options-
Cons-
Somewhat clumsy animations-
Rate of currency earned in proportion to KDR and points earned is low-
Highly overpriced weapons and vehicles in accordance with earned income-
Current engine optimization may or may not boost performance, in my case, it lowered it severely.
I recommend this game to anyone looking for a fun Massive Scale Battle Experience, and already have done so to a few of my friends. There is room for much improvement but it is still a fun way to pass the time. My self-determined overall rating is 7/10.
