Overall it is a decent game to me. Though the storyline and the character weren't as good as expected, mainly the overall gameplay was good.
Combo/Chain combat system was quite sufficent, but still you have to figure out all of the chain/combo(s) by yourself since there is not tutorial about it, only online guides.
Multiplayer is decent, since sticking together as a team works pretty aweomse, but most of the time people like to go their seperate ways and there is no penalty in doing so, and it works too.
Controls were good, except for the ranged combat, its quite hard to shoot at the desired target.
GameModes though only 2, its quite sufficent for me, since the Storymode can be quite long, and Horde mode is fun to play in on multiplayer. Though storymode can be improved by cutting down the distance needed to travel from point to point.
The Enemies/AI was good, many people complained about blocking and having to wait to counter-attack, again, pretty much a lot of things they didn't figure out thats why. If you have figured out a lot of things on how to destroy blocks and cancel attacks, you would get what I meant.
The key part is, you can never play the same level again in the same way.
The leveling system as well as different characters offers variety of playstyle for that certain level. Hence? Unless you intentionally do it, you can never play a certain level again in the same playstyle as before.
Mainly I find that bad review/comments come about from having no in-game tutorial to state the ways to play, etc. Hence having some players get misconception(s).
Overall, if you are a person who
- Don't mind repeating some stuff (levels)
- Like to figure out things on your own
- Like to constantly try out new things
Then this game is just for you.
Else, it would be a 50-50 chance that you would like this game.
But if you are opposite of those, then don't buy this game.

Alright, obligatory stuff first: I am a huge RWBY fan. I've been a fan since the White trailer and my wife and I both watch the show religiously. I bought this game in its alpha to show my support to Rooster Teeth because I liked their franchise so much. Steam shows me as playing only two hours but I'm not sure why. I'd wager I've played roughly six hours of the game. I understand that's not a whole lot but the game is simply painful to play.
When everything is said and done there are two problems with the game: The characters are not fun and the gameplay is worse. Yes the story is meh, but I'm ignoring that because it isn't as important as the other two.
Problem the first, none of the characters feel how they do in the show. I get that it's hard to make witty interactions between characters difficult, especially when you don't know who's going to be on the team at any given time but considering Rooster Teeth invented RWBY and the show has charm pouring from its eyeballs, it should have been possible for them. Almost all the dialogue feels robotic and dull and the fact that the show's voice cast fill their same roles here makes that pretty sad.
Problem the second, this game has some of the worst combat I've seen in any game and there are zero variations in gameplay throughout each level. The game goes as follows: Run until a group of enemies appears, kill all enemies until able to run again. Occasionally the game will be punctuated with a "horde"  section where you guard a doohicky until you kill X amount of boring, samey grimm. That's it. No seriously, that's it. There's absolutely nothing else to it.
What makes this worse is that some varieties of grimm will block your attacks and make you wait until they are open for a counter attack. Remember when Nora killed an Ursa on accident in the first season? Well this game doesn't. Instead of casually murdering Ursa, she now has to stop wailing on them until they put their indestructible arms down and let her hurt them. The worst scenario that happens way too often is when you're surrounded by blocking enemies and have to simply wait them out. As soon as one goes to attack, simply hit the counter-attack button then rinse and repeat. That gets boring in about ten to fifteen seconds depending on your level of tolerance. Team-attack setups do kind of exist but they boil down to "one player stunned an enemy, another player boops in and hits the counter button to finish it." Once again, not interesting.
Between fights every player on your team makes a mad dash for the next combat area, stopping only if they know where the hidden artifacts in each stage are. The artifacts give 250 exp to whoever touches them and I personally believe this was a huge mistake. This game should be all about teamwork but that mechanic alone makes teamwork break down. Kind of a weird move, I think.
I used to think the game would get better with updates and I kept holding out for changes that never came. I kept wanting it to be as fun as the source material. But unfortunately it never got better. And it's not because it's a "hardcore fans only" kind of thing. It's just a bad game, plain and simple. It was made on a budget and never improved from its alpha. It's not worth the hours I played it. It's not worth the hours the developers put into it. It's not worth any amount of money you're willing to put towards it. Do not buy this game.

The 80′s retro VHS techno war gimmick is great fun and unexpectedly well-executed; lasting long enough to give you your money’s worth, but doesn’t overstay it’s welcome. There are hints of a full-sized sequel, and that causes a bit of concern.  Hopefully the gag doesn’t get overplayed in the process.

If there was ever a game to bring up in the "games as art" debate this would be it. Not because of its graphics or story (even tho both are great) but because of the way it uses interactivity to tell its story in a way that no other medium could have done.
At its core Brothers is a puzzle game with a unique control scheme. You play as two brothers on a quest to find a cure for their sick dad and each brother is controlled using one of your analog sticks. This takes a little getting used to but once you get the hang of it you get to experience some really cool puzzles that are all based on the fact that you're controlling two characters at the same time.
I can't write a review that comes even close to doing it justice so I'll just say that Brothers is one of my favorite games ever made. It's a complete masterpiece and a couple of moments in the game gave me shivers and almost brought me to tears. On the other hand I've seen playthroughs on youtube where the player doesn't have nearly the same reactions as I had to certain key points in the game, but yet they've all agreed that the game is amazing.
Just go play the game for yourself. Worst case scenario you won't regret it and at its best it'll make you re-evaluate what can be done with videogames.

BLUF: It's a puzzle game, it has light platforming, it's all about the feels, it's not very good.
Two brothers set out on a journey in search of a panacea for their dying father. Their mother is dead, so it's just the two of them in the big, cruel world. It's the player's job to guide the brothers, both at the same time, through a fantasy world filled with danger and heartbreak. Except none of that gameplay is particularly good.
Brothers is at its best when it's letting the titular brothers see someone else's story play out. There's no spoken english dialogue, but the designers effectively use animation to convey the plot and characters' emotions. But, the central plot is poorly resolved, with a strained ending that runs counted to all the previous gameplay. One of the plot points has a moral straight out of a Grimm tale, warning that you should never have tight-pants feelings or you could wind up dead. And it all adds up to make the game somehow less than the  sum of its parts.
Mechanically, the game is a mess. Controlling the brothers simultaneously usually isn't a problem, but the puzzles are oftentimes slow and repetetive, and the action sequences are a matter of trial and error rather than skill. Boo. Games looks nice, though.

I gave this game a fair chance.
I spent just under twelve hours of my own time playing this game, and I regret every minute of it. I knew the moment I finished my first game, where I was either gunned down by SMGs at a range where my Gw43 or M1 Garand should have been far superior, that it would be the meta.
Well, twelve hours later over a few updates, the gun gameplay is still - unfortunately - a steaming pile of dog crap. I wanted to like this game, I really did, as I'm a huge fan of World War 2; instead I leave feeling disappointed, but at least I feel somewhat justified when I hit that 'uninstall' fuction.
I don't recommend this game at all.
Poor hit detection, poor matchmaking (Germany is usually the superior team), poor gun balance, poor gun gameplay and quite frankly it's just not fun if you're playing as the Russians or Americans; the German team usually steam rolls right through you, as evident by the war progress.
Those of you who enjoy it I can honestly see why, but I think this game destroys it's own potential by long kill times and poor gun play.
I might give this game another chance, but not before the issues with gun mechanics have been 'fixed' to a more appropriate liking. By that I mean shorter time to kill, better recoil management (even with default rounds) and better hit detection.
Until next time.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided
It took me 24 hours, whereas Human Revolution took me 21, in my first play through (missing 1 side mission), and I loved it. I love the different augmentations you have and how well thought out the levels are.
Unlike Human Revolution there's definitely something for everyone; going stealth, hacking, non-lethal, crawling through vents or remote hacking and jumping up to the rooftops. So much variety. You'll enjoy how the game lets you explore your own play style.
I did New Game + as a way to complete the missed side mission, choose other options and experience the game with more augmentations. Lots of fun and this way took me 13 hours (bit of a speed run).
Did it feel rushed, no not really. But with rumours and DLC coming out so soon, it is easy to believe it was cut up. I think while the ending is a little abrupt, it does build up to it from early on.

There are a lot of great things about this game, the exploration, balance for different play styles, and great replayability. This is truly a worthy entry in the Deus Ex franchise, one of my favorite video game franchises. I know people have bagged on it for having microtransactions and one time use DLC, but neither of those impact gameplay in any way. There's not a shortage of Praxis points (many are hidden in insane places,) but the one time use items are Praxis points and credits and various small items, while the weapons can be used multiple times. Overall, this is an amazing game and I'm saddened to see it marred with aspects that seem to be afterthoughts.

Heroes and Generals is a very good game, however it is not for everyone.
If your expecting a battlefield or COD experience, look elsewhere. The pace in this game is significantly slower and you can expect to do a lot of running and a lot of dying. Furthermore, it takes a ton of grinding to unlock anything. As a result, you will see a lot of negative reviews about balance in the game. Players have put a tremendous amount of time into unlocking a weapon, class or vehicle and the slightest change to their respective stats instantly upsets a massive subset of players.
Having played sinced closed Alpha (long before H&G was on steam) I can say that the game is slowly and steadily improving. Balance, although a point of contention among many, is good (I own 4/5 classes and play both German and American), however there is room for improvement.
Gameplay: Gameplay is a lot of fun. You really need to learn how to best utilize your class and equipment. If you have a bolt action rifle, you'll be a severe disadvantage in CQB, while the opposite is true if you have an SMG and are caught out in the open.
Maps: The maps are quite large, so although there are only a few, they do not feel overly repetive. There are 3 or 4 maps I play consistently and I leave the rest out of the matchmaking (skirmish maps arent the greatest).
Graphics: H&G is not the prettiest game in the market, however its not bad looking either. The foliage is very effective for concealment.
Sound: Again, its ok, but not great
Setting: WWII is awesome!
Overall Feel: H&G is greater than the sum of its parts. All the components come together to create a really great game. It has that addictive feel to it that I haven't experienced in an FPS since BF4. There is a lot that can be done to improve the game, but slowly and surely it is continually improving (in a two steps forward one step back kinda way).
Give it a shot (you won't lose a dime)!
To the devs:
Here are few points on which you might improve your game
1. Three ways battles are terrible. They are boring stalemates where the team who defends the most (and lets the other 2 teams duke it out) wins. They need a signifcant re-think
2. Hire some more map designers if possible
3. Increase the weight capacity of soldiers by a 1-2 points. A lot of interesting gameplay would evolve if soldiers could carry more gear
4. Allow passengers in transport vehicles to fire their small arms
5. Allow players to resupply eachother with ammo (like the medpacks)

Trine 2 is a wonderful physics-based platformer. The levels are all well-designed and afford just the right amount of leeway to let the player figure out creative solutions to obstacles. All three heroes that the player (or players - the game has online co-op that works great) controls have unique abilities that can be combined in clever ways to traverse the environments. Sometimes it feels like you can abuse the physics engine to bypass things, but I'm pretty sure most of it is intentional, as the inverse that is often present in physics-based platformers just isn't there: you'll never feel like you came up with a solution that should have worked but got cheated because the physics went wonky. It's just the right blend of physics sandbox and puzzle game.
The only real issue is the combat. It's super simple, and so long as your warrior is alive, absolutely trivial. It's perhaps best to treat enemies as just another physics toy. Fighting them hand-to-hand quickly becomes dull, but you can pick up enemies as the wizard and see how they're affected by the environment. Thankfully, it's a small enough part of the game that I don't think anyone should be dissuaded by my complaints, especially since respawning at a checkpoint doesn't reset enemies, so you never ever have to go through a fight again.
On the presentation side, Trine 2 is absolutely flawless. The supersaturated graphics are utterly gorgeous. Every single frame of this game would make an excellent wallpaper. It simply is that beautiful. The audio is perfect, with great music and excellent voice work. And the story is simple but very well written and charming. Everything comes together to look, feel, and sound like a fairy tale.

Revolution Ace is definitely NOT one of the best shooters in its genre. It has frame rate problems, the bullets blend in with the background, and generally it's a bit of a mess. But somehow when I was playing it, something made me look past all that and I really did have a good time. It has an upgrade system that definitely helps with the sense of progression, a fun but challenging boss at the end of each stage, and a neat system of air bullets vs ground bullets, forcing you to pick between whether you're shooting in the background or in the foreground.
But by far the best part of the game is the multiplayer. It takes all the problems I mentioned and kinda blurs them out of your mind, because, at least for me, I was more focused on playing a game with my friend and the issues became less glaring. There's also a cool multiplayer versus mode, which I've never seen implimented into a top-down shooter before. It works pretty well.
As a whole, Revolution Ace was like a fat guy sitting in front of you at a playoff game. It's annoying at first, sure, but if you can look past the problems, you have a great game in front of you. It's a fun experience, and you should definitely consider picking it up if you have some friends to play it with.

This may be the best game I have ever played. It is easily the most artistic.
Of course, when I say artistic, I don't simply mean "It HAS art". I mean it IS art. That is not to say that the graphics aren't high quality, they are. The art style is gorgeous, the music is lovely, the voice acting (though incomprehensible) is endearing, the story is well-crafted, the camera work keeps you focused on the action and flows nicely, the characters are deep and relateable. All of these things can be said about Brothers. But these things could also be said of a film.  Fair warning though, it is very dark at parts. Definitely not a game to play with kids watching.
What makes brothers art is how it integrates all of its assets, most especially its story, with gameplay. Without spoiling anything, I can say in this game you control two characters, who are brothers, and the way that you control them adds to your connection with this game. There are many games with good stories where it could be said that the gameplay wasn't necessary. By that I mean that the game could have been a movie and been just as compelling. But this is a game where the story (which is excellent in its own right) is propelled to a much higher level of depth by its mechanics. In a certain sense the mechanics are part of the story. That in itself is an amazing feat which few games have managed to capture.
This is a game that you will have a hard time putting down. It isn't incredibly long, but if you are only playing a game because it has hours of gameplay then you are doing it wrong. Any fool can make a game that has hundreds of hours but no depth. It takes real skill to make a complex game with excellent assets, a compelling story, and home-run gameplay all  wrapped into a tight package that lasts a few hours. Without a doubt this game has the highest overall quality of any game I have ever played, and my only regret is waiting so long to play it.

A genuinely innovative RTS, where rather than simply mashing units together until the enemy is spammed to death, the enemy is an infinite horde that can only be managed rather than destroyed. Your squad consists of only a few individuals, and for them to defend a map's various capture points requires a great deal of care in their positioning and equipment.
Because the aliens randomly mutate (gain new abilities and units) the further you advance, the tactics required for every battle will be different, and the tactical situation within each battle is always changing. For example, a single soldier with a flamethrower may be able to hold of a swarm of basic enemies indefinitely, but when the aliens mutate they may start sending ranged enemies that will eviscerate the short-ranged flame trooper, or armoured tower spawners that will make his position indefensible. A hard decision will have to be made whether to retreat, or to reassign valuable soldiers from other vital points to help him.
Resources have to be carefully balanced to plug every gap in your lines, and because the enemy is always changing, on harder missions your defence is rarely stable for long, and victory cannot be achieved through a single strategy. One of the most welcome innovations in Infested Planet is that all upgrades and defensive emplacements are completely refundable in-game, allowing you to continually adapt your force to counter the aliens.
The only real cons I can think of for this game are that the music is droning and uninteresting, and sound effects and animation arent great, but this hardly detracts from the excellent mechanics of the game, and Infested Planet's visuals make up for this by being crisp and colourful.

Simple but surprisingly enjoyable action/strategy game with tight resource management and a focus on squad management.  It has elements of tower defense, Creeper World, and occasionally evokes classics like Syndicate or Cannon Fodder with its small squad mobile combat.  Resource management, area control and denial, timing, and concentration of force versus surface of defense - these are the sorts of challenges this game is about, and although it tackles them simply, there's enough going on that it's not simplistic.  Although this is not a huge game, it isn't asking for huge game money, and what's there is well put together.  The campaign has slightly above-average video game writing and characters; not worth playing the game for, but skippable, and I didn't skip all the dialogue so it must be doing something right.  Mostly it teaches you how to play the game and introduces some fun scenarios to test yourself against.
Where the game falls down is in its repetitiveness on higher difficulties; it's very easy to fight yourself into a stalemate where you don't quite have the resources to push.  You'll gain ground by inches over tens of minutes, and then lose it again in seconds.  So this game can feel pretty sisyphean at its toughest, which some players might enjoy, but I found sometimes frustrating.  I also wish there was more to the game - the high level techs offer you a decent number of options, and many of them are useful, but it often felt there was either one clear way to deal with a situation, or no good way.  Some more scenarios would be nice - the randomly generated missions are great, but more varied objectives and scenarios would greatly improve replayability.
Still, there's something strangely compelling about the experience, and it has a certain old-school charm.  Certainly not without flaws, then, Infested Planet delivers on its promise with craftsmanship and conviction, and at a very reasonable price point.
If you like Starship Troopers then buy this. Then buy the farm.

My god this is possibly my favorite game when i was younger (other than mario). Me and my buddy would literally dig tunnels with rocket launchers and tear stuff up.
Overall is a very strong game. If you played anything after this one, im sorry. Every Red Faction game after this one was trash.
Compared to todays standards, the gameplay is awkward and quick, but once you get used to it, and all of the NPC chatter(which is legit AF), you will understand why they keep trying to re-create this magnificant beast. (ignore the hours i have played on steam, I have put hundred of hours into it on console).

Strong points:
- Fun and addicting.
- The gameplay holds up pretty well to todays standards.
- Nice variety of weapons that feel good to use and offer very diferent ways to play the game.
- Destructive environments way ahead of it's time.
- Non-linear paths on how to progress through areas.
- Enemy AI is quite clever for a 17 year old game, will hide, move in unpreditable patterns, look for you when you're hidding and will always keep you on your toes.
- Good level design.
- Unbelievably good soundtrack and sound design.
- Vehicles are fun to use and add a new dimention to the game, although control a bit awkwardly at times.
- Interesting story and setting.
- Can last for a good 10 hours if you're of average skill like I am, and if it's your first playthrough.
- Ran without notable issues on my Windows 7 Ultimate x64.
Weak points:
- Needlessly awkward stealth sections that are unfair, poorly optimized and overly punishing, they feel out of place in the game.
- I've experienced some lipsyncing issues in most cutscenes.
- Enemie's running animation sometimes glitches when they spot you from a long distance. (I've encountered this particularly near the end)
- Inconsistent voice acting, ranging from decent to not great.
- There are no great Boss fights in the game.
Conclusion:
Red Faction is a fun and addicting, oldie by goldie game. Destructive envirnoments will at times offer you new paths to progress in the game, something quite unexpected from a game this old. As a shooter is pretty well executed and will put your skills to test without being too punishing. It's surprisingly polished but still has it's faults, I found none of them to be game breaking. Got it on a sale and couldn't believe the amount of fun I had with it. If you like the original Half-Life, chances are you're going to be into this.

Trine 2 is a wonderful physics-based platformer. The levels are all well-designed and afford just the right amount of leeway to let the player figure out creative solutions to obstacles. All three heroes that the player (or players - the game has online co-op that works great) controls have unique abilities that can be combined in clever ways to traverse the environments. Sometimes it feels like you can abuse the physics engine to bypass things, but I'm pretty sure most of it is intentional, as the inverse that is often present in physics-based platformers just isn't there: you'll never feel like you came up with a solution that should have worked but got cheated because the physics went wonky. It's just the right blend of physics sandbox and puzzle game.
The only real issue is the combat. It's super simple, and so long as your warrior is alive, absolutely trivial. It's perhaps best to treat enemies as just another physics toy. Fighting them hand-to-hand quickly becomes dull, but you can pick up enemies as the wizard and see how they're affected by the environment. Thankfully, it's a small enough part of the game that I don't think anyone should be dissuaded by my complaints, especially since respawning at a checkpoint doesn't reset enemies, so you never ever have to go through a fight again.
On the presentation side, Trine 2 is absolutely flawless. The supersaturated graphics are utterly gorgeous. Every single frame of this game would make an excellent wallpaper. It simply is that beautiful. The audio is perfect, with great music and excellent voice work. And the story is simple but very well written and charming. Everything comes together to look, feel, and sound like a fairy tale.

The central mechanic around Brawlhalla is that every character has a different combination of weapons at their disposal, and every character has unique signature attacks (sigs) with those weapons. You have to utilize that character's sigs in combination with regular and aerial moves.
And (here's the best part) it's FREE. Not TF2 "free", no. FREE. no pay-to-win items here, you spend money on cosmetics alone.

First review I've written on here. I often disagree with the general consensus on games that get mixed or negative reviews (The Division is one of my most played and current favorite games, with all of it's issues), but this game is hard to defend. Human Revoluion is in my top 5 of all time games. I'm sure Mankind Divided is just as great, but the PC performance makes the game unplayable. People throw around the term "unplayable," like it's water in the PC community, but this is the first time in my personal experience that I feel it truly applies. I am tyring to play at 1080p with the following:
CPU: i7 6700 (locked version)
CPU Cooler: Noctua D15
GPU: MSI R9 390x (No overclock, typical average load temp of 72-76 degrees)
With every setting turned to the bare minimum, the frame rate in this game dips from 60+ to the high 20s in every area that is remotely open. Apartment hallway? Massive FPS drop. For a game that is meant to immerse the player, this is very aggrivating. At the risk of sounding like an entitled gamer; with my hardware, this is simply unaccetpable.
The worst bug that currently exists in this game is the ambient occlusion bug. Even with this feature turned off, parts of the map will bleed solid black on to the map, which spreads. Within 10-15 seconds, your entire screen is black. This happens frequently, if you sit idly and let it spread, in every area of the game for me.
I hope that Eidos/Square Enix can fix the performance issues, but honestly, I don't have much hope. If you read most online forums, people are not talking about this. I'm not overlocking my CPU or GPU, my airflow is more than sufficient. The problem is with this game, plain and simple. Perhaps DX12 will be the saving grace here, but I sincerely doubt it. Hopefully, they can prove me wrong.
-Chris

Following up something as game-changing as Deus Ex: Human Revolution was no easy feat and Mankind Divided more than lives up to its predecessor. That said, in my opinion, in many ways Mankind Divided surpasses Human Revolution and these elements all come down to the gameplay.
Everything in Mankind Divided is faster, more fluid and more fleshed out overall. Mankind Divided is essentially a prettier version of Human Revolution yet everything is so slick and smooth. From throwing objects, firing weapons, using the new and experimental augmentations, it all comes together to have a much more refined and polished feeling that lives up to the looks of the game.
It looks amazing. This is one of the greatest looking video games I have ever played. The game shines in its incredibly unique and bold visual design that washes over everything and the attention to detail is insane. Shooting feels amazing and weighty and the new cover system is heavily inspired by later Splinter Cell games, needless to say it works well.
The major downside to this game is in the story department. Now we knew going into this title that the narrative would lead up to the eventual start of the original Deus Ex game, meaning that they did not have as much room to expand on certain themes and ideas as they perhaps overwise would have. There are flaws in the main draw to the story too.
------- Minor spoiler warning, skip this part if you want a truly fresh experience -----------
At the start of Mankind Divided Adam and Alex are blown up in a Prague train station and the entire plot of the game is finding out who did it, why it was done and how to stop events like it from continuing. This draw was a little too weak in my opinion to be as engaging as the developers would have intended it to be. The side missions and collectable note items add more insight to the world but it lacks that drive that Human Revolution had; Jensen being thrown through the glass and left for dead to find Megan Reed and uncover a conspiracy that would track him across the globe.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Main story hook aside, the game is fantastic in motion and retains everything that made Human Revolution great and more. It is an unforgettable, customisable and varied experience on a whole. That said the weaknesses are there as well; a puzzle like Portal section that feels out of place, a period where you have to avoid police and a series of conversations that, no matter what you have to say, fail to change the outcome. The final boss is weak too. That said, modern Deus Ex games are known for their weak boss fights and I only encountered one in my playthrough. I had seen videos where he was wiped out in a few taser shots and a melee punch. It took a lot of ammo to take him down but it felt underwhelming.
That is the best way to put Mankind Divided. It is absolutely incredible gameplay wise but where it falters in the story is the main weakness. It feels underwhelming because of what came before as it doesn't quite live up to the massive towering hights of Human Revolution. Yet, not being near perfection doesn't mean it isn't worth playing. Mankind Divided is fantastic and well worth your time.

This game absolutely redefined gaming in my mind. I was generally under the assumption that "puzzle" meant that you apply logic to progress, but that just shows how backwards my thinking is. I spent 10 minutes jogging laps around the starting area, not because the progression path was complicated--it told me with an objective marker that I needed to get through a locked door--but because the crowbar needed to get through the door is hidden in some random place that's nearly impossible to see through the murky brown environment. I turned on a generator at one point only to find out the room had a pair of turrets in it, and lord knows how I was supposed to see that coming or avoid damage. Then I progressed through a series of rooms where the only way to progress is to turn off the lights and have glow-in-the-dark paint bold-facedly tell you where the button is that you need to push to progress, only to reach a big open area with infinitely respawning enemies. It was clear that I needed to hold a button down for a few seconds to get the door open, but any enemy that touches you during that time stops you holding the button down. And good luck trying to get a window of opportunity with 50 jumping zombies and suicide bombers in riot gear that can't be put down with anything but a couple of point-blank headshots with the shotgun. This is not *hard*. The train section from HL1 was hard. This is just arbitrary BS.
Apart from that, it's been a while since I've seen optimization this bad. I have no idea how a source-engine game could have framerate dipping. I have dual 4-GB 960s in my rig and this thing would still dip to sub-30 fps whenever it had to render something stressful, like fighting 3 zombies in an empty sewer pipe. I still got massive bouts of screen tearing even with v-sync on. Loading times are atrocious as well, and I have literally no idea how. It's a Half-Life 2 mod, for Christ's sake. This should be the kind of thing that an FX-8350 with two 960s should be able to handle with a few cores tied behind its back.
It makes me sad, because this game has some great atmosphere, but it's hard to stay immersed when I'm having to pause every few seconds either to consult a walkthrough or fiddle with the graphical settings, and after barely half an hour I already had a headache from the awful framerates.

A classic, aging first person run and gun shooter, with its own at-the-time revolutionary spin, RED FACTION is a must play for all fans of old-school FPS games.
Playing as the protagonist Parker, your reality is a future where private companies explore space and set base on planets, in your case, for ore resources. Earth is being sucked dry of precious resources, so as usual humans have come up with a nifty plan! (Nick some from Mars.) As an abused and overworked miner on planet Mars, you join with the rebel forces of Red Faction to escape and contribute to a communist uprising against Ultor Corporation.
At its time of release and comparable to today's technology, Red Faction was unique. The mechanics and graphics are still amazing for its age, especially with regards to its fully destructible environments outside of the preprogrammed story with Geo-Mod technology.
- Storytelling is solid with no twists to be expected, but it's worth a single play through at least.
- Drivable vehicles such as jeeps and submarines are a nice touch, giving breaks between lengthy shooting sessions, and bringing a little more depth into the 'minimal-is-better' type storyline.
- Has a nice variety of weapons with the standard array of pistols, shotguns, and rifles, but also includes the rocket launcher and its ability to 'blow up' walls and objects.
- The graphics are outdated now, but this is a given for a game released in 2001.
- Voice acting is not the greatest - somewhat monotonous and plainly read from the script, but it is scattered throughout which eased the tedium for me. While the music does fit extremely well with setting, it does become very repetitive after a while.
- So, this Geo-Mod technology. I have to say, that despite this being pushed as one of -the- reasons to play at the time, it is very basic and does not actually allow you to bypass certain checkpoints. Walls do not collapse, rather, holes appear that you can continue to gouge out with explosives until it becomes large enough to crawl through. (Think Minecraft, spoon and playdough style.) This is rather critical of me, but just my opinion.
For players of modern FPS games I will point out that lack of an in-game map may be cause for frustration, and small progression devices such as buttons can sometimes be confusing to locate - which can stagger the pacing (unless you have the giant fudge-off rocket-launcher.)
In Conclusion.
Despite the AI not being the most intelligent,
animations being reminiscent of the Tin Man from The Wizard of the Oz,
that every guards personality bears a striking resemblance to that one jerk boss everyone seems to have, the combat is still fun, fast-paced and worth playing at least once.
This is probably a really great game to play if you are suffering upper-management issues at work (and have little backbone to do anything about it.) Certainly, if you are pro-union, this game is for you.
So to all you stranded miners;
- and don't you forget what others sacrifice for you.

If you're not a fan of the webseries RWBY, I wouldn't recommend this game.
Combat is very shallow. While you have light and heavy attacks, there isn't much variety in the ways you can combine those light and heavy attacks. Characters largely play the same, so there isn't much variety in that regard, either. Gameplay consists of moving from one closed-off square to another and fighting waves of enemies. Enemy variety is small. All of thise makes for a repetitive experience.
Even more frustrating is that the starting characters feel underpowered compared to the DLC characters, so objectively better characters to play as are gated behind a five dollar pay wall.
Now, despite all this, I've clocked in 55 hours at the time of this writing. So, something has to be fun about it, right? Well, this game has a Left 4 Dead influence that adds a bit of chaos to the game. No matter how high you level up, your character is fairly fragile. While this means single player is almost unbearable, it makes multiplayer a lot of fun. Your allies can revive you, just like in Left 4 Dead. Never being 100% safe, never knowing when you or one of your allies might get knocked down, makes the game a lot more fun than it otherwise might have been.
I know this review seems like it's going both ways, but that's because my feelings on the games are mixed. I've had a lot of fun playing it. However, these Steam reviews are asking "Do you recommend this game?" I don't. There are far better games you could be playing. This game needs a lot of refining, and a lot more content (the story mode is about 2 hours, by the way, and there's no real replay value). If the developers build on what they've started here, Grimm Eclipse 2 (if the publisher decide to make it) could be a really good game.
This game, though? It's alright, but I wouldn't recommend it unless you're a fan of the source material.

RWBY Grimm Eclipse is your combat based game. Throughout the game you go to various levels, the styles of the levels will look different to the other levels creating variety in the level design. One boring aspect of the game is that every level despite looking different, all played similarly go from one area to another to fight more grimm either it will be normal fighting or you have to fight through waves of enemies or defend an objective, one good part of the game was the mining area where you had to get rid a bomb and to do that the player had to collect dust and run to the bomb and place in the cart to move the bomb away, this added a level of difficulty that was dynamic to the level and made this level extremely fun to play.
This game can be played in many ways, the game can be played single player by yourself or multiplayer with friends and other people. When playing single player the game can feel a little dull, as written before in each level you go from one place to another fighting grimm some places a bit more difficult then other, this can start to feel tiresome and it will, but the thing about this game is don't play it single player. The game has been designed based on the web series, so in the game in will be best to play the game with friends or others, so you can play as a team, and to make the game more interesting, the more players are in the game the higher amounts of grimm you fight.
You might be thinking you just wrote that fighting grimm will become boring and tiresome, but I was talking about it in a single player way, when you play with others you are able to do team moves, which allows synergy between characters in the game, you get to see unique combinations of attacks when playing with different characters, plus when doing a team move/attack you gain extra exp from doing so, which is great as you want to be at level 10 as quick as possible so you are able to either do the most damage the quickest or be able to do amazing crowd control which really helps in the situations you can fall into.
In RWBY, each character played differently, some characters were more combo based, others were best as a support character helping with crowd control or adding buffs to teammates, with some character abilities they able to stun enemies in a certain way that opens them up for a team move/attack which is great for a game for that is based around team play. Each character is also unique, especially for the lines they say, if you have the team JNPR add on if you play as Nora and use her grenade launcher on her third attack she will make a boop sound, and some other character also sometimes says something to each other I think, this is something I forget sometimes, you know busy killing grimm, sometimes you just don't notice.
The verdict for this game is... buy it, this game is so much fun especially when you have a friend around, if you don't play the game on public and play with others, the game plays at its best when you are in a team. RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is an amazing game, all I hope is that more games are made by Rooster Teeth, they know what they are doing and they are good at it.

This game absolutely redefined gaming in my mind. I was generally under the assumption that "puzzle" meant that you apply logic to progress, but that just shows how backwards my thinking is. I spent 10 minutes jogging laps around the starting area, not because the progression path was complicated--it told me with an objective marker that I needed to get through a locked door--but because the crowbar needed to get through the door is hidden in some random place that's nearly impossible to see through the murky brown environment. I turned on a generator at one point only to find out the room had a pair of turrets in it, and lord knows how I was supposed to see that coming or avoid damage. Then I progressed through a series of rooms where the only way to progress is to turn off the lights and have glow-in-the-dark paint bold-facedly tell you where the button is that you need to push to progress, only to reach a big open area with infinitely respawning enemies. It was clear that I needed to hold a button down for a few seconds to get the door open, but any enemy that touches you during that time stops you holding the button down. And good luck trying to get a window of opportunity with 50 jumping zombies and suicide bombers in riot gear that can't be put down with anything but a couple of point-blank headshots with the shotgun. This is not *hard*. The train section from HL1 was hard. This is just arbitrary BS.
Apart from that, it's been a while since I've seen optimization this bad. I have no idea how a source-engine game could have framerate dipping. I have dual 4-GB 960s in my rig and this thing would still dip to sub-30 fps whenever it had to render something stressful, like fighting 3 zombies in an empty sewer pipe. I still got massive bouts of screen tearing even with v-sync on. Loading times are atrocious as well, and I have literally no idea how. It's a Half-Life 2 mod, for Christ's sake. This should be the kind of thing that an FX-8350 with two 960s should be able to handle with a few cores tied behind its back.
It makes me sad, because this game has some great atmosphere, but it's hard to stay immersed when I'm having to pause every few seconds either to consult a walkthrough or fiddle with the graphical settings, and after barely half an hour I already had a headache from the awful framerates.
It's an awesome game, even if you haven't played the half-life series yet. I hope for a sequel very soon.

This game is unique and familiar at the same time. It feels like a warcraft 3 map with only heroes. You have a team of 3-9 soldiers that will go against thousands of  enemies, literally. The enemies are simple melee at first but develop much deadlier abilities later in the game or even later on the same map. To counter this your team can change skills on the fly to adapt to any situation. Because of this the game now oddly feels like a first person shooter where you can change from invisibile assassin to close quarters shotgunner to sniper rifle and then to flamethrower in just 3 seconds leaving behind assassinated enemy heroes, dozens of dead spitting aliens a destroyed tower and a burning building including the enemies in it. There is no limit to the changes you can make, marines can change an unlimited number of times, buildings can be recycled getting the full resources back, research and upgrades can be sold back as well. The only limitation is that except plain marines everything else uses resources and thus the number of upgrades that you can have at the same time is limited. Thus it is very important to determine which upgrades you need at a certain point in time and establish a strategy before you jump into combat. The game also features a pause button which I rarely use as i prefer real time strategy over turn based mechanics.
You gain resources for captuing enemy points and dragging resource crates back to the bases you own. You do not lose resources when losing a point so while the progress may be slow and incremental, you definetly can try new approaches if you get pushed back after a point capture.
There is definetly replay values with random generated maps and a ladder system that shows how well you did on a map as compared to other players. There is also a weekly challenge and a nice story mode with additional mechanics.
I definetly recommend the game.

Okay. This game is basically the Aliens sentry gun scene, except the entire planet is your hallway. It is incredibly satisfying to set up static defenses and station your space marines to hold off a seemingly infinite swarm of alien buggers. Very fun take on the defense genre, especially since you can't just sit tight to win - you gotta take out the alien hives too. It's a tricky balancing act to set up just enough defenses to allow you to go on the offensive.
Missions end up being a dynamic game of territory control, with the alien hives redirecting their flow of critters in response to your expansion. I can't stress how weirdly satisfying it is to expand your territory, with the swarms of dead (and soon to be dead) aliens to mark the border between Camp Bugmurder and Infested Godforsaken Actual Hellhole.
Anyway. It's a neat game. Consider putting on some Basil Poledouris for an alternative soundtrack and you're in for a real good time.

4. The game still requires polishing, even without the balance issues. This game is adequate for the most part. The weapons are fun enough, The levels are pretty boring to look at but fun to explore, and the Geo-Modification aspect that the game really tries to sell to the player is only used MAYBE a handful of times, to be generous. The music is great, and in fact I would say that's the best part of it. You wouldn't get this game for the story, but that's to be typically expected in a game like this.
So why would I NOT recommend it, although I'm saying the game is okay? Because of the inexplicable difficulty spike around the halfway point of the game. I say "spike," but it doesn't get any easier after this point; it's more like a difficulty
. This is whenever the Masako mercenaries come in.
Before this point in the game, I would almost say the game was too
. Then, with the arrival of these mercenaries, you suddenly (I do mean suddenly; there's no gap between "too easy" and "instant death") and brutally have to switch to a different mode of playing. Whereas before you could almost go guns blazing, now you have to quicksave before you go around any corner, in case there's a railgun-wielding enemy who may or may not instantly shoot and kill you the second you peek around a corner; it seemed to be random. You also have to keep checking your flank in case the game decides to spawn an enemy wielding a railgun behind you. I can't speak for everyone, but having to constantly reload saves and hope that the AI decides to miss me is not my idea of fun. After dealing with this for a while, and making it to the 3/4 point or so, I gave myself invincibility just to finish.
On top of this, at the very end of the game, you have to do a completely random minigame. Random here means two things: it comes out of nowhere, and it's random chance whether you'll get the right choices and complete it successfully. Rather than take everything you've learned to make some sort of climactic ending, the game throws this new, brief concept at you.
There was also the glitches I encountered while playing the game. I'm running a modern Windows 10 PC; any modern desktop can easily handle a game like this nowadays, to the point that the game gets a little overwhelmed. I had to cap my FPS at 30 at certain points so the game wouldn't inexplicably blow up important things I needed to use. The scope on the Railgun was unusable due to some bad texture or other, and the same thing happened to certain in-game display monitors. The game also skipped the final cutscene and instantly started rolling the credits after I completed the aforementioned minigame, so I thought that was the end until I decided to doublecheck.
Ultimately, I would say that while this game is
it doesn't do enough good to outweigh the bad. I really wish they'd done more with the key feature advertised for their game (Geo-Modification.) I can't really say it left any impression on me other than frustration, but even that was only minor. Maybe get it for a sale if you feel like getting back to some oldies?

If you're not a fan of the webseries RWBY, I wouldn't recommend this game.
Combat is very shallow. While you have light and heavy attacks, there isn't much variety in the ways you can combine those light and heavy attacks. Characters largely play the same, so there isn't much variety in that regard, either. Gameplay consists of moving from one closed-off square to another and fighting waves of enemies. Enemy variety is small. All of thise makes for a repetitive experience.
Even more frustrating is that the starting characters feel underpowered compared to the DLC characters, so objectively better characters to play as are gated behind a five dollar pay wall.
Now, despite all this, I've clocked in 55 hours at the time of this writing. So, something has to be fun about it, right? Well, this game has a Left 4 Dead influence that adds a bit of chaos to the game. No matter how high you level up, your character is fairly fragile. While this means single player is almost unbearable, it makes multiplayer a lot of fun. Your allies can revive you, just like in Left 4 Dead. Never being 100% safe, never knowing when you or one of your allies might get knocked down, makes the game a lot more fun than it otherwise might have been.
I know this review seems like it's going both ways, but that's because my feelings on the games are mixed. I've had a lot of fun playing it. However, these Steam reviews are asking "Do you recommend this game?" I don't. There are far better games you could be playing. This game needs a lot of refining, and a lot more content (the story mode is about 2 hours, by the way, and there's no real replay value). If the developers build on what they've started here, Grimm Eclipse 2 (if the publisher decide to make it) could be a really good game.
This game, though? It's alright, but I wouldn't recommend it unless you're a fan of the source material.

RWBY Grimm Eclipse is your combat based game. Throughout the game you go to various levels, the styles of the levels will look different to the other levels creating variety in the level design. One boring aspect of the game is that every level despite looking different, all played similarly go from one area to another to fight more grimm either it will be normal fighting or you have to fight through waves of enemies or defend an objective, one good part of the game was the mining area where you had to get rid a bomb and to do that the player had to collect dust and run to the bomb and place in the cart to move the bomb away, this added a level of difficulty that was dynamic to the level and made this level extremely fun to play.
This game can be played in many ways, the game can be played single player by yourself or multiplayer with friends and other people. When playing single player the game can feel a little dull, as written before in each level you go from one place to another fighting grimm some places a bit more difficult then other, this can start to feel tiresome and it will, but the thing about this game is don't play it single player. The game has been designed based on the web series, so in the game in will be best to play the game with friends or others, so you can play as a team, and to make the game more interesting, the more players are in the game the higher amounts of grimm you fight.
You might be thinking you just wrote that fighting grimm will become boring and tiresome, but I was talking about it in a single player way, when you play with others you are able to do team moves, which allows synergy between characters in the game, you get to see unique combinations of attacks when playing with different characters, plus when doing a team move/attack you gain extra exp from doing so, which is great as you want to be at level 10 as quick as possible so you are able to either do the most damage the quickest or be able to do amazing crowd control which really helps in the situations you can fall into.
In RWBY, each character played differently, some characters were more combo based, others were best as a support character helping with crowd control or adding buffs to teammates, with some character abilities they able to stun enemies in a certain way that opens them up for a team move/attack which is great for a game for that is based around team play. Each character is also unique, especially for the lines they say, if you have the team JNPR add on if you play as Nora and use her grenade launcher on her third attack she will make a boop sound, and some other character also sometimes says something to each other I think, this is something I forget sometimes, you know busy killing grimm, sometimes you just don't notice.
The verdict for this game is... buy it, this game is so much fun especially when you have a friend around, if you don't play the game on public and play with others, the game plays at its best when you are in a team. RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is an amazing game, all I hope is that more games are made by Rooster Teeth, they know what they are doing and they are good at it.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided's story is fantastic in the early/mid stages of the game in which it places you into Prague; a torn society where Augs (people with metal parts in their body to enhance their well being) are being oppressed through constant border/checkpoint control by police along with discrimination from human individuals of high power and just other civilians. You play as Adam Jensen the protagonist from the prequel; 'Deus Ex: Human Revolution' an Augmented agent now working for Interpol in which he is tasked with dissolving the Illuminati and making who ever is responsible for the terror attacks pay for their crimes. This at it's core is AAA story design making you really feel like you are in control of your actions and that whatever you choose to do effects the way the world is around you, this in essence is right to some degree in which most of the decisions you make do affect the ending.
The voice acting in this game is amazing and the character models especially Adam Jensen are really nice with lots of details on their face and around their body allowing you to see what kind of augmentations they have on them (this doesn't really give you much of an advantage it's just nice to see). The conversations with important characters in the game are not just cutscenes. Square Enix have made a really unique system where you have to persuade people through a 'Social Analyzer System', this allows you to analyse what traits they are exerting.
The gameplay is easily along with the character design one of the strongest elements to this game. The missions are based around the idea that you have the freedom to do what you want in terms of how you tackle them and what approach you take. For example; you could infilitrate these missions using complete stealth and never killing anyone just incapacitating all of the guards, you could go in guns blazing or simply sneak past everyone not touching anyone at all. This is the beauty of the game's mission map structure allowing you to exploit certain guard patrols without the need for glitches on the hardest of difficulties like some other games. Throughout the game there is an upgrade system that allows you to gain augments one of the most useful ones is the 'Icarus Landing System' this augment stops you from falling to your death no matter what height you fall from, the upgrades you get in this game are actually useful and some cater to certain play-styles more than others do.
The graphics are really nice however, there was a problem with unoptimisation when the game came out due to the MSAA causing extreme lag on all systems I still think there is this problem at the time of this review so just turn that off in your launcher. However even on the lowest graphics it looks amazing so it's all good.
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided's Story towards the latter part of the game tends to lose it's track and focus in which the side quests you are doing tend to fall off and don't really mean anything in the grand scheme of things (they really should in a game like this). For me personally there aren't that many side quests (this may be fine for you but for me I wanted more since the last game had almost the same amount and it really feels like they put the least amount of effort into these). Prague although very detailed and pretty along the side streets doesn't really have the appeal the last game had in it's environments for example; America (Detroit) rather bright and vibrant and China (Shanghai) dark and gritty.
Now the biggest and most painful kick in the teeth that you have probably heard about by now is that the ending is appauling for a Deus Ex game. I can confirm this, I completed the mission not knowing that was the final one however; as soon as the last cutscene ended it literally popped up with "You have unlocked new game plus" I was like "WTF that's it?". Heed my warning no matter how many people that tell you the ending is bad it will not prepare you for the actual viewing of that abrupt new game plus unlock notification. The whole game literally does not wrap up in a nice neat bow instead it leaves it open for DLC or more likely a sequel; IT WAS A SEQUEL BAIT ENDING!
What is probably more or equally insulting is the bloody micro transactions, just why in the hell did Square Enix put these in? Surely no one in their right mind would buy these!? What is a relief though is that it doesn't force you to buy them to get through the game or even prompt you once for them to be purchased instead you actually have to manually go into the store to even see that they are there so I guess that's bonus points to some degree.
Overall it's a 8/10 for me; it has a good story line for the most part, amazing gameplay, interesting characters and world design. However, it is let down by the failing story in the latter section of the game, the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥abrupt ending and the blatant cash in that Enix tried to make with the micro transactions. Let this be a lesson to all developers:

A fresh modern american styled shmup with online co-op. Online Co-op! More shmups need to be on steam and they also need to have online co-op.
Very good upgrades and weapons customization. Your ship has slots in which you can stick weapons wherever you want. Look at the community hub for screenshots of the shop. You can place weapons on the wings to shoot sideways. You have "scrap" (money for shop), experience points for leveling up your rank (which opens more weapon slots), and perks.
The levels move slow and it may seem like a walk in the park towards the beginning, but don't let that fool you since you can find yourself easily overwhelmed all of a sudden. It's not a "bullet hell game" since there aren't 1000 bullets on the screen, but that doesn't mean you won't run into a bullet infested screen. This is definitely apparent in the later levels. The level of challenge is perfect with this one. It's not too easy and it's not too hard to make you stop playing altogether.
Besides it having campaign co-op, you can split-screen battle a friend to see who ends up with the higher score. There are a few power-ups specific that appear in this mode which will affect the other player. It can either be positive or negative so that you don't just grab every one you see.
You have one life to beat a level, but you have two lifebars. One of them recharges when you stop shooting and once the other one is depleted, you die. Very neat feature.
Bottom line: If you're into shumps, this one needs to be in your library.

I think it's fair to fay that people are giving this game a hard time. Understandably, people are expecting the classic Micro Machines formula, essentially a remake rather than a new game. However what is here is actually good fun, especially the focus on class-based battle modes.
Pros:-
- Has the classic micro machines feel
- Includes both Classic elimination mode and race modes.
- Local multiplayer
- Intense multiplayer battle modes (CTF, Base Destruction and King of the HIll), with varied vehicle classes, each with their own unique abilities and specials.
Cons:-
- Social features are lacking a bit (no in-game chat or scoreboards i.e. K/D ratios, scores etc. ).

I've played several games over the past couple of months that have gripped me with their addicting gameplay, but I can't really think of the last game I've played that truly gripped me emotionally in that same period of time.
Probably Undertale. I think that's the last one, yeah.
Brothers- A Tale of Two Sons is... a tale of two sons. And much like Undertale, I'd be doing this game a disservice if I spoiled what makes this game truly extraordinary. But I'll try not to spoil.
Brothers is a game where you control Naia and Naiee (or, as the game calls them "Older Brother" and "Younger Brother", but we still ended up calling the main character Wander and his horse, Agro, from Shadow of the Colossus, so whatever). You solve different puzzles, and go on an adventure to find a tree with a special water that can heal your dying father.
The game delves heavily into relationships, and the concept of loss in a relationship and it doesn't pull any punches. While the advertising for this game makes it look very kid-friendly and happy, the game has many incredibly dark moments. And quite a few emotional scenes, that left me in tears.
The game has plenty of subtle visual means of telling the story along with its complex, underlying plot. The world is inspired from Norwegian folklore and some fairytale concepts, that give it a look all its own. It'll be a long time before this game's visuals become outdated.
While the controls are awkward, I personally got used to them (and I used a keyboard, not a gamepad). But I can see that being a hindrance for other gamers. And there are moments that were a little campy or overly-convenient in service of the plot. They didn't entirely detract from the experience, as I love what Brothers does well, but I feel that it's fair to note that there were bits within the game that I personally thought were a little ridiculous.
However, I appreciate games that can use gameplay mechanics and narrative, and harmonize them into a truly unique story, that I believe could only be told through the means of video game narrative. This game deserves what recognition it's received, and deserves to be played. I'm giving Brothers- A Tale of Two Sons a 9/10.

Given both the mod community and the generl love for this game, Torchlight II offers a lot to anyone who wants to run around dungeons, kill weird and interesting monsters using ridiculous abilities, and collect an insane amount of loot. Will it get frustrating? Yes. Certain points in the game where the level suddenly shifts can be brutal. Will it attempt to murder you in interesting and creative ways? Yes. Will it make you occasionally load it up over and over again to watch as you gib your way through an entire level of monsters? Yes. Is the community still there and working to make the game even better? Yes.
It's a fun, lovingly made game.

Some background: I was a bit late to the Torchlight II party, having purchased this game several years after its initial release. I also never got a chance to play the original Torchlight. And, all things considered, I'm still relatively new to this game. I've owned it less than a month, which isn't very long at all for a game of this sort.
As for the review...
I'll keep this one relatively short and sweet. I was one of those folks who loved the original Diablo and absolutely adored its sequel Diablo II, but then was bitterly disappointed with many of the choices Blizzard made to the third installment of their beloved franchise. Diablo III isn't a terrible game by any stretch, but it has a multitude of features I strongly disagree with (and in some cases, outright condemn) and in any case, I feel that Blizzard is no longer the dev studio it once was. Which isn't exactly a novel thought by now, nor one I'm alone in thinking, but y'know.. it's a big part of why I'm so pleased to have Torchlight II.
Torchlight II is, due largely to the nature of its creation and concept, a Diablo-style lootfest ARPG very similar (in the way its skill, combat, and item systems are set up) to the oldschool-style ARPGS like Diablo II, which I adored and I largely prefer over games like Diablo III and many other more 'modern' ARPGs. Torchlight II's skill tree system is very reminescent of Diablo II, which I consider a good thing. I personally happen to really dig that system.
The cartoony art style is pleasing to the eye and refreshing for the genre. The addition of the very useful companion critters (called pets) is great, and they can even do your shopping for you so you don't have to make trips to town. Pets aid you effectively in combat, and as an animal/monster lover, I really love that the pets are a feature of the game and especially the fact that they're so far from useless. The way they were designed and the functions they serve (plus how you can modify said pets!) make them a blast.
If you enjoy randomly-generated loot and hack 'n slash gameplay in the Diablo vein, this is for you. This is, in many ways (but not all) what Diablo III should have been.
One of the most critical things for me is the ability to play offline, unlike the third installment of the Diablo franchise. I love to play Torchlight with my friends, but I also enjoy solo runs and offline play when my internet decides to act wonky. I don't want to deal with any sort of DRM ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t when it comes to this sort of game; I already tolerate it when it comes to Path of Exile, which is a stellar game with the exception of that fact. So yeah-- being able to play offline is a really big plus for me, and I count that as important.
The one area I feel Torchlight II is really lacking is in is its story. Lots of others have pointed this out so I won't go into too much detail here, but I agree. And that's a bit of an issue for an RPG, especially if you prefer to play solo. But if narrative drive ain't your thing and you prefer sticking to co-op fun with friends, this game is excellent. The mechanics are spot-on, it's fun, it looks great, and it's simply better than Blizzard's nearest offering.
There is plenty more I could add, but I think I've said enough. I recommend Torchlight II to fans of the genre; it's more than worth its $20 purchase price, and if you get it on sale you're getting way more than your money's worth. This game is hella fun, especially with buddies. Get it and enjoy it.

At first glance, this looks like an old, outdated, ugly game. It is, but the amount of freedom you get is almost unmatched. The game can be described as a medieval politics and combat simulator.
You travel around in a map view with armies represented as small models moving around it. The game then instances battles into randomly generated maps. Armies range in size from a dozen men to 300+ strong armies full of cavalry, archers, and frontline fighters.
Fighting is not the only thing you can do in the game. You can hang around the large towns and find out the best goods to transport around to make money as a travelling merchant, or you can raid the caravans of other nations, if you like. There is an entire courting/romance system. You can marry into power by marrying the son daughter of a noble. Of course, if being nice to everyone isn't your thing, you can become a bandit and raid villages, towns, castles, and other parties to gain wealth.
There is a module system that makes it very easy to change the game to your liking. Mods range from texture packs to full blown overhauls that change the entire game.
But as said, the game is old and outdated. The graphics are probably some of the worst when it comes to character models (mods help a little with this), and the massive battles the game hints are are limited unless you modify a file to increase the size of battles. This can make the game unstable, however.
The difficulty of the game can be a problem too. If you get unlucky and lose your army, you might find yourself in a loop of constantly getting beat down by the bigger armies. Other lords hate if you attack them, but have no qualms about going 300 vs. 20. Those lords also are able to very quickly raise large armies of upgraded soldiers. Often much quicker than you can. It can get a little frustrating if you're trying to play at higher difficulties.
Mods can help alleviate a lot of the problems. The game is still more than worth the cost.

This game was my childhood so I may be a little biased but that point aside lets begin. Red Faction puts you into a Orwellian future on Mars playing the role of Parker, a down on his luck run of the mill guy looking for a fresh start... or so he though. The game promptly begins with you getting off your shift and as you begin to return to your barracks all hell breaks loose as miners are instructed to begin an armed revold against the mines ruler the Ultor corporation, who is now of Saint's Row fame. The fun starts right away as you fight your way through the mines and into a cheesy but compelling story nonetheless. The aformentioned cheesy writing paired with well dated graphics and AI are theis games issues but if you can get past those issues you'll be in for a fun action packed story with some of the best in game music ever composed as well as a game series that had so much potential and survived long enough for one reboot but its follow up killed it. Red Faction is a diamond in the rough and a great addition to the lexicon of early 2000's shooters.

Well, this one is a classic. I originally played this one, probably like many people did, on the PS2 and immediatly thought it was an awesome game. It had great music (action tracks as well as awesome atmospherical tracks), a cool setting (the Total Recall inspired mines of Mars), great map layouts (the maps are very well made and fun to explore), and just enough of a story to get you propelled into the action.
Now, I will admit, part of the fun in the this game came from its "blow holes into walls and make your own path" gimmick. While it was pretty innovative for the time it came out, many games have done this since then, making this game feel more gimmicky than anything else by todays standards. Plus, I found myself only using the destructable environments to my advantage for the first half of the game, the latter half I essentially forgot about it and was playing the game as a standard shooter.
The length of the game is pretty short, especially compared to most games that are out now. At the time of writing this review, Ihave 5.4 hours logged into the game on steam. I've not only beat the game, but I also played a match or two onlne, messed with a number of in game settings, as well as had the game running as I got up to answer the phone. Now, it's true that I HAVE played the game before, so it's possible that it was from the fact that I remembered much of the game, but not only has it been many years that I've played it. But I also died quite a lot too, so that had set me back a little as well.
However, despite the fact that the game is gimmicky and short, it's well worth the $10 on steam. As I said before, it's definitely a classic as you not only see elements of earlier games, but you can also see the impact it had in later games. It's destructable environments (which WAS new at the time), the fast paced action, the cool setting, and great level design make it stand out in an otherwise stale FPS genre.
This is not worth a dollar, this should be free and even then I wont like it. It has a very unexciting story characters and conclusion.

Thiss will be less of a review and more of my thoughts of this game and how to compares to Human Revolution. Lets start with game length. I did damn near every side quest and Point of Interest (protip: don't sell any Neuropazyene for credits) and clocked in somewhere between 25-30 hours (minus idling) while taking my time with everything from hacking to stealthing and exploring while playing a pacifist run. This is about as long as Human Revolution, but by the end I was left wanting more.
Speaking of the end, the ending was pretty crappy. Whether this is due to me liking hardly any game ending or this being a recurring trend in Deus Ex games I can't say. I was not at all invested in the end boss or his motives nor did the last mission feel as epic and final as it should have, it was just another mission.
The release version of Human Revolution got a lot of flack for having uninventive boss fights that you were forced to shootbang til they keeled over. They later updated this with things you could hack and sneak through to deal with the big bads. I only faced 2 enemies I would consider a boss: one was in a side mission and the other the final boss. While I didn't find anything I could hack, There were mines and lasers everywhere and many places to hide, I assume you could use the mines to your advantage. I was able to beat both bosses without killing them.
Lets finish with micro transactions, Deus Ex Universe, and the new aug abilities. As I said I did damn near everything in the game and I ended up with pretty much every aug I wanted. If you want to buy augs to artificially make the game easier or try the new stuff out earlier thats up to you. During the game you find Triangle Codes you can scan in a phone app called Deus Ex Universe. I can't speak for anyone else but I was unable to ever register/log in to ever scan anything, perhaps they will fix this but for now its just a wasted unused feature. Finally, the new aug abilites are mosty useless, don't get me wrong some of them are cool but for the most part it was a waste of my precious batteries. Even the one that should have been the most useful for my pacifist run, the TESLA, was mosty overshadowed by the new and improved stun gun. Out of all the new augs remote hacking was by far the most useful to me.
Overall I very much enjoyed Mankind Divided. The gameplay was top notch, I just wish the antagonist and ending were just as good. And maybe make it longer.

This is a overall a good game with solid gameplay. It looks nice, good music and sounds, good stealth and combat gameplay. Following in the footsteps of human revolution, it still offers a lot of options on how to play. This game also improves on the bosses from human revolutions, which felt really out of place if you played a stealthy character (this game features
a single boss and it can be beaten stealthilyy)
Unfortunately, this game lacks the little spark that could make it go from "middling" to "great". The characters (including the protagonist) are mostly one-note and uninteresting. The plot has good ideas but ends up bogging down the game by delivering a huge amount of confusing and not especially interesting exposition - and then delivers a weak ending that doesn't manage to justify or earn all of the exposition this game put you through, instead giving an abrupt end that screems "to be continued" - remains to be seen whether the true ending will come in a DLC or an eventual sequel... Many plot threads also go nowehere and just vanish or are left unresolved.
Also this game tries for theme, as it has a segregation theme, but besides being an intriguing background this doesn't really go anywhere and the game has nothing
smart to say about it. Finally, the gameplay, while very good and refined, is fairly repetitive - all missions feel the same, the game finds a formula and sticks to it without trying to vary too much, for instance asking me to break twice into the exact same location.
