To put it simply, I enjoyed the game. However this does not mean I cannot see all the glaring flaws that make this .. 7/10 for me? This game could have easily been 10/10 GoTY material if these points were addressed. Definitely an easy pickup in a sale for maybe £20-30 (25%-50% off) but at full price, considering the elements I'm about to point out, avoid unless you like wasting money or have nothing better to play currently (this was my dilemma, nothing to play).
#1 Gameplay
The gameplay was as expected although I would say that the takedown "mini cinemetic" is somewhat immersion breaking. Like honestly, felt rather cheeseball. When you've got a game series like the Arkham series to compare to for stealth takedowns... yeah the takedowns in this game straight up suck in comparison. Like I mean they have it fade to black and into and out of the cinemetic takedown. Inexcusable in a 2016 AAA game.
#2 Graphics
While they are certainly "good enough" I wouldn't have said they are spectacular (GTX 980 w/ i7 and plenty of RAM here so don't get panties in a twist). Frankly I found the graphics to be rather laughable at times with plenty of clipping issues with character's hairlines and the complete lack of lip sync to the character's speaking which was also very immersion breaking in a game that has A LOT of talking in it face to face. Go speak to the boys at Rockstar behind LA Noire for pointers please.
#3 Stability
I experienced 5-10 crashes to desktop with this game in 30 hours of gameplay. This. Is. Not. Good. Enough.
Apologist attitude to this kind of stuff is how it becomes commonplace. Why should we accept a product that expects full price with such a proportionally high crashrate compared to say.. an indie game? Sorry but no, this is horrendous.
#4 The Story
I was fully engrossed in it myself although I must admit, I found Fallout 4's story very engaging until I actually thought about it at the end. And we all know how that story ends... how our choices mattered so much. I would say in Deus Ex Mankind Divided I appreciated the little side story missions and the future tie-ins which there are several, like you bump into characters you had interactions with further down the line, but in the grand scheme of things they don't actually serve any purpose towards the main missions so it's rather a moot point.
As for lethal vs non-lethal I have only played through once but I don't know if there is a massive difference between the two. The only time it seems to matter is the end mission which if you do decide to kill one of the guards, it seems to skip a portion of mission and cut to the end boss fight.
Speaking of which, this end boss fight is a joke if you find a certain item halfway through the game in a certain facility. In general I found the bossfights or lack thereof to be somewhat disappointing. There was none of those "oh ♥♥♥♥ I pulled that off?" moments for me.
But basically, you beat this end boss and sit through what must've been about 1/2 an hour of credits for 2 credits cut scenes which leave you with even more questions than answers. The cliffhanger ending here is absolutely unacceptable considering it's more or less a DLChanger ending.
===
In summary, Mankind Divided is a good game from a gameplay persepective for the most part (I would say activating Augs controls could have been better done and the menus are definitely suffering from consolitus) but the story elements and certain gameplay elements are just done so poorly that it fails to reach it's full potential.
This game could have easily had another hour or so of gameplay at the end to wrap up the story although if the DLC is well done and not a cash grab that's fine too I guess. But it's Square Enix we're talking about here, the same people behind the absolutely ridiculous Hitman reboot that is essentially a pay now play later deal.

Good game overall. As you may have already read, the plot isn't conclusive, but it's left open for further development; however, this doesn't mean that what you play isn't engaging.
Gameplaywise, you are offered with a significant number of options when it comes to tackle objectives, ranging from the stealth approach to the full-terminator; during the game you can upgrade Jansen, as in DE:HR, with the augments thats suits your favourite playstyle.
The game is not that difficult overall: having played it at normal, I found myself with 15 unused praxis points, since I never actually felt the need to max out everything - side note: the mirror cloack is so overpowered that kills all the fun of a stealth run, so I would suggest to ignore it if not strictly needed.
On a technical point of view, the game is graphically gorgeous, though bad optimised (at the time I am writing, the directX 12 are still not available). I would recommend to play a bit with the graphical settings, using the internal banchmark to identify the best setup for your hardware. Just mess with the options until you are happy with the results.
Most of the dayone bugs have been taken care of, even though some minor annoyance still remains: in my case, I sometimes experienced a lock in the walk/run command after a game load and - maybe three, four times at most - a bug in the controls of the hacking mingame (couldn't give the commands at all, could just exit the hacking screen, though a quickload would solve the iussue).
About the microtransations, it's just a ridiculous cheat code shop, so that what you once obtained with codes, now you get by paying real money. It's stupid, it's really not needed (if you can't finish the game, even on easy mode, without buying praxis kits, you should just git gud), but I'm not going to penalise the game for a questionable choice that doesn't have any inpact on the gaming experience.
Bottom line, I'm happy with what I played, despite the minor bugs and issues. 8/10 would buy again; must buy if at sale.

The thing that really turned me off this VN was the lack of effort put into the English translation. The story itself was already fairly generic, but had the writing been fleshed out a bit more before releasing, I could understand the glowing reviews it had somehow snatched up. I had only briefly skimmed the reviews before downloading it for myself, and I went with the assumption that there'd be a little more atmosphere and tension given that its a halloween theme, but that was a mild disappointment.
A huge part of a VN's essence stems from its ability to captivate a reader with engaging visuals and music, to which Trick or Treat didn't deliver. The background work felt lazy at times, and given that there was only art for two of the characters, it would have been nice for a few different facial expressions or movements. The music was overall okay, but didn't really add anything to the experience.
Since its free, its not a complete waste of time for those who are pretty hardcore about VNs. I'd recommend it as a good cure for really desperate boredom, but not if you're after something with a bit more impact. Perhaps later works might have more promise, but this VN was mediocre at best.

If you really like VNs and want to try it then it's not so bad that you feel to aggrieved for having played it. If you've never played a VN before, I'd advise trying others before you try this one.

I love Gone Home and Dear Ester and tend to enjoy platformers and pretty, somber things, and from what I'd heard I thought I'd be really into this short/sweet experience. Unfortunately, there's not much sweet (or effectively somber) about it. The game's tone switches from "adventure!" to "prevent a survivor from committing suicide" to "adventure!" to "free a maiden from a somewhat offensive spear-weilding tribe" too often, and not with the art that allows better dramas to make you laugh, cry, and laugh again.
The problem, I suspect, is that the game offers up very little to think about as you blindly push Forward from setpiece to setpiece. The world is full of sadness and loss, clearly meant to echo the loss of the Brothers' mother and the potential loss of their father, but there's rarely much commentary or depth to these scenes, just flavors of loneliness. Then, when the game abruptly moves on to riding mountain goats for fun, it's clear that the action scenes don't serve as meaningful counterpoint to the sadness you keep being witness to. During these patches of straightforward nagivation puzzles, there's simply not much to think about. The relationship of the brothers doesn't change, nor do their fears or hopes. They're curiously static against a constantly changing backdrop of sadness and lighthearted adventure. It's hard to put into words, but the game's insistence on dwelling on the world's misery without considering it more deeply makes the whole experience feel like spending a room with a person in the middle of a bad breakup: neither insightful nor very much fun.

The original Trine was an original concept, that was unfortunately broken by a lackluster gameplay. In solo, Zoya was so good, that you could use her almost exclusively, bypassing puzzles. It was fun to use the grappling hook, but it's still felt rather empty.
Trine 2 is nothing like that. First, the characters have been rebalanced, and the level design enhanced, so that each character has opportunities to shine. Pontius is somewhat underpowered, but Amadeus is great (magnetized crates for the win) and Zoya is not as omnipotent as before.
So the gameplay being good, you take upon that journey with more enthusiasm. And what a journey ! Frozenbyte has created a fantastic world, full of magic and colors, it's a pleasure to discover the different environments (though the "mandatory ice and fire levels for platformers" could have be avoided, Frozenbyte shines by doing original stuff not copy tropes).
Special note for the DLC that is included in Complete Story : it's even better than the main story. Better story with cutscenes and more dialogues, more variation in the environments, and lots of interesting challenges that use all 3 characters. You should really play it if you've finished the main game.

For someone like me who's witnessed several console generations and to that effect played plenty of games in his life, there are those few but legendary shiny pearls, which – just like movies, music, books, people and parties – really stand out as well as in mind and adhere to fond memories. For me, one of those pearls surely is Red Faction, a first person shooter whose vibes, unique setting, gameplay twist and soundtrack were burnt into my flesh-and-bone covered hard drive some 16 years ago. As its graphic content (blood, burning enemies, corpses) was cut back then, I happily bought it on Steam as the uncut version has been taken off the German Index recently.
The title, first installment of a bigger franchise developed by Volition and published by THQ, sends you to Mars which is only a stone's throw away. A whopping 225 million kilometres away (at least on average). You play as the miner Parker, a man who left Earth and went off to new frontiers, to find his luck by working as an official employee for the Ultor corporation under the surface of the ancient war god's planet. What initially appeared to be a good idea filled with hope, promises and exciting adventures is now nothing more than a degrading and humiliating endeavour: Ultor treats its inferiors with hardly more respect than we do with bugs.
Those who neglect work can expect penalties. Those who protest can rest assured to meet the security guards' electrically charged batons. To make matters worse there is a mysterious plague that kills more and more miners, if they aren't disappearing under equally mysterious circumstances. Resentment is slowly spreading on Mars and graffiti tags which clearly militate against Ultor and favour a person named Eos do the rest. The tension's rising and all that's missing for this powder keg is the last spark.
The game starts off with this keg's explosion: During a mining schedule, one of our colleagues simply has enough and expresses his dissent in front of an Ultor guard, who pulls out his baton. A brawl ensues, a shot's fired. And then a literal war breaks out. After playing the game as a teen on my PS2 a fair amount of times, the miners' revolution against the totalitarian corporation filled up to seven hours on my Steam clock. What can I say? After all these years it hasn't lost a single iota of its charms.
I count myself among the people who care the most for the story in a medium (closely followed by gameplay, sound and then graphics). And let's be honest: The story's nothing special here, which doesn't mean it is utter crap. The main theme knows how to please, depending on what kind of person you are: The oppression of the weak, exploiting people who try to build themselves a (new) life and are taking high risks to achieve that goal and, naturally, fight for their freedom. In use of soundtrack and gameplay that main theme is delivered pretty well. The story development however, as well as some 'twists', aren't the Holy Grail of narration by today's standards. Nevertheless, the miners' fight for freedom sends us from the deepest places inside Mars to climbing higher up, level per level, to see the surface and sky again. A literal uprising that kept me really interested in Parker's fate. But consequently, the upcoming three pillars (as I like to call them) carry the whole game to the greatest extent.
Of course, the graphics are inevitably behind time: Objectively speaking they are horrible and setting up Red Faction with a high 16:9 resolution is only achievable through mods or tweaking on your end. The textures are beyond muddy for our spoilt eyes, the polygon count equals the IQ of religious fanatics and even the GPU based AA optimising can't eliminate the jittering completely. But if we all take a moment and look at how people put the graphics of the first Deus Ex from 2000 aside and cherish it for the gaming milestone it is because of its atmosphere, Red Faction's other qualities also still prevail.
Two things I have to highlight on a positive note: First the art design – a factor willingly ignored while reviewing older games. The design of the characters, vehicles, buildings, weapons, everyday items and propaganda posters is rock solid; coherent concepts of what creative people thought a gritty, dirty science fiction story on Mars would look like during the very early 2000s. My second point is the level design. Apart from how the developers built and filled Mars' innards with interesting sights to look at, there often is more than one way to reach your goal, firstly because of the their intentions and secondly because of the game engine - but more on that later on. So keep your eyes peeled for hidden passages.
The soundtrack is simply unique and contributes to the game's atmosphere brilliantly. Of all games I've ever had the chance to play and listen to, Red Faction's score is one of the soundtracks I kept in my mind and ear. The rich synthie sounds either come breaking down on you pretty upbeat while you're exchanging bullets with Ultor guards, mysterious creatures and insentient bots, or they sneak up your tympanum with calm, sometimes menacing soundscapes, while you're exploring the countless caverns, tunnels, underwater areas and man-made facilities. In my eyes and ears the sound altogether seems to be paying homage to science fiction flicks of the late 80s and 90s; I for one was reminded of many of them and welcomed it.
The gameplay of this old gem is well-tried, classical ego shooter fare: Using a broad arsenal of weapons you hit, shoot and throw your way through hordes of enemies. The vehicle sequences every now and then round this picture off: I can't deny that I was grinning like an idiot every time I explored the ingame world for quite a while and found an abandoned inviting vehicle such as jeeps, submarines, tanks and gunships, ready to be used. Those bits still play like a charm and giving enemy units what they deserve with a few rockets or the howl of your minigun is still a lot of fun.
This is the part where we talk about the aforementioned gameplay twist: The GeoMod engine 1.0! For the first time in the history of interactive media the destruction of your environment (at least large parts) with the aid of explosive weaponry became reality with this game's release. You don't have the key to open this particular door? Yes, you have – it's called an explosive charge! Just make your own door right next to the closed one! You're sitting in the cockpit of a gunship and the guards far below barricaded themselves inside a guard tower, annoying you with their tiny rifles? Send your regards by trimming their tower with a good ol' rocket! The enemy bot is behind a column and you can't hit it? Give the bot a wave, while you're 'eyeball to camera lense' with it after removing that nasty obstacle with a grenade! When Diablo 2 began to struggle with the modern age and local servers shut down, it was a very difficult time. This game offers a lot of what the best classic RPGs had to offer. Graphically it is fantastic and it is quite a fresh take on RPGs, the game is quirky and fun on screen with a cartoonish style but great character. The storyline is great if not slightly predictable, but side quests are where a lot of fun happens. It is a great game both for its story and its incredibly fluent and high paced gameplay which is where it really stands out.
At higher levels you often find yourself re-approaching hordes of monsters to try draw them out so you can chop them down slowly as rambo-ing in gets you nowhere. This aspect makes the game strategically satisfying and yet surprisingly difficult at the same time.
This game packs a lot of punch, it is fantastically replayable and very rewarding! I still have yet to try out any of the mods, so this review is solely based on playthroughs.
I loved Diablo II for its dark, serious undertone and eerie music and find myself nostalgic about the PVP and Hell Baal Runs. What fun it was! The only drawback I can think of (and I compare this to D2) is the limited number of classes (there are only 4) and the skill trees are perhaps not as large as they could have been.
But then again I am basically awaiting a remastered Diablo 2 :P
Rather look at this game as if it were a different animal, and as that it is a polished and glorious product!

If you loved the previous game and you got some money in your wallet, buy DMC4: Special Edition and relive the nostalgia with the new additions.

Cat Goes Fishing can be summed up in the title, you play as a cat and you fish. The game however goes farther than the premise. There are two modes to play, classic and realistic. Classic is a mode where you can catch any fish and they will not fight back, in realistic the fish fight your reel and the bigger the fish the bigger the fight. There are over 40 different species of fish to catch in the game which fall into the categories of small, medium, large, and huge. The fish also all have different sale values. There are many different fishing rods and even more rod upgrades to buy as well as boats and bait upgrades. All the upgrades in the game can truly change the mechanics of the gameplay which is fun to evolve into how you want to play. There are also over 20 hats to find and collect in the ocean which give various upgrades and buffs also changing gameplay. The game can be a grind at some points saving up for more expensive items, but the grinds do not last very long. This game is very calming and relaxing as well as intense. It is a load of fun exploring the ocean and fighting to catch a new fish you just saw or completing the quests you have been assigned. Overall Cat Goes Fishing is a very fun addictive game and is a cacophony which is all new and original, and the wealth of things to do will keep you coming back for more. I can beyond a shadow of a doubt recommend this game to anyone and everyone interested. Fish on.

While I am disappointed with the length of the game, this is a single-player first run review of the game.
Pros: / Cons:
Game Story 3rd Best across the Deus Ex Universe (HR 2nd / DE 1st)
Game Mechanics Best across the Deus Ex Universe
Game Inventory Best across the Deus Ex Universe
Game Sound / Music 2nd Best of the Deus Ex Universe (HR 1st)
Game Grasp / Hold 2nd Best of the Deus Ex Universe (DE 1st)
Breakdown:
Game Story ++ / - (Good Not Great)
Is short, had I breezed through it and not taken a few additional side quests and different turns, it would of lasted maybe a few more hours, my initial play through was Non-Violent / Ghost (Which can take time) and it took me about 15 - 18 hours to get through the game. (Pretty Short Considering the Deus Ex Previous HR took me around 40 Hours. Content in those hours was good, though it felt a little repetative, given I only had one place really to visit with the exception of end game points.
Game Mechanics +++ (Great)
Gives you a lot of room to micromanage and find ways around certain obstacles and locations with going to different routes over others. The use of Augs and the new Augs definately provide better advantages along certain routes than others, but given the length of the game it felt like as I was getting the Augs, it wasn't being tested too far beyond what I was given in time.
Game Inventory +++ (Great)
Upgrades and Customization up the @$$, you have so much more you can adapt than just stick a scope on to rifle, you can individually modify weapons and equipment further with parts you find laying about. THere are some old come backs from DE, and a few additional items that I found interesting and useful that weren't in HR. The game inventory system is still mildly the same, and based on your Augs, but its a little more flashier and easier to maintain and update without having to spend half the time in the game organizing everything.
Game Sound / Music ++/-- (Meh...)
For the installment of Jenson Return I would of expected something a bit more epic, but its like they picked up a mediocre producer for the music after giving us that spectacular trailer nearly a year and a half ago. Seriously Square Enix WTF?!
Game Grasp and Hold +/-/+ (Some Here Some There)
There are times you want to put it away and other times you want to keep on going deeper, work and school be damned.
Overall 6.25 / 10.00
Replayability - Sure
My main issue is content shown, vs. content played, there is a lot of things I was hopeful for, including a longer story plot, more locations, and possibly some information regarding characters from the previous HR game. Beyond Serif.
It was a good buy for me, as I enjoy the Deus Ex Universe, but I am desperately hoping that like any of the 2's (Mass Effect 2, Dragon Age 2, and now Deus Ex: Mankind Divided) that the third installment will blow the other two away and give us that incredible insight and game power we have come to know and love.
(PS: Seriously lets get out of the "2's" Being disappointments, its getting agitating)

Literally the only negative things I can say about the game itself are that the story ends halfway through the arc it set up, making it a sufferer of "middle of a trilogy syndrome" where the first entry is a full story and then 2 is a lead in to 3, and that the final boss was only okay. And I'm hoping some optimization patches mean I can turn up the graphics a bit. That's it.
I guess I would have liked to see more focus on organized crime, and corrupt business politics... but that's what Human Revolution was for, isn't it? Despite being the middle child of the Adam Jensen saga, Mankind Divided was still a ♥♥♥♥ing phenomenal game. Every single encounter can be won by kicking down doors guns blazing, sneaking in and leaving no trace aside from a few hacked email accounts, killing everyone in a psychopathic rampage, leaving everyone comatose with a broken everything, or any number of combinations of those and more. The environments are amazingy detailed, full of world building just in the design and decorations. The characters are engaging and well written. The character models and graphics in general are a huge step up from the last entry, though optimization on all the pretty new features could be better. The hub city is absolutely HUGE, to the point where I spent hours just running around all the secret paths and bumbling my way into the incredibly well done side quests.
If it sounds like I'm gushing about this game, it's because I am. It was great. I'm probably going to go play it again. The story wasn't as good as HR, plot wise, but it still managed to touch on a lot of issues relavent to both real life and the setting of the game in a mature and engaging way. It did it's job and transitioned us out of the golden age of mankind seen in Human Revolution, and put us one step closer to the bleak world of the first Deus Ex. I felt things, I had to think about some big concepts for once, and I was entertained through out it all.
They say the game was split in two. The ending does kind of fell like it. Hell, the sequel has supposedly been in development for a year at this point.
Good. I want more like what I just played, and this means I don't have to wait long to get it.
♥♥♥♥ the microtransactions, though. That's just a stupid♥♥♥♥♥idea.

I asked for this game, but I never asked for THIS game. Something that spends so much time winding up a hell of a pitch only to drop the ball and hit you up with credits. Truly it is the MGSV of the series, the fabled would-be magnum opus of the franchise that closes the loop and ends the last game where the first one begins - only for the game itself to be essentially neutered and cut in half, ending after a singular Boss Fight with a mere C-grade Terrorist in stark contrast to Human Revolution's 3 (4 if you include the Panchaea Fight).
Locations are quite limited in this installment, hosting a singular (albeit impressively large) hubworld, whilst visiting a maximum of 3 other environments - but those are just mission specific, nothing to shake a finger on Human Revolution's 2 Hub worlds, and 4 mission-specific environments.
In all, the characters are reasonably fleshed out, as are the worlds and detail in each level, and even the story itself for the most part builds promise and tension, the combat is a lot more fluid, along with each conversation piece you have with other people. But it's unfinished, it's missing it's entire Third Act, leaving you feel ultimately unfufilled. Aside from the takedown of one vaguely important individual (The only Boss), you have contributed nothing else of actual value to the world, you're just some task-force agent, and live up to exactly that.
In Human Revolution, the world itself is at stake as you risk your life to alter the course of Mankind.
In Mankind Divided, you save some buildings full of people in London while the world continues without you.
I recommend the game because it's still part of the Deus Ex series, it brings up and addresses socio-political issues like it's predecessors have before it. It's not as bad as Invisible War, but in it's current state, it only stands inches above it compared to how many miles it falls short of the depth and complexity of Human Revolution, let alone the original Title. It's too concerned with giving you exposition, and not a narrative.

Have played WWII games since Day of Defeat, including Call of Duty and Medal of Honor. As far as a WWII themed shooter, H&G is fairly average. The vehicles are interesting and don't overwhelm combat as much as you might imagine they would. Where H&G falls apart is where most WWII shooters falter: weapon balance.
The starting weapons are desperately useless and players are limited to a single choice. I started with the Americans, and the Garand is pretty insufferably underpowered. Roll your eyes as much as you like, but a bullet at the end of a cartridge that's this long, [---], isn't going to do anywhere near as much damage as a bullet that's rocketing off of the end of a cartridge that's this long, [-------]. A Ball 30-06, which the Garand, Springfield, and BAR all fired, is going to ruin someone's day, even if it doesn't kill them. The major difference between a Garand and a Springfield and a BAR should be accuracy, Not range. Not damage. And most certainly NOT all three.
Automatic weapons are absolutely overpowered, doing damage far above the handgun rounds that they fire. The MP-40, for example, fires the same 9mm round that the German pistol did. Semi-Automatic and bolt action rifles are pathetically underpowered. Do NOT invest in the starting rifle, don't buy a grenade, don't buy a shovel. Save your in game money and buy an automatic. Keep getting better and better autos. Never look back.
Also, I've seen players running around and firing MG-34's and MG-42's while standing upright. It's clear that the guys that developed this title have NEVER fired so much as a .22 rimfire and lack even the most basic understanding of kick or muzzle climb. My advice to them is to get away from the computer for a day and spend a day at the range and familiarize themselves with how guns ACTUALLY work, not how they think they do because all the games they play.
Now, after dealing with all the gun-nerd stuff, the game is, as I said, fairly average, though the graphics are obviously looking a little dated now. The interface is a bit unintuitive and not being able to edit key maps outside of matches is kind of frustrating. Also, talking about in game money, buyer beware, this game is pay to win. If you give them money, you get access "veteran" perks, including additional weapon slots in battle and an additional "combat perk" (like toughness, stealth, etc.). So, yes, definitely pay to win.
It's free, but so are other titles that offer far more freedom for the same price and aren't pay to win.
All in all, a solid C- title.

I was playing one of the side missions, where every base you killed spawns an alien that runs away and spawns a new base if you don't kill it fast enough. Pretty simple.
2 hours later, I'm still playing the same damn mission. There's 9 bases left, and they're all sitting in a cluster. Most of them are covered by a healing field. Every one of them has 9 powerups. I have to defend on 3 fronts from the swarms of aliens that are crawling toward my bases with no respite. Here are my options, and why every one of them won't do anything:
Kill the healing field: This isn't an option. I can't even get near it, and even if I killed it, it would just come back in 20 seconds.
Slowly whittle away at a corner until I can get a foothold: This is flat out never an option in any situation in this game. the second you stop attacking something, all of its turrets or spawners respawn. You can only make a dent if you do enough damage to kill a base in a single attack.
Mass everything I have and push to take a base: Probably the best option and still utterly impossible. When I attack, 5 bases start sending dozens of kamikaze exploder bugs per second at my face. The continuous mass of ranged spitter bugs is still coming. The base I'm attacking shields itself so all my attacks tickle, and on top of that it's being healed. My attacks hurt me because of reflect, base turrets that far outrange me are hitting me and knocking my soldiers back with every shot. On a regular basis waves of assassins come to shoot my commander, and I have to blow missiles to kill them. While I do this, I'll lose my bases on every other front because I can't defend them and attack, and to top it off, the best case scenario is that it spawns a relocator that there's no way I'll be able to kill, that will just set up a new base somewhere else in the cluster.
Restart, make sure I don't get into this situation: And there lies the problem. I couldn't stop it. There was a cluster of 3 here before the game started, and I couldn't defeat them without a lot of powerups. while I was taking out other bases, I couldn't stop all of the relocator bugs, because they're decently fast and very tanky, and it's impossible to follow them since every other one of the bugs that's attacking you slows you as well.
Here's the issue: the game is designed with HUGE power asymmetry. you get a few troops and upgrades, and you're up against a dozen bases that swarm thousands of enemies at you constantly. every game is a war of attrition. The game feels like a chore. It's like a sailing game, where you don't sail the boat but you just sit there with a cup and bail water, but you can't plug the leak until everything else is dry.
yeah, not every mission is that brutal. Yeah, there are other options, I could buy some one time power ups from farming easier missions and try again, or just skip it. Yeah, I could probably bash my face into the problem for another few hours and eventually win, because it's basically impossible to actually lose. Yeah, there are plenty of good points to the game as well. But nothing makes up for what an utter chore the game is. I'm not saying it's not fun, it is fun to an extent. I'm not saying don't play it, maybe it will be more your thing. I'm just saying that I found it a frusterating mess and I'm surprised it's rated so highly, so I wanted to throw my opinion in. If you want a similar game that's not only better, but cheaper, go play creeper world.

I'm convinced that most real-time strategy games shouldn't bother with an actual lore and storyline. The ones with better storylines usually crib their source material from conflicts in history, and I usually gloss over those because there's a sense of THIS IS ROOTED IN HISTORY, IT'S LIKE I'M ACTUALLY THERE via gameplay (what I like to call the Saving Private Ryan approach). Beyond that... oh Christ. The Dawn of War series comes to mind as my first go-to answer for why RTS games shouldn't bother, largely because Warhammer (40K and otherwise) is a gigantic batch of poorly written juvenile♥♥♥♥♥♥with all the depth and appeal of a moody teenager sitting in a dark room slapping the dolls from all of his Collector's Edition video games together. ("Anything by Blizzard" is an immediate runner-up, mainly because Blizzard rips off Warhammer lock, stock, and barrel and any attempt I've made to read any lore for one of their universes made me wish I hadn't.). Infested Planet ALMOST sidesteps this.
Infested Planet is a wonderful distillation of the real-time strategy genre. It pares the structure of a typical RTS down to a few buildings, a few soldiers, and the ability to instantly change your soldiers and abilities on the fly. The enemy is entrenched and reacts to upgrade itself, and sometimes you'll find that the strategy you're employing won't work at all in the face of shielded buildings and mimic squads that copy your squad exactly to kill your own soldiers. And even if the enemy succeeds in kicking your♥♥♥♥♥and taking your bases, you can refund your previously built kit and try a new strategy. The enemy captured your siege cannon? No prob, just switch a grunt from a sniper to a scout and have that scout weaken the building while the rest of the squad puts lots of bullets in it. Want to destroy a series of hives and then set up an area to protect your new base of operations? Go with an officer and four minigunners, kill them all, then switch to shotgunners and flamethrowers and spend the rest of your resources on defense encampments. It's a wonderful game that allows and forces players adapt to unforseen developments (and there are plenty of those that the enemy is willing to pull out in order to destroy your dumb little squad of soldiers).
If you're going to play it, however, I recommend that you play the campaign up to a point, because that's where the game keeps the 'random' missions. The campaign is almost where I fell out of love with Infested Planet. Not just because I have to play something I don't want to play to unlock features inside the game, but also because the campaign's learning and difficulty curve moves up too slowly, and it also keeps taking away the focus from the free-wheeling dance of terror with a plodding story about an army that invades a bug-infested planet and then the planet fights back and then the bugs kill the army and then the stranded sexy female scientist pulls out a bioweapon and the big bug hivemind is destroyed in the last mission and it is told with the same amount of care and excitement employed in this run-on sentence. A lot of the included campaign is boring and stifles what makes this game great. Infested Planet doesn't need a campaign mode and a cast of characters talking over soldiers shooting alien bugs to 'flesh out the lore' (but if the developers insist, get someone who can actually write this sort of thing). Infested Planet's magic lies in its skirmishes and random missions.

short version:
the game is authentic to the middle earth mythos and has tremendous detail.
it is easy to learn with good tutorials and the classes and races feel unique in how they play.
a halfling burgler [bilbo baggens is a burgler class character] is different than a human burgler.
rangers are quite different from lore masters.
and i love it.
longer version:
i started playing the game long before it was on steam.
i bought the game when it was REQUIRED to pay a monthly subscription fee for access to the game.
i have seen the game expand and grow to what it is now.
i approve.
if you don't know the mythology that was built around middle earth, this is a great game and has many different ways to play.
you can play casual or intense and you will find a community that is the most helpful and friendly of any multiplayer online game i have seen, and i have been playing online games since the mid '90's when they were all text games.
the game is primarily "co-operative" player mode where you see and know and interact with many other players.
there is PVP where you can take your characters from the co-operative world and have fun at PVP and return to the co-operative part of the game with the treasures and experience earned in the PVP area.
you can be a burgler. a traveling mistral ,a warrior, or a maker of jewelry and pies.
oh yes and a spell caster also.
you can probably find some aspect of the game that appeals to your "style".
if you know about middle earth you will be pleased to see that the team that developed, and is still developing this game are also familiar with the stories and have taken great care to be true to the original concept put forth in the books years ago.
one example of this would be walking past a stone troll standing on a hill in the middle of a swamp in a certain area, and you knowing the story behind why it is there. no sign posted with the story, no explanation offered, but if you have read the story you know why it is there.
and many other things like the last homely house and you get to meet tom bombadill at his house.
when or if you meet bilbo baggins, elron, strider or gandalf it is done in a believable way that does not break or even stretch the known original story lines from the books.
and being free to play with micro-transactions does not mean "pay to win" in this game.
the ability to earn turbine points from actions in the game [turbine points are what you pay real world cash for]  makes this game different than other free to play games that i have seen, even among those other games with ways to earn points in the game.
so you can learn skills and do deeds that are supporting of the "middle earth mythos" and be rewarded with points that can otherwise be bought.
points in the game are earned mostly for working along lines that advance or support the "feel" of middle earth.

Maybe by playing this game fifteen years after its initial release I had a hard time grappling with it. The game clearly only exists as a tech demo for its environment destruction engine (geo-modding, I seem to remember it being called). And to that end, it's pretty impressive for its time. But, that's really all that's done well here.
The shooting mechanics are wonky and bullets fly in inexplicable directions. On some vehicles bullets will exhaust, and on others they won't but in all cases you have an ammo counter. There is no auto-save function at all. The stealth mechanics make GoldenEye's seem comprehensive and intelligent, and it's forced on you, like it or not. In a stealth section, you cant just say "forget it," shoot a guard, take his assault rifle and go crazy. Nope, you have about three clips of silenced pistol ammo and that's it. By the end of the game, you will hate the rail rifle: it goes through walls and one shots pretty much anything. Sound cool? How about when almost every room has at least one guy carrying it and they are one-shotting you. Gets old really fast.
The game lasted me about 7 hours, but it felt like I spent days playing through it. I found the game pretty hard, and a lot of my 7 hours can be attibuted to repeated dying. If you're in the mood to play something in the vein of classic Half-Life, this one is an okay pretender. You might also be interested in a bit of backstory and context for Red Faction: Guerrilla, which this game does provide.
Ultimately, this game is a mediocre game from the past that has not aged well. Unless you have a very specific reason for wanting this title, you should probably pass on it.

Summary:
Transmissions: Element 120 is a Source engine developed indie game set in the Half-Life universe. It consists of four well-made if somewhat short chapters that provide a few encounters with your favourite crab-zombies and combine soldiers. The overall feel and setting is designed to be a mixture of horror and puzzle solving, with a little hint of combat at key moments.
PROS:
. More Half-Life style play.
. Great care and attention to create an immersive environment and detailed locations, take this small team's effort a step up.
. The custom made soundtrack elevates the tension and key encounters to another level.
. Its short and can be played in two to three hours.
. Achievements are simple to obtain but can be missed if not careful.
. Its free.
CONS:
- Not much really. If anything there could have been a little more spoken narrative / dialogue included to help build up a better picture of the scenario.
- Some of the AI routines stop working for combine soldiers and they just stand there doing nothing. Happened a few times.
- Progressing through some of the physics-based doorways/exits can be confusing. So if thats not your thing make sure you are happy to consult a guide.
AND THE ORDINARY:
* The engine may be dated but the developers have maxxed out as much as possible with the tools they have to make this more than just a mod.
* There isnt much combat with it being staged in key set-pieces towards the end of chapters.
Conclusion:
Short, well-made but enjoyable nonetheless. If you are waiting for Half-life (Episode) 3 you could do worse than check this out! Its one of the best free-to-play efforts that you are bound to find on steam. Fans of Half-life should enjoy this no question. Otherwise if you are after easy/quick achievements or just like to pass the time with free games then you would be a fool not to try this. If however you are after a pure or heavy-focused shooter then this is not for you.

I will start by saying I'm part of the game's recommended audience, so perhaps I'm a bit biased, so take this review with a grain of salt.
I'm a huge fan of RWBY, and I loved playing this game. I like hack-and-slash games like Dynasty Warriors, but they get a bit old after a while. RWBY: Grimm Eclipse it a great game - for about ten hours, or maybe a week if you don't have a lot of time to sit down and play.
I still enjoy it, but the sheer lack of content kills it for me. You have a campaign that lasts about four to six hours depending on your skill - and since every character's combos don't go on for more than a maximum of maybe four or five buttons before you have to get creative with dodge-rolls, the skill ceiling isn't that high - and after the campaign is Horde mode.
I've played for fourteen hours total and have experienced pretty much everything in the game at least -TWICE-. The game, while fun, suffers from a crippling lack of content. As previously stated, the story lasts at most six hours, and if you're good, maybe as few as three. You have two modes - Story, and Horde. The story isn't phenomenal, but it's just good enough to keep you going; there are no big secrets or plot twists, and it's just about average, really, which isn't bad - but there's room for so much more. As for Horde mode, it's far better with friends, but there's only three maps, so you'll be seeing the same places over and over. Difficulty fluctuates between fair and Dark Souls-levels of "I want to cry." When you're fighting Grimm, Horde mode is okay - but the robots you have to fight sit firmly on the OP side. While a good player can still deal with it, the difference between the two types of enemies are night and day - Grimm can be combo'd and dealt with, but are dangerous in a group to those who are not cautious - while two Swallow-wielding robots can combo-lock you to death, and two grenade-launcher robots can instakill you if they hit you within three seconds of each other.
Again, a good player can still deal with it, but there's a lack of balancing here that can absolutely ruin a good Horde run.
Character progression could use a bit of work as well. There are more perks than you have points for without a certain community mod (which, by the way, has the game developer's seal of approval - but you still won't have enough points to get all the perks) or without hacking. However, you really won't even NEED all of those points, as there's only a handful of perks even worth getting. Just as an example, perks for the characters' ranged attacks - absolutely unneeded in anyone who isn't named Weiss, Blake, or Nora. I'm looking at YOU, Ruby, with your absolutely PATHETIC gun. Even on the characters with good ranged attacks, there's only ONE path down that ranged tree that's worth using at all. Blake needs the wide blade beam, Weiss needs the freezing projectile, and NEVER use Nora's perk that turns her grenades into landmines.
The game was marketed as this super exciting thing with lots of polish, but this is so far from the truth that it borders on blatant lies.
If the game had more content, perhaps some of these issues could be alleviated. However, I'd say that twenty dollars is really just about the absolute limit of tolerability for a game such as this. I enjoy it, and it's good fun - but the fun comes to an end far, far too quickly. Unless you are an absolute die-hard fan of Dynasty Warriors-style hack-and-slash games, and an absolute die-hard fan of RWBY, this game probably isn't for you. If you're just a passing fan of RWBY, your twenty-five dollars would be better spent on the bundle for the three currently available volumes of the web animation, which will keep you occupied and entertained for far, far longer than this game.

A quite charming visual novel, with quite an emotional true ending.
There are two things that let it down though : There are a fair few grammical errors in the English text, and whilst the graphics are nice, they aren't as good as they should be really.  Animations for the characters are limited.

Quite a splendid little visual novel. Being free and not from a great host of people, the resources naturally are limited, but they were put to good use. The general atmosphere was most successful and served the story exceptionally, along with the music. Short as it was, the story was still captivating and constructed well. A wise man once said a good story knows when it's the time to end, and this one did know. The routes were crafty but not frustrating for such a tiny VN, which I consider worthy of a separate mention. Considering the limited amount of time available to build them, the characters worked surprisingly nicely, and adapted to the routes more than appropriately. The art might not have been earth-shattering, but I found it pleasant to the eye and fitting for the story.
If I had to mention a single thing to do better next time, it would be to get an additional English proofreader. Especially in an unvoiced VN, perfect language would make a difference in professionalism. Native English speakers shouldn't be that difficult to recruit for such a purpose even with no pay.

Improvements over original DMC4:
* New playable characters and new difficulty modes, of course!
* Better graphics. My PC runs original DMC4 smoothly at highest quality, but now I use a quality setting that's a little lower than highest, and it still occasionally lags.
* When out of battle, the increasing of running speed happens after 2 steps instead of about 5.
* In places where you roll a die, originally when you first strike the die, a disturbing instruction comes out, and your strike is wasted. Now your first strike will count, and the instructions show up after the move is complete.
* When Nero operates the "big top", you no longer have to wait for it to become activated after first strike.
* All progress and purchases are saved automatically, and there will be only 1 save slot. (Maybe not an improvement to some players)
Complaints:
* Game fails to recognize the d-pad on my joypad. As a result, when controlling Dante, I have to use JoyToKey to map d-pad to keyboard keys 1, 2, 3 and 4.
* Boss battles lack variety. That's a really good way to cut down the cost of designing bosses, right Capcom, by having two characters fight the same boss twice. Some Positives/Negatives from my experience...

+The Game Retains the same feel as it did before, boasting a decent combat system.

-Some of the DLC, while optional, shouldn't be a thing at all.  I mean, yeah, the cosmetic DLC for Trish & Lady is nice, but really?  Proud Souls?  Red Orbs?  Blue Orbs?  Mode Unlocks?  Secret Character Unlocks?  These are all things easily done from within the game.  Why botch it up with this crap?  Maybe I'm just getting a bit elitist on such things...
-Lady & Trish is basically just Nero & Dante with fewer cutscenes.  Literally.  It seems pretty damn lazy, but this is Capcom we're talking about.  These folks only seem to be able to create an original idea once every few years, then recycle it endlessly.

Cat Goes Fishing can be summed up in the title, you play as a cat and you fish. The game however goes farther than the premise. There are two modes to play, classic and realistic. Classic is a mode where you can catch any fish and they will not fight back, in realistic the fish fight your reel and the bigger the fish the bigger the fight. There are over 40 different species of fish to catch in the game which fall into the categories of small, medium, large, and huge. The fish also all have different sale values. There are many different fishing rods and even more rod upgrades to buy as well as boats and bait upgrades. All the upgrades in the game can truly change the mechanics of the gameplay which is fun to evolve into how you want to play. There are also over 20 hats to find and collect in the ocean which give various upgrades and buffs also changing gameplay. The game can be a grind at some points saving up for more expensive items, but the grinds do not last very long. This game is very calming and relaxing as well as intense. It is a load of fun exploring the ocean and fighting to catch a new fish you just saw or completing the quests you have been assigned. Overall Cat Goes Fishing is a very fun addictive game and is a cacophony which is all new and original, and the wealth of things to do will keep you coming back for more. I can beyond a shadow of a doubt recommend this game to anyone and everyone interested. Fish on.

Pros:
+ Wide variety of options in regards to how you complete objectives
+ Lean, focused story that's easier to comprehend than Human Revolution's was
+ The single city-hub is a lot more detailed and explorable than one may think at first
+ Augmentations, combat, movement, etc mechanics have been tightened up since Human Revolution
Cons:
- The leaner storyline makes Mankind Divided's events feel less exciting/impactful
- Wasted potential concerning the setting
- Too many questions left unanswered
- Numerous technical issues within the first two weeks of release
- Limited variety of locations to explore/conduct missions within
- Character animations continue to be rigid and repetitive
The Bottom Line:
Given that I consider Human Revolution to be one of the best game's I've ever played, it would be an understatement to say I was excited for Mankind Divided. Unfortunately, as usual, personal hype and high expectations can cause issues and Mankind Divided - despite its merits - didn't live up to those hopes and dreams.
While the game certainly improves upon many aspects carried over from the previous game, it finds itself lacking in two major regards: the story and the setting.
Mankind Divided clearly sought to counter-act the overly-convoluted and downright confusing plot presented in Human Revolution, and while it succeeds in some respects it leads to an experience that's lost a lot of the gravity, emotional investment, and impact that the previous game had. While Human Revolution had you unravelling conspiracy within conspiracy within conspiracy, Mankind Divided opts to give you something much more lean - getting to the bottom of a series of terrorit attacks. Yet, by the game's end this rather simple plot leaves the player feeling rather unsatisfied as your accomplishments feel limited and your victories hollow. While Human Revolution made you feel like you truly achieved something - in spite of still not entirely knowing the Illumanti's role in all of it - Mankind Divided has you deal with the present, known threat and keeps you guessing as to the many questions left hanging. And when you're left with more questions than answers you can't help but feel a little cheated as now you've got to wait years for the next game to continue onwards.
The smaller-scale storyline also leads to a rather limited number of environments the player gets to explore. While maybe, in the end, Mankind Divided only has two or three less locations than Human Revolution, that doesn't change the fact that Mankind Divided's environments lack the same kind of variety (but certainly had more exploration options).
The storyline and locations aside, Mankind Divided's other major flaw is its setting. Human Revolution is set in the augmentation Renaissance/Golden Age. This new technology is taking the world by storm and because of this we see the kind of impact it has on social, political, and economic life as well what augmentations mean on a philosophical and spiritual level. With the support of the storyline, characters, and in-game lore we get a good sense of the world in which Human Revolution takes place and we get to see how all these different viewpoints and beliefs manifest themselves amongst people and organizations both big and small.
By default, Mankind Divided's setting should be MUCH more interesting than Human Revolution's. We're now in a world that is still reeling from the Aug Incident and has reacted to this by largely taking an opposing stance to augmentation and those who are augmented. Augmented humans are now viewed as second-class citizens, they're seen as dangerous, frightening, and untrustworthy and this in turn has led to their oppression and rejection by "natural" society. Many nations across the world have become police-states where augmented citizens are stripped of their rights, seperated from soceity, and even forced into ghettos for their own good.
Yet, while Mankind Divided's setting SHOULD be vastly more interesting and emotionally charged we just never get a sense of that.
While Mankind Divided is a worthy - but not superior - follow up to Human Revolution make no mistake. You will not find many other games out there that put as much emphasis on exploration and freedom of gameplay than this. Issues and personal feelings concerning the story and setting aside, from a gameplay perspective Mankind Divided is quite an enjoyable experience and should certainly be on your radar if you're looking for a solid stealth game.

I should note that OpenIV, the main thing that caused this review to be written, has had it's Cease and Desist notion backed away, so I guess it is back and running? Not too sure, take a look for yourself.
Right, I believe I should post a review about the game, considering the recent controversy that has put GTA in a bit of a spotlight, this time negative imstead of positive.
As folks know already, the modding tool OpenIV has recieved a Cease and Desist notice, essentially terminating Singleplayer modifications (Important note: Singleplayer)
This essentially makes the singleplayer component of the game stuck with essentially the same old same old, that being the same game with the same protagonists with the same you know already. No room for customization like that Rick Sanchez mod that was a thing.
I will admit, it has been noted that Modding was not exactly a welcome sight, due to Take Two (Mostly them) and their concern that Singleplayer modding would leak in to their Online portion. Something that was pretty much impossible with OpenIV as it was not designed to cheat in the game.
So of course that is the whole backlash thing. I guess I can also talk about the game, since this is a review after all:
Singleplayer: Everyone and their amoeba probably know what the singleplayer is about at this point in time, so no need to talk about it. Except that it used to have extensive modification options, but not really now.
Multiplayer: Something that is literary the only reason most people play the game for, except some people still on the Singleplayer (Because honestly, SP is still a pretty solid story to play through), as it is the main thing that is being supported by the developers. Although I would say that ovee time, it started from what sounded like a good time in to a game of "Whoever has the biggest gun". I started it off as a street urchin, and I gotta say it was pretty exciting, but now that my character is quite a high level, I feel like it is no longer a fun game, but more of a slog of "Eh, another day, another dude with a fighter jet nuking me".
Not to mention that hackers/cheaters are also quite frequent, folks running scripts that make them immirtal, make money drops or just screw with people. It is something that is simply not fun.
This was written on a quick notice, so some things might sound a bit odd, so there's that.
Anyway, would I recommend the game? For the singleplayer, I would say yes as it is a pretty solid experience. For Multiplayer? I would say no because it is a dismal place that multiplayer, where you are forced to either grind for a long time to get somewhere, or spend hundreds of your money to get something nice and pretty. Not to mention Take Two's controversy being a sore thing.
Overall: No, I wouldn't say that the game should be purchased.

I want to recommend this game, but at the same time I can't recommend it.
Pros
- RTS without mining for currency
- Cost me about $5 with the DLC
Negatives
- Hives randomly spawning under you
- You upgrade your marines and when they die, the computer will spawn a duplicate of them for themselves, yes the computer will copy your upgraded marines once they die, you had a flame thrower that died?  Now the computer has a fresh flame thrower.
- Same thing goes for turrets/siege towers
- Double costs of towers, you pay for the tower, and then there's the privelege of paying to use the ability of the tower.
- Grind, grind, grind
- If you're crazy enough to beat it, there is ZERO replay value.
The difficulty ramps up on each mission the closer you get to completing it.  You destroy part of the enemy base and the enemy gets a mutation that makes the mission more difficult but it stays somewhat balanced, however at times the computer goes into cheap mode and spawns a whole lot of crap out of nowhere.
On the final mission there is no such destroy mechanic.  The computer gets mutations based on time, so the first one at 10 seconds, next at 20 seconds, and so on and so forth meanwhile you are barely getting by until eventually you become overrun at which point you need to grind previous missions to get money to give youself extra resources for that final mission.

Aaaahhh RWBY, my favorite series, I've been in love with it from the first episode, I saw through that buggy animation and weird lipsync, to the heart of the series below, its beauty, and creativity. < Sounds poetic, but seriously, It's an amazing series xD
But, This is about the game, soooo here we go!
This is the only (so far) official game for the RWBY franchise, It features 4 playable characters by default (8 with DLC) with simple, solid gameplay for each. Each of the 4 playable default characters controls the same, but their attacks have different power, AOE, speed, things like that, each character also has unique special abilities. The 4 playable characters are the members of team RWBY, and the story present here is original to the game, which means if you want to see all of RWBY, your going to want to play Grimm Eclipse.
Now Grimm Eclipse is a Hack and Slash game, it's rather simple, but the fighting is fluid and fun! the problem is, just as with any Hack and Slash game I've played, the combat is very repetitive after playing for a while. Fans of RWBY will probably love the game simply for being from RWBY, but the game isn't amazing xD It's not revolutionary, in fact its very simple, it has a simple leveling system, simple combat, simple story, simple combos, simple enemies, and simple objectives. The game also isn't very long, it doesn't take much time to complete the game, and max all your characters through grinding of previously completed missions. All this makes the game have virtually no replay value, after you finish your playthrough, all thats left is to max the characters and obtain every collectable.
However the game does have 1 other game mode, Horde Mode, it consists of the players (up to four play online co-op) surviving agianst, hordes, of Grimm and defending objective points. Combat is exactly like the games story mode.
All in all Grimm Eclipse is a game I really like! It's got simple, but fun mechanics, it's enjoyable, the graphics look just fine (like Season 4, but the graphics settings allows a "Potato" mode, which is basically Season 1 graphics XD) I don't play it much because its very repetitive, but if your a fan of RWBY, or just want a simple and short game to entertain you and some friends for a while, Grimm Eclipse is great! As a fan of RWBY I wish for a complex game where you could create your own weapons and hunter / huntress, and play through the game with much deeper combat and customization options, but I'm still really happy this great show received a game ^-^
Recomended!

For a long time, I've wondered why I never play RWBY: Grimm Eclipse, because I remember LOVING the pre-alpha demo developed by a single guy a few years ago.
I just played it again and realized why I absolutely DESPISE this game.
1: It has the worst sound design I've ever heard, hands-down. Sounds play for actions that I haven't even done, there are no sounds for things that NEED it, and everything's so quiet that I need to change the set-up of my speakers (or headphones) just to hear the effects over the music and poorly-placed voices. This failure in sound-design leads into reason 2: There is zero satisfaction in what you do. On controllers there's no vibration at all, and there's no screen-shake or environmental impact to indicate the weight and damage of heavy moves, so it feels like all of the enemies are dead grass being cut with a whiffle bat. Because everything's so quiet and there are MISSING SOUNDS, it's like watching an action movie without any of the post-production put into it. All you have are the sounds on-set captured with a mic that's too far away.
3: The camera is awful and there's no lock-on system. I feel like even if there was, it would feel as poor as the movement does. The characters are floaty, the dash is too short to feel like a dodge, I can't see where the enemies are or know how many are on the battlefield at once because the only indication you have of anything behind you is sound, which, as I stated, is so awful that I can't tell what's in front of me and really quiet or behind me and really loud.
4: It's definitely a co-op game, which is mostly fine, except that it doesn't seem to compensate for when you're playing alone using the single-player option. It's extremely difficult to fight every enemy and survive because the characters control poorly and don't do enough damage on their own. I've played this with friends before, and we had a blast because we were just mindlessly destroying everything in our path and talking about either the show or other things.
The game was poorly made, and has the potential to be an amazing co-op hack n' slash, but a bunch of poorly put-together jumbles of game systems (and lack thereof) make it difficult to enjoy unless you aren't paying attention to it.

First of all, one of the biggest issues, the control. The characters have pretty much no flow to their actions whatsoever. When you attack it's a single sudden motion with no smooth speeding up / slowing down in the animation. Pretty much the characters are set to move at a constant speed starting from 0, then at the end of the animation it sets back to 0. It's so fast that you'll miss it if you blink, and it couldn't be further from natural. On top of this, when you attack an enemy, you pretty much snap right to the enemy. This is especially noticeable when you try to attack while in the air. It's not like in games like Kingdom Hearts 1 & 2 where you'll sort of gain some momentum and float towards the enemy so you can hit them, you'll just instantly face them and move in front of them in a fraction of a second. It's as if the laws of physics are breaking themselves to help you or something. Oh, and don't even get me started on the jumping. It's super fast and unnatural with no feeling of momentum. It's almost identical to having a constant speed going up, then having the same speed going back down. And the jump doesn't even go that high.
There's issues with the control scheme itself. There's not any option to precisely set the controls to what you want. And with my gamepad, it has the D-Pad to moving instead of the left stick. This isn't inherently bad (I mean it's definitely a serviceable control scheme), but there's no way to change it to the left stick, and I honestly don't think it feels good to move around with the D-Pad in a 3D space. It feels kind of sudden, stiff, and unnatural, just like the combat in this game. It's not unplayable by any means, but it's another lack of polish. Polish can really go a long way, and this game really doesn't have any. And another gripe I have is that you can't zoom out the camera. It zooms automatically, and up / down on the right stick tilt the camera. I'm always trying to control the camera so I can see everything I need to worry about all at once, but all I can do is try to fiddle with the camera and move my character around to try to sort of do so. It's like it's fighting me a little, and I end up never being able to see everything.
Now let's talk about the fighting mechanics themselves. All combos are basically press X until you press press Y. And pretty much all of the characters only have 1 attack that has a large area of effect, in a game where you're constantly being swarmed by groups of enemies. These two things wouldn't be so bad (Hyrule Warriors has the same combo mechanic), but since all of the enemy attacks are pretty much instantaneous just like your attacks, and a lot of the time their range seems to reach way farther than it should, there's no art to trying to take down crowds like in something like the Batman Arkham games. There IS a counter mechanic, but it has the same problems as the normal attacks, it never seems that effective, and it's done via a button prompt. The button prompt wouldn't be so bad, but when it's included with all of the problems I mentioned before, it makes it feel like random bits of nothing that you can sometimes do whenever the game feels like it. It's not good, to say the least.
The level design isn't better, either. So, this game is basically run from point A to point B, with terrain that's mostly claustrophobic, with lots of areas where it seems you can go a certain direction, only for there to be an invisible wall. This game, let me tell you, loves invisible walls. If you hate them, this game will drive you insane. Now this wouldn't be so bad, just a nitpick really, if the areas themselves were good. But it's just a boring walk through an empty hallway that goes on a little too long, with some artifact collectibles lying around that have seemingly no value or reason to be gotten, until you get to the next room of agonizingly tedious waves of enemies. There is veriety, like sometimes you have to defend a tower thing from being destroyed, or sometimes you have to defend a minecart from being destroyed, or sometimes you have to defend a tower thing from being destroyed, or sometimes you have to defend a tower thing from being destroyed, stuff like that. But let me tell you, the battles go on for way too long, and there's not much veriety in the enemies in each wave. This isn't something like Kingdom Hearts or Doom where there's lots of enemies of varying types, where they all reoccur at some point in different configurations to keep things interesting. This is lots of enemies with very few variations that are actually that different. It's like they wanted scaling enemy classes where there's diferent tiers of the same type of enemy that are introduced that are tougher than the last tier, but then they used all of the diferent tiers as if they're unique enemy types themselves.
The game does have good points, like it looks fairly decent for a (I guess?) 3D indie title, which is helped by the art style. The music is just adapted music from the score of the show (which isn't inherently a bad thing to do) and is fine. But there's not much else.
Honestly, I haven't beaten this game. And I don't want to. Apparently the final boss is the worse definition of a damage sponge you could possibly imagine, and the ending is unsatisfying. That, and the story of this game is completely unrelated to anything in the series, will probably never come up again, and only exists to have an excuse for the game to exist. It's suppose to be an in-between story for Volume 2 and 3, but honestly it's just a lot of made up stuff that doesn't matter.
Oh yeah, and the game really short.
I was debating whether to buy this game or not about a month ago. I had read a bunch of reviews, and noticed a few things. One, all of the positive reviews were mostly from early access when the game was still being "developed" and people were much more likely to forgive problems by the assumpmtion that they'll be fixed later. Two, most of the recent reviews were all negative, and went into convincing detail as to why the game is mediocre / bad. Three, most of the positive reviews were one to three sentences of "rwby is great" or "love the show, loved the game", or "the game is great so fun playing as rwby characters rooster teeth is BOSS", things of that nature; nothing ever going that in-depth as to why it was good. And four, coming off of all of the problems about the game I was reading from the reviews, I would of had to pay $25 dollars to get access to a possibly bad game, whose main appeal is the promise of updates to "improve" it, the hope that it could be enjoyable to some degree, and that it starred Rwby characters. Well, I got stuck on this decision and forgot about the game eventually, until yesterday when I decided to look it up again and see if there were any updates to it that would warrent a purchase. I bought it when I saw it was on sale. And quite honestly, it's not even worth the sale price of $20.
And one last thing that really bugs me about this game. The developers themselves. I don't mean anything against them, but in the updates they're all so proud and fun sounding. They try to sound so silly and fun. They, honestly, don't deserve the right to be like that about a game that isn't that good IMO. They say things like "NORA AND TURRETS! NEED WE SAY MORE?", and it makes me shake my head. It implies that they think the game is fine the way it is and is perfectly enjoyable when it's not, and it's frustrating to see them not realize their mistakes, especially when it means that the game will probably never get better from updates. I only hope they see this review and take another look at their game. Plus, they're making paid DLC for this game. Again, I feel like they don't deserve the right to do that, especially when the DLC is four more playable characters for a game THAT CONTROLS LIKE♥♥♥♥♥
Anyway, character limit. No offense to anyone, but this game isn't good.

I don't get the appeal.
I mean, I get it
. TG2 presents itself as CK2 minus the strategic gameplay, with more of a focus on the characters themselves. That's pretty cool, right? Being able to forge a strong dynasty, play the political game, rise to power, govern a fiefdom, all while taking care of the day-to-day activities of medieval life. Who wouldn't want to play something like that?
Well, that's not what you get. For $10.99, you get a glorified city management game that plays like it was designed for mobile devices. You know all those terrible cash grabs you find in the app store? The ones where you click on some materials, click on a building, and are awarded gold and a big neon CONGRATULATIONS sign? That's essentially the gameplay you're paying for with TG2.
Sure, you can construct buildings, but that's essentially a matter of having enough gold and clicking on a large enough empty plot. Sure, you can get married, but the relationship system makes DA:Os look positively lifelike. Sure you can design your character, if you're happy with choosing from five beards, six hairstyles, and a couple of skin tones (rough estimates, not actual numbers).
I know this review sounds harsh, and I know I'm using some pretty strong rhetoric here. However, when you listen to how 4Head describes their product ("the shining successor of the ultra successful medieval life sim...", "State-of-the-art role playing features...", "a beautifully crafted and immersive 3D world...", etc.) and read the significant number of positive reviews on the store page, the objective and experienced gamer can't help but feel a little misled.
