After watching the "Let's play the game" about The Guild 2, I decided to buy the game and try it out.
The first thing you'll find out, that's it's quite unclear what you should do.
The tutorials give you the basics about control and actions you can take.
But anything worthwhile is player made and quality varies.

You have the different 'classes' you can try:
- Patron
- Craftsman
- Scholars
- Rouges
I chose craftsman and started a blacksmith making tools.
Bought wood and iron and all went quite well.
After a while I bought a woodcutter, which helped in making more money.
In the meantime I went on adventure in the political arena and made it to some low-ranking office.
Got some kids, expanded my buildings a little.
After a while you get how the game works and all goes more easily.
Instead of buying an already existing mine, which was getting more and more expensive,
I instead send my thugs to attack and conquer it. After which, my wealth exploded.
Because the mine was making much more then it was selling and wasn't controlled by one of the houses.
Expanding my little empire, I ran into the rank problem which required you to buy an higher title to build more buildings. And decided to build stuff in another town.
Meanwhile I had reached the highest political rank, with two children on the two 2nd tier positions.
Making it easy as pie to stay in position and also to quel my oponents.
And everybody was bribing me to get any position, which was a nice income as well.
But at this point, the game lost my interest. There was little challenge left and only 'chores' that remained.
The scope of the game doesn't magically increase. The city and villages around it are you playground, forever.
Which means once you got enough buildings and such, you basically won. No endless games.
You can make the AI 'run' your buildings, which is nice and all that, but mostly poorly worked out.
1) You cannot setup 'routes' like "Bring XX wood from woodcutter to blacksmith, then bring XX iron from mine to blacksmith"
2) The AI buys the resources needed, not necessarily at your resource-producer
3) You cannot set your building to sell only to -your- carts, thus you cannot set a lower price for yourself
4) The AI ignores your "only work in current city" setting from time to time
Besides that there are various annoying buys:
1) Translations in dialogues are missing or buggy. Resulting in German speech.
2) Carts standing next to a building (or in it) don't show up for interaction in the building
3) Various other glitches
All these combined result in my regretting buying the game.
It was fun for a maximum of 9 hours, but after writing this review and deleting the game.
I highly doubt I ever will touch the game again.
It has a very interesting concept, but glitchy AI and graphics end up destroying this great game. Due this, my vote is no, do not recommend. 4/10.

I have a confession to make, I absolutely love cyberpunk. My favorite anime is Ghost in the Shell, one of my favorite movies is Blade Runner and one of my favorite game series is Deus Ex. So while I’m talking about this game I will have both a bit of bias and a little more criticizing for the new one, Deus Ex Mankind Divided.
Deus Ex in its heart has always been a story driven fps with an inventory system and various augmented powers that the main character has access to all the while unlocking new ones as they progress through the game. That is where the new iteration really shines, the gameplay. Eidos Montreal might have scaled back on the map size but what they lose in size they more than make up for in details and that includes various routes that a player can take. In Deus Ex, the big draw of the game has always been the player gets to play how they want. If you want to sneak around, hack locks and walk through vents to get to your objective then you can. If you feel like you want to go guns blazing and kill all that oppose you that is your prerogative as well. That goes for the bosses as well. You can silently knock them out, lay traps to get them to kill themselves, take over bots that will kill them or take them down with your own two hands. The choices you can make is what makes the Deus Ex series one of the best.
In DE:MD, you have various weapons that allow you to get your objectives done; lethal vs non-lethal and close quarters vs long range. On top of that you have some of the base augmentations from Human Revolution and seven new ones including a nano-ceramic blade, a protective nanoshield, a time slowing system and an electric shock bolts system that is attached to your fist These add new dynamics to the options you have while playing the game.
Other than those features Deus Ex is a run of the mill FPS in that you run around completing objectives to different missions but those augmentations and the different paths is what makes the game lots of fun. Pulling up your vision Aug to look through a wall to see two guards on the other side, proceeding to cloak and then shooting one and quickly turning to knock another out with your finisher is a lot of fun. All during the games (especially the late stages) I felt like a super powered James Bond as a traversed around the different areas. The gameplay is truly where this game shines and makes you want to come back and play a 2nd time just to experience it differently even if you just put 30 hours into your first run.
Mankind Divided follows the continuing story of Adam Jensen after the events at Panchaea and the “Aug incident” in which everyone with augmentations had a switch flipped that saw millions killed and many more injured and created a huge divide in humanity. The idea now was not that Augments helped humans improve themselves but a lot saw it as a threat to humanity as a whole and thus began the “Mechanical Apartheid”. Those that were augmented were separated from society and looked down upon. Augmented couldn’t get jobs and they were seen as lesser humans and thus slum cities like Mankind Divided’s Golem City was formed where the state police could be in power over augs and so that the augmented wouldn’t be seen by other “Naturals”. Having written this review about a week and a half after the game launched I’ve been able to see a lot of others thoughts on whether “politics” (yes I put that in quotes) should be welcome into a game like Deus Ex. As long as it doesn’t feel forced and makes sense in a narrative setting why not? The idea that augs killed millions of humans would scare any government into forcing those out and separating them from the rest of society. It, unfortunately, feels like a proper result of an incident that left millions dead.
That said, you play as Adam whose main task now is a lot more focused than it was in Human Revolution. Adam is playing a double agent in which he is a part of a special task force in INTERPOL called TF29 in which he is investigating the bombing that occurred at a main train station in Prague all the while he is also an agent of the Juggernaut Collective, a group of global hacktivists that are dedicated to discovering the identities of the Illuminati, yes that is the name of the secret group, and fighting them to not let them control society. Though the focus of the story is better in Mankind Divided the amount of conspiracies from local all the way up to corporate feels excessive. Also I feel like Mankind Divided suffered from too many trailers syndrome. Everything you needed to know about the story, the main events, the main plot points, the main bad guy, was all revealed in the trailer leaving very little in the game itself. The only big plot twist didn’t happen until during the credits which allows for a bit of speculation for the next game is kind of sad that it took that long to reveal something you might not have known from watching the trailers. If you were one of the lucky few that haven’t seen anything about the game, I envy you.
Another strong point of Mankind Divided was the characters, at least the major ones. All of the major characters felt like they had a personality. If you were to ask me to describe each character I would be able to give you various character traits that were clearly established. Now that said a lot of the minor story characters all felt incredibly bland. It was surprising how much level of detail went into the major characters personalities but the minor ones just seemed like a couple notes on a piece of paper.
Although Mankind Divided was smaller map size and not as many locations as Human Revolution the amount of detail, both graphically and aesthetically, is much greater. Now that also is due in part to Eidos’s new engine, Dawn Engine. That said, every building, every location felt very different and well designed. There were little details everywhere that we haven’t seen much until the more recent powerhouse engines we are beginning to see. The graphics are also equally impressive in that this is one of the first games (VR excluded) that pushed my 780Ti to its limits for 1080p 60fps. I had to turn off MSAA and only had the graphics options on high, looks like it is time to upgrade to the 1080Ti later.
The audio is also fantastic which included a great soundtrack. Each area had its own ambient song that fit the location perfectly. An upscale more quiet classical for Prague during the day, a harder techno for the red light district Prague during the night and a sad kind of depressing song for Golem city. Eidos also did a fine job with the voice acting in which a lot of characters actually sound like they were from where they were originally born or lived.
Overall Deus Ex Mankind Divided is a fantastic game that excels in most points including graphics, sound, gameplay and performance however it falls a little flat on its face from over excessiveness in its stories and bland minor characters. Now there is one complaint about the port in that Nixxes (the pc port developer) left in mouse acceleration and the only way to disable it is to mess with windows registry keys and though I got used to it by changing some of my mouse DPI settings I know others were not able to. Also another friend was having graphics textures not loading though that seems to be a somewhat rare occurrence and Nixxes was working on a fix for that.

Halloween theme/timeline.

Neutral -
Artwork. Nice, but not a lot of variety.
Translation. A lot of negative reviews are based on this, and while there were some parts that were poorly translated, they

fit. That said, I have seen much worse translations and while it might make a reader hesitate in the flow while reading,
it's by no means unreadable, nor something to earn a negative review imho.
Short. I suppose this could be a pro or a con, depending on if you're in the camp looking for more in depth character
development, or the "reading is hard" camp.
Cons -
Music. The musicbox portion of the soundtrack got really grating after a while. Otherwise this would sit in the neutal
portion.
Overall, a nice, free VN that if you're OK overlooking a few mistakes that the grammar police would likely pull you over and issue a citation for, can give you a few hours of light reading and a couple of easy achievements. Consider the DLC if for no other reason than to support these guys and/or gals in the hopes they continue to develop quality VNs.

As someone who's played the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the Devil May Cry games, I enjoyed what was all added here in the Special Edition. The three new characters are fun to play and are pretty unique from Dante and Nero, which was nice. Lady is probably my personal favorite of the added characters, with the focus on ranged combat feeling the most fresh gameplay wise. The new game modes are also welcome, providing additional challenges for experienced players. All the characters also have a bunch of costumes to unlock, which is always fun. I was a bit disappointed that the new characters didn't get their own music or separate set of levels, but I can't complain too much in light of everything they did add.
On the technical side of things, the game is pretty well optimized. It runs at a solid 60fps fairly reliably, it never seemed to drop below that even with a ton of enemies on screen at once. Granted, it has been quite a while since I played the original version, so I may have just simply forgotten what it used to look like.

With the added features you get a pretty good amount of content for the price (five characters, seven difficulty modes, and bloody palace) compared to most similar games. If you're a newcomer to the series it's not a bad place to start either, since none of the games are strongly tied to each other. Highly recommended.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is a four player hack-and-slash set in the world of Remnant, and was made in part to be a new way for fans of the RWBY series to jump in and have fun themselves. It was originally developed independently by Jordan Scott, then later picked up by Rooster Teeth and became the first title officially developed by Rooster Teeth Games. An early access version was made available in December of 2015, and recently was fully released on July 5th, 2016. .
In Grimm Eclipse, you take on the role of one of the four members of Team RWBY (pronounced “ruby”) and set out to find what is disrupting Beacon Academy’s security system. You fight against swarms of Grimm (the catch-all phrase for monsters in the RWBY Universe), but look for answers: who is behind all of this? How are they doing it? And why won’t Yang stop telling awful jokes?  Can a game based on an animated series live up to the hype?
The Good
This game has gotten a lot of polish since the last time I talked about it. The lag issues are totally gone, which is a major plus. The graphics are much better than they were, and the art style really captures the show’s unique feel. Combat has also been revamped with the addition of heavy attacks, counters, and finishing moves, giving it a lot more depth.  The fighting is quick and clean and flows smoothly throughout the game. It’s a simple system, but sometimes simple is best.
The four characters (Ruby, Weiss, Blake, and Yang) each have a distinct fighting style, allowing you to pick the one that suits you best. Grimm Eclipse also has a level up system that allows for a small degree of customisation. You’ll quickly realize that the level cap of ten doesn’t give you nearly enough points to purchase every skill in the game, so it’s up to you whether you want to focus on survival, brawling, long-range attacks, or what have you.  It adds a small RPG, stat element to the immediate rush of combat that Grimm Eclipse is built on, and it doesn't detract from that fighting.
Speaking of characters, the voice acting is all done by the actual voice actors. Aside from your team members shouting their one-liners throughout the game, you get running commentary and advice from Professors Port, Oobleck, and Ozpin. There is no game that can’t be improved by Dr. Oobleck’s coffee-fueled ranting.  In all seriousness, it's nice to see that this game doesn't feel like a throwaway attempt to make money off the series, but instead adds lore and character to what's happening.
In welcome news, they’ve also ironed out the matchmaking for finding co-op allies online. You can now choose your preferred difficulty and which level you’d like to play, and the game will find people to play with you.
The Bad:
I have to admit that I was disappointed by a few things about the final release.  For one thing, Grimm Eclipse is very short; the campaign only takes about 2-3 hours to finish, and the story leaves a bit to be desired. Remnant is a rich world with a long and colorful history, and all of that just becomes simple scenery for your battles against the Grimm. We do end up getting a bit of background lore, and tidbits of interesting detail are sprinkled throughout, but nothing earth-shaking comes out of the plot.  I was hoping for something with a bit more gravitas, or some new angle to help me enjoy the world a little bit more.   Instead, it feels shallow in comparison to what could have been.
The Final Word

Transmissions: Element 120 is a Source engine developed indie game set in the Half-Life universe.  It consists of four well-made if somewhat short chapters that provide a few encounters with your favourite crab-zombies and combine soldiers.  The overall feel and setting is designed to be a mixture of horror and puzzle solving, with a little hint of combat at key moments.
+ More Half-Life style play.
+ Great care and attention to create an immersive environment and detailed locations, take this small team's effort a step up.
+ The custom made soundtrack elevates the tension and key encounters to another level.
+ Loved the clever use of luminescent paint in certain areas.
+ Its short and can be played in two to three hours.
+ Achievements are simple to obtain but can be missed if not careful.
+ Its free.
- Not much really.  If anything there could have been a little more spoken narrative / dialogue included to help build up a better picture of the scenario.
- Some of the AI routines stop working for combine soldiers and they just stand there doing nothing.  Happened a few times.
- Progressing through some of the physics-based doorways/exits can be confusing.  So if thats not your thing make sure you are happy to consult a guide.
* The engine may be dated but the developers have maxxed out as much as possible with the tools they have to make this more than just a mod.
* There isnt much combat with it being staged in key set-pieces towards the end of chapters.
Short, well-made but enjoyable nonetheless.  If you are waiting for Half-life (Episode) 3 you could do worse than check this out!  Its one of the best free-to-play efforts that you are bound to find on steam.  Fans of Half-life should enjoy this no question.  Otherwise if you are after easy/quick achievements or just like to pass the time with free games then you would be a fool not to try this.  If however you are after a pure or heavy-focused shooter then this is not for you.

I liked this game its fast paced and easy on the eyes, there were some challenges along the way, but with the power of friendship and team work we managed to beat it.Its Hitch's most briskly entertaining movie, and one of his most comic, adventure-caper type movies, largely thanks to the persona of Cary Grant. But its also one of his most suspenseful - in the fact that Grant is being recognised as someone else, and that he may be put in jail for someone else's crime.
I've finally come to realise just how great This game is. The reason you should love Hitchcock is he put entertainment upfront. Hitchcock was not interested in whether this or that would happen in real life: he was interested in what would make the most entertaining scene for the movie. Trine 2 is a peak in this regard. The dialogue and situations intentionally throw reality to the wind - the double-entendre dialogue in the love scenes is not supposed to be the way people talk!
If you said to Hitchcock "as if he'd keep driving" or "as if she'd do that"
he would just laugh at you and say you've missed the point. This is 100%
movieland, and once you get used to the fact, and that this is not a fault in the film, but done intentionally, you'll love it. Its expressionistic - everything happens in movie language: the people laughing at Grant in the elevator, the way he keeps driving drunk near the beginning, the way he grabs the knife and everyone stares at him after someone's been stabbed.
It flirts with the idea of identity. I thought it was interesting how Grant first is dismissing, then incredulous that people should be calling him by another name; then, as the tries to find out who this guy is, he enters the hotel room of this new identity, then he puts the suit on, and finally he identifies himself as George Kaplan.
A succession of fantastic, memorable scenes, a great leading man in Grant, and one of Hermann's essential Hitch scores make for a movie i can put on at any time.

I have played this game for quite a while and I have enjoyed it a lot. I will start with a simple list:
+Good graphics
+Very fun gameplay, it take quite a bit of micro-managment
+Very satisfying, there is something that feels so good about killing thousands of aliens.
+Has a good difficulty, not to easy, not to hard
-No multiplayer (Yet this game feels perfect for it)
-It is rather repetitive
-The game lacks replay value
-The campaign is rather short
So for the graphics, what can I say? They are alright. AAA titles will put it to shame, but graphics mean little in a game unless they are downright horrible or put strain on performence. Because the aliens tend to attack on multiple fronts and resources are limited, you have to choose what the spend it on carefully and arranges your troops well. Will you send your entire squad to take down a group of hives and risk losing a point? Or will you split you team up and chance it? Wil you split you team up and back up your assault with heli strikes? There are plenty of options. The difficulty isn't to bad, though not to easy either. (Unless you spam seige cannons) Occasionally there will be that ONE factor that screws you such as losing a support building or a tower spawner messing up your base. The mutations also add a whole layer of depth into the game. There are 33 different mutations that buff the enemy when you take a hive. Basically, the closer you get to winning, the harder it becomes.
Now on the bad side, the game doesn't have multiplayer. This game feels perfect for it though. You can have a marine commander pitted against an alien commander and they try to beat each other. The alien commander could draw paths for the alien swarm to follow and unlock new mutations, hives, and build turrets. This could even go a step further and allow a few other players to play as hero units General Magusson, The doctor, or drake where they move around, shoot weapons with crosshairs, and throw grenades at the cost of ammo. That would cater to the more action players while the RTS players play as the commander above them.
The gameplay gets rather repetitve during long play sessions. This is because most missions are pretty much "Capture the points" or "Kill all the hives" The campaign puts some variation into the missions, such as convoy, supply recovery, etc. Overall the game needs a few more modes. After the campaign is over, the game lacks replay value, there just isn't some kinds of in-game acheivment system or secret unlocks. It just makes you lose intrest. You can still make highly customizable skirmish modes and do daily challenges though, so that is addition content if you feel the desire to play them. It took me about 10 hours to beat the campaign, and that manages to defeat most AAA games. I just feel that the game could use more story content and a better story. (The story is basically "Kill all the aliens")
To summerize, the game has weak replay value, no multiplayer, and a weak story. The gameplay is solid the graphics have their charms and the feeling of killing thousands of aliens as well as the metagame make this very fun to play.

This is a great game while it lasts, if this game has a good multiplayer added I would bump the rating up the 15$/60$. ...to be able to run this game. I consider the original DMC4 on PC one of the very, very best ports ever made. But this port? Comparison is at the end.
Capcom updated the engine for this title, so now there's Motion Blur, Depth of Field and "God Rays" light effects. So, um, good news? Not really, and that's the funny thing: It looks worse now.
Motion Blur in itself is completely sick, because its actual purpose is to conceal the low framerate in movies (which run at 24 FPS). So you essentially spend graphics power to simulate a lower framerate (at least that's my explanation). And Depth of Field looks just... weird here, the same with God Rays. The game was just not made with them in mind. And not only does Motion Blur and Depth of Field look bad here, they also need a lot of graphics power.
So, why am I going so much into detail with these effects? If you don't like them, just turn them off, right? Well, jokes on you: You simply can't. You have to edit the Executable of the game with a hex editor to disable Motion Blur and Depth of Field. Good news is that it's very easy to do and there's even
.
My Specifications:
Intel Core i5-2500K @ 3.30 GHz
(from 2010)
Now, about the performance... I can play the original with max settings at 1920x1080, probably 4xAA, with solid 60 FPS ingame and in cutscenes. This port? I can play with (almost solid) 60 FPS ingame and 25-45 FPS in cutscenes at 1280x720 with 4xAA, and that's only after I disable Motion Blur, Depth of Field and God Rays. This is worse than the Xbox 360 version of the Original, which runs with almost the exact same settings (only difference is that it has 2xAA) with constant 60 FPS.
The reason I still recommend it: It's still a fantastic game and Capcom shows that the old DMC isn't dead. It's just a shame that the port is somewhat shoddy. But if you have the graphics power, don't worry.

DMC4 is my favorite stylish action game. Now you get 3 new characters. That's CRAZY. And they are super well-designed. It's a Special Edition re-release that has more new mechanics than most sequels.
Maybe you thought Nero played pretty differently from Dante. Vergil, Lady, and Trish are on a whole other lever. Hell, I think they feel more distinct than 2013's DmC does, and that game was supposed to be a reboot. And we're in a time when most new action games are Batman clones. These characters are a reminder that, yeah, there's a lot of uncharted territory in action game mechanics.
Vergil is a character about moving slowly and striking efficiently. He has a "concentration" gauge that fills up by standing still and walking, and drains when he misses attacks or runs. So you get to pace around enemies like a badass as you summon phantom swords that do the work for you, before teleporting to enemies and slashing them up. You get this cool back-and-forth between slow pace and fast pace. And instead of attacking / dodging / running like you normally would, you rely on your teleports to dodge and don't miss a beat with your attacks. It matches his style from DMC3 cutscenes.
Lady only has guns, and melee is a very minor part of her playstyle. She's all about distancing herself from enemies and raining down rockets and bullets. After buying yourself time, you can choose from a variety of ranged combos. The most damage she can deal out is by charging up her rocket launcher, which deals pretty ridiculous damage when fully charged. Like Vergil, Lady introduces some slower-paced decision making with her mechanics. She's the most unique character of the 5 IMO.
Trish is a less wild departure from traditional Devil May Cry. She can throw out her sword to spin and trap enemies in an AOE, and her moveset changes when she does this. She also has the ability to leave lightning streaks in the air after one of her arial attacks, which also trap enemies. You can use these tricks to maximize damage on one enemy, or keep enemies occupied while you work on different threats. You can also get really creative with how you knock enemies into your AOEs.
I have gripes, and they are the same gripes with the original DMC4. It still sucks that you backtrack for the 2nd half of the campaign. The story is still not as interesting as DMC3's. The lock on system will still occasionally not select the right enemy, and some of the fixed camera angles are awful. The last points I wish they would have fixed in the Special Edition.
Also, the 3 new characters get the same campaign minus cutscenes. It's... fine. But given how good the characters are, it's a shame they don't get something unique to play (or at least variations on the campaign). But hey, it's not a sequel.
At the end of the day, the characters are the important part, and they totally deliver.

Now, I love the series of RWBY, and this game is by no means bad. However, since the game is supposed to be fully released at the time of this review, there are some rather glaring problems that shouldn't be ignored. First and foremost is that the "single player" is a joke. All it is, is a mode where people can't join you. Enemy difficulty and number are hardly affected. Normally, this wouldn't bother me much, but there are some enemy types that use strong attacks far too frequently. You can counter, sure, but if you're in the middle of a horde, you can only counter one. And due to the frequency of strong attacks, you die near instantly. The other glaring problem is that, to the best of my knowledge, there's no way to focus on an enemy. You have to deal with an Auto-targeting system that will target the least threatening opponent. The game is still fun, don't get me wrong. I personally love carving through Grimm with Ruby and her delightful comments, it's just the few problems I notice tend to break my immersion.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons, an indie puzzler with significant emphasis on storytelling, is probably one of the most surprising purchases I have ever made. The story is intriguing, the world is wonderful, and even though there is not one bit of comprehensible dialogue for an English speaker such as myself I could not help getting swept up through the use of unique storytelling cutscenes and the use of the environment. This is a game that makes the player confront the issue of death not just through the story but also through its mechanics. It is styled like a brief epic, drawing on what I can only understand as Nordic mythology and folklore to create a fantastical environment of characters and landscapes that I honestly have to admit are both breathtaking and impressive for a game. They know it's good, so they made sure you could enjoy it by placing little benches throughout the levels if you ever wanted to just stare at it. The game is also relatively short and can be completed within a few hours like I just did, but unfortunately I failed to even attempt to find the many gaffes and secrets hidden throughout the levels, so that may add some additional time on. My one major issue is going to have to be the control scheme and to a much lesser extent I found the lack of video options slightly irritating. The control scheme is particularly awkward when you are winching lifts, which - thank god - only happens twice in the whole game, but then again I did not use a controller for this game and they highly recommend it. For anyone who appreciates a good, heartfelt story of family, brotherhood, death, and perhaps even becoming an adult, then this is for you.
TLDR Version
+++Magnificent, fantastical story
++Beautiful landscapes
+Strong theming
-Lacking video settings (only gamma is adjustable, no resolution for window preferred users)
--A control scheme that screws with your head, especially without a controller
---A control scheme for stubborn keyboard users that makes elevators your worse nightmare
++++A control scheme used in such a way that by the end of the game you will try not to cry and cry anyway
11/10 would send children on a dangerous quest again in airbrushed mountains

Survive that, and you find a beautifully done game, although, like I said, a little depressing.

Some time ago, I reviewed Fabio Ferrera's
, where my closing comment was essentially along the lines of "You can take it or leave it, but for me, I'll LEAF it" and not much has changed, though I believe I would prefer the linear prequel over this open-world experience.
Unlike it's predecessor,
is a non-linear open-world game that basically drops you in game without telling you where to go.  Instead, everything is simple implied save for one area, which is the area to the left.  It suggests that you follow the gravel path to lead you to the fairy tears (giant water drops) to restore the area tree guardians.  The sad part here is that often times, you'll find fairy tears off the path so long as there's activity in an area off-path (berries, enemies, steps, air gusts), though most of the time, you'll only be treated to dead-ends by these red herrings.
As you play, you'll deal with awful camera angles, poor platforming (where you'll sometimes fall through platforms), and getting lost in the big open world when you stray too far from the gravel paths.   You may also be overwhelmed from dealing with one massive world along with the load times as it starts to boot up some assets for other areas.  Each load time ranges from 30 seconds to a full minute of your time...sometimes you'll even be lucky enough for the game to crash during these load times.  (Fun!)
Clearly more work went into this game as detailed by all the structures and models used, but most of your experience will be filled with big empty spaces where you'll be running for a while before you reach your destination (I miss the house hub teleportation system of the predecessor).  In some areas, you'll see doors that you can just walk or jump around to bypass the switch.  In other areas, you may end up seeing floating bushes or underneath floors of distant platforms.  That said, this game is clearly an incomplete project with plenty of bugs still there.
The achievements here are pretty easy to get, but there's one that's particularly grindy (collect 10k berries, easiest in the snowy peaks).  Worse is the achievement for playing local coop, where the developer says you must have TWO controllers (no, keyboard does not count here) for local coop.
Overall, I cannot recommend this Woodle game either.  Though I can appreciate the effort that went into it, but it's still quite a mess in need of further work.  As other reviewers have said,
is a project that feels like it had decent potential, but as a "finished" product, it feels quite rushed.  The asking price for this particular game is $4, but as a final product (as it currently stands), I can only see myself recommending this game for $1 or less.  I was honestly bored and disappointed with this game and you might end up feeling the same.
2/10  Second score.  Same as the first!  (+credit for effort on the open world.  -credit for a boring, non-linear mess.)

The next installment in the Deus Ex franchise is here, but does it live up to the hype? Yes and No. Before I start this review I would like to say that this does DOES indeed have microtransactions but you are not informed about them or forced onto them at any point (I only learned about them via the community hub), that being said I do not condone the use of microtransactions in general and would suggest avoiding them completely if you do decide to purchase the game.
The microtransactions only give in-game credits and praxis points (in-game skill points), they are one time use (who tought of this stupid idea), but simply playing the game netted me dozens of praxis and tens of thousands of credits, I never felt as if I was earning too little so nothing justifies the use of microtransactions.
The story is good in some parts and dissapointing in others. If you expect a story much better than the one in Human Revolution then this game will probably dissapoint you in that regard, I know it dissapointed me.
The story revolves around Adam Jensen, an augmented former cop who's trying to find the real culprits behind some terrorist attacks. Some of the characters are preety well written while others only get a few lines and only feel akward.
Without spoiling anything, what ruined the story for me was by far the abrupt and cliffhanger ending. You play the game with this constant feel of build-up, you feel like you're gonna get answers or a big revelation in the end and just when you tought the story is about to pick up, it ends. Your choices don't matter, going lethal or non-lethal doesn't matter, it just...ends. Sequel bait at its finest.
The soundtrack is preety good altho not as good as the Human Revolution one, there's some amazing tracks that stand out as well as some repetitive ones that keep playing over and over, overall it does give you the feel and atmosphere of a futuristic open world.
Here's a sample of the soundtrack:
The ambient sounds, even tho not the best, are used preety well to create the feel of a big open world and for the most part work preety well even tho there is certainly room for improvement.
The gameplay has certainly improved since Human Revolution, Adam can now move fluidly through the world, climb on buildings and objects, the cover system feels a bit wonky but overall it feels like an improvement over HR.
The biggest annoyance I had was the transition from gameplay to a short scripted cutscene whenever I would use a takedown, it felt out of place and awkward. There's a large variety of both lethal and non lethal weapons to choose from as well as dozens of Augmentations, alot of them new which diversify the ways to play.
Each mission has multiple ways of approach and almost all missions have multiple ways to end depending on your dialogue choices and how much you investigate. In that way, I found the side quests were better written and organized than the main story.
This one is tricky. Some people will tell you it runs horribly on a GTX 1080. Some will tell you it runs well on preety old machines. I was one of the lucky ones I guess. On my FX 8350, GTX 760 and 8GB RAM I hovered around 45-50 fps on High settings with AA, Vsync and Contact Hardening Shadows off. It was very playable and it never felt like it was stuttering.
Something around the lines of the recommended system requirements will give you 60 fps or more on the High preset at 1080p. The very high and ultra presets are almost impossible to run well with the current hardware.
I did experience one crash towards the end of the main story, thankfully the developers didn't take the EA way (ignore the fanbase) and instead aknowledged the crash on twitter, announced they were working on a fix, said the ETA was early next week and actually delivered. I had to wait 2 days to continue playing, but at least they had the courage to treat this like a real issue and not just blame the customers with stuff like "install latest driver/get a better pc".
The graphics are incredible and a huge step up from HR, the detail in the city of Prague and everywhere else is just amazing, as a person who worked in the video game industry I was really impressed by the detail that was put in the world and the locations, the small details make it come to life. Character animations and faces are just as bad as HR tho with some awkward dialogues.
It took me roughly 32 hours to finish the game, having completed every single side quest in the game and the main story. I went lethal in my first playthrough, some scenes could be entirely skipped if you went non-lethal. I would say the main story is around 15-20 hrs depending on your style of play, the rest being side quests and exploring.
There is only one hub in the game, Prague, which altho very detailed is not that large in size and can only offer you a limited amount of exploration.
If I were to replay the game going non-lethal, doing all the remaining achievments, I would probably be looking at around 60 to 70 hours played. But why would I do that, since my choices don't really matter in the game.
A game that is good but not great, Deus Ex Mankind Divided dissapoints in story and writing but makes up for it with improved gameplay and a very detailed city. Mankind Divided is a lot like a big brother to Human Revolution; they really do appear similar, but one's got more experience than the other. And they're definitely different people. What I mean by that is, you can tell Eidos Montreal knows how to make a Deus Ex game by now. While the formula of Human Revolution is most definitely present here, you'll find that it isn't the same game.
Oh, and I've already played the game twice. In less than a week. I know, it's kinda sad but that should attest to the quality of the game.
: Eidos knows when to not mess with a good thing. The gameplay feels very similar to that of it's predecessor, excepting one major thing; you can actually enjoy combat now. The guns aren't hugely varied but exploration will yield special versions of guns and experimentation will tell you which ones you like best. They all feel great and they work very well, making for a fun experience. With the ability to change weapon mads and ammo on the fly, you'll find combat is truly fun. That being said, don't buy this game if you want a shooter, because the combat is easy as long as you're careful the engagements are usually short.
The stealth is a lot like Human Revolution. It's fun, tricky, and there's a million and one ways to stealth through any and all environments. Every single area is designed with your potential upgrades in mind, so each new upgrade can yield a new path. The A.I. has been rebalanced since HR to mke them a little smarter, adding some nice challenge to it. If you're looking for a stealth game, this is worth considering. (Oh, and if you're gonna do stealth - Remote Hacking. You'll need it.)
The character system is fantastic. There are seven new augs, and each one of them useful for their respective styles. The focus enhancement (slows down time) for example, works really only in combat. The TESLA (can tase up to four people at a time if upgraded) is best paired with stealth, though it can be used in combat. Nearly all of the augs have a purpose, depending on your playthrough. If you explore and play stealthily, you should have over half of the augs by the end of the game. It's definitely not a grind to level up.
There's a crafting system. It's the simplest one I've ever seen and is VERY useful. You can basically craft ammo and consumables. Not really much to talk about there, but I like it a lot.
So, to sum up gameplay - play the way you want to. The game allows for and respects any gameplay choices you do make, so have fun!
: It's top notch. Stuff is so well hidden I once took a path to a room and then couldn't find out where the path was when I was leaving. Exploratiuon is useful and heavily rewarded. There's emails to read, pocket secretaries to find... You'll find any number of things while exploring, but there's a lot of well hidden stuff you really have to look for. The level design is clever and lends to stealth or gunplay without compromising on realistic cyberpunk atmosphere.
: They're not the best I've ever seen, but they're still pretty good and they help make the atmosphere.
: Voice acting is generally great, and thank god they got a guy to replace David Sarif. I mean seriously thank god. Guns and augs all sound good, really fitting. To be honest I didn't really notice the soundtrack but I did like what I actually heard.
: Fantastic... except for one thing. There is supposed to be real hate for augs, and yet Jensen experiences none of it. I pretty much only used the "Naturals" lines and train cars and was never once penalized for it. Shop owners never refuse to deal with you, and no characters refuse interactions. It really damages the atmosphere but all the rest was great.
: Overall, good. Except for the fact that I never felt like any of my choices really mattered. I'd go into more detail, but I don't want to even hint at spoilers. True, one or two choices did make a difference but none of them very big. Again, I'd love to explain, but I'm not going to. Forbes tippeed me off to an event in the game that kinda ruined the surprise, and I'm not going to do that.
Also, the story ends at least one or two missions too soon. The end (at least if you're nonlethal and or stealthy) feels very anticlimactic and truly disappointing. I want to say I hope there's a DLC for it, but that's ridiculous. Shouldn't need a DLC to get an ending to the story that's actually satisfying. And yes, there is a credits scene.
Oh and also, while the side missions don't really change the plot they are very interesting. Definitely worth checking out and the XP rewards are really great. I felt like I spent a lot of time finding and doing them, but I'm positive I didn't do them all. They definitely add to the games charm and replayability.
So, to sum it all up - This game is amazing. If you liked Human Revolution, wait for a sale. If you loved Human Revolution's gameplay, you have to buy this. If you loved it's story, wait for a sale and don't compare the two -- unless you like feeling dissapointed.

Ok, so if anyone is really mad at WB for abandoning this game I can't blame them. It's a pretty rotten thing to do.
However...
I bought this game after the drop of support had already been announced, so I knew what I was getting into on that front. And once I got past that, I've been more than amazed by the game. I've been an MK fan since I was a teenager playing the original arcade cabinets, and this is easily up there with MK2 and MK9 as the best games in the franchise. Graphics and sound are excellent, the level of detail is ridiculous (just watch some of the stories play out in the backgrounds and you'll see what I mean), and the combat system is easy to pick up yet deep. It's a rare fighting game that both amateurs and hardcore players can excel at, and I much prefer the a la carte combat system in this game to one where I have to push eight buttons in a row or nothing happens.
Also - the living towers in this are genius. Just genius. Sometimes, if I have a few minutes but not enough to play a ton, I'll log on and see what the hourly tower is, play it, then go about my day.
I've logged almost 20 hours and I've only finished half the story and played with half the characters (only a few with all three forms). I've only truly mastered Kitana, and there are even a bunch of her moves/kombos that I haven't fully explored yet. I'm so excited to keep trying new things, and it's going to take me a long, wonderful time to get to it all. The amount of content is staggering.
So bottom line - if the abandonware issue is a deal-breaker, the don't get it and I won't blame you. But if you can live with it, this is truly one of the best fighting games I've played in forever, and it is worthy of the MK name.

Transmissions: Element 120 is a Source engine developed indie game set in the Half-Life universe.  It consists of four well-made if somewhat short chapters that provide a few encounters with your favourite crab-zombies and combine soldiers.  The overall feel and setting is designed to be a mixture of horror and puzzle solving, with a little hint of combat at key moments.
+ More Half-Life style play.
+ Great care and attention to create an immersive environment and detailed locations, take this small team's effort a step up.
+ The custom made soundtrack elevates the tension and key encounters to another level.
+ Loved the clever use of luminescent paint in certain areas.
+ Its short and can be played in two to three hours.
+ Achievements are simple to obtain but can be missed if not careful.
+ Its free.
- Not much really.  If anything there could have been a little more spoken narrative / dialogue included to help build up a better picture of the scenario.
- Some of the AI routines stop working for combine soldiers and they just stand there doing nothing.  Happened a few times.
- Progressing through some of the physics-based doorways/exits can be confusing.  So if thats not your thing make sure you are happy to consult a guide.
* The engine may be dated but the developers have maxxed out as much as possible with the tools they have to make this more than just a mod.
* There isnt much combat with it being staged in key set-pieces towards the end of chapters.
Short, well-made but enjoyable nonetheless.  If you are waiting for Half-life (Episode) 3 you could do worse than check this out!  Its one of the best free-to-play efforts that you are bound to find on steam.  Fans of Half-life should enjoy this no question.  Otherwise if you are after easy/quick achievements or just like to pass the time with free games then you would be a fool not to try this.  If however you are after a pure or heavy-focused shooter then this is not for you.

First, make sure to use PureFaction in order to get the game to work on modern systems and to get widescreen resolutions, see the Steam Guide on how to set it up. Red Faction is an OK game - it has a unique Geo-Mod technology where the player can blow up walls and the environment, however it is severely under-utilized by giving minimal explosives and weapons to blow things up. Furthermore, there are a lot of walls and other environments where you simply cannot blow up. When you take away the Geo-Mod features you are left with a plain and ordinary shooter that does not really excel in any category. The AI is odd, sometimes enemies will just stand in one spot or on the other hand they will run around and shoot chaotically. There are also some gimcky weapons that often take the player out in 1 shot which leads to frustrating areas near the end of the game, also the boss fights seem to be really overpowered in favor of the boss. The areas are all the same dull brown Martian color and the interiors are all the same dull and washed out colors and area after area (level after level) feels the same which gets really boring fast and the game sometimes is vague on what is the next objective leaving the player sometimes wondering what they need to do next. Lastly, the game tries to mix the pace up by throwing in some stealth missions where you go undercover and are stripped of all your weapons - these levels do not really add anything but slow the game down for no necessary reason. The campaign story is okay, nothing too captivating and thankfully is not too long (~5-6 hours). Overall, I had fun in the beginning where you really got to utilize the Geo-Mod technology but after the first couple of levels the game became bland as an ordinary shooter and not fun any longer dealing with inaccurate weapons and seeing the same scenery over and over. Compared to Half-Life which came out around the same time, it feels that this game was lacking in every department and became underwhelming.

This is a mechanically great shooter that is completely ruined by a pay to win model. Here's how your experience will go:
You start with a junky semi auto weapon (with a rounds per minute cap so even if you have a fast trigger finger you wont be able to shoot more than a couple shots per second) with no sights, no sidearm, no vehicles, no grenades, no mele weapon, noequipment at all. It's just you and your semi auto rifle for hours and hours and hours of grinding. It's really enjoyable in the beginning when you're only matched with other noobs with similar setups but eventually you get thrown into the regular lobbies and will get utterly anniahaliated by people who have unlocked the good ammo, good weapons, optics, grenades, etc.
At that point your options are to either continue to get stomped on for another 2 dozen hours until you can start getting decent unlocks or buy gold to unlock more weapons and xp buffs.
You decide to grind and now you've put in 25 hours of play and you finally have enough currency to unlock a new weapon. Now you get to choose between upgrades for your current junky gun to make it medicore, unlock the worst smg, or unlock the worst sniper. That's right you don't get to save up and buy the weapon you want - you have to go in order or worst in class to best.
So you decide you want to snipe and spend your weeks worth of grinding to buy a recon class. Turns out the basic sniper is not great at all. Unless you get headshots it's hitmarker city. the scope is not great and the handling is difficult. Now your options are to either grind for another 2 dozen hours to buy upgrades, grind for 50 hours to unlock the next sniper in the class, or spend $ to unlock the next tier.
You finally grind up and unlock a scope and more powerful rounds and a decent barrel. Now you can finally land some one shot kills and be effective. then you learn that the good unlockable gear deteriorates and runs out. So now you have to either slow your grind way down to maintain your premium weapon equipment or play with your junky sniper and speed up the grind to unlock the next tier, or pay $ to repair the premium equipment and buy more good bullets.
Fastforward and you have grinded for 100s of hours and your sniper is maxed. Want to play as in infantryman? Want to play as a sub machine gunner? Want to be a pilot? Want to be a tank specialist? Well guess what. Start the grind over for each and every one of those.
In summation your options are either grind for 100s upon 100s of hours or pay tons and tons of $. If you don't pay the majority if your time will be spent leveling up a gun that you don't really like or aren't that good with. There are better FPS out there. Don't waste time on this one.

I've written quite a lot about the game in their forums here on steam and have also streamed new updates and made a video review so I have a ton to say about this game, but ultimately it's simply unfinished. Its flimsy fighting mechanics are extremely susceptible to dominant strategy and don't lend themselves well to it's awkward direction. It's greatest sin, however, is that each of the characters are basically all exactly the same.  They've made some progress with the animations differing between characters, but if you were to blindfold me and ask me which character I was playing I wouldn't be able to tell you based on how the game changes (or doesn't) between characters, because the dominant strategy is rooted in the basic mechanics of the combat system.
I really want this game to be great, and I feel like it's so close!  However it still needs a lot of work!

The thing I dont like, is how the story is told. The story is quiet basic yet somehow a bit cloddish. Since the character do not speak a real language, you can only imagine what they are "talking" about.
To be fair, through the gesture of the characters it's not hard to understand what's going on, but there is a lack of depth in the narration.
Like " Oh no your father is about to die. Go there to find the only thing that can revive him " - "OK" -
The other thing I dont like, is the overall lenght of the game. About 3hours... it's short.
Well all in all, if you really like atmospheric adventures and dont want to spend too much time, give "Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons" a try.

First review, I just usually cast my vote instead of doing a review.
If you enjoyed Deus Ex Human Revolution then you will enjoy this game (to a certain degree), but don't expect it to completely live up to the amazing Story depth of Human Revolution.
The Story of the Main Game is great leading up to last mission, but then the story just falls off. I'm sure others can agree with me that the way the game ended is pretty sudden and lackluster. And you fight

I enjoyed doing the side mission in the game, not really going to delve into it too much but it was fun doing them. Especially doing The Harvester Mission.
Due to the never ending of DLCs that we've somewhat had gotten accustomed to, the devevlopers now believe they can get away on completing the Story through DLC, so they can earn more money. Sadly, they will get away with it. I can see adding DLC to do additional story content, but piecing the story together to finish it through DLC is just unacceptable in my eyes.
Well, off to the gameplay. Gameplay is great. I thoroughly enjoyed my Pacist playthrough, and snagging that Foxiest of the Hounds achievement felt great as well. Hacking was the same as in HR and just as rewarding for doing so. Exploring can be of some benefit. Persuading NPCs in the story was fun. Being invisible, seeing through walls, remote hacking, and much more... the new augmentations are fun as hell. I do recommend doing a New Game+ playthrough because you save your Praxis Kits from your previous playthrough, of course Koller would Reset you again and you obtained all of your Praxis' Kits, then after just experiment with different augs.
My only issue in Mankind Divided was that going in a Lethal route wasn't as fun. Going Guns Blazing type route wasn't fun (well for me)... but it was great sneaking around and popping people with suppressors.
Graphics are amazing for this game. I still truly believe this game isn't that demanding at all... You only load one big area at a time. The only place I can think of having some FPS drops is Golem City, everywhere else I don't think. It's all just bad porting. But hey guys just remove MSAA... yeah, it'll fix all of the fps issues.
There is some Replay Value, if you want to get all the achievements you missed on your first playthrough. Don't care for achievements? Then one playthrough would be enough. I did all of the campaign achievements and obtained "I Never Asked For This", in which you cannot die in the playthrough, if you do then your game save is deleted and have to start all over.
Overall the game is great and I'll give it a strong 7.5/10. Would be higher if the story didn't just abruptly ended like that and probably go more in-depth about the Illuminati in the main game instead of discovering more about them through DLC.

Gameplay wise this was an absolute blast and you always feel really clever when you've found ways around otherwise difficult objectives. Storywise? Absolute travesty. "Lacking depth" has been the generous term thrown around but it's so much more than that. If you're going to buy this game, please have 0 expectations for anything above a 5/10 story.

Aaah, Mortal Kombat X.
What catches my eye the most in this game isn't the just the interestingly hyperbolic X-ray/fatality/brutality animations, but in fact are the interactive stage backgrounds, and the "crypt" reward system.
Even if you have not played any other Mortal Kombat, chances are you probably have an idea of what this is about, a fighting game with an unholy amount of attack combinations for each character, each, with its own well-done animation.
While probably other reviewers more interested in the upgrade of certain game mechanics, let me talk you into these new stages and crypt...
Stages:
Before, the stage was just a picture making a location in which the avatars were playing, well, now it is not just a context filler, but an actual part of the battle. Now you feel that you are battling somewhere in a more tangible way. You can interact with certain parts of the scenario to perform "ambient" attacks or jumps, which add a VERY nice touch as to how the integration of the context slips inside of your battles. Plus various animations make it more "cinematic"-like, certainly, from my perspective this changes a lot the emotion.
Crypt:
Now this is highly entertaining for me. I'm one of those people who in games like Fallout or Dark Souls needs to look under every rock and see what I can find (which as you can imagine has got me killed countless times in those two), instead of a plainly boring "upgrade" menu, the crypt introduces an interactive way to adquire your unlocks, as it places you inside a much bigger area than you'd actually expect, with hidden secrets for you to find, puzzles, spontaneous attacks, all for the loot. I have enjoyed exploring this area far more than the battles themselves to be honest. Great work in this.
Should you buy this game if you have not played all the other ones? Well, I'll be honest, I am not exactly the biggest fan around, you could consider me a casual player along the series, hell I didn't even know very well the story until I started playing this one and found out more about it. But have I fully enjoyed this game nevertheless? Yes. Graphically and gaming mechanics-wise, I found it greatly appealing. So don't be afraid to get it! Give it a try!

I'm actually not quite sure why I enjoy this game so much. It's like the Starcraft missions where you lead a few marines into swarms of melee-only zerglings, and the marines mow them down right & left while trying not to get overwhelmed.
Likes:
-- No diddling with resource harvesting: There are some resource & ammo crates, but otherwise resources come from capturing the enemy bases.
-- Death is temporary: If a marine dies, they get resurrected after a delay.
-- 100% refund on recycled buildings: Recycling one turret and adding a new one closer to the front has a net cost of zero.
-- Small numbers on resources: 12 resources means one fixed turret and a soldier upgraded to shotgun. Once you get a few more resources, do you recycle that shotgun to build another fixed turret?
This combination means you're constantly considering what the current situation needs and where to apply your limited resources. Which is nice.
Dislikes:
Really my main dislike is that unit subtleties aren't clear: it badly needs a unit encyclopedia. Is a normal marine effective against one of those bigger beetles with spiky armor? No--this is a useful fact to know, but the game doesn't make this obvious. There's a science/exploration theme to the campaign, so an in-game encyclopedia would fit.
The tougher missions would be more palatable if I could regroup and figure out where I went wrong...but without knowing unit strengths & weaknesses it's tougher to figure out.
Overall: worthwhile, totally worth the sale buy.

Disclaimer: I feel the need to mention that I worked at Volition 5 years after Red Faction came out.  I worked on Red Faction Guerrilla and Armageddon both.   I no longer work at Volition and my employment there has only minimal effect on the review (I learned how hard it was to deliver Red Faction to the fans.)  However I feel that I'm able to write this review with out a bias.
Red Faction is a very unique game.  Playing it 15 years after it came out, and the strongest feeling from playing the game is how gimmicky the famous Geomod destruction is.  At the same time, there's quite a bit to like about Red Faction, and even for a "gimmick" Geomod is really unparalleled as an accomplishment.  Even later games in the series never reach the same heights as the original.
To get it out of the way, THE reason to play this game is the Geomod destruction models.  And honestly, it's one of the coolest features.  The player has the ability to use explosives to blow holes walls and buildings, and is able to use those holes to enter the building.   There are stalactites all over the game that can be knocked down with a simple explosion.  The world actually has physics on all these objects.   From a technical standpoint this really is a unique feat, especially for a game that came out around the time of the PS2, but from gameplay side.  Well there's the problem.
Red Faction Guerilla (the third game in the series)  shows how cool destruction can look and feel during gameplay.  The issue is in Red Faction, the player never feels like he has a wealth of these weapons.  In addition explosions do huge damage the the player, so he tends not to use explosives.  in addition there's not many explosive barrels in this game as others, and when a computer explodes it appears to not to damage to the ground or building.
Add to this the fact that a decent number of walls/ground and areas seem to be impervious, it makes it less likely the player is going to use geomod effectively  That's a real problem in my book, because it's a major feature.  A  major feature that the player doesn't use.
As for the rest of the game.  Well if you excuse the old style of gameplay, you'll actually find a pretty good game.  I was wrapped up in the story.  In fact there was a good amount of the game where I just wanted to see what happens next.
The story involves a miners' revolt on Mars, and a resistance.  The resistance though is a bit laughable because every time you meet someone from the resistance it seems they live just long enough for you to find them and then they die.  Luckily you are the great hero in the game.  Not one of prophecy but the one who actually can fight and not die (mostly).
The story is worth playing through, so I won't go over it, but honestly, there's not a ton of twists, just solid story telling.  I enjoyed the story more than I expected, and that's kind of impressive for such an old game.  There's almost constant discussion and interactions with people.  Again that's quite unique for the time.
The one thing with the gameplay is the AI in this game is a little weak.  Granted most shooters at the time were weak, the AI in this game tends to zigzag all over the place.   Half life came out the year before and had slightly better AI (or at least different).  The thing is the enemies in this game are a bit hard to kill, so that's works.  It's just a bit silly looking at time.  Otherwise the gameplay is solid for it's time.
The other thing to mention is that the game does take the player through enough areas with a lot of variety that they don't get tired of it.  The rock formations are dull brown, but this was before everything had to be brown.  There's office buildings, facilities for the planet.
One thing that annoyed me is after about 70 percent of the game, the sound started cutting out.  now I had done a marathon gaming session, about 7 hours, maybe something ran out of memory and stopped talking, but it seemed pretty reproducible, so I missed some of the final area's dialog, and that annoyed me.
The other thing is I had to use a cheat code.... on easy mode... for a boss.  Because that boss was... I'd call it broken.  I'm kind of shocked how hard he was so I cheated just so I can see the rest of the game and story.  It was really annoying, but that was the only place where the game had a huge difficulty spike.  As long as the player autosaves reasonably often they'll make it through the game with out a lot of problems.   But watch out for Capek's boss fight.
Overall though Red Faction is a great game for 2001.  And playing it now, it's interesting.  I won't call it the best game ever, however it's an interesting technical feat, and the game and story is quite good.  The graphics have aged, very poorly, but overall the game is entertaining.  If you want to see something that's old but still works great, Red Faction is a good pick up.  Just don't expect anything like the later sequels, which took the destruction in a different direction.

A disappointing mess.
I played the first Woodle Tree, and I really enjoyed it a lot mainly because it was a simplistic design with a relaxing tone to it. It was divided into worlds that were easy enough to access and explore. I finished the game in hopes there would be more.
Come to today, we have Woodle Tree 2 : Worlds.
Woodle Tree 2 is everything Woodle Tree isn't and more.  This game is not only incomplete, it's not even stable.  There is a vast world out there with lots to explore, but it's a cluttered mess of colors and designs, that you really don't know where you are a lot of the time. Something like this could of used a mini map, but instead it leaves you trying to find 3 Water Drops per world in what I saw to be quite an empty design.  I see so much area just empty, and you're able to explore it too.
Controls took a downgrade in this edition, as at times they don't work with jumping, or double jumping. Sometimes attacks won't respond, and sometimes for no reason at all, the game will freak out and put me into a turbo speed walk that I would need to jump in the air just to stop.
Sounds are pretty bleak, but the last game kind of suffered that issue too, so nothing changed there.
Music is....sadly feeling missing at times. The first game had an enjoyable soundtrack that was peaceful to listen to. This game, seems to either be no music, or the music is so low that you don't even know it's playing unless you really try to listen.
Story is painful. You are tossed in this vast world, and you need to stop whatever evil came into town and you're own your  own from there. I can't talk to anything or anyone, but they see me and like to watch me walk around, so it's pointless to bother figuring it out. The game just wants you to go out and figure it out I guess.
Game is colorful, and retains that feeling, but it's sadly so mixed up in colors and designs that it's not even pretty or enjoyable to look at.
Overall, Woodle Tree 2 : Worlds is rushed mess. A series that I would of hoped to be something more, seems to of taken a road to rushing to get something on the market fast. This game could of been something so much more had it had the time, and was developed more.   Unlike the first title which I recommended and enjoyed, I can't recommend this one. It's empty, it's depressing to play, and it's missing all potential in a good action platformer. I should also add, the load times are very painful to get through.  Areas load and it could take up to a minute. The game loading alone to just start is almost 2 minutes.

Don't be discouraged by the negative reviews... a lot of them are there because people are up in arms about microtransactions and/or initial problems running the game (i.e. stuttering, bugs, etc.). I personally experienced little to no problems running the game and there is absolutely no need to purchase anything to enjoy the game.
Mankind Divided offers a more fluid and natural game-world compared to Human Revolution (no zoning out to fight bosses until the very end) and truly offers various ways to solve/navigate missions.  In this aspect, it is a step up from Human Revolution and I hope the developers continue to evolve this side of the game in a positive direction for future games/DLC's.
The story, while not as good as Human Revolution's, isn't as bad as people make it out to be as well.  It suffers from a "rushed" ending, leading to some plot threads being resolved in a less than satisfactory manner... but a story should be judged as a whole and not just with the resolution, and overall, people need to stop having a cow and just enjoy the ride.
While I wouldn't go so far as to rate Mankind Divided as an all-time great... it is a very good game and one that I highly recommend.

Combat gives you zero satisfaction challenge wise since there are virtually zero bosses and enemies that require some kind of tactics in order to counter their skills/arsenal. Plus you end the game with ample EMP, armor piercing ammo, grenades and whatever nifty stuff, but you are just not needed to use them.
Another weak point of the game is the story line, which brings you to a climax when you least expect it in tandem with the most unimaginative boss you've ever seen. Right after that you get one of the most boring cinematic you've ever experienced, then in a sudden the credits start rolling and just can't believe that the game ended after a measly 20 hour or so trip in cyber-wonderland.
Sadly this is a slapdashed game. The developers probably invested too much time creating and/or customizing an engine not really suited for this kind of experience. And the creative department suffered the loss. Compared to Human Revolution this game is subpar on every level.

Blood Dragon is a magnificent standalone expansion to Far Cry 3. It features a near polar opposite premise to the original. It is the 80's perception of the year 2007, ravaged by Vietnam 2. You emerge as a cyborg badass all American hero. Your objective? Kick cyborg♥♥♥♥♥ kill the badguy, and get the girl. Not necessarily in that order.
My favorite aspects of this expansion pack are how similar to Far Cry 3 it is, and yet how different. The game's side content is very similar, coupled with the open world nature of the game. However, the aesthetic is completely different. Resembling a cross between G.I. Joe and Terminator, with dozens of allusions to almost every single 80's movie ever created.
Add to that is a top notch soundtrack, with tunes reminiscient of Terminator and Daft Punk. You definately get what you pay for with your 15$.
Some mild critiscms include the general lack of major gameplay innovation over Far Cry 3. It's very similar to that game, and if the aesthetic differences don't appeal to you, nothing else will. It's also not a full length game either, and it is very possible to 100% complete the game in a single sitting.
Yet I have nothing but good memories of this game, and it's in general a sign of good things. Blood Dragon could easily be compared to Red Dead Redemption's Undead Nightmare, and eventually I hope more titles could be added to that list.

Great game. The missions are quite easy in the beginning, but they get challenging soon enough.
What I like:
- Excellent mix of big strategy and small-scale tactics.
- In most other RTS, there is a tipping point where you know the AI won't recover, so the rest of the mission (often a big part) is just clean-up duty. In this game, however, the aliens get stronger and more vicious the more you advance, so it stays interesting until the end.
- You get a full refund for salvaged *and* destroyed buildings, so you can experiment and adapt during a mission. (Think "control/supply points", not "money".)
- *Lots* of alien carnage - alien kill counts in a mission are typically >10.000 :)
- Great music + sound effects
- Overall, a very well thought-out game and UI
Before buying, I was a bit sceptical whether I'd like the visuals, but they actualy work out quite well in-game.
The only downside is that there are only few actual campaign missions - 16, I think, including some very easy ones. But there are various random missions (at different levels) and weekly challenges that are a lot of fun on their own, so there's enough play time as it is.

Your main objective is to move little space marines around a map and capture outposts from the alien swarm.
You can upgrade individual marines to different specializations such as, Officer, Scout, Sniper, Flame, Shotgun. Each with their own advantages necessary to take over the map.
Aliens will start off weak, but give them time and they will mutate and become stronger, no sitting around in this game if you want the advantage.
I lost interest in the game after the first few missions, it is very repetitive and arcade like. Move marines, kill kill kill, capture base and set up defence, rinse repeat.
If you are looking for deep tactical stratedgy games this is not it. But this IS a great ball fun and you'll waste a few hours very easily. At this price during the Monster Sale it is worth adding to your collection.

and also watching his LP (Let's  Play) video and I was just hooked enough to get the game.
It's a Top down strategy game where you control a few armies against swarm of aliens trying to eliminate one of their hive after the other.
Simple concept but it has a lot to offer for an indie game.
Every time you advance things get a bit tougher because of the alien mutations plus they sometimes went on a rampage at some point of the game each time you destroy one of their hives. But not only that. Since they're scattered across the map, they tend to re-capture undefended base and turn them back as hives. So there's a lot of micromanaging going on. Sure a few missions are manageable but as you progress, the game will encourage or even unleash your hidden strategic think-tank that's been cooped inside the core of your head for a long time and you don’t have a choice or else you'll lose the game.
But not to worry, perks like weapon modifications and support units (air drops, air strikes...etc) are in the game and usable on each mission. However, if you want to use them you have to earn money and to earn money you will have to win a couple of previous missions in order to advance and all that are in the game with no microtransactions required.
So this game is recommended to those who like RTS (Real Time Strategy) and/or wants to know how it feels like to get swarm by aliens with a few number of units to control like one of those bugs from

- Rico from the movie. But in the game's case, Aliens will run you over.

"Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons" is an amazing indie puzzle storytelling with beautiful graphics and a touchin' plot mixed with funny moments. It's game control mechanic is creative and transmits a powerful message: you need to control both brothers together to progress through the game. If they don't work together correctly, you'll fail and will be stuck. They need to work together properly during all the game - and isn't that what a good brotherhood is all about? Also, it can be played as a local co-op game with a friend - each one of you controlling one brother.
The world is detailed, charming and vibrant. Despite the game story being only 3-4 hours long if you have good coordenation (I've a pretty bad one, so I've suffered a lot and spent like 10 hours to full complete the game and get all the achievements), it takes you through a multitude of environments and a rollercoaster of feelings. Every chapter feels fresh, compelling and interesting.
Sometimes in a adventure, we grow stronger but there is so much that we lost along the way... "Brothers" showed us how immensely powerful a game can be, when it's gameplay and story complements each other perfectly.

Cat Goes Fishing is a very relaxing fishing game.
The fishing is very well though out in which you start out upgrading your fishing rod and then move on to buying a boat to get to deeper waters.
The game offers a very unique physics for the casting which help you cast either very far or just right in front of you. You always start with small bait and must catch a small fish then recast to catch a medium fish with which you can catch most large fish but some fish have certain requisites to catch them. (like using a puffer with a large hook to catch the swordfish). We also see the sadness of overfishing with one of the species in the game. If you fish a certain species they will be extinct.
The visuals are very simplistic and colorful. The vast mayority of the fish are very distinguishable by their color and shape.
The sounds and music are very well made. The underwater sounds resonate with the depth that your in and the music on the surface is quite tranquile.
All in all you have a simplistic fishing game that is nice and tranquile for those afternoons when you just need to space out. Rod in one hand, a joint in the other.

If you like games like Uncharted or Tomb Raider... this game is a bit like that in the sense that there is a lot of climbing and puzzle solving involved. There are no voices (just gibberish) and no definitive story line (although the game is linear) but it is an adventure game set in a medieval fantasy of two brothers embarking on an adventure to find some sort of cure for their ill father. The graphics are fantastic and the humor and amusement is off the charts (at one point you can cover a white bunny with soot to 'un-alienate' it from a group of black bunnies. There's another mini event where you can play medieval 'basketball' with a girl).
What sets this game apart is that you play as both the brothers. This adds challenge as each brother has their own specialties in interacting with the game's environment to progress... both rely on each other to make it throguh the game. The controls are simple if you are using a game controller. The joysticks move the brothers and the triggers is a multipurpose "interact" button. You don't need a controller but it plays much better. On the keyboard its the WASD and arrow keys. Overall, a must have game for fans for beautiful ly visualized puzzle games with a story told through actions rather than words.
